div1.p: The editors are very grateful to the National Endowment for the Humanities, which has generously awarded the project a three-year grant (2018–21) under the auspices of its Scholarly Editions program, and to the Research Libraries Program of the Gladys Krieble Delmas Foundation, which has provided invaluable grant support for the Carlyle Letters Online. We are also grateful to the Binks Trust for its continuing financial contributions to the funding of the Edinburgh editorial team and office. The editors again express their gratitude to the British Academy, which made the Carlyle Letters a British Academy Research Project and continues to support us with an annual grant, and to the members of its Committee on Academy Research Projects and its assistant secretary, Ken Emond. The editors also express their gratitude to those private individuals who have made donations for the support of the Edinburgh Carlyle Letters office, to the University of Edinburgh Development Trust, and to Joyce Caplan and the Friends of Edinburgh University Library.

We remain extremely grateful for the advice of Paolo Mangiafico, Scholarly Communications Strategist and Co-Director, ScholarWorks Center for Scholarly Publishing, Duke University Library; and we continue to extend our appreciation for early critiques of the electronic edition to the late David Chesnutt, formerly of the Model Editions Partnership at the University of South Carolina, and to Natalia Smith of the DocSouth project at the University of North Carolina. Brent E. Kinser serves as coordinating editor of The Carlyle Letters Online in addition to his editorial service to the print edition. DNC Data Systems of Mumbai, India, has electronically encoded volumes 1 through 47 of the Carlyle Letters. Colin Wilder and the staff at University of South Carolina host the online edition at the Center for Digital Humanities.

The letters in this volume cover the period October 1873 to November 1875. Notable topics addressed in the letters include: TC’s enthusiasm for J. A. Froude’s expeditions to South Africa in 1874 and 1875, an ill-advised and unsuccessful mission given to Froude by Lord Carnarvon with the secret aim of creating support for a South African federation1. A. F. Pollard and William Thomas, “Froude, James Anthony (1818–1894), historian and man of letters.” Oxford Dictionary of National Biography. 23 Sep. 2004; Accessed 22 Nov. 2019. https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-10202.; the award of the Prussian Order of Merit in February 1874 for Frederick the Great and an honorary doctorate from Harvard University in November 1875 (received by TC with some reluctance and embarrassment); the offer of a knighthood in December 1874 (refused politely by TC with surprise and gratitude at the magnanimity of Benjamin Disraeli). The deaths, griefs, and serious illnesses of family (most notably TC’s niece Margaret Stewart), friends, and acquaintances—particularly the deaths of Betty Braid and Maggie Welsh and the decline of Rose Froude, J. A. Froude’s daughter—are also noted in correspondence. TC characterizes himself in these letters as wallowing in idleness, but the letters belie TC’s harsh assessment. This volume records a varied and continuous program of reading, focused research, editing, and writing. TC published two major new works during this period: “Early Kings of Norway” and “The Portraits of John Knox.” Both projects inspired TC to carry out extensive
research, with the assistance of Mary Aitken and many of the correspondents in this volume; but notably, both works received similar critical receptions from informed contemporary readers, who commented privately and publicly on a serious decline in the quality of TC’s scholarship. As the letters in this volume show, TC was made aware of the vulnerabilities in his arguments prior to publication, and chose to publish even so: there is no record in these letters of any sense of concern for his reputation as a historian.

TC had first projected a work on medieval Norwegian history early in 1872. He wrote to his brother John A. Carlyle that he thought he could “write a rather bright and useful little Book” about the early kings of Norway, were it not for his shaking right hand and weak grasp of Icelandic (TC to JAC, 20 Jan. 1872; 48:32). Neither obstacle proved insurmountable: Mary Aitken acted as amanuensis, and TC used English and German sources (Samuel
Laing’s English translation of Snorri Sturluson’s Heimskringla [1844] and F. C.
Dahlmann’s Geschichte von Dännemark [Hamburg, 1840–43]) to research early Norwegian history. Samuel Laing’s introductory essay on Snorri places the author of the saga in “the Valhalla of European literature” alongside TC himself.2. Samuel Laing, The Heimskringla; or, Chronicle of the Kings of Norway. Translated from the Icelandic of Snorro Sturleson, with a Preliminary Dissertation, by Samuel Laing (1844) 3. Initially, TC intended the text that would become “Early Kings of Norway” to be the preface to a new English translation of the Færeyinga Saga (the Faroe Islands Saga). TC used C. C. Rafn and G. C. F. Mohnike’s multilingual edition of the saga3. C. C. Rafn and G. C. F. Mohnike, Færeyínga saga oder Geschichte der Bewohner der Färöer im isländischen Grundtext mit färöischer, dänischer und deutscher Übersetzung (Copenhagen: Jens Hostrup Schultz, 1833). as his source, basing his translation entirely on their German text rather than the edition’s parallel Icelandic, Faroese, and Danish texts.4. Chris Vanden Bossche, “Carlyle’s Færeyinga Saga Translation,” Carlyle Annual 10 (1989): 64–79; 65, 78 n. 7. He completed his translation by December 1871 and sent it to John A. Carlyle. TC’s translation was not published and only a portion of the manuscript has survived (Vanden Bossche, see below). TC had completed the preface by 14 February 1872 (Froude, Carlyle 4:417).

TC asked John A. Carlyle for his opinion of his translation of the Færeyinga Saga and the lengthy preface. The result was, as Cowan puts it, “a minor showdown” between the brothers (168).5. Edward J. Cowan, “The Sage and the Sagas: The Brothers Carlyle and Early Kings,” Bibliotheck 9 (1978–79): 161–83. Unlike TC, John was accomplished in Icelandic and familiar with contemporary Norwegian historical scholarship. He read and corrected TC’s translation of the saga in December 1871, finding the text “very readable, though incorrect in several places” due to mistranslation of Icelandic terms; the saga itself was “not without merits, though one of the poorest I have read” (JAC to TC, 25 Dec. 1871 [MS: NLS 1775E.105]). He also attempted to correct the preface, but after a long period of silence admitted to TC that he had withheld comment because the preface was so poor it was impossible “to keep all the good passages in due coherence” after dispensing with its numerous errors. Attempting to correct the manuscript had made him “ill … with vexation” (JAC to TC, 28 April 1872 [MS: NLS 1775E.143]). He repeatedly criticized TC’s overreliance on Dahlmann’s “obsolete” opinions and neglect of the authoritative scholarship of Jacob Aall and Peter Andreas Munch (JAC to TC, 31 March [MS: NLS 1775E.131], 25 April [MS: NLS 1775E.141], 28 April 1872). John warned TC against risking his reputation by publishing this irredeemable work: “To one who knows nothing about Norsk History the MS is excellent reading, but it
would be unsuitable for you to send forth anything unauthentic after having gone to the bottom of so many matters of History, & some of the errors are great” (JAC to TC, 28 April 1872). Reluctantly, he volunteered to bring the scholarship TC had neglected to Chelsea, but dreaded the prospect of editing TC’s preface: “I fear you would be too impatient, & I myself also too thin-skinned and too unwell” (JAC to TC, 28 April 1872).

“Early Kings of Norway” has received little attention from Carlyle scholarship. With the exception of Edward J. Cowan’s article on John A. Carlyle’s Icelandic scholarship, Chris Vanden Bossche’s editions of “Early Kings” and the surviving portion of Carlyle’s translation of the Færeyinga Saga, and Alice Chandler’s analysis of TC’s body of work on German, Icelandic, and Norse medieval history,6. Alice Chandler, “Carlyle and the Medievalism of the North,” Medievalism in the Modern World: Essays in Honour of Leslie J. Workman. Ed. Richard Utz and Tom Shippey (Turnhout: Brepols, 1998) 173–91. “Early Kings” is usually passed over with minimal comment or dismissed as evidence of TC’s cognitive decline. This inattention is understandable, given the weakness of TC’s grasp of relevant scholarship, but one consequence of this critical neglect has been underappreciation of TC’s interest in Norse mythology and his investment in a myth of Norse origins for British civilization, notwithstanding Froude’s attempt to convey TC’s view that “all the virtues we possessed he believed to have come to us out of our Norse ancestry” (Froude, Carlyle 4:78). If, as Jude V. Nixon argues, “Carlyle viewed Norse and Saxon history in a unified way,” then “Early Kings” is an extended meditation on the Norse influence on English history that TC claimed was insufficiently acknowledged in most histories of England.7. Jude V. Nixon, “Thomas Carlyle’s Igdrasil,” Carlyle Studies Annual 25 (2009): 50–51. Taking its cue from Samuel Laing’s introduction to his English translation of the Heimskringla, which emphasizes Norse influences on early English history in precisely the way TC complained English historians failed to do, “Early Kings” is in part English history, with its Norse elements emphasized: Olaf Haraldsson’s legendary destruction of London Bridge, and the dedication of London churches and streets to his memory as St. Olaf; the heritage of Harold II of England; the Norse version of the battle of Stamford Bridge; the Norse ancestry of William the Conqueror, “the man famous to England, and momentous at this day, not to England alone, but to all speakers of the English tongue, now spread from side to side of the world in a wonderful degree.”8. Thomas Carlyle, “Early Kings of Norway.” Historical Essays. Ed. Chris R. Vanden Bossche. Strouse edn. (Berkeley, Los Angeles, and London: Univ. of California Press, 2002) 340. But “Early Kings” is not only a history: it is also an argument against contemporary democratic reforms by way of analogy. As Alice Chandler argues, Norse “history is a secondary consideration” for TC in “Early Kings,” and his “real
subject” is the “democratization of English society” and the Reform Act of 1867 (Chandler 182). “Early Kings” is punctuated with inapt allusions to Victorian concerns: the Oxford Movement, income tax, utilitarianism, and, in particular, democratic representation. Thus, Sverre Sigurdsson is maligned as a stump orator, suspicious to TC because of his “unctuous Parliamentary Eloquence or almost Popular Preaching” (Carlyle, “Early Kings” 421). TC represents the conflict between the rebel party that brought Sverre to power, the Birkebeiner, and their opponents as a precursor of the French revolution: “an armed mob of poor people,” “a kind of Norse Jacquerie,” risen up against the “tyrannous Bourgeoisie” (Carlyle, “Early Kings” 421–22). TC resolves the history of the Norse kings with a meditation on the cosmic purpose of tyranny, as it is revealed in medieval Norwegian history: his kings and rebels, unconscious of the forces motivating their actions, prove to be the agents of “Despotism and Democracy, arbitrary government by one and self-government (which means no government, or anarchy) by all.” “Dictatorship with many faults” triumphs over “Universal Suffrage with little possibility of any virtue,” and the violence of despotism, in TC’s analysis, brings about “the first transformation, so mysterious and abstruse, of human Chaos into something of articulate Cosmos” (Carlyle, “Early Kings” 425–26).

The first reader of “Early Kings of Norway,” John A. Carlyle, had delivered an emphatic critical opinion that the work should be suppressed for fear of damaging TC’s reputation as a historian. Despite his justified concern, devotion to TC overpowered John’s critical judgment, and he promised to attempt to correct the manuscript (JAC to TC, 29 April 1872 [MS: NLS 1775E.145]). In December 1874 TC informed John that William Allingham, recently appointed editor of Fraser’s Magazine, had persuaded him to publish “Early Kings” in the form of three articles in the journal; Allingham had promised to edit the MS and incorporate John’s “notes” and “corrections,” and TC would only be responsible for correcting the proofs. Perhaps mindful of John’s view of the work, TC professed to regret having given permission for publication, and promised that John would “have no further trouble with it” (TC to JAC, 11 Dec 1874). TC strikes the same note of regret in a second letter to John about “Early Kings,” claiming he recollected little of the third portion of the text, and would never have permitted publication had Allingham not been so “passionately anxious” for it: “Except for the encouragement or other benefit it may give to poor Allingham nothing cd have induced me to bother with it farther” (TC to JAC, 30 Jan 1875). Against the better judgment of its author, “Early Kings” was eventually published in January–March 1875 as a series of articles in Fraser’s Magazine and as a single volume (with TC’s essay on John Knox) by Chapman & Hall in the same year.

The Edinburgh Review gave “Early Kings of Norway” a lengthy notice that recognized the manifold problems with TC’s text. It commented on the
surprising brevity (even printed in large type) of “Early Kings,” given the scope of the subject matter; much of the review is dedicated to addressing gaps in TC’s knowledge of Norwegian history. The review identified the same fundamental flaws John A. Carlyle had found with the unrevised manuscript, namely TC’s overreliance on a handful of sources, some out of date; his failure to consult standard modern authorities; and his use of a “doubly second-hand” translation of a translation as his primary source.9. “Art. VIII. The Early Kings of Norway; Also an Essay on the Portraits of John Knox. By Thomas Carlyle. London: 1875”, Edinburgh Review, 1 July 1875, 203–32. In addition, the review noted that histories of England had not ignored the connections between early Norwegian and English history to the degree claimed by Carlyle.10. Edinburgh Review, p. 204. The review ended by damning “Early Kings” with faint praise, praising its “music” but not its scholarship, treating it as the work of a great writer but not a capable historian of Norway. The book was commended as a “brilliant but most kaleidoscopic sketch … a remarkable and a suggestive work, not only for what it says but what it omits to mention. Had he [TC] known more of his subject and availed himself of materials close to his hand, his work would have been better still.”11. Edinburgh Review, p. 232. The Atlantic Monthly was stronger in its critique of the historical failings of “Early Kings,” noting TC’s evident ignorance of Icelandic, his lack of sympathy with his subject, and the absurdities generated by his overly schematic division of Norwegian monarchs into “anarchs” and “anti-anarchs,” with little regard to recorded history.12. “Recent Literature”, Atlantic Monthly 36 (1875): 493–502 (p. 499). Its verdict was damning, and fulfilled John A. Carlyle’s prediction that TC risked his reputation as a historian by publishing “Early Kings”:
div1.q: It is difficult to repress a sense of disappointment and pain at seeing a name which we have been taught to revere attached to a volume so flimsy in its construction, so slipshod in style, and altogether so unworthy of a scholar as these essays of Mr. Carlyle’s on the Early Kings of Norway. … [W]e hope for his own sake that his more lasting contributions to literature will not lend a pernicious immortality to this hasty compilation of ill-digested facts.13. “Recent Literature”, p. 498.
div1.p:
In contrast, the Atlantic found that the second essay in the volume, TC’s essay on “The Portraits of John Knox,” marked a partial return to form. “On Scottish ground he waxes warm with holy zeal, and his lively sympathy with the character of John Knox and his eager partisanship occasionally stimulate him into a vehemence of diction which cannot but remind us of the time when
Sartor Resartus and the essays on Burns and Goethe and Jean Paul Richter kindled our blood and widened our vision.”14. “Recent Literature”, p. 500. The Atlantic recognized that TC’s enthusiasm was stronger for John Knox than it was for the early kings of Norway; but the declining scholarly rigor identified by the reviewers of “Early Kings” would also be discovered by those who engaged closely with TC’s theories about the portraits of Knox.

TC had been interested in the physiognomy of Knox since at least 1847, shortly after his friend David Laing published the first volume of his edited collected Works of John Knox. At this time, TC seems to have been willing to accept Laing’s argument that Beza’s portrait of 1580, said to be a picture of Knox, might be an authentic portrait.15. Marinell Ash, “David Laing and Carlyle,” Carlyle Newsletter 4 (1983): 27–31. But he became enthused by an alternative candidate for the authentic portrait of Knox, that printed in Charles Knight’s Pictorial History of England, known as the “Somerville” portrait because it had been in the possession of the Somerville family and their descendants. TC records that on first sight he “unhesitatingly believed in it,” and had a copy of the engraving hung on the wall of his study.16. Thomas Carlyle, Works 30:360. In July 1866, according to Allingham, TC first showed Laing a purported portrait of Knox, which can be identified with the Somerville portrait due to the reference to the subject’s baldness and small beard. Allingham’s description of this uncomfortable encounter between TC, Laing, and the engraving, anticipates the dispute in 1875 that would bring Laing and TC’s friendship to an end:
div1.q: They were looking over some engraved portraits, and C. singled out one, asking pointedly, “Whose face do you call this?” Laing suggested that it might be So-and so, or So-and-so, C. saying “No, no, no!” and at last, “I perceive that you can throw no light on the matter.” It is his own conviction that this (a shrewd humorous face with bald forehead and scanty beard) is the only authentic portrait of John Knox.17. William Allingham, William Allingham: A Diary, ed. H. Allingham and D. Radford (London: Macmillan, 1907), p. 138.
div1.p:
By 1873, Laing was attempting to organize a campaign to raise funds for a memorial to Knox, with the ultimate intention of erecting a memorial in Edinburgh’s St Giles’s Cathedral; skeptical of Laing’s ability to lead the campaign, and believing the lack of a statue of John Knox shamed Scotland, TC began to gather materials and evidence to prove the authenticity of his preferred candidate for the one true portrait of Knox. The letters in this volume record an intensive program of investigation into various portraits of Knox, including the woodcut in Beza’s Icones. TC worked collaboratively with artists and art
historians to develop a more informed understanding of the works in question. Unlike “Early Kings of Norway,” “The Portraits of John Knox” draws on considerable research, and permits the reader to evaluate both the evidence adduced in support of TC’s conclusions and the mode of analysis. TC engaged in correspondence with Selina Constance Smyth, b. Somerville, then owner of the portrait, who in April 1874 brought the picture to London so that it could be examined by experts and TC (TC to SCS, 27 April 1874).

Numerous letters in this volume record TC’s growing conviction of the Somerville portrait’s provenance, a conviction that, in fairness to TC, is based in part on his investigation and research; but the letters also betray that TC’s enthusiasm for the Somerville portrait is, ultimately, an article of faith, based on an unverifiable and instinctive belief that Knox must have had a distinguished physiognomy, which TC found only in the Somerville portrait. In letters to Laing and in “The Portraits of John Knox,” TC returned repeatedly to his strength of feeling, as if it were evidence. Writing to Laing after an Edinburgh meeting about the proposed Knox memorial, TC called for investigation into his favored portrait, but concluded: “Physiognomic evidence has long appeared to me to be complete; every lineament is Scotch, and expresses in my opinion, with singular completeness, the wiry vigour, the perfect veracity, the loving earnestness, modesty and yet long-suffering contempt which dwelt in the grand soul of Knox” (TC to DL, 10 Dec 1873). The final section of “The Portraits of John Knox” concludes in similar tenor, with a statement of faith on the part of Henry Merritt of the National Gallery, approved by TC: “My opinion is in favour of the Somerville Portrait being of Knox. Strongly marked features like those were not likely to become confounded with any other man’s. The world has a way of handing down the lineaments of great men” (HM to TC, 9 Jan. 1874).

Laing, the recipient of several letters about the Somerville portrait, and unsolicited autotypes of it, from TC, was unwilling to accede to such declarations of faith in physiognomic truth, and was dismayed at TC’s method of reasoning and willingness to publicize his belief based on weak evidence and instinct. The dispute over the portraits of John Knox proved to be the end of a longstanding friendship. As with John A. Carlyle’s unavailing warning to TC that the evident flaws in his Norwegian scholarship risked his reputation as a historian, Laing’s attempt to warn TC off the subject proved unsuccessful. Laing wrote:
div1.q:
You will excuse me in still saying I have no faith in your Somerville Portrait, and as to getting you to change your opinion of Beza’s “wooden block” or figurehead is equally hopeless. Being, what you may call, an obstinate blockhead, I will maintain as I have done for the best part of 40 years past, that the said woodcut is the only genuine & well-authenticated
Portrait of the Reformer. But there is no need of our quarrelling in such a matter. (DL to TC, 31 March 1875)
div1.p: It was, according to Ash, the one angry letter of Laing’s life, and although there may have been no need to quarrel over such a matter, the long friendship was irreparably damaged by TC’s public subordination of historical method to strength of feeling. TC’s essay on “The Portraits of John Knox” was published in Fraser’s Magazine in April 1875, and in a single volume with “The Early Kings of Norway” later that year. The essay commends Laing’s scholarship on Knox, but attempts to discredit Beza’s woodcut and all other reputed portraits of Knox that bear any resemblance to it. Laing did not respond publicly, but in 1875 Carlyle’s arguments in “The Portraits of John Knox” were systematically refuted by James Drummond, curator of the National Portrait Gallery of Scotland, in a paper read to the Society of Antiquaries and privately printed. The work may have drawn upon Laing’s own notes.18. Geoffrey Bullough, “David Laing Letters,” Scotsman, 6 June 1932, p. 2. None could fault TC for merely expressing an opinion of his ideal image of Knox, Drummond wrote, but to publish that opinion and attempt “to substantiate this myth as a historical reality … is too much.”19. James Drummond, The Portraits of John Knox and George Buchanan (Edinburgh: For private circulation, 1875), p. 6. TC is accused of misconstruing and distorting the written opinion of the artist Robert Tait, who had examined the Somerville portrait, and is made to sound confident in its authenticity in “The Portraits of John Knox”; Drummond reproduces Tait’s complaint that TC presented an “imperfect and even misleading impression of what he had written” through selective quotation.20. James Drummond, pp. 21–23. Drummond expresses dismay, even contempt, at Carlyle’s “style of argument … (if argument it can be called),” quoting at length from numerous instances where Carlyle sets his personal dislike of the personality expressed in Beza’s picture against historical documents from the time of Knox, as if these were equivalent forms of evidence; Carlyle’s argument was “mere personal opinion,” Drummond concluded.21. James Drummond, p. 11. (Drummond somewhat undermines his own defense of the historical method by concluding his argument against the Somerville portrait with a complaint that its weak chin is inconsistent with Knox’s history as a leader of men.)22. James Drummond, p. 30

Drummond’s essay contains serious critiques of TC’s scholarship, handling of sources, and mode of argument. As with “Early Kings of Norway,” the principal impact of “The Portraits of John Knox” was a negative one, affecting TC’s reputation among contemporary reviewers and historians. He appears to have been untroubled by the reception of the essay, not noticing
the substantive critiques of the essays in his letters. A letter to John A. Carlyle after completing the proofs of “The Portraits” would seem to express his view of his new published work: he found the essay “feeble,” but even so regards it as of vital importance to him, personally, because it represented valuable, meaningful work (TC to JAC, 30 Nov. 1874). It is not certain that TC recognized the present limitations of his power to compass and execute a program of research, and then to critically evaluate historical evidence; there is little to no concern noted for his personal reputation in these letters; but the imperative to work, and the impact of work on his sense of self-worth, was as marked as ever, even if the outcomes were disappointing.

The letters record considerable activity in addition to work on “Early Kings” and “The Portraits”: regular meetings and correspondence with acquaintances and family, and an ongoing program of reading that encompassed classical and modern history (Lubbock, Michelet, Plutarch), life writing (of subjects including Touissaint L’Ouverture, John Stuart Mill, and John Wesley), essays (Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera) and literature (Goethe). When TC writes that he is idle, the claim must be put in perspective; he may be idle in comparison to the unrelenting toil of the Frederick years, but there is little quiet time recorded in these letters.
Katherine Inglis

div1.p: October 1873–November 1875
October 1873–November 1875

October 1873. TC writes his regrets on the death of Provost Dods of Haddington: “His worth was well known to me” (6). He invites Lady Ashburton to visit any day in Chelsea (8); she visits on the 9th. TC thanks John A. Carlyle for taking care of distributing books to family in Scotland, and tells of a dinner at the Forsters’ (7), of walks with William Allingham, and of Lady Ashburton’s life in London (11). He asks John’s advice about an (unidentified) Icelander’s enquiry about possible translation or teaching work. Tyndall writes to TC. James Fitzjames Stephen returns to London and walks with TC. Mary is editing her Scottish Song, a Selection of the Choicest Lyrics of Scotland (1874) for Macmillan (18). TC writes Ruskin to thank him for the early copies of his lectures on Val d’Arno; asks if he has read John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography (31).

November. TC thanks Charles Eliot Norton for news of his safe arrival in the U.S. and the gift of his translation of Vita Nuova, “a truly welcome gift,” and praises Ruskin very warmly: “I hear at the present time, no other Voice like him in this dreary Mother of dead dogs which is still commonly called a world” (3). He apologizes to John for tardiness in replying to letters, sends family news from Canada, and dismisses Mill’s Autobiography—“I have never read a more uninteresting book” (5). He dines at Forster’s (11) with Spedding and Tennyson (15). He thanks John for sending Fitzjames Stephen’s lectures, which he finds very unclear, though he speaks generously about Stephen himself. “I am still as idle as ever” (15). His sister Mary has renewed the lease of the Gill, and TC agrees to send £50 to help with drainage. A German visitor talked wearisomely on Faust part 2, “really a singularity to look at and to hear” (22). TC is tired of the newspapers, including a false story that he was writing a pamphlet on the Pope and Kaiser, and he writes Blackie firmly to deny it (24). He still receives many invitations. He is sending German books to John in Dumfries. He attends a grand dinner at the Taylors’ (27).

December. TC writes Miss Hope-Scott to ask, on behalf of ballad editor Francis James Child, for permission to quote from manuscripts at Abbotsford (2), and to David Laing to explain why he did so (3). He then has to write Norton to explain that there will be delay since Miss Scott is abroad, but that David Laing may be able to help Professor Child (8). Laing is also trying to organize a memorial to John Knox. TC writes Mary Smith to thank her for the gift of her book (8). He recalls to his brother John the Edinburgh Professor Jameson (Geology) and
contrasts his general dullness with David Laing’s prompt and helpful replies (9). TC wishes to propose to David Laing the creation of a bronze statue of John Knox in Edinburgh to be put in the “College Square” as the “Typical Scotsman … and the bravest we ever bred.” He would like to make John Knox’s house in the Canongate a popular monument too. He writes to Laing that “all Scotland would respond with alacrity” to an appeal for money, and discusses portraits and likenesses of Knox (10). He tells his brother John that Laing has replied positively to the idea of a bronze statue (20). Ruskin has visited several times, “lean but ardent, vehement”; with Froude he takes TC to see Holman Hunt’s “Shadow of Death.” Forster is still in poor health, but near the end of his Dickens biography. TC visits the Tennysons (20). He writes to David Laing about his ideas on a genuine picture of John Knox, and strongly urges the Somerville portrait, explaining that he had been mistaken in calling it the Torphichen likeness (30).

January 1874. TC writes to his brother John on family matters, praising David Masson’s new book on Drummond of Hawthornden (“full of excellent correct information”), but regretting he cannot persuade David Laing to join him in pressing for a public memorial to John Knox—which TC is very determined to see accomplished in his lifetime (1); the next day he writes John with second thoughts about making any public fuss on the matter (2). He sends considerable sums to John to put on deposit in his Dumfries bank, and records visits from the Leckys and Dean and Lady Augusta Stanley, and from Ruskin (“full to overflowing with far glancing projects”); letters come from Norton in the U.S. (8). He writes cordially to Norton assenting to Emerson’s suggestion that he should leave his collection of TC’s letters to Norton (29). He writes James Manson to correct his wrong information about Mme Brentano and Goethe (30).

February. TC gives a long account to his brother John of continual colds and digestive problems, though he still manages to walk with Froude up to four miles at a time; he experiments with medicines, and with alternations of his normal bathing routine. He hears from Birmingham of his niece Jenny Scott’s death, and writes of his concern for Jamie. He is glad to have news of Alexander Carlyle and family in Canada. He finds the third volume of Forster’s Dickens “far better done than I expected,” and offers to send it on (4). He receives confirmation and the insignia of the Prussian Order of Merit that he has been awarded (12). With recovered health, he feels more cheerful and resumes his normal walking habits. He forwards to John a letter from d’Eichthal, who had also visited while TC was unwell. Finally, he passes on the news of the death of Froude’s wife (14). He congratulates Forster warmly on the third volume of his Dickens (16). He writes John with news of much recovered health and energy, and details of family photographs (25). He writes Thomas
Constable to congratulate him on his biography of “your worthy and distinguished father” (25).

March. A real increase in health prompts TC to resume his morning bath, to take a hearty breakfast, and to walk in the afternoons—preferably with Froude, whose The English in Ireland TC praises warmly to John, “fairly the best Froude has ever written.” George Cooke visits and advises on investments (7). Health steadily improving, TC busies himself with research on likenesses of John Knox, sending some to John in Scotland, along with other plans for their investments. He is keen to persuade John to come to visit him in London (21). He thanks Lady Derby for her help in tracking down portraits of Knox (23), and tells his brother John about her efforts on his behalf. The Blakistons visit (25). TC writes David Laing in some detail about his views on the likenesses of Knox; he has 50 autotypes made of his chosen favorite and sends Laing six to distribute (26).

April. TC thanks Selina Smyth for her husband’s help in tracing details of Knox portraits, and sends autotypes (1). He writes to Robert Horn to put on record his indebtedness to the Advocates’ Library in Edinburgh (3), and to brother John with news that Emerson is to stand as rector for Glasgow University, and records his indignation that Laing does not agree with his views on authentic pictures of Knox (4). TC and Mary dine at the Forsters’ with the Earl of Shaftesbury (4). TC writes in friendly style to try to cheer Froude, still devastated by the loss of his wife, and congratulates him on the good reviews of his book on Ireland. Froude has invited him for a visit to Wales, but TC hesitates to accept (10). He writes to Robert Horn in Edinburgh, trying diplomatically to enlist Laing’s help in securing copies of portraits, while still disagreeing completely with Laing about authentic likenesses of Knox (10). This business, he tells his brother John, is the only “vestige of real work I can still be said to have on hand.” Forster, “still poorly,” is writing on Swift, “and certainly he slowly improves” (11). Maggie Welsh arrives for a month’s stay (18), allowing Mary a holiday. TC sends Norton three autotypes of Knox, the “inexorable preliminary” of any memorial being a “credible resemblance,” which is what TC is busily seeking (23). Selina Smyth, delayed by an accident, arrives in London with the Somerville portrait of Knox, which TC has been eagerly awaiting (27). He writes a recommendation to the Times editor, John Thadeus Delane, for an article by Lattimer (29).

May. TC gives his first sitting for the Boehm statue for Lady Ashburton (1). John A. Carlyle arrives for a visit (4). The Somerville portrait is widely inspected, and TC admits (6) that it turns out to be a copy, not the original. TC declines Helena Martin’s dinner invitation, having been “discovering that I was grown unfit for dining out” (6). He asks anxiously for news of Lady
Ashburton, and tells her of Forster’s bad health. Boehm has had four sittings for the statue, “decidedly promising” (13). Ruskin has written from Naples; TC in his reply praises the new Chelsea Embankment (13). He declines an invitation from Lady Derby to meet Alexander II, czar of Russia, saying evening outings are now a thing of the past for him (18). Boehm is examining Knox pictures for TC ([30]).

June. TC passes on to Woolner an invitation to paint Captain Cook for the Premier of Sydney (10). He is sorry not to have accepted Froude’s invitation to spend part of the summer with him, but “I am as idle as a dry bone.” Forster’s health is improving slowly (20). TC is glad to have news from Ruskin who is in Italy for the summer (20). He thanks Selina Smyth for her help concerning the Knox portraits (27). Gavan Duffy visits (28).

July. TC is sorry to miss a visit from Forster, and grateful for the gift of a fine bound set of his Dickens. Froude has agreed to go to South Africa on a diplomatic mission, and TC is enjoying Swift, “re-reading after some sixty years” (3). John leaves for Lerwick (8), and George Bancroft calls (11). He thanks Robert Horn for his “kind and entertaining letter” on the Knox portraits (12), and Froude for his cordial good wishes (13). TC finds the heat oppressive, and is considering a holiday out of London with his brother John (13). He sends his annual gift and good wishes to Betty Braid on the date of JWC’s birthday (14). He thanks Ruskin for his letters and news from Italy (15). He meets the crown prince and princess of Germany (16), organized by Lady Augusta Stanley (18). TC decides against accepting Froude’s invitation to take a holiday in Wales, instead preferring to plan a trip with his brother John (18). He writes to Ruskin in Florence to thank him for his continued correspondence (30).

August. Samuel Laurence visits to discuss the Knox pictures (2) and Froude visits (3). TC tells his brother John of the many visits and opinions people have made to view the various pictures of John Knox, though TC has made up his mind as to the only authentic one. Allingham has become editor of Fraser’s Magazine. William Brookfield dies (12 July). TC is “diligently” reading Boswell’s Johnson, while Mary is learning to draw, having completed her anthology of Scottish Songs. He replies to a question about free will and fate recommending the writer to “dismiss it” as unknowable (3 and 4). Laurence is keen to paint a copy of Selina Smyth’s portrait of Knox, and TC writes to ask her permission (4); Laurence begins to copy it and by 27 August has almost finished. Lady Ashburton invites TC to Seaforth, but he declines (7). TC leaves for Edinburgh with Mary (22), meets Laing and William Stirling Maxwell, but happily finds himself “perfectly incognito” he tells John (27). He visits Comely Bank and Haddington; “in fact I spoke to nobody except to
honest David Laing and Masson.” Froude leaves for the Cape of Good Hope (23). At Provost Swan’s invitation, TC and Mary move to Kirkcaldy and stay in his house (31).

September. “I feel myself better today than I have been not only since leaving Chelsea, but for many months before that,” writes TC to John, describing the quiet of St. Brycedale House in Kirkcaldy and the excellent sea-bathing (1). He is happy to offer Friedrich Althaus a testimonial for a professorship teaching German Literature at University College, London (5). He declines an invitation to visit Sir William Stirling Maxwell at Keir (16).

October. TC and Mary return to London; Mary writes Betty Braid to apologize that TC had had no opportunity to visit her (16). TC begins to plan out his writing on portraits of Knox, though diverted (he tells John) by problems with the drains in Cheyne Row (17). He has seen Tait, Allingham, and Erasmus Darwin; Forster is too ill to be visited. He misses Edward Twistleton (d. 5 Oct.) and Brookfield; Miss Bromley is “deeply distressed,” he tells John. News and a photograph come from Alick in Canada (17). TC tells his brother John that William Allingham, now a frequent visitor, is “an innocent, ingenious creature,” but “very far inferior to Froude” (23). “I do nothing but lazily read,” he tells Forster (26). He writes Betty Braid to console her on the sudden death of her husband (30).

November. Still looking at new images of Knox, TC urgently asks Boehm to visit to give him his opinion (4). Ruskin begins regular visits from Oxford; Forster is at Seaforth. John has sent the news of the death of their niece Margaret Stewart. Allingham encourages TC to publish his article on the portraits of Knox in Fraser’s Magazine (6). TC writes a friendly letter to Edward FitzGerald, encouraging him to re-visit Edinburgh (6). He thanks Robert Horn for all his help with the Knox pictures (11). He tells John he has actually begun to write on Knox’s pictures (17), “probably the last thing I shall write in this world.” John is considering a possible move to Chelsea; Ruskin is a regular visitor, as is the newly-married Allingham. TC thanks Forster for keeping in touch, “regardless of my stupid looking silence” (19). He complains of bad weather and bad health to John, but encourages him to consider a visit to Chelsea (30).

December. Forster (in poor health) is in London and TC meets him (9). TC is still dictating on Knox to Mary and complaining about the bad weather, but he mentions that Allingham has been very helpful (11). Ruskin visits with drawings from Italy (18) and TC writes urgently to John about finding and returning books for the London Library (19). TC writes a formal but grateful thanks to Disraeli, declining the gift of a baronetcy and a royal pension (29), and sends a copy of his letter of refusal to Lady Derby (who was the originator of
the scheme), acknowledging that Disraeli’s letter is “magnanimous and noble” “after all the hard things I have said of him” (30).

January 1875. London is experiencing severe winter weather, with blocks of ice floating on the Thames (1). Early Kings of Norway is finished, The Portraits of John Knox almost so. The Allinghams call (11). Boehm is working on a plaster model, which became the bronze of TC that now stands in Chelsea Embankment Gardens. Arthur Watt (John A. Carlyle’s stepson) visits in Chelsea. TC tells his brother John that he occasionally feels, despite his increasing infirmity, “glowings out again of intellectual & spiritual clearness” (30).

February. Froude returns from South Africa (3). Forster is too ill to see TC when the latter calls (2). Lady Ashburton is also suffering from cold. Samuel Laurence thanks TC for a gift of £100 for “my small doings in the years that are gone—as you tenderly put it” (10). TC invites his brother John to Cheyne Row, but the cold weather induces John to decline (11), while TC admits to John that “I have felt in general health almost rather better than in the two past winters” and “Thank heaven we have at last got Knox done.” “Froude comes to me or I go to him every second day or oftener.” Forster is still unwell (13).

March. TC assures Lady Ashburton he will find her a photograph of Charles Sumner (3). He writes a long letter to his brother Alick in Canada with family news; Craigenputtoch, he notes, has fallen into a “mournful state of degradation as a residence, the woods all cut away” (4). He and Froude dine with Forster (5), and TC discusses with John his investment plans. Knox proofs are soon to be delivered (7). Miss Bromley returns to London. TC is now reading the Knox proofs (15). Spring weather arrives. TC asks W. E. Forster if he can help Rosetta Frankau in her charitable work (30).

April. TC hears from Norton in the U.S. that he has asked Whistler for an etching of his portrait of TC, but explains he cannot contact Whistler to request copies of the portrait, “not of my poor features, but of the clothes I had on” (1). Boehm’s statue is finished, and is destined for the Royal Academy exhibition. TC has a daily walk on the newly-completed Chelsea Embankment (1). He promises Edith Forbes to arrange for her to have the letters he received over the years from her father, R. W. Emerson (2). TC asks Lady Ashburton for news of her health; his own days, he confesses, are “mere inarticulate musings and dreamings” (9). He writes his sister Janet in Canada with a gift of money: “I have grown very old … and am very weak and useless” but he passes on family news, and hopes that his brother John may visit later in the month (12). He is glad to have a long letter from Lady Ashburton (15). He assures brother John that his room in Chelsea is ready for him (17). He thanks John Lothrop Motley for his letter which “touches me to the very
heart” (19). Robert Herdman begins work on his portrait of TC (22). TC tells John that Froude is still in Torquay looking after his daughter, who is dying: his own health is satisfactory, though he has lost a front tooth (24). Maggie Welsh dies in Liverpool (29).

May. John A. Carlyle arrives to stay at Cheyne Row. TC writes Jeannie W. Chrystal to commiserate on Maggie’s death (5). He writes to congratulate Émile Montégut on his marriage (15). He writes to Walter Welsh in Auchtertool also to commiserate on Maggie’s death, and to send a book (26).
June. Norton writes to TC with news of the award of an honorary LL.D. from Harvard University (30).

July. TC writes, on what would have been JWC’s birthday, with a gift of £250 to Walter Welsh in Auchtertool (14). He writes to Lady Ashburton in Scotland, telling her of his visit to Lady Marian Alford, and of his visits to the Forsters who are to holiday in Melchet Court. Froude returns to South Africa (23).

August. Lady Derby writes (26 July) inviting TC to use Keston, their holiday home. TC acknowledges an honor from a U.S. historical society (4). He writes to thank Forster for his life of Swift, and confirms that a visit to Keston is almost decided on. He thanks Froude for his letter: “I wish with my whole heart you were here again, for I am very solitary without you” (6). Mary and he leave for Keston (11). Brother John remains in Cheyne Row until 19 August, then leaves for Scotland. TC writes to Forster from Keston to thank him for his letter and the good news of his recovery of health, and praises the quiet and surroundings at Keston Lodge (19). He writes to George Hoggan expressing his detestation of the practise of vivisection (28). He thanks A. P. Hood for his volume Thomas Carlyle.

September. While TC and Mary are at Keston Lodge, a “tumult of universal cleaning, sweeping, painting, washing, uncarpeting and general noise and confusion” is taking place in Cheyne Row. TC feels his health improve, he tells Lady Ashburton, though he is anxious for more news from her (1). “The silence day and night is the completest in the world,” he tells brother John (2). TC and Mary visit Charles Darwin and his family, and call on Sir John and Lady Lubbock. TC reads Ruskin (“very hard reading”) and Hood’s study of Carlyle himself (“confused and more or less absurd”). TC and Mary take daily drives, to Beckenham, Croydon, Westerham, Eltham, Shooter’s Hill, Sevenoaks. He agrees with John that their sister Jean Aitken should be invited for a holiday in London (9). He writes cordially to Edward FitzGerald (15). Mary writes (16) to Ellen Conway to report she has engaged a servant for Chelsea. TC writes to Forster to thank him for keeping in touch with “pleasant little weekly dispatches” (17). He is reading Michelet, and Southey’s life of Wesley,
and with Mary attends a Harvest-Home at Wickham Court. They visit the Darwins, and meet Tyndall out walking in the countryside. They return to Chelsea (30) to a spring-cleaned house and two new servants.

October. TC repeats his hope that sister Jean will come for “a good quiet visit and unlimited conversation” (2). He is glad of news of his Canadian relatives (2). He thanks Lady Ashburton for writing from Inverary and hopes to see her in London. Caroline Bromley is in Crewe (7). Masson pays a surprise visit (9). London is quiet; TC tries to visit Erasmus Darwin, and is visited repeatedly by Allingham, he tells John (9). TC begins a course of dental treatment for “a new set of teeth” (16). Darwin is “looking miserably ill” (16) but Forster, who has been “dreadfully ill,” is better (17). Jean in Scotland is preparing for her visit to Chelsea (21). The new teeth are fitted and “will really be of use to me” (26). Jean is enjoying her London visit. TC is re-reading Goethe with pleasure. “The town is beginning to be populous again,” and TC has seen Lady Ashburton, who is preparing for a visit to Egypt (26). TC writes disparagingly of both Tennyson and Ruskin’s latest works.

November. TC complains of the mixed weather, though he enjoys the company of his sister Jean, “who is a superior walker, much stronger than I” (6). Lecky and Allingham are “my most frequent visitors,” and TC visits Forster once a week in his own room. The new teeth are proving troublesome (6). The weather is wet; the Thames is running very high (13). TC thanks brother John for the trouble he is taking to translate Goethe for him. He is reading Thucydides. The new teeth are a failure. TC’s honorary degree from Harvard arrives (20) and TC writes to Harvard president Charles W. Eliot, with thanks (23).

As volume 49 enters the final stages of editing, we received the news of the death of its managing editor, David Southern. He had been with the edition since 1997 and was a crucial and invaluable contributor to the project. From the outset, he was a natural fit for the position. He had a lifelong interest in the written and printed word, and prior to joining the Carlyle Letters had served as a typesetter, graphic designer, and publisher, particularly of poetry. He was a pivotal figure in guiding each Carlyle volume through the proofing stages, characteristically insisting upon a complete oral reading of the text before delivering the penultimate version back to Edinburgh. With patience, tenacity, and droll humor, he made the project the center of his professional life. He was a devoted bibliophile, and he cultivated an extensive range of friendships with scholars, librarians, collectors, and auctioneers that resulted in the frequent discovery of new Carlyle letters and manuscripts. David was also an early advocate of the Carlyle Letters Online and worked tirelessly to ensure that the digital version matched the printed volumes for the highest standards of design, layout, and accuracy. His colleagues will fondly recall his warm hospitality on visits to Durham, and his deep knowledge of North Carolina’s literature, history, culture, and landscape. His genial and reassuring presence will be missed on both sides of the Atlantic.

div3.sourceNote: TC-PD [PDO], 6 Oct. MS: R. R. Campbell, purchased from Sotheby’s sale, 29 Oct. 1968. Pbd: Glasgow Herald, 13 July 1901. Text is from MS copy in an unknown hand. Col. Peter Dods (1828–1905), eldest son of JWC’s old friend William Dods (1795–1873), provost of Haddington.
div3.head: TC TO PETER DODS

docBody.p: It was a sharp surprise and shock to me to receive that little note from Haddington a week ago.Peter Dods wrote, 2 Oct.: “A notice was sent you a day or two ago of my fathers death [29 Sept.]. I am now writing a few particulars to some of his old friends.” It was but a short while before that I was there almost at his door;TC had been in Haddington visiting JWC’s grave, 5 Sept.; see 48:220–21MW to SW, 9 Sept. 1873. and only did not see him because he was much more pleasantly employed among his children in Lancashire,Dods wrote: “He [William Dods] had paid a visit to myself in Cheshire & to two other sons in Manchester & returned only a week before his death.” Peter Dods lived at 10 Palmerston Pl., Edinburgh, so was presumably having a holiday in Cheshire. William Dods had eight surviving children from his first marriage to Harriet, b. Shirreff (ca. 1804–53), six sons and two daughters; see 37:265. His second son, John (b. 1830), was an East India merchant living in Springfield near Manchester; it is not known which other son lived there. and now in a moment it is all ended, and in this earth we shall behold his face no more! His worth was well known to me, his great kindness, faithful and punctual service on all points on the most mournful of occasions is a thing I can never forget,William Dods helped with arrangements for JWC’s funeral in Haddington, 26 April 1866, and TC stayed with the Dods family the night before the funeral; see 43:216–17JAC to WDO, 24 April 1866, and 249–50TC’s Journal Entry on JWC’s Death. For a photograph of William Dods, see 39:63JWC to JAD, [21 Feb. 1863]. and while life lasts he must be connected in my mind with what was dearest to me in this earthly world.

I thank you much for the second note you sent and for its clear and pious account of what the circumstances were. It is a consolatory thought that his death was so easy, that he had not to suffer any of the miseries that attend old age or disease, and that he passed away to his Rest in that gentle and blessed manner.Peter Dods wrote that his father was in excellent health when he last saw him, but some days after returning home “he felt out of sorts, but no-one thought much about it, he was conversing & going about as usual & while in conversation with my Mother at 7 pm he raised his hand as if to shade his eyes, laid his head on the arm of the sofa on which he was sitting & without a struggle the mortal put on immortality.” He died of “fatty degeneration of the heart” (death certificate).

To your dear MotherJane Dods, b. Wilkie (ca. 1809–85), William’s second wife, m. 1854. I cannot venture to say anything, I know too well how importunate are all condolences in the depths of one’s own silent sorrow and bereavement, only in time and pious reflection is there gradual assuagement
to be found or hoped for. I beg you all to accept my human sympathy, and my best good wishes, and to believe always yours and especially hers with very many regards

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], [8 Oct.]. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand with TC’s signature. Dated by TC to JAC, 11 Oct.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Except within the first ten days, which were spent at Blickling, I fared ill rather than well in my Scotch excursion;TC stayed at Blickling Hall, Norfolk, at the invitation of Lady Lothian, 2–13 Aug.; see 48:214–19TC to JAF, 30 July; TC to JF, 1 Aug.; TC to JF, 8 Aug.; and TC to JAF, 12 Aug. He then went to Scotland, 13 Aug., returning to London 15 Sept. and indeed on getting back hither found myself quite unusually weak and out of order. And in that state have continued nearly ever since. The hope of getting round to my old average has never quitted me; but almost till today, if even today, I cannot fairly trace any steady first step towards that modest result. However, I continue to hope and in a sense to believe.

I am at home all day till three o’clock tomorrow, as every day; I am delighted to hear of Mary’s recovery,Lady Ashburton’s da.’ Mary Florence; she had been unwell over the summer; see 48:209TC to LA, 6 July 1873. and of your safe arrival home: I shall hope to see you sometime tomorrow; and shall try, on my own strength, after three o’clock—if you have not managed to alight here beforehand on your own.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 Oct. MS: NLS 527.97. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Within the last two weeks I have received various little kind notes and messages from you, which I ought to have acknowledged,—and would have, had I not been so utterly torpid, stupid, sad and idle The latter adjective does indeed involve me in blame for no degree of do-nothingism could have been more complete. I have sat merely reading, reading books of little worth to
me, some solemn doctrinairism by Benjamin Constant;Henri Benjamin Constant de Rebecque (1767–1830), Swiss-French political activist, writer on politics and religion. Doctrinairism was a kind of liberal constitutionalism popular in post revolutionary France. a spasmodic epigramatic work on the French Revolution by an Eduard QuinetEduard [Edgar] Quinet (1803–75), French historian and writer; TC presumably refers to his La Révolution, 2 vols. (Paris, 1865). surprising to me slightly rather than in any way instructive;—latterly Moore’s Utopia,Sir Thomas More (1478–1535; ODNB), Utopia (Louvain, 1516); TC owned the (Frankfurt, 1601) edn.; see Sotheby’s (1932) 90. with some biographies of said Moore, disappointing rather than cheering to me; and this day in particular nothing at all but Ritson’s Introduction to his Scottish Songs:Joseph Ritson (1752–1803; ODNB), antiquary, song and ballad collector; his Scottish Songs (Glasgow, 1794; 2d edn. 1869), had a particularly long and detailed introduction. —waes me, waes me! The chief or sole excuse for all which is my miserable state of stomach of which I say nothing more, hoping always it may soon mend a little. I do usually have some hours of heavy sleep; the absolute silence of my poor sleeping place being at present almost the only earthly blessing that I can recognise. SomnusIn Roman mythology Somnus was the personification of sleep. is defined as the Brother of Death; the first I may take as a present solacement, highly welcome in its way; in the second Brother’s help I am calmly certain of a perfect remedy. No more, no more of all that.

Your last Message, today’s, came an hour ago. All is there perfectly settled on the practical side: the Trench’s BookUnexplained; possibly Richard Chenevix Trench (1807–86; ODNB), clergyman and writer, archbishop of Dublin 1874–84; he wrote many books, his most recent being Plutarch; his life, his lives and his morals. Four lectures (1873). He also published several works on philology, and had previously corresponded with TC on that subject; see 43:19–21TC to RCT, 24 Oct. 1865. now probably in Forster’s hand; the Ruskin letter a mere double of one received here yesterday come safe to hand.Ruskin wrote two letters to TC, 9 Oct., sending one to Dumfries and one to Chelsea, as he did not know if TC was back in London yet. John A. Carlyle had apparently forwarded the Dumfries one to TC. The Chorley BiographyHenry Fothergill Chorley (1808–72; ODNB), journalist and writer, Henry Fothergill Chorley, Autobiography, Memoir and Letters, 2 vols. (1873); Chorley was the brother of TC’s friend John Rutter Chorley (1806–67; ODNB; see 19:135TC to JWC, [early Aug. 1845], and 22:30TC to JAC, 8 Aug. 1847). handed over to Jean,—Jean’s copy of Bridekirk’s hunting“Bridekirk’s Hunting,” song written by Adam Carlyle (d. 1734), Laird of Bridekirk; see 37:53TC to JHB, 4 Dec. 1860, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 17–18. conformable in every point to my remembrance of Jamie Pool’sJamie Pool of Borgue, Annandale schoolmaster; see 46:26TC to JCA, 11 March 1869. which is to go into Mary’s Song BookMary Aitken was compiling Scottish Song A Selection of the Choicest Lyrics of Scotland (1874); see 48:228TC to JAC, 27 Sept. 1873. She added a footnote to “Bridekirk’s Hunting”: “The author of this song, the Laird of Bridekirk, was a well-known man in Annandale, Dumfriesshire. Carlyle of Inveresk [Rev. Alexander Carlyle (1722–1805; ODNB)], speaks of him as a kinsman. Fifty or sixty years ago, there were many traditions of his exploits, current in that region, amongst others that on one hunting occasion his voice had been heard from ‘Woodcockair to Wintrop Head’—a distance of ten miles as the crow flies!” (Scottish Song 158). as much preferable to the one she already has. All right, all right.

We were at Forsters dining last Tuesday night, àpropos of Norfolk Elwin;Whitwell Elwin (1816–1900; ODNB), clergyman and editor, rector of Booton, Norfolk, 1849–1900, old friend of Forster’s. which adventure did me none of the mischief I expected; but rather did some good; and was pleasant beyond hope while it lasted. Poor Forster, I am sorry to understand, does not feel himself improving, but the contrary. I myself struggle to be of a different opinion but he is evidently in deep depression, much bothered about his third vol. of Dickens;Forster was working on the third and final vol. of his Life of Charles Dickens (1872–74). and evidently in painful case, as he looks around him and ahead.

Froude has been away since Tuesday or Wednesday last, visiting a Lord Ducie;Henry John Reynolds-Moreton (1827–1921), 3d earl of Ducie. is due today and probably already come. Meanwhile Allingham has started up; taken me two long walks,William Allingham; during the summer months many people left London, so TC had had little company since his return; see 48:227TC to JAC, 27 Sept.; Allingham noted in his diary that he himself had returned to London, 8 Oct., and walked with TC both 9 and 10 Oct. (Allingham Diary 227). with inducement to speak at least, which is better than absolute nothing in such a case. None else of my friends has turned up, except indeed Lady Ashburton, who was here two days ago, and is lodging still for a few days more at Thomas’s HotelLady Ashburton was having Kent House, Knightsbridge, built, 1872–74; see Surtees, Ludovisi 151; in the meantime she stayed either with friends or in hotels when in London. in Berkely Square; busied about many things; but well in health, both her Mary and she and purposing to live at Hastings or Brighton for the winter. The clipping of the Glasgow Newspaper refers to the young Lady you met at L. Luichart.Julia Charlotte Sophia Stewart-Mackenzie (1846–1937), niece of Lady Ashburton; John A. Carlyle stayed at Kinlochluichart with TC, July 1871; see 47:218TC to JAF, 25 July 1871. Her husband is eldest son to the Earl of Tweedale and a man already in the forties;Julia Stewart-Mackenzie m., 8 Oct., (as his 2d wife), Arthur Hay (1824–78), son of field-marshal George Hay (1787–1876), 8th marquess of Tweeddale. and will have a large fortune, probably before long.—Except my love to all and each you see there must not be one word more Return the Tyndall letterFor John Tyndall’s letter, see TC to JTY, 16 Oct. when you write next.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JT [JTY], 16 Oct. Addr: The Lord Warden Hotel / Dover. Typescript: Royal Institution RI TYP/1/207. Pbd: Francis O’Gorman, “Ruskin’s ‘Fors Clavigera’ of October 1873: an unpublished letter from Carlyle to Tyndall,” Notes and Queries 43.4 (1996): 430–31.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN TYNDALL

docBody.p: I never yet hear whether you are come home from your Dover investigation, but as I still see nothing of you, fancy that you are not yet in my neighbourhood. The very day before your letter came to me,Tyndall wrote from Dover, 9 Oct.: “I am here much exercised in the investigation of sound signals intended for warning to the mariner in case of fogs.” Tyndall pbd. his conclusions in “The Transmission of Sound by the Atmosphere” (1874). I had seen, and not till then, the strange wandering, meandering number of Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera, which contains his ill-natured remarks on your Alpine-Glacier investigations;John Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera: Letters to the Workmen and Labourers of Great Britain (1871–84); in letter 34, “La Douce Dame” (Oct. 1873), Ruskin attacked Tyndall for dismissing the work of James David Forbes (1809–68; ODNB), physicist and geologist; in his Occasional Papers on the Theory of Glaciers (1859), Forbes had described the motions of glaciers as like that of viscous fluid, but Tyndall, in Forms of Water (1872), supported the earlier theory that predicated glacier motion on fracture and regelation. which naturally seem to me very little called for in that place or any other. But throughout that number, R. seems in a specially prickly humour ready to strike out right and left in a more than usually violent manner upon everything that comes above his horizon. Witness that of Sir Charles Adderley, “boiling and eating his mother” instead of burying her;Sir Charles Bowyer Adderley (1814–1905; ODNB), politician; Ruskin began “La Douce Dame” discussing the contrast between “noble sentiment” and “unsentimental desire” as motives of human action. Adderley had recently criticized the terms of a debate on the relationship of the United Kingdom to her colonies as “purely sentimental”; Ruskin argued that a familial relationship, which includes that of a mother country and its colonies, is by definition “sentimental”; he gave examples from the Greek historian Herodotus (ca. 484–ca. 425 BC), Histories 3.38, and his story of differing cultures’ attitudes towards eating or burying their parents, and the biblical story, 2 Kings 6.29, of mothers eating or hiding their sons during the famine in Samaria. compared with which all he says of you is almost an amenity rather!— Ruskin himself I have not seen for many months, nor heard of except in the most transient way.

As to his criticisms on you and your ideas of glacial movement, my clear opinion is that you should take no notice of him whatever; such being the one dignified, wise and proper course on your part.Tyndall replied, 17 Oct.: “Be it as thou wilt!— I shall do as you advise, because I feel that your advice is the best and noblest that can be given to me.” To no mortal that knows you will it for a moment be credible that you had any private grudge against Professor Forbes’s “fame” in that respect, or private favour towards Agassiz
or in fact the least purpose in your mind, but that of clearing up the subject and rendering it visible to the bottom, as everybody knows to have been your invariable custom hitherto.Forbes had been visiting Jean Louis Rodolphe Agassiz (1807–73), Swiss-born biologist and geologist, author of Études sur les glaciers, 2 vols. (Neuchatel, 1840), at the Aar glacier in 1841, when he developed his theory, in contradiction of the established idea still followed by Tyndall. Be silent, then, and don’t weaken your cause by asking everybody or anybody whether that is not the fact. And go on silently doing the feat, what yet remains of it, as if there were no Ruskin there,—a nine days of raining Ruskins not having yet set in.Tyndall was deeply hurt by Ruskin’s attack; in his letter of 9 Oct. he wrote: “[F]or over and over again when in private conversation he has been subjected to far graver attacks than he could possibly direct against me, I have defended him. … He attacks me on a
subject in connexion with which I have only sought to do the right. … And this … shall be done if it rained Ruskins nine days running.”

I have been here for above a month; visibly not a little smashed and worsened by my painful pilgrimage to northward. Only within the last few days have I begun to feel as if slowly getting back to my old average instead of the better I had counted on. Evidently my time for touring is gone by; “stay where thou art” the rule for me henceforth.Tyndall replied: “I think you must not give up the notion of quitting London from time to time. I believe the chief problem in your case—and indeed in mine—is rather one of meat and drink than of any thing else.” Let me hear from you, or still better see you when you return.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 Oct. MS: NLS 527.98. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your letter and all your messages or signals, especially the Newspaper with the Pope and Kaiser letters,Pope Pius IX (1792–1878) wrote, 7 Aug., to Kaiser Wilhelm I (1797–1888), emperor of Germany 1871–88, to complain about the persecution of Catholics in Germany. Kaiser Wilhelm, 3 Sept., rejected this claim, contending that many of his Catholic subjects had conspired with opponents of his government in “open revolt against existing laws.” The Kaiser insisted that his aim throughout was “to protect internal peace, and preserve the authority of laws in the States whose government has been entrusted to me by God” as a matter of “kingly duty” (Annandale Observer and Advertiser, 17 Oct. 1873). came all safe at their due times. The Pope and
Kaiser Letter has been much noticed and admired here; I have not seen for many a long year in any Newspaper so manfully quiet honest and solid a word spoken by any person especially by an official person to the wretched old Prince of Humbugs as this of Kaiser Wilhelm. I suppose BismarckOtto von Bismarck, chancellor of the German Empire. must have been at the writing of it. Would to Heaven there were any English Minister now extant, or soon likely to be, who durst stand up in the name of this country (which was once the country of Cromwell, and protestant to the bone) and tell the accursed son of ChaosOne of TC’s names for the pope; cf. 45:122. a similar story!In Britain as in Germany the rights of Catholics were limited, particularly their access to education and various areas of employment. Both countries suspected and feared that Catholics’ primary loyalty was to the pope rather than to the secular ruler. But that is a vain thought.——

The enclosed Letter from a thrice dreary IcelanderUnidentified further. has brought me in mind of Vigfusson,Gudbrand Vigfusson, scholar of medieval Scandinavian history. John A. Carlyle wrote, 13 Oct.: “Last week I had a letter from Mr Vigfusson. … He had been reading your French Revolution with great admiration for the first time, & found things in it superior to every thing else he had read in English with exception of ‘some of Shakespeare’s plays & the Bible.’ He may possibly call between two & three some afternoon this week & take his chance of seeing you & perhaps of taking a walk if you have no other engagement. He is a very lively man when he feels himself welcome, & knows more about all Norse matters than any one I know of.” who has not yet called; but with whom I should like to speak for a few minutes about this new dismal being. You I think merely saw him here; and know of him nothing farther? I had totally forgotten him and can yet recal almost nothing of him, except only his lean angry face and the impression he gave me of total impracticability, distress and absurdity. He seemed to have a pique at Vigfusson, and declined my recommendation to go and speak with or ask counsel of him.John wrote, 21 Oct.: “The Icelander’s letter I also return. I had some talk with Vigfusson about him, just after he had called at Cheyne Row in August or July; & Vigfusson gave him a very bad character, & advised me to have nothing to do with him on any account. And perhaps your best way would be to let his letter lie unanswered, at least till you see Vigfusson & hear what details he has to give.” John had been staying in Cheyne Row May–July 1873; Icelander unidentified further and his visit unrecorded. His project of translating an Italian or any novel or thing into English for the press is practically impossible,—for this one reason, were there no other, that he clearly does not know English; and the process of getting to know it would be much too “tardive” in the posture he is in. I see not anywhere the faintest prospect for him, except in giving lessons of Icelandic, could he find any customers ready to receive him. Towards this, Vigfusson might give him a certificate; and I daresay would, on finding him worthy?—— I might indeed succinctly dismiss him, by mere
silence on this occasion; but somehow I feel sorry for the bewildered outcast; seemingly near starving, and Lessons in Icelandic here in London or Oxford or somewhere seem a possible resource and the sole one. Tell me what you think on next writing.

I also enclose Tyndall’s Letter in answer to a word I sent him; it is better that din is kept down than stirred up. From Ruskin we have not heard a single word, after his eager two notes of preparation. He talked of sending me “books”; but I have not the least guess of what they were. Last Sunday, which was a complete day of rain, James Stephen walked in here; I put on my Mackintosh; and went out on a longish walk with him; tho’ the rain still continued pouring. He appeared to be in good heart, in spite of his Dundee experiences and other disappointments:James Fitzjames Stephen stood in a by-election as a Liberal candidate for Dundee, Aug. 1873, but lost; see 48:214–15TC to JAF, 30 July 1873. His other disappointments unidentified. I agreed with him in regard to Dundee that with such a prospect of stepping at once into a Solictor Generalship in Parliament (more especially as he was flattered with the confident hope of his easily coming in at Dundee), it would have been all his life after a kind of haggle of doubt whether he had not missed his chance by holding back;—he evidently miscalculated the Dundee opinion about Gladstone, and one’s frankly declaring oneself a soldier of his.The by-election was won by James Yeaman (1816–86), a Scottish Liberal who later became a Conservative, so was perhaps less in sympathy with William Gladstone. Stephen is coming to Edinr early next month to deliver 2 Lectures to the Philosophic Institution, on “Popular Government,” and the good and evil of that now established state of things: we shall see them in print I suppose;Stephen delivered lectures on “Popular Government” to the Edinburgh Philosophic Institution at Queen St. Hall, Edinburgh, 11 and 14 Nov.; they were pbd. in the Contemporary Review 23 (Dec. 1873 and Jan. 1874): 1–19 and 165–81. and find whether there is anything fruitful in them or not. He is a very honest robust and courageous man, this Stephen; but has ahead of him a thorny enough wilderness to make his way through.—No other person or thing worth noting have I met with; no news even about myself and my “state of health” have I got to send you; and as three oclock is fairly come, I ought to cease.

Mary is very diligent at her Songs and seems to think she may have the Ms. in Macmillan’sMacmillan & Co., publishers; it was pbd. May 1874. hands very shortly. The collection I do really believe will be a tolerably good one, superior at least to any other that I know. I myself make feeble, altogether feckless attempts at some real or even imaginary work: but in this state of the digestive apparatus nothing really is possible, except to be patient and to take things easy, or the sorrowfully easiest one can. Thank Jean for her little note which was very welcome last Monday. Were the shirts done (which I suppose must now be shortly I shall look for the a/cs of these and
of the trousers and waistcoats,Mary Aitken recorded in TC’s checkbook: “Chelsea 31 Oct. 1873 / Mrs Aitken (shirts trousers &c) / £5 .. 6 .. 3½” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). which latter, though I have only had on one pair and one waistcoat appear to fit quite well. Give my love and blessing to everybody. I am, as always,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JR [JRU], 31 Oct. MS: Viljoen. Pbd: Collingwood, The Life and Work of John Ruskin (1893) 2:431–32 inc; Ruskin’s Works 23:lv; Cate 174.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: After several weeks of eager expectation I received, morning before yesterday, the sequel to your kind little note, in the shape of 4 bright 4to lecturesRuskin wrote, 9 Oct., that he had “some little books” to send TC once he knew where he was; see TC to JAC, 11 Oct. (forwarded by an Aylesbury printer) on the Historical and Artistic development of Val d’Arno.Ruskin delivered ten lectures on “Val d’Arno in the Thirteenth Century” at Oxford Univ., Oct.–Nov.; the first four lectures were delivered 20–31 Oct., and although not pbd. till 1874, apparently the printers, Watson & Hazell, Aylesbury, sent TC early printed copies which Ruskin used when delivering the lectures; see Ruskin’s Works 23:5. Ruskin, Val D’Arno: Ten Lectures on the Tuscan Art Directly Antecedent to the Florentine Year of Victories, Given before the University of Oxford in Michaelmas Term, 1873 (1874); see Ruskin’s Works 23:1–178. Walter Hazell (1843–1919) and George Watson (b. ca. 1816). Many thanks to you for so pleasant and instructive a gift. The work is full of beautiful and delicate perceptions, new ideas, both new and true, which throw a bright illumination over that important piece of History and awaken fresh curiosities and speculations on that and on other much wider subjects. It is all written too with the old nobleness and fire, in which no other living voice to my knowledge equals yours. Perge, perge [Go on, go on];—and, as the Irish say, “More power to your elbow!”—

I have yet read this Val d’Arno only once. Froude snatched it away from me yesterday;James Anthony Froude; Ruskin replied, [ca. 1 Nov.]: “I have ordered two copies of the lectures to be sent to you and one to Froude.” and it has then to go to my Brother at Dumfries. After that I shall have it back.— Your visit to me still hangs in the vague; your very pen to me-wards continues uncomfortably stingy;Ruskin wrote: “I am very careful … about not doing too much, — If I do not write to you think how many things I must leave undone.” but we will hope, we will hope. I am not very well; but it is mainly Old age that ails me; so that there is nothing to
be said, or complained of. Have you read poor “Mill’s Autobiography,John Stuart Mill, Autobiography (1873), pbd. 17 Oct. ” and did you ever before read such a book?
Adieu, dear Ruskin. Work while it is called today!Cf. John 9:4.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 3 Nov. Addr: Cambridge / Boston / Massachusetts. PM: London, 3 Nov. 1873. MS: Houghton. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p: You sent me a kind announcement directly on your safe arrival home,Charles Eliot Norton had spent much of the winter of 1872–73 in London, leaving 15 May; he wrote, 28 May: “We reached home night before last, after a prosperous voyage. … The country here is beautiful with the spring flowering. … But the trees and the shrubs are as Yankee as the people, and in every aspect New England is different from Old. … To you I am more grateful than you can ever know.” which I read with great pleasure, and was very grateful for. Not very long after, there arrived your excellent translation of the Vita Nuova;The New Life of Dante Alighieri, translated (with essays and notes) by Charles Eliot Norton (Boston, 1867). a truly welcome gift; this latter ought, by all right and reason, to have drawn an immediate answer from me; yet, alas, it did not. The little book was very curious and interesting to me: I had never fairly read or understood it before, and your translation made it thoroughly transparent, and seemed to me faithfully, modestly and gracefully done; I had indeed a real satisfaction in getting this new glance into the inner soul of Dante; and felt it to be at once psychologically curious and deeply pathetic,—on the whole entirely intelligible to me. My Brother, a great Dante student, next had a reading of the Book; and pronounces it to be “excellently well done”; a fact, I believe, which has already been testified to you by many witnesses.

The duty of announcing all this to you was at once as clear as sunshine; and few days since has it been absent from my poor conscience, from my poor heart, as a thing evidently needful, evidently profitable to be done;—which nevertheless as we see is only now taken in hand! Miraculous enough; and caused solely by “Diana in the shape of continual IndigestionDiana, the huntress in Roman mythology; cf. “Diana in the shape of Hunger,” The French Revolution, Carlyle, Works 2:130. ,” nothing
else but she (sorrow on her)Coterie speech; see 46:96TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1869. has created this mysterious phenomenon, Cruel Diana, worthier to be called Hecate or one of the GorgonsHecate, Greek goddess of magic, sometimes identified with Artemis, the Greek name of Diana; TC previously named them as responsible for his indigestion; see 8:114TC to JSM, [3 May 1835]. The Gorgons were three sisters whose gaze turned people to stone. in my case! For I am still under her influence; and have to feel that inexorable fate will keep me so, under heavier and heavier pressure from her till the End come. Patientia, patientia; that, too, I can believe is all right, and springs (as your friend Dante says), it, too, as Malebolge itself does, out of Eterno Amore [Infinite Love].Malebolge, the eighth circle of Hell in Dante’s Inferno.

But to descend to historic prose. I made a pilgrimage to Scotland by Norfolk and the east shores; obliged to fly from London and its blaze of July heat, and unmelodious noise.
