We went, my little Niece Mary, who writes this, and I, first to a grand old place called Blickling,Blickling Hall; see TC to Lady A, [8 Oct.]. some 10 or 12 miles south of Norwich, the birthplace of Anne Boleyn,Anne Boleyn (ca. 1500–36; ODNB), queen of England 1533–36. and variously otherwise distinguished,—to me most especially by its spacious silence, fine old libraries, old trees, and breezy expanses of green environment; it is among the very finest bits of palatial architecture I have ever seen (built, as it tells us, 1620–26) perfect yet, every brick and every plank of it;For TC’s stay at Blickling Hall, and descriptions of the house, see 48:214–19TC to JAF, 30 July; TC to JF, 1 Aug.; TC to JF, 8 Aug.; and TC to JAF, 12 Aug. —inhabited only by two youngish ladies and their invalid old mother (Dowr Marchioness of Shrewsbury, who seldom or never shows herself to a stranger):Lady Lothian and her sister Lady Gertrude Chetwynd-Talbot; their invalid mother was Lady Sarah Elizabeth Chetwynd-Talbot. the likeliest of all places for a creature who, like me, hates justly every kind of noise. There for a couple of weeks we did admirably well; saw with satisfaction the interesting phsiognomy of Norfolk (uninvaded yet, this corner of it by the tartarean railway whistle or any of its adjuncts); saw Oxnead, old residence of the Paston Letters’ people,Letters written by several generations of the Paston family (per. c. 1420–1504; ODNB), who owned various estates in Norfolk including Oxnead, 11 mi. (17.5 km.) N of Norwich; the letters were mostly written between 1418 and 1509, and were discovered at Oxnead in 1735, and first pbd.1787; they are considered “the richest source there is for every aspect of the lives of gentlemen and gentlewomen of the English middle ages” (ODNB). a really beautiful old place still, as in the hands of a gentleman farmer, who keeps the place all trim as velvet; has daughtersOxnead was currently owned by Thomas Mack (b. 1848), eldest son of John Mack (ca. 1795–1867); he was unmarried, but had five sisters: Elizabeth Charlotte (1850–1917), Margaret Mary (1852–1937), Catherine Susanna (b. 1855), Alice Octavia (1859–1946), and Frances Ursula (1865–1958). playing croquet, has smooth yew hedges or fragments of such, 20 feet high; smooth paths and venerable fragments of ruined magnificence scattered in his grazing paddocks: next to
this in interest was ancient Norwich itself and its grand Cathedral the interior of which was more impressive to me, I think, than any similar edifice had been; it is of immense height the interior all white, of pure white stone in shapes serenely grand; bidding the human soul a little, ‘Be thou, too, grand, thou miserable little article so far as thou canst!’— There in Norfolk we did very well; and I got some real improvement and alleviation; but after that, our travels by sea and by land, our sojournings and visitings were all, or nearly all, inimical and hurtful to me. So that at last I bethought me of returning home, such home as was still left me in the world, where at least there was the blessing of solitude and physical quiet to be expected; and shot home accordingly (Mary as my little Ariel,Ariel is an airy spirit in Shakespeare’s The Tempest who serves the magician Prospero. ministering in all things) at one stretch about the 10th or 14th of Sep.;TC and Mary returned to London 15 Sept.; see 48:223TC to JAC, 20 Sept. where I have lain here quiet ever since. I was in Edinr 2 days and 1 night; but spoke only to 2 persons;Presumably Maggie Welsh, who accompanied TC and Mary Aitken to Edinburgh, and David Masson, who arranged for their accommodation; see 48:220–21MW to JW, 9 Sept. 1873. the mute dialogue with things was naturally more extensive, but could be edifying to nobody but myself. I had one little errand in that region; one and no other in Scotland, or properly in the world;Visiting JWC’s grave. that done, we hastened back Chelsea-ward; and are intending to continue quiet, or, if it must be, torpid, here, as more conveniently than elsewhere. I have now got company enough and to spare, which fails not to do me a little good; but I shall much miss your company; and the really human sort of dialogues we used to have together last winter.TC wrote often about how much he enjoyed Norton’s company; see for instance 48:199. Norton replied, 16 Nov., saying how happy he was to hear from TC: “There is nothing in my life to take the place of our walks.” I think the continual rain of last winter, the rainiest I ever saw, did me more mischief than frost would have done; but on the whole I feel to be coming round to near the point where I used to be, and I am in truth, not much or at all more weakened than another year of time has a fair right to have made me. I read a great deal, almost approximately happy when I can get a good book which is rather rare: whether I shall ever have the audacity to write anything again is highly uncertain,—and even to myself highly unimportant. The base black deluge of atheistic “science,”TC presumably refers to the writings of Charles Darwin, Thomas Huxley, and
Herbert Spencer (1820–1903; ODNB); see 48:73TC to UC, 23 June 1872. very falsely so called, will evidently run its course in spite of all conceivable writing, reasoning or persuading; let us look on it holding our nose well with a composed mind; and know that at length, it will clean thoroughly out the Augean stableOne of the labors of Hercules in Greek mythology was to clean the stables of King Augeas of a great accumulation of filth, untouched for many years. & leave the poor world free to begin again.

Ruskin is writing some beautiful things, which I persuade myself you regularly see. His Lectures on Robin Redbreast and Swallow,Ruskin’s Love’s Meinie. Lectures on Greek and English Birds. Given Before the University of Oxford (1873); see 48:226TC to JAC, 20 Sept. 1873. the most delicate and brilliant things I almost ever saw, came to me while at Blickling; he sent last week four new Oxford Lectures of which others are to follow, entitled Val d’Arno; a most ingenious, instructive and genial kind of thing; the man himself I do not remember to have seen at all since you left us. Apropos of these Val d’Arno Lectures, or rather of my answer to them, I had a grimly sad-looking letter, of a very stoical tone, though not of an unhealthy; but disclosing to one that Ruskin also is treading the Winepress alone;See Isa. 63.3. and sometimes feels his labour very heavy. God be with him, poor fellow. I hear at the present time, no other Voice like him in this dreary Mother of dead dogsCoterie speech; see 41:11TC to JWC, [6 Sept.]. which is still commonly called a world.

Poor Forster, who I think rather regularly hears from you and answers, is still under heavy suffering, almost continual; but I persuade myself nevertheless is steadily, though slowly, getting better.—Did you see poor John Mill’s Autobiography? It is loud among the penny a liners, or was, two weeks ago, the whole fraternity of them under visible astonishment, struggling to spell out from it, “The great Thinker of the Age.” I never read any book at all like it in my life; it resembles more the Autobiography of a logical Steam-engine, than any human creature’s;Norton replied, 16 Nov.: “I have not read Mill’s Autobiography. One who knows anything of the Vita Nuova and of the Divine Comedy may be pardoned if he smile compassionately at poor Mill’s experience of love. There is room for improvement, doubtless, in the regulation of our passions, but to regulate them out of existence is to go too far.” and gives me, whenever I reflect on it, a peculiar, and dreary sense of desolation, disappointment, blighted pity and discouragement of mind. No doubt you have read it and will understand all this.

Through Forster I heard that your good and dear old Mother, had been in extreme danger,Catherine Eliot Norton; she had been ill during most of the summer. but that she had marvellously recovered and was restored to your love yet again. God be thanked; it is a sore parting that with a Mother, and such a Mother; this is a unique event in the history of us all, that have been lucky in our birth.—A very stout large gentleman named Field, from Philadelphia, called here the other day, with Sculptor Story;John White Field (1815–87), Philadelphia art patron and collector, and William Wetmore Story (1819–95), American sculptor, art critic, and poet; both were friends of Norton’s. TC had previously met Story at the Grange (Lord Ashburton’s house in Hampshire), Oct. 1862; see 38:241JWC to MR, 21 Oct. [1862]. and gave me still fresher news of you; all well, he said, and my dear little Sally (little gipsy that she is!) diligently playing her fiddle,—did you ever hear of such a thing!
Kiss her bright little cheek for me; and say I am still true to my old feelings.Sara, Norton’s eldest da.; see 48:200TC to MNO, 9 May. Norton replied: “My little Sally is true to her old love. She will never forget him.” God bless the whole household of you, young and old.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 5 Nov. MS: NLS 527.99. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:420; Carlyle Encyclopedia 325–26. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Many thanks for your patience with me, for your liberal pair of letters this morning! I have been sorrowfully negligent, or rather altogether not negligent, but powerless or defective in power; the genius of perpetual indigestion is one of the ugliest fellows I ever met with; and the weight of him naturally grows heavier not lighter as I get older day by day. I am very glad to hear that things are not yet so bad with you (nor, as I guess, perhaps ever will be); and that your dietetic plans are so rigorous, correct and successful. Go on and prosper;—go on especially with your readings at night,John A. Carlyle wrote, 4 Nov., a detailed account of his diet and exercise regime. He continued: “[A]fter [dinner I] read a book or two of the Iliad to Jean & the two lassies [Anne and Margaret Aitken] downstairs. The Odyssey has already been read all through in that way”; see 48:228TC to JAC, 27 Sept. 1873. and your walks in the morning.—— I need not say how glad your second letter was to me, and how well worth writing; it is very good news indeed that poor Mary and her people are to be left quiet in the old environment; and it is beyond any hope I had that they would get the place for such an increase of rent as £20.John wrote again, 4 Nov.: “Since I wrote … Mary has come from the Gill, & desires me to tell you that a new lease had been signed … today; with only £20 advance in rent—which seems to us all a very small sum considering the present high price of all farm produce.” Their sister Mary Austin and her husband, James, farmed The Gill, near Ecclefechan, and their lease was up for renewal from 2 Feb. 1874. John wrote later, 1 Jan. 1874: “The factor … told James Austin that he would not have got the new lease at the rent he offered, unless the Marquis himself had decided the matter by specially requesting that the family might remain at the Gill.” John Sholto Douglas (1844–1900), 9th marquess of Queensberry, landowner. A lasting dreary kind of anxiety hanging about one for the last year and more is hereby tumbled away.—The family had been anxious about the lease renewal for many months; see 48:177TC to JAC, 12 March 1873. Yesterday morning came this letter from Alick.Alexander Carlyle, their brother, living in Canada. I did mean
to send it yesterday; but actually could not get time,—such a tumble of things absolutely foreign to me came raining in before I had got my breakfast (very late breakfast) fairly done. Alick’s letter is in a mournful kind of tone; but it means nothing bad that I see; nay the issue is at last good; that the young man has got hold of his bit of territoryProbably Alexander’s son James who had been looking for a farm; see 48:184TC to JAC, 29 March 1873. and that all else goes on much as it did. When you can write poor Alick a letter, it will be a benificence to do so.John replied, 7 Nov.: “Yesterday I wrote to poor Alick … & gave him all the news I could.” I am always thinking to do something of the kind, but, alas, my right hand has lost its cunning,TC was suffering from an increasingly shaky right hand; see 47:2TC to TC, 4 May 1870. and the Genius of Dyspepsia, surely he will temporarily lift his ugly hoof off my neck one day or other!— The Yankee letter was for an Autograph.John had enclosed with his letter of 4 Nov. a “rather questionable looking American letter” which had arrived for TC at Dumfries; “It does not seem to be one merely asking for an Autograph & therefore it is sent on.” I enclose it here as a curiosity, along with another, which came from Glasgow yesterday: the power of stupidity in this present epoch is very strong.

You have lost nothing by missing of the Autobiography of Mill.John wrote, 4 Nov.: “I have not yet seen John Mill’s Autobiography, but the reviews & extracts from it promise little.” I have never read a more uninteresting book; nor I should say a sillier, by a man of sense, integrity and seriousness of mind. The penny–a–liners were very busy with it, I believe, for a week or two; but were evidently pausing in doubt and difficulty by the time the 2nd, editn came out; and I should judge that there will not soon be any need for a 3rd do. It is wholly the life of a logic-chopping engine, little more of human in it than if it had been done by a thing of mechanized iron: “Autobiography of a Steam Engine” perhaps you may sometime read it as a mournful psychical curiosity, but in no other point of view can it interest anybody—I suppose it will deliver us henceforth from the cocka leerie craw about “Great Thinker of the Age”; wh. will be a kind of deliverance, welcome, though inconsiderable. The thought of poor Mill altogether, and of his life and history in this poor muddy world gives me real pain and sorrow.

Ruskin’s new Fors, which I also have read, is quite what you say.Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera (see TC to JTY, 16 Oct.), letter 35, “Song of Songs” (Nov. 1873). John wrote, 4 Nov.: “Ruskin’s last Fors is worth nothing, otherwise I should have forwarded it to you.” But by the next post here are 4 Oxford lectures, under the title of Val d’Arno, which seem to me of first rate quality. I send them to you by this post;For Ruskin’s Val d’Arno, see TC to JRU, 31 Oct. John replied, 7 Nov.: “The parcel of [Ruskin’s] four Lectures was not delivered here till late in the evening. … I have read the first Lecture & find it rather difficult to understand thoroughly.” they dont require to be returned at all; for there is a second copy of them coming to me and
indeed a second copy of Lecture V has already come. There is to be a sixth lecture; when it arrives, I dispatch V & VI together. Please return the Ruskin letter. It is the only one I have had from him these many months; a heavy laden letter indeed.Ruskin wrote TC a long and very gloomy letter, [ca. 1 Nov.]. Adieu, dear Brother, We hope to write again, some of us in a few days. My blessing on you all Ever your affecte

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-JR [JRU], 12 Nov. MS: Yale. Pbd: Cate 175–76. Text from Cate.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: My uncle bids me say how very much he has been surprised and gratified about your Appendix. He says that the work is beautifully done; that you have seen into the very heart of the matter; and that he is more flattered than he can express by the trouble you have taken in this matter.Ruskin was writing an Appendix titled “Notes on the Political Economy of Prussia” for his new edn. (1873) of The Crown of Wild Olive (1866) about the Prussian economy with specific reference to the first three books of Frederick; it was intended as an appendix to the chapter on “War” although in the event the chapter “The Future of England” was placed between them; see Ruskin’s Works 18:515–33. Ruskin replied to Mary, [13 Nov.]: “It is a great relief to my mind that your uncle likes the Appendix” (MS: NLS 555.66).

My uncle thinks that it would be much better to refer to the people’s edition (which is only 2/ a vol., and is extremely popular) than to the little 1869 editn. I have therefore in each case substituted the page of it in the parenthesis for that of the one you had chosen; so that should you agree with him, and not have time to look it over, you could send the proof direct to the printer,Ruskin used page numbers from both the 6 vol. first edn. (1858–65) and the people’s edn. (1872–73). He wrote: “So many thanks for the beautifully made alterations. I’ve sent them straight to printers” (MS: NLS 555.66). —the numbers are perfectly correct (I have been used to doing work of the kind for him). If you in the least care for a copy of this edition, which is very pleasant to read, being in small voll. easily carried about & light to hold, he would be delighted to send you one at once. If your Ms. is already in the printer’s hands, I should be so very happy to alter the numbers in the parenthesis of the proofs which are still to come.
With all kind messages to you from Uncle,
docBody.closer: Yours affectionately & respectfully, / Mary Carlyle Aitken

bibl.sourceNote: TC-AF, 14 Nov. MS: Univ. of Virginia Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Albert Fleming (ca. 1846–1923), author and lawyer, later a follower and friend of Ruskin.
bibl.head: TC TO ALBERT FLEMING

docBody.p: I read your Pamphlet; and have the clearest sympathy with your disgusts and indignation at what you see and experience in this “House of Rimmon,”Fleming sent TC his pamphlet, In the House of Rimmon (1873). The title is taken from an incident in the Bible and means to compromise one’s principles for the sake of worldly goods and advancement; see 2 Kings 5:18. Fleming’s pamphlet is a tirade against the inhumanity of the modern industrial and mechanized world, written in the form of a letter to an anonymous friend. which the modern life of England is growing more and more to be.

I have good hopes that you yourself will grow to be an exceptional figure, and will make out for yourself a noble life yet, where so many are ignoble and even inhuman. This is in all times and in all places possible for a faithful and willing mind; but is at no time easy, and perhaps never was more difficult than it even now is. But a man always can find in the world some honest work, honest and fairly commanded by the Maker of him, which he can learn and strenuously do like a true and faithful worker,—accepting for it quietly what minimum of wages is honestly procurable; and the smaller his wage I need not tell you the more a noble man he is. Meat, clothes and fire are essentially all that wages can do for a man, and these even now I believe are procurable in our own poor country as in others. Perhaps you have even some real talent for Literature, the divinest endowment of capability a man can have? This is a question well worth your serious enquiry; perhaps your serious preparation for & experimental trial of? Fine literature, as a business, I believe to be the most painful & the worst paid of all; and unless one finds himself actually possessed of some real faculty for it, ought in no case to be gone into.

One chief thing I had to advise is that you, so soon as possible, subdue your indignation; and reduce it into noble central fire not seen on the top at all; in other words that you invoke omnipotent “Patience,” and make her more and more you[r] tutelary goddess! This is absolutely necessary, indispensable; and can only be a work of time and devout continual effort. The German proverb says, “Patience can subdue iron and adamant”; it can conquer all earthly hindrances; and without it, no hindrance can be conquered.
Hoping for you, and heartily wishing for you, I remain

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Nov. MS: NLS 527.100. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:300–1 inc. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:423–24. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature in blue pencil.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
You sent me duly the FitzJames Stephen Lecture in the Scotsman, wh. I should not have seen otherwise so soon; it was carried off the same day by Froude as a thing he was eager to see. The second and concluding lecture you most likely have today;For Stephen’s lectures, see TC to JAC, 18 Oct.; the lectures were pbd. in the Scotsman, 12 and 15 Nov. & on Monday morning I may expect to see it here. Stephen had been talking of it to me more than once; and I found it a very curious piece indeed, delineating one of the most perfect dust whirls of administrative Nihilism and absolute absurdities & impotencies; more like an Elective Government Apparatus for Bedlam, elected and submitted to by Bedlam than any sane apparatus ever known before;—and strangely enough it is interlarded withal with the loyalest assurances every now and then that it is the one form of Government for us for an indefinite period; and that no change for the better can be practically contemplated.In the first lecture Stephen declared that “Parliamentary government has been irrevocably established amongst us, and it is impossible to suppose that it will be seriously modified in any period to which we can look forward. … I see no use in discussing the question whether this is a good thing or a bad one. For all practical purposes it is enough to say that it exists, and that it is the part of all rational men to make the best of it, as they make the best of the climate, the soil, or the national character of their country” (Scotsman, 12 Nov. 1873). The second lecture wh. was to show us some shadow of the per contra side I shall be curious to see.In his second lecture Stephen’s argument is that the more people involved in decision making the more inefficient it will be, but that people would rather that, “than that it should be well done at the price of being put into the hands of a small knot of officials forming what is called a bureaucracy. … To give the country a really efficient government it would be necessary … to restore a considerable degree of real power to the King; and this cannot be done” (Scotsman, 15 Nov. 1873). Poor Stephen has evidently got intertwisted with Gladstoneism and the prospect of Solicitor-generalship to a distressing and bewildering degree. His Dundee failure of Election has been the most awkward event: it cost him, they say, £800 of money; and the Gladstone Solicitor-Generalcy is gone from him like a knotless thread,—one Vernon Harcourt,Following Stephen’s defeat at Dundee, John Duke Coleridge (1820–94; ODNB), Attorney-General 1871–73, urged Gladstone to appoint Stephen as Solicitor-General; see 48:215TC to JAF, 30 July; but the post went instead to Henry James (1828–1911; ODNB), Sept.–Nov. 1873, and then to Sir William George Granville Venables Vernon Harcourt (1827–1904; ODNB). TC had first met Harcourt in the early 1850s; see 34:111JWC to TC, [9 Aug. 1858], and more recently at Addiscombe, July 1869; see 46:65TC to JAC, 23 [30] July 1869. questionably eloquent,
greedy and ambitious quack, coming in in his stead; both Froude and I are almost rather of opinion that he ought to join with DerbyEdward Henry Stanley, 15th earl of Derby, leader of the Conservatives in the House of Lords. and by one bold stroke cut loose from the People’s WilliamWilliam Gladstone. altogether; but I believe neither of us has yet spoken to him in that strain. He is a very honest man, Stephen, with a huge heavy stroke of work in him; needs a great deal of money for the big young familyStephen had eight children. he has; and at present has no means of earning but by journalist legal & other piece work. He himself takes his Dundee disappointment with a courageous indifference; and fears nothing. A German proverb says, Every year a cheese, [few]Word missing, edge of paper torn. cheeses, every year a child is many children. Enough of all this, far more than enough.

I am still as idle as ever; do nothing but read (poorish books, alas); walk daily a 3 or 4 miles talk the while, if I have any company;—have always, alas, to spend so many hours out of my four and twenty in mere sleeping, misdigesting, and drearily endeavouring in vain to manage not insupportably the wretched dilapidated clay house where I have still to linger till the term come. In general my mood is mournful; but seldom or never to be called quite miserable; occasionally strangely wonderful, tender and even solemn. With the great change so near there is no conceivable reason for complaint except one’s own weak folly.

Tuesday last I went again to dine at Forsters Tennyson & SpeddingAlfred Tennyson and James Spedding, both longtime friends of TC. there and no other company. Tennyson was distinctly rather wearisome; nothing coming from him that did not smack of utter indolence, what one might almost call torpid sleepiness & stupor; all still enlivened however by the tone of boylike naïveté and total want of any malice except against his Quarterly & other unfavourable reviewers.Tennyson had recently suffered several bad reviews; a comparison of Byron and Tennyson, Quarterly Review, Oct. 1871; a review of Harry Buxton Forman, Our Living Poets (1872), Quarterly Review, July 1873; and a review of “Gareth and Lynette” and “The Last Tournament” (1872), part of his Arthurian cycle The Idylls of the King (1859–85), London Quarterly Review, Jan. 1873 (39:394–405), which began: “There is some ground for hoping that the Laureate has now really finished his ‘Arthuriad,’ and passed out of the atmosphere that has so long been the bane of his poetic genius” (394); and concluded: “[W]e come back once more to the hope that we have the last of the ‘Arthuriad’ in our hands, … a subject or set of subjects whereon he has failed to throw the full human interest necessary to make narrative poetry of the highest value” (405). He had the look of being very ill washed (tho’ in fact, I believe washing could do no more); but his face has big rope-like wrinklings, there is a large dull coloured plate of baldness on his crown; and
I guess he feels himself growing old and his “si-news beginning to stiffen,” as the old Burgher preacherUnidentified. said; tho’ he bragged often of his still undiminished strength. Poor Tennyson, after all!Coterie speech, an early phrase of John A. Carlyle’s; see 1:211TC to AC, 19 Dec. 1819. Spedding looked a good deal better; clean as spring-water, serious, simple, something of reverend in his aspect. He has actually finished his Life of Bacon,James Spedding’s The Letters and the Life of Francis Bacon, 7 vols. (1857–74); the Athenaeum announced, 15 Aug. 1874: “Completion of Mr. Spedding’s Life of Lord Bacon. The seventh volume of the Letters and Life of Francis Bacon … Collected and Edited by J. Spedding … With a copious Index, Completing the Work, is now ready, price 12s.” the last page of it gone to press; a right notable feat for Spedding; which I emphatically praised. The eldest of his three beautiful Nieces (Tom’s daughters)Margaret Emily Spedding, da. of James’s brother, Thomas Story Spedding, d. 2 June. is dead last Autumn. S. gave me the history of the event; in very calm but rather touching terms.— Forster still suffers a great deal in these cold, windy & often foggy days; has not once been out I should think for almost two weeks back.

A mass of letters, wh. were intended for Jean has been accumulating: I stick them in if they can interest her or you for a few moments. Tell her I did faithfully mean to enclose them in a letter to herself; but absolutely cannot now; repentance itself will surely urge me to write to her soon. My best blessings be with you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 Nov. MS: NLS 527.101. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
It is evidently proper that poor Mary’s needful £100 be furnished by one or both of us together,Their sister Mary Austin had just renewed the lease on their farm; see TC to JAC, 5 Nov. John A. Carlyle wrote, 18 Nov.: “It seems to me a good thing in the new lease, that part of the wet land is to be drained, the landlord paying half the cost … & when drained the tenant will have all the profit at least for fifteen years.” John then wrote, 21 Nov., enclosing a letter to himself from Mary, [20 Nov.]: “We think if we had £100 pounds it would do a good deal in draining and perhaps laying on some lime. The proprietor takes charge of the cutting and all other things about the drains. Our folks have the tiles to cart, and pay for every thing except the tiles” (MS: NLS 1775E.266). —I am myself perfectly indifferent which way you decide it to be; and the money shall be furnished in either case whenever
you declare it to be necessary.John wrote, 21 Nov.: “I purpose that we make up the £100 she wants by cash sending her one half of that sum; or I could send it all from here if I had your sanction.” Of course, I suppose, you will require some legal receipt from the AustinsJohn wrote, 7 Dec.: “I heard from Mary that the draining at the Gill is to begin very soon, & sent her my £50 at once. I did not think it necessary to get any legal receipt for the money.” For TC’s £50, see TC to JAC, 8 Jan. 1874. to keep matters exact on the incidents of events which cannot now be distant: decide it altogether by your own judgment, you that are on the spot, and know better.

Except certain foolish and superfluous letters that have come to me, I have nothing to send to you in the shape of new tidings or occurrences. The first letter from the poor Falkirk body contains in it a sheet of cursiv schrift, of which I made out no word except the signature which is that of the Alsatian distracted commentator on Faust,“The Falkirk body” unidentified further; he had sent TC Samuel Moser’s book Goethe’s zweiter Faust, oder der geöffnete Walpurgissack [Goethe’s Faust part 2, with Commentary] (Weissenburg, 1864) in Sept.; see 48:223–24TC to UC, 20 Sept. 1873. He now forwarded him a letter from Moser, dated 18 Oct. from Weissenburg, in the province of Alsace, then in Germany, now Wissembourg in France. and the title, wh. is to indicate his reasons for said distracted commentary;Moser’s letter was headed “Why did Goethe write his second Faust?” followed by a quotation from Goethe’s poem, “Lines on Seeing Schiller’s Skull”: “But to me an adept the script was written, / The sacred meaning was not revealed to everyone” [editor’s translation]. had it been in Roman hand, I should have been a little curious to know what they were and have read the paper; but as you are at least far better qualified for that kind of cursiv than I or Mary, I hand it over to you, who, if you have not, as I rather dread, sufficient interest in the thing to carry you through it, are hereby freely permitted to fling it aside and send it back to me on the chance of somebody coming in who can at once do it without trouble. I have been reading 3 or 4 earnest but feeble and wearisome disquisitions on the 2nd part of Faust by very dull, though eager and vehement people; which and some better things (especially an account of Goethe’s lustige Zeit at Weimar,Johann August Diezmann (1805–69), Goethe und die lustige Zeit in Weimar [Goethe and the Funny Time in Weimar] (Leipzig, 1857); it is quoted in Moser, Goethe’s zweiter Faust 16–17. viz: his history during the first ten years there; wh. I will send you, if you care about them,—but first of all they will require to be bound;John replied, 25 Nov.: “I shall be glad to see the book about Weimar when bound. We could have had it bound here, only part mt have been lost by post.” having in the reading, in spite of the gentlest management gone all into a heap of loose leaves. Of Vigfusson, or of the other IcelanderFor Gudbrand Vigfusson and the “other Icelander,” see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. I have heard nothing farther; but there came one morning to the foot
of the stairs another semi-articulate foreigner, whom, at the loud sound he was making, I went down to meet, and see into: he proved a strange rusty bald headed impetuous looking man called Dr Something; who had come hither from Berlin to give “German Readings”;Berlin doctor and his German readings untraced. & had sent me two tickets; and two importunate fractions of cursiv-schrift, the second of wh. was answered by Mary to the effect, “Cannot come; will send my Niece instead” (which latter also had failed to go); Nay the poor Man himself came down to tell me that he had had no audience whatever; and had given up the enterprise till a better day. “Gut, sehr gut [Good, very good]!” I kept this Dr nearly half an hour talking in broken English eagerly about Goethe, particularly eagerly about his 2nd part of Faust; and really was a singularity to look at and to hear. He spoke loud, but not without a certain ridiculous enthusiasm which kept one on the edge of laughing outright; the rather as he had a pair of large blythe eyes, no hair to speak of on his big broad head, or long bare pillar of a neck; and had taken, generally, a strong resemblance to a strong gigantic goose. He carried away with him Moser’s extraordinary book on Faust; and promised to return it; and to send along with it another commentary in his possession before the week ended, wh. he has not yet done.

Letter 2nd is an answer from him of the House of RimmonAlfred Fleming; see TC to AF, 14 Nov. John wrote, 18 Nov.: “‘In the house of Rimmon,’ by Mr Fleming, was read zealously by us all.” wh. requires only if read at all to be flung into the Wastebasket. No 3. Blackie’sJohn Stuart Blackie; see TC to JSB, 24 Nov. empty indistinct bow-wow refers to a paragraph wh. has got into the Newspapers, destitute of the smallest shadow of foundation, that I was busy writing a Pamphlet on the Pope and Kaiser;The Cork Constitution reported, 8 Nov.: “It is said that Mr. Carlyle is engaged upon a brochure on the struggle now going on between Germany and the Pope.” On 17 Nov. the same paper announced that “The Birmingham Morning News confirms the statement that Mr. Thomas Carlyle (as we recently reported) is writing a pamphlet on the controversy between Emperor and the Pope, a subject in which he takes a profound interest.” For TC on the Pope and Kaiser, see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. letter from some Leipzig publishing House had already come two days ago: I have met with nothing more absurd & baseless in my life. Enough on these absurd subjects. Dizzy’s speech, of which at first I heard from Froude some laudatory account, I got yesterday from Allingham’s Daily Telegraph;The Daily Telegraph, 21 Nov., reported Benjamin Disraeli’s visit to Glasgow, 20 Nov., and his address to a delegation of textile factory workers from Glasgow and Dundee who were seeking a reduction in their hours of labor. Responding to their petition, Disraeli declared: “The elevation of the working classes depends upon two causes: if their wages rise and hours of toil diminish, they are placed in a most favourable position, and if they do not avail themselves of that position they only prove they are unworthy of it. With regard the first point—the financial considerations, with respect to wages—no Legislature can interfere. … The rate of wages must be left to those inexorable principles of political economy to which we all bow. They depend upon demand and supply, and upon the financial circumstances of a country. But when you come to the hours of labour you leave financial considerations, and you enter into social ones. And these a Legislature can interfere with … to the advantage of the country and of the working classes.” & ran through it, with the feeling that I had never
anywhere read a more flimsy piece of cunningly devised Nothingness; and that the man Dizzy was even more a silly fool, intrinsically, than I had before supposed him. The rest of my evening was wasted too on Public Opinion;Public Opinion, a weekly review, 1861–1951. —I find more and more that reading in the Newspapers is little other than a douche of putrid dirty water better to be avoided than gone into.— — We are engaged to dine with Froude and Theodore Martin;Theodore Martin (1816–1909; ODNB), Scottish lawyer, biographer, and translator. whom perhaps you may have heard of; it is at the said Theodore’s earnest desire and I could not well refuse Froude’s evident eagerness. Monday 7¼ is the time; no other company there. Several days before, Henry Taylor, or we should say Sir Henry Taylor, with a brightish stranger lady had alighted on me;Sir Henry Taylor (1800–86; ODNB; see 6:40TC to MAC, 10 Nov. 1831), poet and diplomat, old friend of TC’s, knighted 1869. The “brightish stranger lady” unidentified further. The Taylors were spending the winter in London at 66 Eaton Sq. and brought the imperious demand of a dinner on the Thursday now next coming. The imperious Sir Henry wd take no refusal; his brougham to be at this door punctually at 7¼ p.m; and a young lady in it to see with her eyes whether I was really unable.TC had refused an invitation to visit the Taylors earlier in the year; see 48:163TC to LT, 11 Feb. 1873; Taylor wrote to a friend, 25 Nov.: “I paid Carlyle a visit a few days ago, and I think the account you had of him can scarcely have been correct. I heard nothing but the customary grumble, and when I told him he would have to dine with us on Thursday (the day after to-morrow) he laughed, but made no real resistance, and he is to come accordingly. He does, however, look a little more withered that he did last year” (Correspondence of Henry Taylor, ed. Edward Dowden [1888] 327–28). Taylor’s wife was Theodosia Alice, b. Spring-Rice (1818–91), m. 1839, and they had at least two daughters, Una Taylor and Ida Alice Ashworth Taylor (1847–1929; ODNB), biographer. That also therefore stands before me. In the interval between Froude and Taylor the Duke & Duchess of Argyle, whom I had not seen for nearly 2 years and who were very good and human to me,George Douglas Campbell (1823–1900; ODNB; see 42:16TC to JAC, 11 May 1865), 8th duke of Argyll, m., 1844, Elizabeth Georgiana, b. Sutherland-Leveson-Gower (1824–78). TC had dined with them, 9 Dec. 1870; see 47:119–20TC to DUA, 5 Dec. 1870, and 124–25TC to JAC, 10 Dec. 1870. came in with a third invitation, but this never so sublime I had absolutely to decline.—Alas, alas, the very light is done—I must finish abruptly. I have not written to Jean; indeed I heard she meant to write to me. I can only send my love to her and all of you for this week. Whether the next week, equally idle, will be equally
unproductive even of a readable letter we must not prophecy. Adieu & blessings to you all,

closer.note: The signature has been cut away.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JSB, 24 Nov. MS: NLS 2631.74. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN STUART BLACKIE

docBody.p: There is not, nor ever was, the slightest vestige of foundation for that foolish rumour of my writing about Kaiser Wilhelm and the Pope.Blackie wrote, 21 Nov.: “I am glad to hear you are about to project a thunderbolt. The Pope is a foolish old gentleman; not for his benefit, but for the benefit of those who believe in him, a stroke or two of good flailing, in your style, will be seasonable.” See also TC to JAC, 22 Nov. At no moment in the last half century has the Pope appeared to me other than a scandalous Phantasm, altogether despicable and altogether damnable; awakening in every earnest man only the question, how long, Oh Lord, how long?Cf. Ps. 94:3. till this Father of Hypocricies is thrown out of thy earnest world?

In Bismarck I firmly trust, and indeed have never doubted but this Blasphemous Humbug had found his fit man for dealing with him: so that speech about such a matter was not needful. Let the dead bury their dead.Matt. 8:22.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 29 Nov. MS: NLS 527.102. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:301–2; Wilson, Carlyle 6:305. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I am much obliged by the pains you took in deciphering that foolish MoserA letter from Samuel Moser; see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. John A. Carlyle wrote, 25 Nov.: “I began Moser’s letter, could read the first words easily, began to copy it for you & did not like to yield to the great difficulty of reading the rest of it; & by several hours labour got through the whole of it. … I have almost quite lost the old facility I used to have on reading such German writing.” He sent the copy to TC.
for me. I could not, any more than yourself make out the indecipherable word; but it was of no consequence whatever; the whole paper being utterly dark as to the one subject of curiosity there cd be in it, viz, What on earth or under the earth could have induced poor Moser to adopt that style of interpreting Faust, and even to regard it as a salutary inspiration of Heaven, which had rendered the “half of his life” sublime and memorable among the sons of men. Leave him there to fight his own battle, poor devil. The gigantic Human GooseGerman doctor, unidentified further; see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. has sent me back in safety the Moser treatise with no commentary, except one borrowed from Voltaire that of cutting off the last letter of fin and andWord repeated in error. substituting a note of exclamation which makes it, fitly, fi! Fie upon it then with all our heart. Gigantic Human Goose himself was happily on the invalid list, and troubled me with no farther interview with himself.

In regard to the Lustige Zeit in Weimar and the other German bookFor Die Lustige Zeit in Weimar, see TC to JAC, 22 Nov.; the other German book was probably Karl Rheinhold von Köstlin, Goethe’s Faust (Tubingen, 1860); John wrote, 25 Dec.: “As to the two German books, I have read Die lustige Zeit in Weimar which amused me very much; but have not yet got through Köstlins book on Faust, & dont find it of much use to me. However I will return both to the London Library in due time, & am glad to have seen them.” (of which two pieces only the former is worth much examination from you); We tried this week to have them sent on direct to you unbound; but to be bound at Dumfries; the Library people wd not “continue their refusal if I insisted” but evidently did not like the proposition and engaged to have them bound here ‘immediately’ (i.e. within 10 days). After which you may begin to expect them. I myself have been reading nothing German; merely wandering in mixed mood over Lanfrey,Pierre Lanfrey, Histoire de Napoléon, 5 vols. (Paris, 1867–75). Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821), French soldier and statesman, emperor of France 1804–14. Vol IV and certain other poor Napoleonic matters. Lanfrey’s Book is hard and dry, but not without intelligence brevity and vigour; and says throughout the very worst that can be said of that wonderful man. It is not worth your buying but it might be of your reading; in which case I could probably get it for you here. In Lanfrey Napoleon gradually delineates himself as the nearest approach ever made to Lucifer, called otherwise Satan Salthoun:TC likens Napoleon to Lucifer, the archangel whose desire for power caused his fall from heaven; “Satan Salthound” is TC’s version of “Mahoun,” an old Scots name for the devil, probably originally derived from Mahomet; see 11.45. but I found there were grave omissions in that delineation and that the man was actually human after all. Hardly ever man so strangely situated and so strongly tempted in this world before!—

I am sorry I have nothing to send you this week; even in the form of letters that would be worth their postage. I am told Jean sometimes finds an entertainment
in looking over these fractionary emblems of London life. They cannot to almost any other person be other than dull and worthless. This morning I recd from some dreary gentleman in Kensington a book about Education and Religion[David Kay], Education and Religion: Their Mutual Connection and Relative Bearings (1873). distinguished by being almost all in the form of footnotes and excerpts from nearly every kind of extant authority, good bad and indifferent upon these topics. I think I will send her or you that miserable waly dreg [weakling] of a book with do do letter enclosed; so soon as I have looked at them once more and seen whether any answer or none would be the fitter for the poor soul.—

I got through my Taylor dinner,See TC to JAC, 22 Nov. wh. was very splendid indeed; and was home about 11 at night ready for one glass of Sherry with 2 waters pipe of baccy and 2 hours more of quiet reading. Lady Minto,Emma Eleanor Elizabeth, b. Hislop (d. 1882), countess of Minto, m., 1844, William Hugh Elliot-Murray-Kynynmound (1814–91), 3d earl of Minto, Liberal politician. blooming beautiful Countess was the heroine of the evening; hero or quaisi-hero, Sir John ColeridgeSir John Coleridge; see TC to JAC, 15 Nov.; TC had met him at Forster’s in March; see 48:173TC to JAC, 7 March, and had then remarked on his likeness to his great-uncle Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834; ODNB), poet, whom TC met in 1824; see 3:90–91TC to JAC, 24 June 1824, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 288–89. a tall straight up gentleman, utterly bald and clean washed, whom I had seen before and could again recognise in him, a good deal of the element of Coleridge hum-bug, with abundant parliamentary and advocate faculties. Irish and other ladies, more or less sublime with their respective gentlemen, kept me in plentiful talk.— Altogether unprofitable to me till I got away. Adieu, dear Brother, four ocl’ is striking and Nights wet curtains are swiftly rushing down. My love to Jean & the rest. Blessings be with you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-MMH-S [MMHS], 2 Dec. MS: EUL. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Mary Monica Hope-Scott (1852–1920), only surviving da. of James Robert Hope-Scott (1812–73) and Charlotte Harriet Jane, b. Lockhart (1828–58), and great-grand-da. of Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832; ODNB), poet and novelist. Mary Hope-Scott had inherited Scott’s house, Abbotsford, near Melrose in the Scottish Borders.
bibl.head: TC TO MARY MONICA HOPE-SCOTT

docBody.p:
Will you permit me to intrude upon you,—to whom I have not the honour of being personally known but whose illustrious Forebeers, especially your
Grandfather Lockhart,John Gibson Lockhart (1794–1854; ODNB), writer and editor; he m., 1820, Sophia, b. Scott (1799–1837), Sir Walter Scott’s eldest da.; they had three children, including Charlotte Harriet. TC first met him Jan. 1832 (see 6:101JWC to JCA, [23? January 1832], and Froude, Carlyle 2:233), and they remained friends until Lockhart’s death (see 29:102TC to JCA, 16 May 1854). and his amiable family I did know, and shall remember in love and honour while I live,—to intrude upon you for one moment with a small request, or rather bit of testimony, which seems to be required of me, not on private grounds alone, but in some degree on public too; and which I hope will not be very disagreeable to you.

It seems, Professor Child of Cambridge, New England, a man of very distinguished merits in regard to Scottish Ballad Poetry, who is preparing, with immense diligence, fidelity and use of all his possibilities, a new edition of his excellent Collection,Francis James Child (1825–96; ODNB), American scholar, philologist, and folklorist; he was compiling a definitive collection of English and Scottish ballads, and was requesting information from scholars all over the world for his master work, The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, 5 vols. (Boston, 1882–98). TC had already asked John A. Carlyle for help in contacting sources; see 48:132TC to JAC, 30 Dec. 1872, and 134TC to JAC, 4 Jan. 1873. Child was a neighbor of Charles Eliot Norton, who wrote to TC on the subject, 16 Nov.; see TC to DL, 3 Dec. has applied to you for liberty to get copied, in the Edinburgh Signet Library, two Mss. which are now at Abbotsford; and which are the two documents alone wanting to him now, after the almost endless researches he has been making in regard to this matter.Child already had material from Sir Walter Scott’s Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, 3 vols. (Kelso and Edinburgh, 1802–3), but he knew there were further manuscripts at Abbotsford. To yourself I well understand how precious these two Mss. (one of them in Sir Walter Scott’s own hand) must be: but I have great confidence and pleasure in testifying as Professor Child requires, and adding my clear opinion that there will be no danger in complying with his request.

I entrust this note to Mr. Laing of the Signet Library,David Laing; see TC to DL, 3 Dec. who, I think, must be well acquainted with Mr Child’s great merits and high editorial qualities; and who, I doubt not, will think as I do of Mr Child’s petition to Abbotsford (and, in a sense, to Scotland itself!); and take faithful charge in case of your compliance.
With very many regards and perfect good wishes, I remain always

bibl.sourceNote: TC-DL, 3 Dec. MS: EUL. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO DAVID LAING

docBody.p: There came to me two days ago, from Charles Eliot Norton, a valued new–England friend of mine, a message from Professor Child, who is is [sic] neighbour, in regard to that new Edition of his Scottish Ballads,See TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. which is occupying so much of his attention. Child, it appears, has secured all the documents, aids and evidences he can hear of except two, now at Abbotsford; one of them described as a “Ballad Book, used by Scott in compiling the Border Minstrelsy, and another, a sort of Scrapbook also at Abbotsford, in which it would seem Scott had copied out some ballads he had heard.” Norton continues: “Child wishes much to get exact copies of these Abbotsford Mss.; and has lately written to Miss Hope Scott begging to be permitted to have copies taken, either at the British Museum or at the Library of the Writers to the Signet in Edinburgh. He is afraid that Miss Hope-Scott or her Counsellors may know nothing of his Work, and may turn a deaf ear to his request; and he asked me, as we walked, whether I thought you would be willing to state that he was a respectable character, to some person who might convey your gauranty to the fair demoiselle, to whom fate has brought so many precious possessions.”

I have accordingly written to Miss Hope-Scott to whom I am a perfect stranger; but to whose Grandfather, Grandmother and Mother I was familiarly known, testifying and requesting, as the meritorious Child requires. I am very dim as to all the details about Abbotsford, Child or this interesting young Lady; but I am very anxious that his poor request should be complied with.

It strikes me that you must be already acquainted, better perhaps than myself, with Child’s high editorial merits, and faithful exertions in regard to his new Edition; nay perhaps are in communication with him about this same Abbotsford matter; at all events I commit the little note I have written to your care; and beg you to write the name of the post townThe post town for Abbotsford is Melrose. with your own hand;—and either to write a word along with it or directly after; and in short to help the poor missive and its purport, as you, of all men known to me are best able to do;The preface to Child’s The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, 5 vols. (Boston, 1882–98) notes: “In 1877 Dr David Laing procured, ‘not without difficulty,’ leave to prepare for Mr Child a copy of the single manuscript of ballads then known to remain at Abbotsford. This MS., entitled ‘Scottish Songs,’ was so inconsiderable, in proportion to the accumulations which Sir Walter Scott had made in preparing his Border Minstrelsy, that further search seemed to be imperatively necessary. In 1890 permission to make such a search, and to use the results, was given by the Honorable Mrs Maxwell-Scott” (English and Scottish Popular Ballads 1:xxviii). Mary Monica Hope-Scott m., 1874, Joseph Constable Maxwell-Scott (1847–1923). at any rate please forward the letter at once to where the young lady
is. I reckon it would be a kind of slur upon Scotland, if it did not help, rather than hinder or neglect the Enterprise Child is now upon in favour of a subject so far away from him, and yet so dear to him as well as to Scotland. I found his bookChild’s earlier collection, English and Scottish Ballads, 8 vols. (Boston, 1857–58). full of merits wherever I examined it; and to you, I doubt not, it is far better known and more capable of being judged of.
Somewhat in haste; but with many friendliest regards; and the sure hope, that you will do what you honestly can in this matter, I remain always,
docBody.closer:
dear Laing,
Yours sincerely,
T. Carlyle.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 8 Dec. Addr: Shady Hill / Cambridge / Boston Massachusetts / U.S. AMERICA. PM: London, 8 Dec. 1873. MS: Houghton. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p:
Today I enclose you David Laing’s return-message about the Hope-Scott letter, to put Professor Child into clear understanding as to his outlooks in regard to those two Ballad Mss. he is anxious about. Laing, you will see, retains my poor Note, unable for perhaps 4 months to add the distinct Hope-Scott address, or at all decisively stir in the matter. On Miss Scott’s return ‘from Algiers,’Mary Monica Hope-Scott was currently in Algeria and would not return to Abbotsford until the Spring. about that time he appears to concur with me that there can be no real difficulty put in the way of getting said Mss. copied if Child still wishes it but he seems to testify that in his own opinion it may scarcely be worth while; for proof on this latter point, he refers me to a poor Book called “Illustrated Exhibition-Catalogue for the Scott Centenary” (a noisy more or less nonsensical and hypocritical delirium of a “Centenary” from which I had to keep studiously aloof):The Scott Exhibition. MDCCCLXXI. Catalogue of the Exhibition Held at Edinburgh, in July and August 1871, on Occasion of the Commemoration of the Centenary of the Birth of Sir Walter Scott (Edinburgh, 1872). The exhibition included a copy of Ballads and Lyrical Pieces, which contained ballads “already published in different collections, some in The Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, others in The Tales of Wonder, and some in both these Miscellanies” (Scott Exhibition 126). For TC on the Walter Scott Centenary, see >47:155TC to JAC, 10 Feb. 1871. I had afterwards, in due time, a copy of this Catalogue sent
me; but found it of little or no interest, and I think must have given it away;—at least I cannot now lay hands upon it here; and can only flatter myself that you or Child, if you find it necessary, can probably easily fall in with it in some Boston Library or Bookshop.

With or without that latter help it will be good for Prof. Child to apply at once to Laing with whatever question he may have to ask as to the likelihood of benefit from those Abbotsford Mss.; and so decide on the best evidence attainable whether he will wait for them or not. Laing is an excellent, goodnatured, solid old gentleman, full of Scotch good sense and prudence; and is by far the best informed man now living about all matters of that kind. “David Laing Esq, Signet’s Library Edinburgh”:—but doubtless Child has already been in correspondence with him; nay, Laing himself tells me, missed finding him last Autumn, to L’s regret.Norton replied, 22 Dec.: “Your prompt and serviceable kindness in the matter of the Ballad-Mss. is recognized most gratefully by Child & myself. … He will write to Mr. Laing, with whom he has already had some sort of correspondence.”

“As to the enclosed, written a day or two ago,”Presumably this refers to an enclosure in Laing’s letter connected with the Knox monument; a committee had been set up in Edinburgh to discuss the possible erection of a monument to mark the tercentenary of the death, 24 Nov. 1572, of John Knox (ca. 1514–72; ODNB), religious reformer. all I have to say is, That it refers to the melancholy fiasco of a Monument to John Knox, which I did discern was a true wish all over Scotland, but a thing lost amid the roaring oceans of unwise palaver sure to arise on such an occasion where the least worthy are sure to be heard first (such the length of ear and excellence of windpipe):—and now out of all that, poor Laing and some silent Committee are anxious to realize some reasonable bust or statue of Knox, that if possible the roaring oceans and the braying throats (and the few subscribing pockets) may not have raged for absolutely nothing at all. Upon this he requests a few words from me; and today’s ought not to go without my trying to say something. From the Knox–monument fiasco as from the Scott do I kept absolutely apart till this day.TC had so far refused to get involved; see 48:130TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872, and 139TC to JAC, 8 Jan. 1873. Norton wrote: “I am glad you felt inclined to write some words to further the project of a memorial to John Knox. They will save it from the unreality of feeling which generally is the characteristic of such things.” — —

I return many thanks for your clear and affectionate letter; the reading of which has given real pleasure to me[.] I wish truly, tho’, being myself so dumb a correspondent, I have little right to hope confidently, that you will often write again, and keep me on a level with American tidings and aspects of any
moment; for I do honestly think of America as if it were still a bit of England (or England a bit of it, if you like that better), and all Americans, more especially all good and wise Americans as my born countrymen and brothers. Your own prophecies about that huge country, I perceive, are not very joyful or exstatic more than my own, but I always know of such vast phenomena that the best lies hidden; that on the whole in a garden of such huge extent, were there nothing more, “Time is always pretty certain to bring Roses.”— There has arrived hare a third huge Vol. of Andrew Marvell for you (580 pp. of very thick paper, beautifully printed): it contains altogether the Rehearsal Transposed,The Complete Works in Verse and Prose of Andrew Marvell, ed. A. B. Grosart, 4 vols. (1872–75); vol. 3 (1873) contained The Rehearsal Transpros’d (1672). Rev. Alexander Balloch Grosart (1827–99; ODNB), literary scholar and theologian; vol. 1 was dedicated to TC: “By express permission and ‘all good wishes’” (Complete Works 1:iii). Norton replied: “The big volume of Marvell that you so kindly promise me will be very welcome whenever it may come. But I am in no haste for it.” both parts of that and nothing more, except feeble notes; if you are in any haste about it, tell me so, and I will at once find some safe conveyance; if you are in none, it may wait until some turn up.
With many kind regards and affectionate good wishes to all the Shady Hill inmates, including little SallySara, Norton’s eldest da.; see TC to CEN, 3 Nov. and her violin I remain

bibl.sourceNote: TC-MS, 8 Dec. Pbd: Mary Smith, The Autobiography of Mary Smith, Schoolmistress and Nonconformist (1892) 316–17. Mary Smith (1822–89; ODNB), schoolmistress and radical.
bibl.head: TC TO MARY SMITH

docBody.p: I well enough remember the transient shadow of fine relation which you once had in this household;Smith had corresponded with JWC between Jan. 1854 (see 29:20–21JWC to MS, 16 Jan. 1854) and April 1865 (see 41:205–6JWC to MS, 10 April [1865]); they had also met once or twice in Carlisle; 41:205. and in a mournful changed condition must always have; nor do you miscalculate the value I put upon it, or the feeling it awakens in me.

In looking over your bookMary Smith, Progress, and Other Poems; the Latter Including Poems on the Social Affections and Poems on Life and Labour (1873). Smith later wrote that the collection “in some measure came from my reading Emerson, together with my study of history” (Autobiography 1:284). I am well pleased to find, what is rare in books, a perfect sincerity and worthiness of purpose; and I can easily believe that
those clear utterances of your convictions and emotions about social and domestic matters may benefit many serious readers, now and in years coming. The question has sometimes arisen with me whether if you wrote down your ideas and feelings in simple and distinct prose, it might not be still better for your readers and yourself. This is a question I cannot pretend to decide; but my guess, if your circumstances suited and your inclinations prompted, would be clearly as above.

As to “Progress,” about which there has been such chanting and trumpeting for the last half century, especially for the last score of years, I confess I could never see much in it, or decidedly discern any progress except in Smithwork and its adjuncts;The industrial revolution; cf. “Signs of the Times,” Critical and Miscellaneous Essays, Carlyle, Works 27:56–82. —a very sooty, shrieky, and to me contemptible kind of progress,—yielding, as I often say, immensities of gold to those who least of all deserve it among us; and who can do, when one reflects upon it, nothing but mischief by being thus made kings among their fellows.

For the rest, I quite agree with you. All, or almost all the “Progress” in Smithwork and gold nuggets, is due to the Puritan ages; a fact which, on contrasting their moralities with our so miraculous smitheries, is a very melancholy one.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 Dec. MS: NLS 527.103. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:304. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
You answered GeikieArchibald Geikie (1835–1924; ODNB), geologist and historian. John A. Carlyle wrote, 7 Dec.: “I enclose these notes from Professor Geikie. … Burn them after having looked at them.” with great propriety in regard to his requests about Jamieson.Robert Jameson (1774–1854; ODNB), geologist and natural historian, regius prof. of natural history at the Univ. of Edinburgh 1804–54, from whom TC took classes 1812–13 (see Wilson, Carlyle 1:87), and again 1818–19 (see 1:149–50TC to RM, 27 Nov. 1818, and 162TC to RM, 15 Feb. 1819). By no means could I have given him anything suitable or useful about that worthy and industrious but dull individual whom I remember with a kind of sympathy and even gratitude to this day; though his mode of
lecturing was barren and awkward beyond most.Geikie had visited TC, March 1870 (see 46:181TC to JAC, 25 March 1870), when TC talked at some length about his memories of Jameson; Geikie reported: “He laughed when he gave us some of his reminiscences of the lectures of Robert Jameson, the Professor of Natural History at the University. He said that Jameson had never done him any good, had no power of interesting him in the subject, and rambled so widely from one topic to another that it was hardly possible to follow him. … Jameson was probably somewhat dry as a lecturer. … [B]ut he certainly had the merit of inspiring some of his pupils … with a love of natural science” (Archibald Geikie, A Long Life’s Work: An Autobiography [1924] 133). I daresay you yourself remember the awkward beck he used to make, holding his hand on the belly of his gown; and looking so helpless as he handed some specimen to be sent round; nay I think it was you that first noticed and pointed out as a risibility, that curious gesture of his. I remember too his large mournful eyes, thrown up towards the ceiling as he spoke; the mournful metallic voice,—in general the bashfulness, seriousness and intrinsic solitary dignity of the man; who did a great deal of work too in his day; and first brought the hide-bound Edinburgh Plutonists to know that there were real German Mineralogists, withal.Jameson had studied at Freiberg, and encouraged TC to study German in order to translate treatises on mining and geology. He introduced TC to the “Neptunist” theory of Abraham Gottlob Werner (1749–1817), who argued that rocks were all formed as deposits from the primeval ocean covering the earth, as distinct from the “Plutonist” theory that certain rocks came from the layer of molten rock under the earth’s surface. For the rest I could learn really next to nothing from him or from them; nor has there yet almost anything of what I could call truly useful light arisen for me, out of that province of things. Darwin & Co’s hypothesis that I was once an oyster or an ape,See TC to CEN, 3 Nov. For JWC’s outrage at being told she was descended from an oyster, see 36:53JWC to MR, [28 Jan. 1860]. and that Almighty God is merely Caloric does not seem a useful result!—

The obliging Laing almost directly answered my request in the Abbotsford Matter; but unfortunately on enquiring into Miss Hope-Scott’s present address he found that she was off to Algieria for the winter and would not be back for 4 or 3 months; so that till that date, he keeps my Note lying ready for her; and in the meanwhile apprizes me that he has seen the 2 Mss in question; and judges that there is little or nothing in them. This letter of his I forwarded yesterday to Norton that he might read it to Child and bid him be patient and, in the meantime, write freely if he liked to Laing,—whom he missed last Autumn on calling, to Laing’s regret. And so that matter stands, concluded for the present.

But along with this came another letter which I now enclose to you (not worth returning), wh. touches on another matter, namely, the Knox Monument,Presumably the enclosure in Laing’s letter mentioned by TC to Norton; see TC to CEN, 8 Dec. —by no means so easy to conclude! Upon that matter I have been thinking ever since;
and I imagined to myself yesterday I had at length found out a feasible kind of solution; and meant clearly to write to Laing today explaining myself with due emphasis on the affair: but, alas, I last night lost most of my sleep; and feel so stupid bewildered and foredone that I must fairly put it off till tomorrow. My plan was to have a bronze statue of Knox, which could be got, I believe, moderately true to the actual physiognomy and figure by good sculpture and good and faithful inquiry into that old traditionary portrait now at TorphichenAt this time TC was confused about the naming of the various Knox portraits; see TC to DL, 30 Dec. The epithet “Torphichen” appears to have become attached to the “Somerville” portrait, which TC believed to be the true likeness; the actual Torphichen portrait he believed to be a copy of the portrait in Theodore Beza (1519–1605), French theologian and scholar, Icones (Geneva, 1580); see 48:126–131TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872, and Carlyle, Works 30:330 and 360. The Torphichen portrait belonged to James Walter Sandilands, 12th Lord Torphichen, living at Calder House, Torphichen, Midlothian. For reproductions of the Beza, Torphichen, and Somerville portraits, see 48:127–29TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872. (the only likeness of Knox I ever could for a moment believe in); and for a place to put it in I thought the fit one might be on a pedestal in the centre of the College Square;TC probably means the quadrangle in Old College, Univ. of Edinburgh. A statue of John Knox, by John Hutchison RSA (1832–1910), was finally raised in New College quadrangle, 1896. mutely proclaiming in this way, “The newest Spiritualism of Scotland still understands this to be, in many, and these the most important, senses, its Typical Scotsman; worthy to rank among the truest, noblest and bravest we ever bred; and a benefactor to Scotland, such as few ever were.” This would be my notion about the statue; and I think if it could be rightly done, so as actually to resemble Knox, as near say as Shakespear’s Statues do S. (wh., by wise and strenuous guiding seems to me possible), it would fulfil what could well be required in that respect: all of reality, riddled clear of falsity and humbug (which are unsuitable to Knox, as they hardly ever were to any other man)—all of reality that can now be done by mankind after the 300 sad years of confusion and neglect.

Another bit of reality and certainty connected with Knox is that of his dwelling house at the head of the Cannongate;John Knox House, Canongate, Edinburgh. The house was built in the late 15th century; there is some doubt as to whether Knox actually lived there, as he apparently lived nearby in the Manse in Warriston Close, 1560–66. which I remember well in its old ragged and sternly impressive condition; but which I have never seen in its new and improved form. With this also, if there were funds remaining after the bronze statue, something might perhaps be done,—a repository for authentic Knox remains (original editions of his books), documents on the History of the Reformation &c &c; but this is comparatively a minor matter. I wonder who at present is the Proprietor of that Knox House?The building was restored in the mid-19th century, and opened as a museum in 1853, managed by the Free Church of Scotland; it now belongs to the Church of Scotland. It ought to
be at least the Town Council of Edinburgh, properly the City of Edinburgh, or even the whole of Scotland or some altogether immoveable entity!— This is mainly what I had to say to Laing, and instead I have said it first to you.

Nay in my present humour I dont see how to get it ever said to Laing; for of course he must mean that it shall be made public as possible; that is to say printed in the Newspapers,—which you know how much I scunner at. But we will wait till tomorrow at any rate; perhaps it will then look less impossible.— — Alas, alas, here has been a flight of Thackery ladies and others;Presumably Anne Thackeray (1837–1919; ODNB) and Harriet “Minny” Stephen, b. Thackeray (1840–75; ODNB); other ladies unidentified. beyond expression unfurthersome to me. I will end I will end. With my blessings on you all, sad and sincere.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-DL, 10 Dec. MS: EUL. Pbd: Wilson, Carlyle 6:315–16 inc; Scotsman, 6 June 1932 inc. Quot: Marinell Ash, “David Laing and Carlyle,” Carlyle Newsletter 4 (1983) 29. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. The Scotsman incorrectly attributes part of this letter to Laing.
bibl.head: TC TO DAVID LAING

docBody.p: Many thanks for your prompt attention to the Abbotsford matter.See TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. Please keep the Note till the young Lady becomes accessible: I at once forwarded your letter to Child’s neighbour;Charles Eliot Norton. my impression is, that Child will still demand a correct Copy on Miss Hope-Scott’s return; you can, therefore, be thinking of some proper Copyist, and be at once ready for him when the time comes. But, no doubt, he will himself write to you long before that.— As to the Knox monument affair I have been much thinking of it ever since you wrote; I am right well pleased to hear that you determine to start again from that ruinous downbreak;—and the following is mainly what I have to say upon it.

It has always been evident to me that there could be no cause of failure in the Enterprize of a Monument to Knox, but the want of a rational proposal of what is to be set up in honour of him. Fix upon something that would represent in any way moderately true, modest and feasible the real relation of Scotland at thisWord repeated in error. time to John Knox, now three centuries distant from us, and I have not the least doubt but all Scotland would respond with alacrity, ready to
accept and help, and that money, in particular, to any fit amount from Scotsmen here and in all parts of the world would come in.In Dec. 1872 a committee had been formed to look into the erection of a memorial in Edinburgh to celebrate the tercentenary of Knox’s death, and had decided to raise money first and then decide what to do with it; see 48:130TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872. At a further meeting, 26 Feb., it was reported that almost £2000 had been pledged, and a statue agreed on, but since then nothing had happened. At a meeting, 8 Dec., Laing moved: “1. That the committee limit their object to obtaining a marble statue of John Knox for Edinburgh, to be placed in a public building, whether Church, or gallery, or hall, as may be afterwards found most eligible; and, should the funds at their disposal be sufficient, with an ornamental pedestal of appropriate designs as sculptured basso-relievos. 2. That artists be now invited to prepare for public competition. … 3. That these resolutions in the meanwhile be submitted for approval to parties who have already become subscribers to the Knox Memorial. 4. That the promised subscriptions be now paid” (Scotsman, 10 Dec. 1873). With a foolish, untrue or impracticable plan; still more as we have seen, with no definite plan at all, it has naturally been different. In the case of Knox,—the figure of whose existence both outward and spiritual has grown so dim to us, and in whom all of us know mainly, that there was no compatability with lies; and that to him of all men, anything of falsity, bombast or (half-involuntary) hypocrisy in short would be the most unsuitable,—the question What to propose is unusually difficult. Truth, distinctness, simplicity, these are the qualities that would be most available in the answer given.

Like yourself I am clear for a Statue as the thing to be tried for at this stage of the business. If there is any actual likeness of the person of Knox procurable and ascertainable, the very dictate of Nature herself is for a bronze or marble statue, faithfully modelled from the same. The first question therefore is, Does there such a likeness of Knox exist? My own poor notion is, as you know, that there does: in that traditional Portrait at Torphichen, an excellent Engraving of which has been many years beside me. In no other portrait Icon or Image of Knox is there the least of a physiognomy that I can believe to be Knox. The Icon in your own 6th vol (Works of Knox)Laing had included an image of Beza’s woodcut of Knox in The Works of John Knox, ed. David Laing (Edinburgh, 1846–64) 6:xiii. has a mouth and chin (could one see them for the beard) which seem to resemble; in hardly any other is a feature that I can imagine to have belonged to him. The excellent Wilkie’s imaginary PortraitSir David Wilkie (1785–1841; ODNB), “John Knox Preaching Before the Lords of the Congregation, 10th June 1559,” oil painting on wood. of him is beyond all others disgusting to me; and wide away from any shadow of conceivability to anybody who has gained a knowledge of Knox. You have warned me more than once that this Torphichen Portrait has externally nothing for it but traditionary evidence; and I think you said even this had never been investigated to the bottom. Such investigation with the aid of wise Artists Sculptors &c ought to be now gone
into; and I do trust that the evidence for it (constant tradition, namely) is as good as what there is for any other Portrait. Physiognomic evidence has long appeared to me to be complete; every lineament is Scotch, and expresses in my opinion, with singular completeness the wiry vigour, the perfect veracity, the loving earnestness, modesty and yet long-suffering contempt which dwelt in the grand soul of Knox. An excellent statue might be modelled from it; the Geneva Gown would be drapery to the ancles (stature and general make of body I suppose is known to you):—in short I could expect from a well-chosen Sculptor, preceded by rigorous enquiry all round, an altogether venerable interesting and even credible statue. As credible for instance as the Shakespeare statues now accepted among us;—to me, on the mere physiognomic basis, much more credible than any of these. The statue, I am clear, should be in bronze, in a simple preaching attitude as the picture has it with the venerable head bare, and almost no gesticulation; only attitude and face denoting what depths of earnestness there is. I would gladly have the old big Bible introduced too; but the kind of pulpit or stand that would be necessary for that might probably be vetoed by the Sculptor.

The one site I can think of as at all suitable would be the centre of the College Square on a pedestal of Scotch whinstone or most enduring rock; far away from the sorry populace of statues, which Edinburgh too much swarms with already. There in the centre of its University it might seem to speak what in truth will be for ever profitable to all Scotchmen; and Scotland might seem to answer, through many generations, “Yes, the newest spiritualism of Scotland still reverently recognises in you its spiritual Father (changing only in the garment of your intellect, but in the essence of it clear and eternal); and for certain one of the Noblest Sons Scotland ever had; and at this hour her benefactor beyond all others that could be named.

There is one other actuality still connected with Knox: the old house he lived in at the Head of the Cannongate. It used to be extremely venerable to me. I have never seen it in its new shape; but have sometimes asked myself, Is that settled on a true footing? Who is Proprietor and Director of it just now? Could not something of a Knox Museum (or the like for old editions of Knox’s books &c &c) be made of it? But all this is of course of a very minor importance; and indeed of none at all, till the other is finished. Go ahead then, dear Laing with all your strength, and all your loyalty of soul; none wishes you more heartily goodspeed than I.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 20 Dec. MS: NLS 527.104. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I have nothing particular to tell you either of good news or bad; but will write a word by way of testifying that fact more distinctly before the week end. We have excellent Decr weather; the mildest and best I almost ever saw at such a season; and if the poor Digestive Apparatus could be persuaded (which it can’t) to behave with any propriety at all, I might follow my idle existence reading all day, without any special complaint.

I got Laing’s Letter some days ago, and enclose it here. It contains nothing; merely indicates in one short sentence that apparently he means to go on with the Bronze-Knox project, which it was rather welcome to me to hear. I had written to him quite to the effect you already heard; and was a little dubious whether he would catch at it: it is very uncertain to me still whether they can with any success accomplish the thing I had in view; but if they cannot, I see nothing else worth attempting, and must own to myself that poor Scotland is absolutely without the power to honour its Foremost Man and itself with any memorial of a not unworthy character. We shall see, we shall see.

Ruskin has been here several times since I wrote. He looks lean but ardent, vehement; and is very talkative and speculative. The first time we met, he had come from Oxford expressly to see Hunt’s picture the “Shadow of Death.”William Holman Hunt (1827–1910; ODNB), “The Shadow of Death” (1870–73). He staid with Froude with whom he had appointed to go next day; and I volunteered to accompany.
