The Picture seemed to us all three an absolute failure; to Ruskin, who has a high value for Hunt,Hunt was one of Ruskin’s protégés. a quite lamentable proof of the blind delusions a gifted painter could be led into by a noisy deluded world, and its pruriencies and cants; to Froude the poor Christ, a feckless looking, long eel of a creature seemed as if he had been the “Handsome Man” selected from some minor Theatre: in short I believe the thing to be condemned by all people of any senseAugustus John Cuthbert Hare (1834–1903; ODNB), author, visiting TC soon after he had seen the picture, reported TC saying it was “the most unnatural thing that ever was painted, and the most unnatural thing in it the idea that the Virgin should be keeping her ‘preciosities’ in the carpenter’s shop” (Augustus Hare, The Story of My Life [1900] 4:155). TC apparently first met Hare earlier in the year; see 48:212TC to LA, 6 July 1873. though there go to it 1500 visitors a day; and he has sold it, one hears, for £15,000.

Poor Forster has been prisoner in the house for many weeks,Forster suffered from a chronic severe cough; see TC to CEN, 3 Nov. in spite of the altogether genial weather, sometimes altogether bright and sunny and generally
with a temperature generally above 50°: he dare not venture out, he declares, lest he should get lamed altogether, and be cut off from finishing his Dickens.Forster’s The Life of Charles Dickens, 3 vols. (1872–74); the Athenaeum advertised, 10 Jan. 1874: “Completion of Forster’s Life of Dickens. / On the 29th of January will be published, with portrait and illustrations, / The Life of Charles Dickens. / By John Forster. / Vol. III. 1852–1870.” I was astonished to hear yesterday that he has it actually within 2 chapters of the end; he has written it all truly in tormentis, as King Friedrich Wilhelm used to paint, Fredericus Wilhelmus in tormentis pinxit.Friedrich Wilhelm (1688–1740), king of Prussia 1713–40, father of Frederick the Great; he suffered from gout, and when in pain and unable to sleep would paint, mainly portraits, and sign them thus; see Frederick, Carlyle, Works 13:141. — Froude is over head and ears in his Irish vol;Froude’s The English in Ireland in the Eighteenth Century, 3 vols. (1872–74); vols. 2 and 3 were pbd. April 1874. greatly ardent on the subject; and has sent the half of it sometime ago to the printer. He comes oftener than any other person to walk with me, but does not often get eloquent except on this topic of his own. I have seen Tennyson, with his two boys,Tennyson’s sons were Hallam and Lionel. this week; and, day before yesterday, Mrs TennysonEmily Sarah Tennyson. called, who is very weak and old looking but full of innocent eagerness and I believe ardour in smoothing down all asperities from her Alfred’s sublime career; writes all his letters for him &c &c. I ought to call thereWhen the Tennysons were in London they shared a house at 4 Seamore Place with Lady Jane Franklin, b. Griffin (1792–1875; ODNB), traveler and explorer, widow of Sir John Franklin (1786–1847; ODNB), Arctic explorer, who was Emily Tennyson’s uncle. Emily noted in her journal, 28 Oct.: “We took up our abode at Seamore Place in the house we shared with Lady Franklin, and A. likes it the best of any house we have had in London” (Hallam Tennyson, Alfred Lord Tennyson, A Memoir, 2 vols. [1897] 2:151). In a later undated entry she wrote: “The boys walked with him to call on Mr Carlyle, who thought that we were to be ruined by a ‘government of party, headed by a gentleman Jew who sits at the top of chaos.’ However he preferred Disraeli to Gladstone. Mr Carlyle called upon me, and was very interesting and touching about old days, and was afraid of tiring me by over-talking” (Alfred Lord Tennyson, A Memoir 2:152). this very day, and will, never having done it before; & they go, it seems, on Monday morning. Poor souls after all.Coterie speech. Poor Allingham has a mighty scheme in him of renting a small house instead of lodging, as hitherto; but it may be doubted whether he will actually accomplish it;—being a man of many Bedenklichkeiten (anxieties).

n.p.TC inserted “n.p.” to indicate a new paragraph. I hope you like your two German Books,See TC to JAC, 29 Nov. or rather I only hope about one of them. The criticisms on Faust have to me been, one and all, fairly rather intolerable, and I have now got another by Dünzer;Probably Johann Heinrich Joseph Düntzer (1813–1901), Goethe’s Faust, 2 vols. (Leipzig, 1850–51). which with its
bad print, and wire-drawn janner is almost unendurable and shall be my last adventure in that kind.

This sheet is ending, dear Brother; and I must not go into a second. Write me the first hour you feel disposed; at the greater length (you know always), the better. Did I ever thank Jean for my excellent hareskin bosom friend,Jean Aitken sent him a hareskin vest each winter; see 46:124TC to JAC, 2 Dec. 1869. & night caps? I almost fear not; but feel them to be excellent properties, not the less. Adieu, my blessings on you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-DL, 30 Dec. MS: EUL. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO DAVID LAING

docBody.p: I suppose you to be very busy with the “preliminary arrangements” about Knox,See TC to DL, 10 Dec. —which will naturally be many and intricate and require much serious consideration and manipulation;—in which I by no means wish to hurry you, though I am very often thinking of you and them and really feel interested and eagerly wishful about them.

Ever since your answer came I have been consulting and considering about your possibilities of finding a real and credible above all things a veritable and actual likeness of Knox;—which I doubt not you agree with me is the first and inexorably necessary step before issuing your proposals at all or again appealing to the public on that subject. The more I think and enquire, the more am I driven and drawn towards that “Torphichen Portrait” (as we called it), as with the intimation “Here or else nowhere!” Permit me two or three words more on that subject, not answering unless you like, or till you are ready.

In the first place I cannot find, unless it were you that taught me, where I got the epithet ‘Torphichen’ as attached to it: No where hitherto have I met with an Engraving of it except in Knight’s Pictorial History (Vol II p. 748);See TC to JAC, 9 Dec.; the portrait that TC believed to be a true likeness, engraved by Benjamin Holl, was the Somerville portrait. TC noted in “The Portraits of John Knox” (1875) that he had first seen it in Charles Knight’s publication of George L. Craik and Charles MacFarlane, The Pictorial History of England (1849) 2:opp. 548; see 48:131TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872. TC has here mistaken the page reference. which
refers to it as from a picture “in the possession of Lord Somerville,”At the time of the publication of Knight’s book the Lord Somerville was Admiral Kenelm Somerville (1787–1864), 16th Lord Somerville; after the death of Aubrey John Somerville (1838–70), 18th Lord Somerville, the title became extinct. not Torphichen at all!— But at this point, my Niece, who is now writing for me, testifies that there is at Dumfries an Engraving identical with my own, which is considerably superior in finish and distinctness to Knight’s and which bears legibly the reference Torphichen (slit away from mine by the careless framemaker). So that I am driven to suppose there are two pictures, an original and a copy, of which certainly Torphichen is more likely to have the original than Somerville, who I think continued Catholic through Knox’s time.The Lord Somerville in Knox’s time was James (ca. 1519–69), 5th Lord Somerville, who remained a Catholic, although his father, Hugh (ca. 1484–1549; ODNB), 4th Lord Somerville, had been Protestant. Accurate and strict investigation therefore ought to be held at Torphichen a correct Photograph taken and copies given about, the best artistic opinions got upon it; in a word, a verdict about it the best attainable as the preliminary of all. I have shown it here to persons of judgment who uniformly pronounce it excellent and probable,—especially one painter of great insightUnidentified. and quickness of feeling seemed quite in love with the face and sanguine about its capability about a Statue;—but he has no knowledge about the History of Art and the dating of pictures, and the counsel of such a one, or of more than one, is a plainly necessary preliminary. In short there ought to be an altogether serious and quasi-judicial enquiry made into this picture; and if the verdict falls out any way decisively no - I really do not at present see what farther is to be done. I find in the only Granger which I have access to (a Granger in 40 or more voll.)James Granger (1723–76; ODNB), English cleric, biographer and print collector; his A Biographical History of England, from Egbert the Great to the Revolution, 2 vols. (1769), was a collection of portraits with short memoirs of each person; by the 5th edn. (1824) it had reached 6 vols. (see 44:31TC to LASM, 6 Aug. 1866), and continued to be so successful that later editions, added to by other contributors, were expanded to fill many volumes, and the epithet “Grangerization” was coined to describe the process; Forster owned several editions, which TC had previously consulted; see 46:121TC to JF, 29 Nov. 1869. only 2 portraits of Knox a mere couple of those Icones which are worth nothing; And indeed seem to me flatly incredible which is worse than nothing. In LodgeEdmund Lodge (1756–1839; ODNB), biographer and historian, Portraits of Illustrious Personages of Great Britain, 40 vols. (1814–34). again I find besides the scraggiest Biography of Knox, only an altogether feeble figure said to be from a picture in Glasgow University most probably known to you, which to me had the air of a possibly real drawing from Knox, but by a totally incompetent hand, under which it had turned out, like the others, a mere zero; a poor empty profile without character, almost without expression
of any kind,—as if it had only eaten its victuals while here. This is all the length I have yet got in all my poor attempt at enquiry. And this is all I will say to you at present. I need not repeat what becomes more and more evident to myself That unless we can produce a fairly credible (and as far as we can search) and actually veritable likeness of Knox, it will be unworthy of every true lover of Knox to propose to his fellow Scotsmen any statue at all,—the venerable original being of all Scottish or other men the very truest and least compatible with any shade of unveracity in thought, word, or deed!
Dont bother yourself writing a word of answer, dear Laing; only be busy with your best strength (as I am persuaded you are) in pushing on this really good Enterprize.

I forgot to add in reference to the Torphichen picture, that, in strict comparison with those Icones,See TC to JAC, 9 Dec. wh. we know too well, I find in some of them a faint similarity in the expression of the mouth and chin, and, withal, on very strict inspection a similar kind of nose in the Torphichen; that is to say a longish nose with a rise in the middle, beautifully brought in and visible only from the side; not prominent and vulgar as in that stupid Icon kind.
docBody.closer:
Believe me always, / dear Laing,
Yours heartily, / T. Carlyle

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 Jan. MS: NLS 528.1. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:303–5; Wilson, Carlyle 6:317. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature in blue pencil.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: On Saturday last I intended to write to you what no-news we had; another day too I was disappointed of the same purpose by some intrusion or other; nor am I tempted today by the braw Newyears’ card which has come to me (wh. you may give to Annie,Their niece Anne Aitken. if you like), to wish you the compliments of the season,—compliments of the season alas, alas; and the wish of many happy new years is sadly inapplicable to poor fellows like us! But I had a little thing which I wished to speak to you more about, and have half an hour at my disposal for that and the other objects of a note.

There have several bits of Books come to me, of which I wanted to say a word. First there came one from Edmonstone and Douglas,Edmonston & Douglas, Edinburgh publishers who pbd. TC’s Inaugural Address (Edinburgh, 1866); see 43:165TC to JWC, [5 and 8 April 1866], and 195TC to JAC, 16 April 1866. a very singular
rhapsody of a thing entitled “Business,”Business. By a Merchant (Edinburgh, 1873). The work was described in the Westminster Review: “It is a book written for people who want something to read, and have plenty of time to read it in. It is quaint in its style and materials. … It is full of short poetical quotations, classical and mythological allusions, and fanciful images and metaphors” (Westminster Review 45 [April 1874]: 541). It includes a few brief references to some of TC’s works. of which, if he did not send you a copy too, I think you might accept a perusal,—and shall have it by speaking a word. The Book is by a very singular fellow,John A. Carlyle wrote, 26 Jan.: “The author of the Book on Business, consisting chiefly of quotations, is a Frank Carr [1834–94], merchant, of Newcastle.” Carr also wrote novels and poetry, often under the pseudonym Lancelot Cross. of whom one would like to know some little thing as to his whereabout and figure, though as to the Book itself and any instruction deriveable from it there is nothing to be said but, “Passae, passae, Oh strange, strange!”— A second Book entitled Drummond of Hawthornden came from MassonDavid Masson, Drummond of Hawthornden: The Story of His Life and Writings (1873). William Drummond (1585–1649; ODNB), Scottish poet and laird of Hawthornden, nr. Edinburgh. about a week ago, which I read diligently and generally with great pleasure and approval. If you haven’t got a copy tell me and I will send you this, for you are pretty sure to like it. It is successfully for Scotland and Drummond what M.’s other huge Book should have been for Milton and England;Masson, The Life of John Milton: Narrated in Connexion with the Political, Ecclesiastical, and Literary History of his Time, 7 vols. (1859–81). He pbd. the first vol. in 1859, but had apparently laid it aside while busy with other books and his teaching. TC wrote to Masson (letter untraced), to which Masson replied, 9 Jan.: “You may guess what pleasure your kind & generous letter brought me. It was as welcome a new year’s gift as I could have received; and I return you my very best thanks. / All you have said, and now repeat, about the conduct of what remains of the Milton book, has sunk, is sinking, and will sink, into my mind, and is sure to have effect.” He completed the work, with a revised 1st vol., in 1881. but now, alas, neither is nor can be. It is full of excellent correct information about Scotland in Drummond’s time, and with successful skill, very considerable indeed, plants Drummond sitting observant in the middle of it, not bearing it all on his back, as poor Milton has to do.— I am reading various other books in a desultory manner, such unhappily is all my poor done out existence permits me to do. I will say nothing farther about these on the present occasion.

The two Canada Letters came duly and were worth reading, particularly our poor faithful Alick’sTheir brother Alexander. , whom one is touched to see wending calmly and lovingly to the last down the road we have all to go, each in his several mood, and with his peculiar burdens. Son James’s is as you say a little of the Gill-ha order;Alexander’s son James, apparently living in a primitive or solitary place; see 24:223TC to JAC, 5 Sept. 1849. loneliness, and rubbish all round, the principal scope of it: but we can calculate, withal, the fellow will rally to his tools before long, and by
degrees make something of a Cosmos of what is now so dreary a chaos (Enter Lecky and Mrs,William Edward Hartpole and Catherine Elizabeth Lecky. who sublimely kept me for near an hour!) But indeed the main thing I had in view today was the Letter from Laing, which I here enclose. Ever since you heard last from me, I have been much occupied with the thought of a public statue of Knox; and especially with enquiries among any sculptural or pictorial people I have had access to about the possibilities of getting a real Likeness of him and converting it into a bronze figure of real excellence. This seems to me the one difficulty in the matter; all other difficulties I consider to be easily superable. For I take them to consist essentially in the matter of money only, and I cannot for a moment believe that Scotland, to whom it is a positive disgrace to have no monument to Knox, would, if properly applied to, withhold an abundance of money at least. Since Laing’s last letter I wrote him a second, recording what researches I had made as to that Torphichen portrait, and the considerable approach to complete conviction or persuasion that here was the actual point to begin, viz: that a thorough enquiry by Experts in Scot. History and in pictorial antiquities
should be made into this picture; that photographs should be taken of it, &c &c; and that in short, if a reasonab[l]e conviction in the affirmative were once attained, the question should be put emphatically to all Scotland. Will you help us to make this into a suitable bronze Of the answer, as already said, I have no doubt myself. But today according to Laing’s letter just arrived I find he has no faith whatever;—which has much disappointed me. I will write no more to Laing; at least till he has done with his “Monument in the North Aisle,Laing did not achieve such a monument, but he did get a plate put in Parliament Square at the approximate site of Knox’s grave, inscribed “I. K. / 1572.” See opp. A statue of Knox by Pittendrigh MacGillivray RSA (1856–1938; ODNB) was eventually placed inside St. Giles Cathedral, 1906. See also TC to JAC, 9 Dec. 1873. ”—which in itself shall be quite welcome to me as a fit contribution, but an utterly fractional one to the thing wanted.

figure.p:
John Knox Gravestone, Parliament Square, Edinburgh
Courtesy of Jane Roberts

docBody.p:
In fact I have considerably set my heart on seeing a real Monument set up to Knox, as probably the last thing I shall meddle with in this world; and I wont yet give it up, though Laing has failed. Twenty years younger I would have placed myself in the front and on the top of it; but, alas, at present all I can do is to give my poor £50 or £100 to it, to summon & invite competent persons to consider my proposal and fulfil it, if they can. Tomorrow or next day I mean to write to Masson on the subject,The following day TC changed his mind and decided not to write to Masson on the subject; see TC to JAC, 9 Jan. asking him to request perusal of my two letters to Laing; and after that to consider and consult with all the likeliest Edinr people he can think of. After which, to report candidly to me. Had you been in Edinburgh I should have much solicited your help; but of course at such a distance you can do, I fear, little or nothing.John A. Carlyle had been in Edinburgh when the first meetings took place, Dec. 1872; see 48:130TC to JAC, 27 Dec. 1872. He replied, 4 Jan.: “I was in Edinburgh when the great meetings took place for discussion of the subject, & they were all of the most frantic & disorderly kind, chiefly characterised by ignorant zeal, wild sectarianism & ignorance of all common sense. … [At the] second meeting the most delirious things were proposed, such as raising a Memorial Column as high as Salisbury Craigs or Arthur’s Seat. And I dont think any man in his right senses would consent to be chairman of another Edinr public meeting of the sort. But if one could quietly obtain permission to place the bronze statue you speak of in the College Square … I think money enough might be collected to pay the cost.” Arthur’s Seat is an extinct volcanic hill in Edinburgh, about 820 ft. (250.5 m.) high, Salisbury Crags are cliffs around the hill, about 150 ft. (46 m.) high. One thing I think of: you might transcribe what I wrote to yourself (part of the last letter you had reporting what I meant to say to Laing) transcribe this and send it off to Stirling-Maxwell of KierSir William Stirling Maxwell, living at Keir, 3 mi. (5 km.) NW of Stirling. He was a noted collector of books and prints, especially of portraits; see 46:177TC to WSM, 24 March 1870. with any observations you might choose to add; and especially with the serious request that he would maturely consider it, and ask himself the practical question, “Is the project a likely one, and will you appear as the Head-Committee
man at the top of it” This, I think, would really be helpful; and if Stirling say yes I will engage to stand by him so far as I have any feet left; nay, I think, if he and I both said yes with the proper emphasis the thing would veritably take effect, and that particular “disgrace to Scotland” be at an end. Of course if he liked, Laing would shew him farther the two letters I have written, and put him fully aware of what my poor theory is; and what the dull and stupid facts of the case are. Tell him that I very much request his wisest and noblest opinion on the business; and shall take it the most important light I can have for my own conduct in regard to going farther or stopping short where I am. Dark night is coming down, dear Brother; and I must at length suddenly end. With my love and blessings to you all, Ever your affectionate,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 2 Jan. MS: NLS 528.2. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:425. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I wrote you a long letter yesterday; the latter part of which, all that relates to Stirling of Kier, and the speculation of your writing to him on the subject of a Statue to Knox, must have thrown you into not a little embarrassment, which probably you are struggling with at this moment. I write now to bid you dismiss all that from your mind and not write to Stirling just now, and probably not on that subject at all till we see farther. I woke this morning very early and the first thought that came to me was the pungent one to this latter effect!John A. Carlyle replied, 4 Jan.: “It was a very great relief to me yesterday to hear that you had resolved to do nothing further at present in regard to the Knox memorial.” Fling away your trouble therefore on that score. I do not write to Masson either today or perhaps at all, not at least till I have considered the subject better.

I am indeed abundantly sorry that Laing’s faint heart restricts him to so insignificant an Enterprise in behalf of Knox and Scotland;John wrote: “Poor Laing got his nerves shaken at those large meetings & does not like to venture on any thing of the kind again. He edited the works of Knox most faithfully, collecting materials for nearly twenty years; & the bust in St Giles, if he realizes it, will do no harm.” but I reflect that the step I was about to take would amount in effect to my putting myself at the head of the wider adventure and too possibly involve me in a tide of troubles far beyond what I am fit to bear. At any and all rates, I will hold my peace about the whole matter and consider it still farther before saying more.

Stirling it has struck me, withal, could probably throw some light upon the Torphichen portrait; being himself related to the House.James Walter Sandilands, Lord Torphichen, was the grandson of Margaret Douglas Stirling (1784–1836), da. of John Stirling (1742–1816) of Kippendavie, a junior branch of the Stirling family. But I am myself in no habits of writing to him, and haven’t even spoken with him for a number of years. He might probably enough regard the enterprise as unlikely to succeed and decline taking any presidency, to which of all Scotsmen he seems the most appropriate.— I steadily consider the want of a Public Statue to Knox as a standing disgrace to Scotland; but it may very well be that poor I, so near the verge of my career, was not the man appointed to remove it. In short, leave lazy Laing alone, dear Brother; and let us not enter into a dangerous element till we have examined farther!—

Perhaps you have noticed in the Newspapers some jumble of a story about me and a Prussian Order “pour le merite”The Illustrated London News reported, 3 Jan.: “Mr. Carlyle has been chosen to succeed Count Manzoni on the Prussian Order Pour le Mérite (civilian class).” The “Order Pour le Mérite” was first instituted as a military honor by Frederick the Great in 1740; it was then expanded to include a civilian class in 1842 by Frederick William IV (1795–1861), king of Prussia 1840–61. Recipients held the honor for life; TC’s appointment resulted from the death of Alessandro Manzoni (1785–1873), Italian poet and novelist. See also TC to JAC, 14 Feb. To myself there has no notice or specific word on the subject come to hand; I understand nothing whatever about it; and perceive only that, were it never so well-meant, it can be of no value to me whatever. Dy thee naither ill na’ gudeCoterie speech; see 4:369TC to MAC, 20 April 1828. Adieu, dear Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 8 Jan. MS: NLS 528.3. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Today I send you off those Four Bank Receipts of £1000 each, adding the cheque for £2050, according to your suggestion;John A. Carlyle had been checking TC’s Dumfries bank balance; he wrote, 4 Jan.: “I … found that there is a balance in your favour for £2779 .. 10 .. 9. Perhaps some of it might be put in Deposit; & the old Deposit Receipts which you have at Chelsea might be changed for new ones, with Interest added.” He then wrote, 6 Jan.: “It is more than two months since I paid my £50 to Mary for draining at the Gill [see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1873]. … It might save you a little trouble if you paid your £50 from the cheque for £2000 through me.” TC’s checkbook recorded: “8 January 1874 / Dr Carlyle (for Deposit a/c) / £2050 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). with your usual punctuality
you will announce their arrival, and duly dispose of them. I know nothing of the state of the Stock market, and am sorry to hear it is still in so distressed and fluctuating a condition; I thought cheap stock (since it is all cheap at present) might possibly in some safish or safest place, your Glasgow & South Western for example, might offer an inviting resource;John wrote, 4 Jan.: “It is well that neither of us bought any railway Stock last year as all of it has since fallen very much in price.” Financial failures in Vienna, June 1873, were the first symptoms of a serious economic depression, covering Europe and North America, which lasted for the next twenty years. The rampant investment in railways was one of the many causes. but I leave it all to your own much superior knowledge and am glad to have my hands free of it. Our neighbour of No 4 here, Mr Laisné, it appears, has been speaking to Mary one evening of the high qualities of Russian Govt Stock perfectly safe and an interest of 6 or 7 per cent.Constantine B. Laisné (1833–84), living at 4 Cheyne Row, with his sister Ellen C. Laisné (b. ca. 1835), and possibly also his widowed sister Adelaide Nedham (b. ca. 1831). There is no mention of TC buying Russian bonds at this time, although he did buy some the following year; see TC to JAC, 7 March 1875. I think it might be worth your while to make some enquiries or attempts for solid information on that subject:John wrote, 9 Jan.: “I have often noticed those Russian Government investments in the newspapers, but have no inclination at present to take any share in them. Six or seven per cent is large interest, but it only indicates that Russia wants money very much & that it cannot be got very readily in Britain. I have no one here whom I could consult on the subject.” I should have no objection to venture along with you £1000 or £2000 (not more, till we saw farther!) to the credit of that Great Man the CzarAlexander II (1818–81), emperor of Russia 1855–81. and his potent imperial enterprises;—but probably you will find no actual evidence to be had about it; and will leave it to rest upon its own basis for the present.— Dean Stanly and his Lady Augusta with two rather talkative little kinsfolk, Bruces, a nephew and niece,Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, dean of Westminster, and his wife, Lady Augusta. Lady Augusta had five brothers and five sisters, and several nephews and nieces, the most likely here being the children of her youngest brother, Thomas Charles Bruce (1825–90), and his wife, m. 1863, Sarah Caroline, b. Cornhill (1836–1913): Charles Thomas (1865–1915), and either Elizabeth Marjorie (d. 1929) or Augusta Mary. called yesterday to take leave of me before departing for those hyperborean regions with the view of a certain sublime wedding ceremony there.Dean Stanley was to officiate at the marriage, in St. Petersburg, 23 Jan., of grand duchess Maria Alexandrovna (1853–1920), only surviving da. of emperor Alexander II and Maria Alexandrovna (1824–80), to Alfred (1844–1900; ODNB), 2d son of Queen Victoria, duke of Edinburgh and duke of Saxe Cobourg and Gotha; Lady Augusta was to be one of the official representatives of Queen Victoria. They go tomorrow, are to be in Berlin, Saturday night, stay there
two days, then embark, trebly wrapped in furs for some thirty or forty hours of railway which conducts them to some artificial heat again in Petersburg. I cannot say that in the physical point of view they are favourable specimens of England. But perhaps there may some better arrive before the wedding is over. Lord Sydney, a stalwart old Townsend,John Robert Townshend (1805–90), Viscount Sydney, Liberal politician, Lord Chamberlain of the Household 1868–74. of rather impressive aspect is to accompany the Prince of Wales:Albert Edward (1841–1910; ODNB), prince of Wales, eldest son of Queen Victoria. luck by the way to all of them.

On the whole an immense quantity of literary and other encumbrance has been tumbling in upon me for the last few days, to the destruction of my morning leisure; but I hope it is now mainly over, and fast getting under my thumb. Ruskin has been here again and is coming back, I think, on Saturday; full to overflowing with far glancing projects and speculations; a beautiful new vol. of his, beautifully bound in blue morocco with gilded edges (vol vii of his Works) is by far the most interesting I have received; but except the part of it which is new and relates to Friedrich of PrussiaRuskin, The Crown of Wild Olive. Four Lectures on Industry and War, with an Appendix entitled “Notes on the Political Economy of Prussia” with specific reference to the first three books of Frederick; it was vol. 6 of The Works of John Ruskin (1873), pbd. 11 Dec.; see MAI to JRU, 12 Nov. 1873. Ruskin wrote, [early Jan.]: “Here’s the book—I do hope you’ll like some little bits in it. I’m not sure that you ever saw the end of the Future of England—which is all yours as much as the Frederick part— I find Saturday will be the best day for me to come after all.” I can get no part of it read at present. There came a pleasant letter, too, from Norton in America, which I will enclose if there be room.

Forster, I am glad to believe, seems getting fairly better; had been out in the Horticulture promenadeThe Horticultural Society’s gardens in South Kensington, which had a covered promenade; see 48:174TC to LA, 8 March 1873. twice for an hour when I saw him last; and was near winding up his poor DickensForster’s The Life of Charles Dickens, the final vol. of which was to be pbd. 29 Jan. enterprise. Froude is fiercely busy with his Irish task which is now to be in two volumes of moderate size,Froude’s The English in Ireland (see TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1873); the first vol. had been pbd. 1872, vols. 2 and 3 were pbd. April 1874. instead of one of immoderate. I believe it will be a singular & perhaps the very best book ever written upon Irish affairs yet;—still more disgraceful to England, indeed much more than to wretched Ireland itself; a mere cock fight of monstrous misbehaviours against perpetual mutinies, utter mendacity the soul of both.

Paper, you see, is done; so is time. Give my best love to Jean and them all.
Our weather is not so bad as yours indeed we have generally what may be called wonderful weather for the season & on our roads and pavements hereabout are as clean as a table.

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-UC, 14 Jan. Typescript: Maine Historical Society. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO AN UNIDENTIFIED CORRESPONDENT

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle, my Uncle, bids me say, with his best compliments and thanks for your note, that he is very sorry to hear of your sad condition of health, & that he would gladly do a great more than the small thing which you request of him to help you.

My Uncle knows of no correct or authorized American Ed. of his Works; but Mr Lipscombe of PhiladelphiaTC possibly means J. B. Lippincott & Co., booksellers and publishers, who distributed his works in Philadelphia. sells the English Edition (Chapman & Hall’s, London); the library edition, which is in large type & royal 8vo, & the people’ edition in smaller, tho’ quite clear, type, post 8vo Both editions he believes are equally correct.
With my Uncle’s best wishes I beg to remain, dear Sir,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 29 Jan. Addr: Shady Hill / Cambridge / Massachusetts. PM: London, 30 Jan. 1874. MS: Houghton. Quot: Waldo H. Dunn, Froude and Carlyle (1930) 73. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p:
Your welcome Letter came duly; and was read with pleasure and thanks. I ought, now that I consider it, to have answered at once; and certainly had I been wise, I should have done so: for, latterly, it is evident to me there may be in your mind some scruple of uneasiness about those Emerson Letters;Norton wrote, 22 Dec. 1873: “Four or five weeks ago I had a note from Emerson in the course of which he said,—‘ I shall like to know that I may confide to you the entire file of Carlyle’s letters to me from 1835 to 1872, nearly a hundred, I believe; that you may hereafter make what disposition or destruction of them you shall find fit;—to which I might add, I believe, some manuscript notes of him taken in 1848.’ … I answered,—that I was deeply touched by the confidence he put in me, and that though at first suggestion I shrank from accepting such a charge, yet on reflection I was willing to do so, for I knew no one to whom it could be more sacred, or who through affection and respect for you and for him, would be more desirous to fulfil the charge in a manner, whatever the needful fulfilment might prove to be, such as he and you would approve. … I do not like to have this trust in my hands, and in my heart, without your knowledge of it, and your concurrence in it. Emerson may not write you of what he has done,—and yet, I feel that you should know it, and that your leave should be asked.”
and at the present moment, it is more than usually difficult to me to write anything; and as to the thing to be written, nothing could be clearer to me from the very first. Understand then at once that I entirely agree with Emerson in his disposal of these letters, and have or can have no feeling on the subject, but that if he was going to do anything at all with the stuff he could not in the world have found anybody fitter to take charge of it than yourself. Accept it therefore, I pray you; lock it by in some drawer till I have vanished; and then do with it what to your own just mind shall seem best. If my Brother, Dr Carlyle in Dumfries, or Froude, who are appointed Executors, should ever want it, they will know that it is in your keeping, and will get a just response upon it on application. And that is all I have to say on this small matter,—which I confess grows smaller & smaller to me every day, & every year, for the last forty; the wish rising stronger & stronger in me, were it possible, not to have any Biography at all in a kind of world like this, but rather to be purely silent in the Land of Silence; intimating to all kinds of “Able Editors,” blethering Stump Orator’s penny a liners, or guinea a worders, “Sweet friends, for Jesus’ sake forbear to dig the dust inclosed here.”—Cf. the inscription on Shakespeare’s grave.

This is all of essential I had to say. Needs only that I charge you with my friendliest, fraternal salutations and thanks to Emerson, and hopeful gratulations on all you report upon him.Norton wrote that he had recently visited Emerson: “He is best at home, and it seemed to me that I had never seen all the sweet qualities of his nature in happier activity than on that day. He was well in health, in good heart, and … in full vigour of mind.”

A little more than a fortnight ago, I sent your Vol. of Marvell to TrübnerSee TC to CEN, 8 Dec. 1873. Nicholas Trübner (1817–84; ODNB), philologist and publisher, specialising in importing books from the U.S.; see 42:114TC to NT, 8 July 1865. Norton wrote, 22 Dec.: “As to the Marvell volume, the easiest way to send it [is by] care of Trübner. … He sends a weekly parcel to America.” & had it accepted and taken charge of by him: so that I suppose it may be almost already in your hands. I fear you will not find it very interesting; but it is solid, honest reading of its kind, and ought to have a niche in American Libraries,
as well as here.— Child’s Abbotsford affairsSee TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. 1873. I hope, go all straight; though I have heard nothing from Laing either on that subject or any other since I last wrote to you. I hope the Cromwell Mask was believingly accepted and had its success in your late reunion;TC gave Cromwell’s death mask to Norton, 19 April 1873. Norton noted in his diary at the time: “It is one of seven casts taken from the original mask. He said he had long had one of the common casts such as may be found in the plaster workman’s shops, that had been given to him by John Sterling. It had hung in his dressing-room for years, and his associations with it made it more valuable to him than the one that he gave me; but the cast I was to have was far the better, and much the more faithful likeness” (Norton’s Letters 1:478). Norton wrote, 22 Dec.: “I have been getting together such engravings from portraits of Cromwell as I can find, for the purpose of showing them with the mask at a meeting of our Historical Society.” Norton had arranged the bequest of TC’s books on Cromwell to Harvard (see 46:163–64TC to CEN, 2 March 1870), and he himself bequeathed the Cromwell mask to Harvard; see HCC: frontis. I pride myself on its being the probable Father of all future American likenesses of Cromwell to the gradual extirpation of so many others that swarm there, I doubt not, even as they do here.

For the last ten days I have had a paltry cold, which (or rather the Drs upon which) have been a great annoyance to me— Worse than any Alexander the Coppersmith!See 2 Tim. 4:14. — and have rendered writing, until today when I consider victory to be won, almost an impossibility or what in the language of exaggeration, we are too apt to call such. Light is about closing, too (5 p.m), and I suppose the Mail unless I haste will be shut. God bless you all, young old and middle-aged at Shady Hill.

postscript.p: Ps. Sir Hudibras (according to Butler)Samuel Butler (ca. 1613–80; ODNB), poet; Hudibras (1663), a satirical mock-heroic poem. was about to do a dreadful homicide & all-important catastrophe & had drawn his pistol with that full intent & would decidedly have done it had not, says Butler, ‘Diana in the shape of rust’ imperatively intervened.“But Pallas came in Shape of Rust, / And ‘twixt the Spring and Hammer thrust / Her Gorgon Shield” (Hudibras 1.ii. lines 782–84). The Greek goddess Athena, sometimes known as Pallas Athena, had a shield with the image of the gorgon Medusa on it. TC always names the Roman goddess Diana when referring to these lines, although the Roman goddess associated with Athena is Minerva; see 1:191TC to RM, 14 July 1819, and 25:222TC to TSS, 19 Sept. 1850. This is TC’s response to Norton’s query, 22 Dec.: “In your letter to me of November 3d you mention ‘Diana, in the shape of continual Indigestion’ … and you puzzle me. Why poor Diana should take that form is unknown to me. … Does the inconstant goddess of the Moon rule over the tides of our blood & bile? Pray explain to me.” A miracle she has occasionally upon me in other shapes!

My niece Mary insists upon having added here her emphatic thanks for the LongfellowHenry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–82), American poet and educator; he lived in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Norton wrote: “I owe many thanks to Miss Aitken for the note she was good enough to write to me. … I shall ask you to offer her the enclosed note, and I hope she may care enough for Longfellow to prefer his autograph to mine.” Autograph.

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-JAM [JALM], 30 Jan. MS: Leeds Univ. Hitherto unpbd. James Alexander Manson (1851–1921), literary editor, ed. of the Daily Chronicle 1872–77.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO J. A. MANSON

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me say, in answer to your Note of yesterday, that “Bettine” was not a Child at the time she wrote the Letters to Goethe, but a Mme Brentano, wife of a German Jew at Berlin (herself a Jewess),Elisabeth (Bettina) von Arnim, b. Brentano (1785–1859; see 8:332TC to JOST, [12 April 1836], and 22:163JWC to HW, [19 Nov. 1847]), German writer and novelist; she wrote Goethes Briefwechsel mit einem Kinde [Goethe’s Correspondence with a Child] (Berlin, 1835), a fictionalized account of her correspondence with Goethe, 1807–11, when she was an adult but as yet unmarried; she m., 1811, Carl Joachim Friedrich Ludwig von Arnim (1781–1831), German poet and novelist. Neither were Jewish. who latterly did not live with her Husband. She wrote several useless, tho’ ingenuous novels, which were popular in Berlin; she could find no English translator for her Correspondence; and herself did it with such English as she was mistress of.
Goethe was at the date of the correspondence over sixty years of age, and married; but Mr Carlyle thinks that under no circumstances whatever would Goethe ever have thought of marrying her.
With Mr Carlyle’s compliments,
docBody.closer: I am / yours very truly / Mary Carlyle Aitken

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-JH [JCHA], 3 Feb. Pbd: Copeland 243–47.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO JANET HANNING

docBody.p:
— Your little note arrived duly and was very welcome; telling as it did that all was well with you in your far off home. I have several times lately intended to write to you, spontaneously, but somehow one’s time seems to get so filled up that few of all the things one proposes to do get accomplished. I was very glad of the little note which you sent sometime ago in
answer to one from me, and would have taken up Cousin Kate’sJanet and Robert Hanning’s 3rd da., Catherine. Challenge as to writing, but had a great deal of writing to do at that time and was moreover in very indifferent health,—or I certainly should have written to her. I hope she is getting on well. We had a very good account of her from Alick and James CarlyleAlexander Carlyle’s sons Alick and James visited Scotland and London, July–Aug. 1871; see 47:222TC to SW, 9 Aug. 1871. when they were here.

Uncle has been pretty well all the winter, until a fortnight ago, when he caught cold, which has troubled him a good deal; but he is getting rid of it now. Last August he and I went to Norfolk,See TC to LLA, [8 Oct.] 1873, and TC to CEN, 3 Nov. 1873. and, after spending ten days very pleasantly there, during which time he seemed every day to grow younger and better, we turned our faces to the north. After a disagreeable journey to Newcastle by steamer, went on to Dumfries, where we found everybody well; from Dumfries we made several excursions,—to the Gill, where all were prospering, and especially Jane,Mary and James Austin’s 4th da., Jane. who used to look rather thin and delicate, was looking very well. Aunt Mary is one of the kindest people one ever sees; she looked older than she did when I saw her before; and is generally rather serious than lively. They have got on their farm for another nineteen years at a very small increase of rent,See TC to JAC, 5 Nov. 1873. which must be a great comfort to them. We one day went to Scotsbrig, where I have not been more than about three times in my life. John’s wife,Margaret Carlyle. whom I never saw before, looks very amiable and gentle, rather than clever and smart; they have three children, one boy and two girls,John and Margaret Carlyle had three children when Mary visited: Isabella, Elisabeth, and James; a 2d son was born Dec. 1873. one of the latter about the prettiest little thing I ever saw. Uncle Jamie had unfortunately made a mistake as to the day of our coming; so that we did not see him then; but he came to Dumfries and was looking very well; though, poor man, he has had a hard enough time of it since; for his daughter Jenny has been very ill all the winter; as it was she lost her little daughter; and last Sunday night poor Jenny’s long painful illness ended in death.Jenny Scott d. 1 Feb., see TC to JAC, 4 Feb. I think she has left three children. It must be a cruel blow to Uncle Jamie, who always seemed so fond of her. We have been expecting no other news than this for some time back; but when death comes it never fails to surprize. There have been a great many deaths amongst us the last year or two; you are well off, dear Aunt, to have all your children spared to you. My Mother when I saw her in Summer did not seem to have forgotten those that were taken away.Jean Aitken had two sons who died in infancy, and more recently, Thomas and James. We used to be
very fond of singing songs together in the evenings, but when we once tried it last time I was at home, one after another of us broke down until we had to give up the one solitary attempt. At Ecclefechan I went with the two Uncles to see the houses in which they were bornTC and John A. Carlyle. TC was born in the Arched House, Ecclefechan, and John in a cottage nearby (since demolished) where the family moved in 1798; see Wilson, Carlyle 1:15–17. and also to see Grandfather’s and Grandmother’s graves.TC’s parents, James and Margaret Carlyle, buried in Ecclefechan churchyard. I don’t remember ever to have seen Ecclefechan before. It was a very interesting day we spent; none of us were in high spirits, as you may suppose; but it is very pleasant to me to look back upon the visit. Uncle and I went also to Fife to visit the Welsh’s (Aunt Jane’s Cousins)Rev. Walter Welsh and his sister Margaret, at Auchtertool Manse in Fife. and after two or three days there we spent a day at Haddington; staid one night in EdinburghTC and Mary visited Edinburgh and Haddington, Sept. 1873; see 48:220MW to SW, 9 Sept. 1873. and, after seeing one or two people there, returned to Dumfries, and after a week or two to Chelsea,—having been away in all only about six weeks. Uncle was not very well and complained of the noise of the railway whistle &c. at Dumfries; and so we were not sorry to be back to Chelsea again; I am hoping to get away for a week or two this spring so see them all at home, if Miss Welsh comes on a visit,Maggie Welsh came April–May; see TC to JAC, 17 April. as she may very possibly do. Uncle has not been working at anything lately; he spends nearly all his time in reading. I am very glad to be back with him again, although I was sorry to leave the Taylors,Mary had worked for Peter Alfred Taylor (1819–91; ODNB), politician and radical, and his wife, m. 1842, Clementia, b. Doughty (1810–1908; ODNB), women’s activist (see 48:241), as a teacher and secretary, from Jan. 1873 (see 48:119TC to LLA, 14 Dec. 1872) until June or July; by the end of July 1873 she was living at Cheyne Row again. who are very good people, and were most kind to me. I got on there very well, only I was in bad health nearly all the time. However, I am very much better now.

I have written this note, or rather long scrawl, in great haste; and have been often interrupted, so I hope you will excuse it—as, if I read it over, I shall be sure not to send it off and have not time at present to write another. Uncle sends his kindest love and best wishes,Mary presumably enclosed TC’s check: “4 Feb. 1874 / Mrs Janet Hanning (15 Murray St.) / £10” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20752). as well as thanks for your kind letter, with all good messages from myself.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 4 Feb. MS: NLS 528.4. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
You need not frighten yourself or bother your head any more about my “bad cold.”John A. Carlyle wrote, 26 Jan.: “We have all been rather uneasy about your cold ever since we first heard of it. … It is a very painful & troublesome complaint, more especially when one sleeps badly at the same time. I should be extremely well pleased to hear that you had fairly recovered.” It is nothing but the consummation and topmost crisis of a thing which has been going on ever since you saw me last;TC left Dumfries 15 Sept. 1873; see TC to LLA, [8 Oct.]. and which I can perceive means simply long-continued torpor in the liver, and a refusal of the bowels to do anything but lie stagnant, the prey of raging winds, which, as you yourself know, are a “devil of a thing.” All the time we were in NorfolkTC was in Norfolk 2–13 Aug. 1873; see TC to LLA, [8 Oct.]. bowels behaved in the most handsome manner; and even at Dumfries there was nothing altogether grievous to complain of; but ever after my arrival there, there was a visible deterioration and after my return hither a continuation of the same bad track till at length, for a good few months past, there was an absolute cessation, so to speak (very partially relieved from week to week by some poor hop pill); so that walking was at all times grievous and burdensome to me, though my only relief and sometimes, with Froude, I would persist in it for four miles without omnibus at all, and return home utterly exhausted & sick of the scandalous enemy lodged within me. I had a number of ‘colds’ but they all ran away in the form of “snifters” and a day or two’s continual dropping at the nose; this last cold was the fruit of a trifling incidental exposure but struck, with a new though trifling impression into the top of the windpipe; it, too, might have been subdued with a little more attention bestowed, and especially had I been left to myself to deal with it, for I percieved [sic] clearly by this time that all had risen in my neglect of the occasional blue pill, recommended by Quain,Dr Richard Quain. —a recipe wh. the dirty spoonful tumultuous castor super-added to it, always rendered more or less hateful to me. But Drs were called in (Dr WoolmerJoseph Benson Woolmer (1827–74), surgeon, 71 Warwick Sq., Pimlico; see 45:3TC to JAC, 5 July 1867, and 215TC to JAC, 22 Dec. 1868. especially by poor Mary’s anxiety and clearly against my command); Woolmer, otherwise a most rational & solid man, would not the least believe that my stomach was like no other mortals He threw in squills, one aloeticAloetic, a laxative or purgative made from aloes; see Carlyle, Sartor 167.
pill; and both he & Quain agreed that my cold bathing in the morning was to be peremptorily given up until warmer weather,— which meant that my whole hygienic economy was to be turned topsy turvey, & I, with my inventive faculties in such a brilliant condition, be left to discover another by painful experiment at every step. The consequences of all which, especially of these Drs, have been that I have lain sunk for the last fortnight in the most frightful quagmire or midden-hole of sordid physical miseries that can well be conceived; and am only within the last few days, since Woolmer is quite away, and Quain, a much milder hand, only occasionally looking in, gradually emerging to my old normal state. I take half a blue pill every third day; no castor more, but only as substitute a teaspoonful of some electuary wh. I have not yet tried: the essential is, I intend to prosecute the torpid liver in that way, till it bethink itself; that, I am certain, and Quain with me, is the one evil: and meanwhile, “the tepid or bloodwarm bath” &c &c will get itself reduced from chaos into cosmos; and all will be as well again as usual.

Forster insists on sending his carriage (a harbitrary covePresumably either TC or Mary Aitken wrote in a similar vein to Forster around this time, as Forster wrote to Mary, 25 Feb.: “I wonder you’d write such a thing—with the Bird of Wisdom sitting & overlooking you—or that your uncle has ‘no sort of command’ over me, when you know very well it is he, not I, to whom ‘Harbitrary Cove’ is alone applicable” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 72) The term had been applied to Forster some years before by a cabman; see Percy Fitzgerald (1834–1925), Irish author and critic, Pickwickian Studies (1899) 90. [tyrannical fellow], and the kindest of men). It is easier to drive in than walking would be; but it does me almost no good, nor, in spite of all admonitions, can I find that with warm fleecy clothing about me & wrappage to the chin, the natural air of heaven does me any mischief, or even irritates the windpipe, which latter I rather find to be a trifling item, depending on other causes, not quite known to me, and which, I take it, will disappear altogether, had the blue pill done its work. This the faithfullest wearisome diagnosis I could make of my beggarly case; and I strictly forbid any body to afflict his soul with fears about it, till he hear worse. This day, I will add only, though weak as ever, I seem to feel in a feeble degree really clearer and my remains of coughing, which never amounted to much, seemingly diminished still nearer to insignificance.

We had yesterday morning the sad and fatal news from Birmingham,The death of their niece Jenny Scott, 1 Feb. all over there; which filled us with sorrow, especially for poor Jamie, left again solitary in his dreary old days, and cut off from the one bright joy he had in life. I wrote a few words to him yesterday; but was well aware of how little use they or any words could be. I hope he will go home with JamieJamie’s son James Jr., who lived at Craigenputtoch with his wife, Catherine. and dwell
chiefly there, where there is at least a woman, not a female spooney,Jamie lived at Scotsbrig with his son John and his wife, Margaret, whom TC thought amiable but not a very good housewife; see 48:27TC to AC, 16 Dec. 1871. to look after his real wants and him. Jamie, I am told, is always very affectionate to him, which is the brightest merit I know in that young man. I hope and believe he will conspicuously show this on the present sad & tragic occasion. Poor Jenny’s case, poor little soul, has been very tragic too; but for her one feels it a stern consolation that her dreary sufferings and sorrows are now all stilled in Death; and quietly hushed down into eternal Rest.

This very day, we suppose, they may be busy with the funeral.John wrote, 1 Feb.: “Jenny seems to have no organic disease, but only the same kind of distressing weakness which her mother had for so many years.” For her mother, Isabella Carlyle’s, illness and death, see 35:101TC to JN, 26 May 1859, and 106TC to [JAC], [7? June 1859]. John wrote again, 8 Feb.: “I hope Jamie will come back to Annandale without further delay as the funeral was over yesterday.” God be merciful to us all.

You would get poor little Jenny’s note from Canada. Mary is writing to her today;See MA to JH, 3 Feb. but I hope, withal, some of you, direct from the fountain head, will write before long. Mary had a letter lately from Alick Carlyle junior which gave a nice view of the Xmas family party at Bield & good old Alick senior, with his hoary head, presiding cheerfully at one end, while Jenny, poor old soul sat pouring coffee at the other. Both of these he described as sensibly grown older, as what could we hope other; but for the rest all going on in fair order there. The young Alick himself described his own health as decidedly rather bad; and his weariness of school-teaching in a place so utterly without intellectual society as very considerable; on the other hand he appeared to be reading diligently tho’ not much I think in scholastic ways; and we may fairly hope things will improve with him by and by.

I have just finished Forster’s Dickens, vol. 3:—can you easily get it from your Library? if not I will send it up to the party among you who got the other two;John wrote, 8 Feb.: “It is doubtful whether we shall be able to get the volume from our Library here, as there will be only one copy & many have already bespoken it. So please send it to Jean by post as soon as convenient.” it is far better done than I expected, and indeed the whole Book may be said to be (by the help of those incessant Letters from Dickens himself) a wonderful Autobiography of Dickens; leaving him conspicuous to mankind for as many years & generations as they are pleased to remember him at all.
My love to Jean & my best blessings to you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 14 Feb. MS: NLS 528.5; postscript MS: NLS 528.23B. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:425–26; A. Carlyle, NL 2: 305–6; Wilson, Carlyle 6:321 and 322–23; Dunn, Froude 2:388. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I write you today a very short letter, but it will quiet yr anxieties and be greatly preferable to none. My cold seems quite gone or all but utterly gone; the poor liver itself has been stimulated into regular action (God be thanked!)—and I ought to feel quite well & indeed do in a sense; am able to walk out, well wrapt up for almost a couple of miles daily; and feel only an extreme weakness, which I judge to be the fruit of all the physicing & other miseries I have lately had. For three weeks certainly in such a disgusting and degrading state of misery as I had never lived in before; add to which the chaotic disturbance wrought upon me by the Doctors, every portion of whose “medicines,” except only the salutary blue pill was more or less poisonous to me; thank God, thank God, I am for the present quit of all that; and design even in a day or two to resume my cold bath (made tepid by a good jug of hot water) and preliminary walk in the open air. For the last week or more I take a little well made porridge and milk before getting out of bed: this I design to continue only postponing it till after my walk & closing it up by an immediate subsequent cup of coffee, and poached egg upon a bit of buttered toast served warm, with all the industry and energy that my poor little Cutty of a Mary can strenuously bring to bear upon it.— You are therefore to tell Jean that she must not imitate me any farther in this bad path of winter cold, but take care of herself & get rid of her cold as I have done, with all speed.

The day before yesterday His Prussian ExcellencyGeorg Herbert (1820–1902), Fürst Münster von Derneburg, German ambassador to the Court of St. James 1873–85. Allingham noted in his diary, 13 Feb.: “Carlyle has received the German order Pour le Mérite—black ribbon with silver line near each edge; he dictates to Mary letters to the Ambassador and to Berlin, but cannot phrase them to his mind” (Allingham Diary 231). forwarded to me by registered parcel all the Documents and the Insignia connected with our sublime elevation to the Prussian order of merit. I had a great deal of unwelcome bother reading that accursed cursiv-schrift of theirs & making out what gasp of official twaddle I was expected to answer with: but that, too, is all done; goes off to Berlin by this evening’s post. The papers—all but one,—which enclosed a series of strict enquiries, all in cursivschrift, as to my name, surname, place of birth, religion, social standing (a “Writer of Books”) place of abode, connection with other Prussian honours; & has now gone back with clear answers affixed: and so we have done, thank Heaven, with this sublime
nonentity for ever & a day. The star or symbolical decoration is really very pretty; a bright gold thing like a wheel with spokes about the size of crown piece hung with a black ribbon, with silver edges. Mary has laid it by punctually folded up, probably never more to meet the light in my time, but in sum I am heartily glad to have got rid of the affair; & feel about it, after the fash is over quite as emphatically as I did at first; that had they sent me ¼lb of good Tobacco the addition to my happiness had probably been suitabler and greater.

Preliminary to these high Officialities there came a letter the night before from D’Eichtal junior;Karl d’ Eichthal, son of their old friend Charles d’Eichthal; John A. Carlyle replied, 15 Feb.: “I am glad you liked Eichthal’s son. He got through all the war most creditably. His father is anxious to have him wedded to some English wife, as he tells me in every letter I get from him.” which is far too curious to be omitted, the rather as you need not return it. D’Eichtal had called Sunday gone a week, during my coughing time & sat with me about an hour. He is a tall lean, wiry-looking figure; aquiline in face, not Hebrew at all, and of a complexion wh. reminded me of the late Dr ArbuckleDr. Robert Arbuckle (1802–62), old friend of John A. Carlyle’s; see 38:274. while still young. A decidedly soldierlike good looking young fellow, who speaks the most extraordinary English I ever heard (not without sense in the meaning of it) & tried no other lingo upon me. You might write to him if you liked. He naturally spoke eagerly about you, and your old München connections.John had first met the Eichthals in Munich in 1827; see 5:276–80TC to GE, 17 May 1831.

I shall of course be very glad if you can send me any good news of poor Jamie: after a little while you will doubtless go down to him, and at least report I am very wae about him; this he needs not to be told of and, alas, indeed what good can anybody’s sympathy do him.

I have still one black article of news, the saddest to myself that has befallen for years, to announce to you. Poor Froude, whose kindness to me during this cold was extreme & continual, has in a sudden, almost without warning at all, lost his loving and excellent wife;Henrietta Elizabeth Froude, d. 12 Feb. no doubt the saddest calamity that could have overwhelmed him. For several weeks past, it now appears Mrs Froude was confined with “a kind of Bronchitis,” but neither herself nor any of those about her made the least stir about it; all confidently calculating that to stay in the house was all then needed in the matter. Froude hardly mentioned it to me in his almost daily visits; and seemed cheery & happy beyond wont, just about finishing his Book on Ireland (an excellent Book by far the best ever written on that subject) & rejoicing in the fall of Archquack Gladstone.William Gladstone dissolved Parliament, 24 Jan., and would resign as leader of the Liberal party, 17 Feb. Not till about four days ago did I hear from him the slightest expression of
anxiety on that domestic head: only the next day he returned with a face full of anxiety; said Mrs F. was threatened with some congestion of the lungs or even with inflamation there; wh. had evidently altogether alarmed him; The next day we saw him, Mary & I, at his own door where he came to the carriage we were in; his face speaking nothing but wild despair; the poor lady cd not get an instant of sleep; no sooner did sleep come than breathing stopped and she awoke again in agony. Thursday night at 8 oclock she died, all on a sudden;—and has left poor Froude, I dare well believe, drowned in such black deluges of woe as no other man in London. I am going now to see whether he can admit me for a moment,Froude’s da. Georgina Margaret later spoke of TC’s sympathy for those suffering loss, reporting: “I shall never forget his poor, crumpled figure when he came to our door in 1874 to ask whether he might see my father after the death of our mother” (Dunn, Froude 2:388). but I think it probable not. Adieu, dear Brother.

postscript.p: P.s. I felt about the little Syme passage in the Life of Dickens, exactly as you did;James Syme (1799–1870; ODNB), surgeon; he had operated on TC’s hernia, July 1868; see 45:161TC to JF, 2 Aug. 1868. John wrote, 12 Feb., that he had read vol. 3 of Forster’s Life of Dickens: “One passage about Syme & Dickens’s consultation of him is most ridiculously absurd, & one wonders how Forster could have let it pass. It should certainly be left out in any new edition. It tells entirely against Dickens. As an old friend of Syme’s I felt offended at first on reading it, but thought no one who had ever seen him could fail to see the flatness & insipidity of such a poor caricature. The enclosed letter cutting from the Scotsman will show you what it is.” The Scotsman clipping was a letter from John Brown (1810–82; ODNB), physician, old friend of John’s, quoting a passage from the book [Forster, Life of Dickens 3:417] where Dickens, in Edinburgh Feb. 1869, consults Syme about his painful foot, and caricatures Syme’s Scottish accent and language. Brown wrote: “Now, does any man who ever heard Mr Syme speak, imagine the hideous jargon … was his customary manner of speech? … Mr Syme … spoke as he wrote English … pure, clear, strong, and to the point. He knew well and relished our own rich vernacular, but he never spoke it” (Scotsman, 10 Feb. 1874). I rather disapproved of Dr Brown’s tone; last night I spoke of the matter to Forster, who pleaded hard that no shadow of disrespect had been meant &c &c, I insisting, however, that had Dickens known who & what Syme was he would have strongly refused to jot down such a thing about him in such a dialect. Today poor Forster has just called; and bids me write in virtue of what I and you have said to him (for he objects strongly to the blusterous Brown) he will wholly remove the offensive passage or at least whatever shadow of offence is in it from his Book.John replied, 15 Feb.: “I am glad to hear that Forster is going to remedy the passage about Syme.” This I promised to tell you; and Mary sticks it in after the cover was closed.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 16 Feb. MS: FC. Pbd: Shepherd, Carlyle 2:303–4 inc. Quot: Kaplan 537. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: I am happy to say, as I can with perfect sincerity, that I have read your third vol of Dickens with continued interest and pleasure,—and with a glad surprise, moreover, which heightens all these feelings. Surprise I say, for the narrative flows on with limpid clearness, soft harmony, perfection of phrase and idea; not a trace in it anywhere of the horrid state of pain in which I too well know you to have been all the while.

This Third Volume throws a new light and character to me over the Work at large. I incline to consider this Biography as taking rank, in essential respects, parallel to Boswell himself, though on widely different grounds. Boswell, by those genial abridgments and vivid face to face pictures of Johnson’s thoughts,James Boswell (1740–95; ODNB), companion and biographer of Samuel Johnson (1709–84: ODNB), author and lexicographer; for TC’s earlier praise of him, see, for instance 23:19. conversational ways and modes of appearance among his fellow-creatures, has given, as you often hear me say, such a delineation of a man’s existence as was never given by another man. By quite different resources, by those sparkling, clear and sunny utterances of Dickens’s own (bits of auto-biography unrivalled in clearness and credibility) which were at your disposal and have been intercalated every now and then, you have given to every intelligent eye the power of looking down to the very bottom of Dickens’s mode of existing in this world; and I say have performed a feat which, except in Boswell, the unique, I know not where to parallel. So long as Dickens is interesting to his fellow-men, here will be seen, face to face, what Dickens’s manner of existing was. His bright and joyful sympathy with everything around him; his steady practicality, withal; the singularly solid business talent he continually had; and, deeper than all, if one has the eye to see deep enough, dark, fateful silent elements, tragical to look upon, and hiding amid dazzling radiances as of the sun, the elements of death itself. Those two American JourniesDickens had toured the U.S. Dec. 1867–April 1868 (see 45:51TC to CK, 20 Oct. 1867); Forster’s The Life of Charles Dickens, vol. 3 chapters 15 and 16, covered these journeys. especially transcend in tragic interest to a thinking reader most things one has seen in writing!
On the whole, therefore, I declare you to have done right well, my Friend; and my first and last word about the Book is, Euge, euge [Well done, well done].

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 25 Feb. MS: NLS 528.6. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your letter of this morning;—which, alas, I have no time to answer except by assuring you that I am going on quite favorably; slowly recovering some measure of strength, so that I now (without as yet bathing of any kind) can take my morning’s round of walk before breakfast, and walk slowly, from three o’clock onwards, as far perhaps as Hyde-park Corner & back,About 4 mi. (6.5 km.). after my two or three quiet hours of idle reading (I grieve to say almost utterly idle at present) wh. I resume again after dinner & sleep about ½ past 9. I will not at present ask you for any of the Books you are so kind as offer. TourguéneffIvan Turgenev, Les Eaux printanières et Le Gentilhomme de la Steppe (Paris, [1873]). John A. Carlyle wrote, 24 Feb. that he had not quite finished the book, but would return it soon. you can when completely done with it return by any opportunity. Of Syme’s Life I seemed to get about enough in the Scotsman Review wh. you sent me; of Syme himself I have altogether the same idea as your own.Robert Paterson M.D. (1814–89), Memorials of the Life of James Syme (Edinburgh, 1874). For Syme, see TC to JAC, 14 Feb. There was a long review of the book in the Scotsman, 16 Feb. John wrote: “Syme was one of the most thoroughly honest men, & stood true in all his doings; & he was also most warm-hearted & most modest in the true sense of the word. … [H]e was the best Surgeon of his time.”

The Photograph you send I have given to Mary, who sends her best thanks.John wrote: “I enclose a photograph, which I have [been] getting some copies of lately done by our industrious Mr Wilson here. Please give it to Mary with my kind remembrances.” Robert Wilson (1832–81), photographer, living at 78 Irish St., Dumfries. I find it is not from a face, but from a portrait from poor Laurence,Samuel Laurence; he had painted TC (1838–41; see 10:frontis); this was presumably a photograph of the painting. who never cd much succeed with me. Brother Jamie complained about it (Mary says) about a “scollop on the nose” wh. he had not noticed in the original. The only photo. of our dear old MotherTC had got photographs made, June 1868 (see 45:154TC to JCA, 30 June 1868), of the portrait of Margaret A. Carlyle by Maxwell of Dumfries, 1842; see 13:frontis. and 14:211–12TC to JCA, 1 July [30 June] 1842. wh. is not faded almost quite away here is the one enclosed: but Mary is to go to Elliott & FryJohn Joseph Elliott (1835–1903) and Clarence Edmund Fry (1840–97), photographers, 55 Baker St.; they took several photographs for TC in March 1868; (see 45:120–22TC to JJE, 25 April 1868), so it was likely that they also photographed Margaret A. Carlyle’s portrait; see also 48:69TC to MA, 18 June 1872. & realize from them new copies of both the photographs done by them,—in wh. you shall share so soon
as they get to hand. I am due at poor Froude’s & indeed must set off with all the speed in me.— Tom Wilson’sThomas Wilson, British chaplain at Weimar. Letter is not worth returning or perhaps even reading. Ever your affectionate Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-TC [TCON], 25 Feb. Addr: Messrs Constable, Printers, / Edinburgh. PM: London, 25 Feb. 1874. MS: Morgan Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. On the envelope in another hand is written: “a valuable letter / (Thomas Carlyle).” Thomas Constable (1812–81; ODNB), printer; he printed TC’s Inaugural Address (1866); see TC to TCON, [13 April 1866].
bibl.head: TC TO THOMAS CONSTABLE

docBody.p:
Weeks ago I ought to have acknowledged with many kind thanks your valuable Biography of your Father;Thomas Constable, Archibald Constable, and his Literary Correspondents: A Memorial, 3 vols. (Edinburgh, 1873). Archibald Constable (1774–1827; ODNB), Scottish publisher. which I read with great interest and pleasure. The Book, I am told, has been making an impression up here of a lively and favourable nature; but nobody here, or perhaps elsewhere, could read it with such a vivid and almost personal interest as I myself did; for the period of it is coincident almost with that of my own life, since I first saw Edinr, and brings to my mind, in colours fresh as yesterday, all the noteworthy singular and any way distinguished people that I have lived in the world along with, and am now almost a solitary survivor of. Not even the wretched crooked wonner, Forbes,Rev. Dr. Duncan Forbes (1762–1826), friend of Archibald Constable; see Archibald Constable, and his Literary Correspondents 1:270 and 466–80; TC uses “wonner” to mean wonder, but in a derogatory sense; see 5:130TC to JAC, 6 Aug. 1830. whom your Father was so kind to, failed to start up alive before me again, with all the insignificant, puddles, fooleries and futilities I had known or heard of him!— Among the letters & records of those not known to me before, I think those of Mr HunterAlexander Gibson Hunter (1771–1812), financial partner of Archibald Constable 1803–11; see Archibald Constable, and his Literary Correspondents 1:57–160. were the most entertaining. His tours and feastings in Scotland and England, with the London Murrays and Longmans,Murrays and Longmans were long established family London publishers, Murrays founded 1768, by John Murray (1737–93; ODNB), and Longmans founded 1724, by Thomas Longman (1699–1755; ODNB). Constable published in partnership with both at various times. are full of spirit and graphic life; and many a curious picture he
gives us of the scenes and situations he was in during his too short career at your Father’s side.

The account given of your worthy and distinguished Father is completely a new Chapter in the history of Bibliopolism: a man of high faculties, and of noble and friendly dispositions; fairly defineable as the highest specimen of that class Scotland or Britain has yet seen. One admires, throughout, his magnanimous courage, his deep sagacity and clearness of discernment, his inexhaustible opulence of resource;—he is clearly to be marked as the Author & originator of all this modern phase of British publication “for the Million”Constable’s dream was to sell good books so cheaply that even the poor could afford them: “I’ll make it … impossible that there should not be a good library in every decent house in Britain. … I have now settled my outline of operations—a three-shilling or half-crown volume every month, which must and shall sell, not by thousands or tens of thousands, but by hundreds of thousands—ay, by millions!” (Archibald Constable and his Literary Correspondents 3:309, quoting John Gibson Lockhart, Memoirs of the Life of Sir Walter Scott, bart., 7 vols. [1837–38] 6:31). which has taken, since he left it, such unexpected shapes! A man that made an epoch in his business, and this in so conspicuous and important a manner, must long continue a memorable kind of man.

You have done your task, with touching fidelity, with great filial piety, which I much sympathized with; understanding also well enough the shade of sorrow with which it is all overclouded; for indeed the action is a Tragedy, both as respects your Father and Sir Walter;Archibald Constable was for nearly 20 years, and despite several arguments, the main publisher of Sir Walter Scott (see TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. 1873). Despite being highly successful, he had little capital, and relied on borrowing from banks; during the winter of 1825–26 there was a severe economic recession, with many businesses and banks failing, and in Jan. 1826 Constable went bankrupt, and because at the time there was no limited liability the personal assets of all his partners, Scott included, were forfeit. each of the two contributing to it by action and reaction (little as they could foresee such result) the elements of “pity and fear” are the sad catastrophe of both!—

One thing only I will add: it seems to me you should not be very angry at Lockhart;John Gibson Lockhart (see TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. 1873), in his Memoirs of the Life of Sir Walter Scott, blamed Constable personally for the bankruptcy, attributing it to gross accounting errors and misjudgement. he speaks indeed improperly about your Father here and there; but I can bear witness that the high idea I got of him from Lockhart is essentially the same as I derived from your book. Accept many thanks, my dear Sir, for your kindness to me on the occasion and my best wishes at all times.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-UC, 4 March. Pbd: Kenneth W. Rendell, Inc. Catalog. Inc. Listed as a signed quotation in blue pencil.
bibl.head: TC TO AN UNIDENTIFIED CORRESPONDENT

docBody.p: My first short clothes were of yellow serge; of … I should say, my line short cloth, for the vesture was one and indivisible, reaching from neck to ankle, a mere body with four limbs; of which fashion how little did I then divine the architectural, how much less the moral significance.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 7 March. MS: NLS 528.7. Quot: Dunn, Froude 2:388. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Yesterday your letter came with Tourguenéffs Book;See TC to JAC, 25 Feb.; John A. Carlyle wrote, 5 March: “I send back Tourgueneffs book with many thanks. It is a good book of its kind.” and very glad we were to hear what tidings you could send us of self & kindred. The account of Jamie’s gradual improvementJohn enclosed a letter to himself from their nephew John Carlyle at Scotsbrig, 3 March, in which he wrote: “My father is here just now, I am glad to be able to say that he seems a deal better than when he came home. The pain in his left breast … is not so bad” (MS: NLS 1775F.258). was especially welcome; welcome also your expressed intention of writing to our dear old Alick;John wrote: “I hope to send a few words to Alick by this day’s post, as it seems a long while since I last wrote to him”; he then wrote, 11 March, to report that he had done so. I am myself often sad to think that I have not written for so long & cannot well write, at least not till I get a little better. We appear to have much better weather than you; very seldom, or at good intervals any rain (Hardly above one wet day this long while): harsh tempered mists are not infrequent, but generally the sun gets out for an hour or two; and today, for example, we have, as we had yesterday, a bright, clean and brisk March day all sunshine, tho’ after a rimy night.
