Within the last week I have regularly resumed my morning bath, which palpably does me good; stirs up the internal functions & makes me sensibly stronger for a vigorous morning walking of 20 minutes in my warmest coat. For several weeks past, I have got into the steady habit of commencing my breakfast with a warm little basin of porridge dropt into milk; the porridge is excellent Dumfries meal, faithfully boiled & stirred by Mrs Warren;Sarah Warren, Cheyne Row housekeeper. the milk is very feeble, tho’ I study to believe
that it is real milk & not chalk or sheeps brains. This porridge foundation is distinctly welcomer to me than anything else for many months past; I follow it straightway with a warm cup of coffee & a ditto bit of crumb–toast (Mary loyally slices off the crusts & eats them, and puts on at her best speed “butter for the million”). I swallow down, not with desire, a sound Gill egg;Food was sent regularly to Chelsea from Scotland. and that completes the sublime operation. I distinctly feel to be growing somewhat better; and indeed have not altogether felt so well since I arrived last year at Dumfries from Blickling.See TC to LLA, [8 Oct. 1873]. The town is now very full; and generally there is somebody here intending a walk or otherwise, but nobody gets in till three p.m.; & then I much oftenest go with Froude; who is decidedly the most serious, rational & worthy of all the companions I have. Poor fellow, he says little about his immense calamity, but if you meet him alone anywhere his look is that of one sunk in boundless grief.See TC to JAC, 14 Feb. He resists by work, which indeed is the only human method. The day after his Wife’s funeral, he set to work upon his Irish Book; resolutely intent to do the last chapter of it; and has now done it, & has the whole book in the printer’s hand; out of which it will come into the public in some two or three weeks. I read yesterday and the day before the first half of his last vol.; the wonderful preparative phenomenon of the Irish Rebellion; the next half gives the rebellion itself and its wind up of the union with Britain. It is an excellent Book, fairly the best Froude has ever written, and, by many degrees, the best ever written upon Ireland, and I calculate will do a great deal of good to this & the coming generation, concerned in that scandalous business of “governing Ireland” and of being “governed” there. England one clearly feels, makes a baser figure in that business than even Ireland itself. Shall I send you the Book when I get it here or can you easily procure it at Dumfries.Froude, The English in Ireland (see TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1873). John replied, 11 March, that he planned to buy the book himself.

This morning, after many many months of absence, George CookeJohn George Cooke (1819–80; see 45:44TC to JAC, 7 Oct. 1867, and 22445:biographical notes), stockbroker and financial adviser to TC; he had been a close friend of JWC. called here & talked rationally about various things, especially about the huge & pestiferous influx of foreign Jews, who are threatening to turn every English branch of trade into sheer gambling, ever of an unfair character & on the hugest scale ever seen in the world. He was in Paris lately & found France in great economic distress; very ill off for cash or credit in spite of their sublime payment of the German ransom:At the end of the Franco-Prussian War, the Treaty of Frankfurt, 1871, decreed that France had to pay Prussia an indemnity of five billion francs; they were given until March 1875, but had paid it in full by Sept. 1873. everybody also is in complete uncertainty
as to what will come of the “Conservative Republic”The term “Conservative Republic” was used to describe the French Third Republic (1870–1940), which sought to preserve the achievements of the French Revolution while moderating its radical elements. The notion was endorsed by Louis Adolphe Thiers (1797–1877), first president of the new Republic, 1871–73. The Daily Telegraph, 26 Feb., pbd. a letter by Thiers, summarizing his views: “I see no practicable form of government but a wise, equitable, healing Republic. … For my part, I see no other means than for the electors … by their choice of representatives to enlighten the [National] Assembly without alarming it, and point out the path they wish the nation to follow, which, there can be no doubt, is that leading to the Conservative Republic, in which we have hitherto found, not the troubles that were predicted, but the reparation of the disasters of the most fatal of wars.” they are trying to build. As C. wd not go away I took him to questioning him about Investments for lying money; he described all that as being in a weakly condition; but knew of one investment (of wh. indeed he himself had shares for sale till the end of March) wh. he considered good & safe. I made him write down the particulars; wishing you to consider & consult about it: the title of the thing is Furness RailwayThe Furness Railway operated around the Solway Firth, in the Furness area of Lancashire, NW England. John wrote: “The name of that Furness Railway … is well known to me, & I often see its Shares quoted in the papers. The Solway Junction R.W. was constructed mainly on dependence of Iron ore that was to come from Furness & shares in it were at one time high, & now the Ore is said to be mostly smelted at Furness instead of being sent to Scotland as before, & at all events the Solway Junction has become a very losing concern, not always paying its working expenses. … My own idea is that things are going on rather dangerously as if the usual crisis were near at hand; & I should prefer letting any spare money I have lie in deposit; for I don’t like to be made anxious about such matters.” John was right; the line had been built primarily for the movement of iron ore, with very limited passenger amenities, and there was a downturn in the iron trade in the mid-1870s (Lancaster Gazette, 15 Aug. 1874). (wh. it seems has become a great Irish Highway from some place in Morecambe Bay;—if you cannot understand the scratches he has made, tell me, & I will endeavour to explain. He says the Scotch Bankers know the thing well & accept the shares, as security, at par.— I have not a moment left. Here has StephenJames Fitzjames Stephen. come whom I must endeavour to shake off for Froude’s sake;—clear sign that I must finish. I send my best love to Jean who I wish wd write to me.Jean replied, 8 March: “I am truly glad to hear … that you are farely getting round after yr long & tedious illness. … I had many an anxious thought abt you … wch it would have done less than no good to have given expression to at the time.” I send my hearts blessing to you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 21 March. MS: NLS 528.8. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. The bottom of the pages are torn, resulting in some missing words.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your letter came safe to us yesterday morning, and was very welcome.John A. Carlyle wrote, 19 March, with news that their relatives at the Gill and at Scotsbrig were all well and thriving. We have no news to send you back in return, but happily at least no bad news,—which fact is surely itself worth the price of a penny.

I looked at those Artizan-Dwellings Papers;John sent TC a report of the Artizans, Labourers, and General Dwellings Co. a philanthropic property company in which they both had shares; see 47:139TC to JAC, 13 Jan. 1871. was glad to see the indistinct SecretaryThe secretary was J. Royle Martin. so charmed with his prosperity and able to pay 6 per cent: I will sign my name to that paper of his (for there has no vestige of any “carte” come)—sign my name to the paper & leave you to fill up the blank with any number of new shares you please.By 1874 the company had housing developments in Birmingham, Gosport, Leeds, and Liverpool, as well as London. John wrote that the company “seems to be prospering, & this year can afford to give a dividend of six per cent with ample reserves. … There is an invitation to take more shares … I don’t think the investment would be a bad one on a small scale, & should be ready to join you in taking five or ten additional Shares each of £10 wh might further the undertaking a little.” I myself have no means of gaining any solid information about the thing at all; but if you can fairly discern that it actually pays 6 per cent on what seems a solid foundation I myself don’t see what objection there cd be to filling up that blank with ‘185’ new shares, so as to make it 200 shares in all or £2000 to each of us funded in that way? Do what you judge fittest after well con[side]ring the circum[stances. . . .]MS torn, some words missing. you are satisfied I will willingly conform, be it 2000, 1000 or whatever you like. I confess I dont like that £6000 lying buried in the drawer here at a loss of 1 or of 1½ per cent annually; but I suppose there is no finding of a safe investment or even of an averagely safe one; and that doubtless is a conclusive objection.

Along with this letter you receive two portraits of Knox, which I intend for Sister Mary and Brother Jamie: I wish you to get Mary’s framed in the simplest way before it go to her. I will be answerable for the postage stamps so soon as you report the thing done.— To yourself these two autotypesAutotype is an image reproduced by a kind of carbon printing process; TC had had them made from the engraving of the portrait in Knight’s Pictorial History of England; see TC to DL, 30 Dec. 1873. John replied, 22 March: “I agree with you in thinking that the portrait of Knox, which you send copies of for Jamie & Mary, is the only one that has any likelihood of being real. … Jean has written today to ask you for a copy of the Knox portrait, & I should like to have one too, if you have any to spare.” Jean wrote, [22 March]: “I am pleased to find that your estimate of the Knox Portrait coincides so entirely with my own. I have steadily maintained that this was the one credible likeness I had ever seen of Knox. The one we have here is the same in every respect tho’ mildewed & otherwise defaced it was given more than 30 years ago to our dear Mother either by yourself or the Dr. … If you could kindly spare me one of the new ones to put in the original oak frame I shall feel greatly obliged—as my present one is not fit to put into it since it was torn off seeking the name at the bottom.” TC had sent the picture to his mother, 5 Sept. 1840; see 12:241TC to MAC, 5 Sept. 1840. are to
represent a confused piece of small work which I have been getting done, to ascertain and help to preserve the real likeness of Knox for the Scottish people so far as poor I, without aid of committees & noisy correspondences, or bronze images either could manage to do it.See TC to LDE, 23 March. I have accordingly examined and studied all the pictures that are discoverable of Knox, some eight or nine in whole; have had the best Artist-advice procurable in England; and have become for my own share as good as clearly convinced that the real likeness of Knox is that [. … . .]MS torn, some words missing. eight or nine, there is not one has the slightest external evidence now procurable. There are about five of them that do not strictly resemble a human creature at all any more than the wooden Highlander at the door of snuff shopsSince the eighteenth century it was common for carved wooden figures of Highland Scots, often in the act of taking a pinch of snuff, to be placed outside tobacco shops. does; while of internal evidence this Somerville portrait seems to me altogether full. I have accordingly got 50 ‘Autotypes’ of this sort done of the print; 12 of them are already come and these to you are the first that I send away. The next 10 or so I will enclose to Laing for distribution among persons near him whom he knows to be rational and interested about Knox: of the remainder I can send more to him if he wishes, and in the meanwhile shove them about among people whom I myself may know to deserve them best. In that way as above said I shall have compendiously done all that lay in my small power towards supplying the want of a monument to Knox,—if that is the conclusion Laing has arrived at, as seems to be intimated by his strict silence to me, ever since you heard last about him.See TC to JAC, 1 Jan. Enough of that small matter therefore.

Another thing I want to speak to you about was, If [you] are not intending a visit to London this season? An excursion into a [. . . .]MS torn, some words missing. you will undoubtedly need; some visit to me seems a still more indubitably natural part of your programme. Tell me what your thoughts & notions are as soon as you can. Maggie
Welsh is still about Liverpool;Maggie Welsh was visiting her brother Alexander and family. her I asked to come for a month; and she consents for I think the 17th of April & onwards. Mary’s literary workMary Aitken was working on a book of Scottish songs; see TC to JAC, 11 Oct. 1873; it was pbd. 30 May (Athenaeum, 30 May). seems pretty near ending; this, and Maggie Welsh about the end of April, are all the data,—except the usual fixtures in that kind (my own weak enough but also steady enough state of health and complete indisposition to go out of my quiescence & silence here): consider them and then consider what your own data are; and let me know as soon as possible what you think about it and about the time of your coming.John replied: “Thank you for your kind invitation to Chelsea again. I have looked forward to the usual visit near the commencement of summer, & may make it earlier if desirable.” I am quite tired out even with this poor bit of dictating, and can only send my blessing to you all, and assurance that I little regret my want of strength, unpleasant as that is for the moment. Tell Jean that she will be called upon for new oatmeal before long, porridge now being a steady item of breakfast. No supper of a satisfactory nature can I yet find out.John replied: “I still find the Crawford brown biscuit my safest supper, with one glass of sherry just before bedtime.” William Crawford (1818–89), took over a biscuit makers in Leith, 1856, which originally sold ship’s biscuits, hard biscuits made from wheat flour and water. The following year TC’s checkbook recorded: “9 March 1875 / Mr W. Crawford / Leith (Biscuits) / £0 .. 14/3d” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753).

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady D [LDE], 23 March. MS typescript copy: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY DERBY

docBody.p: Things go successfully with this Knox Portrait;Lady Derby had been making inquiries on TC’s behalf to locate the current owner of the original Somerville portrait of John Knox; see TC to DL, 30 Dec. 1873. She wrote first to Louisa Harriet Henry, a cousin of the late Lord Somerville, 21 Feb., and forwarded her reply to TC, 24 Feb., which said that the painting belonged to her younger sister, Selina Constance Smyth, who lived with her husband, Ralph Smyth, in Gaybrook, nr. Mullingar, Ireland; TC wrote “Knox at Mullingar” in blue pencil on the back of Lady Derby’s letter. Lady Derby then forwarded to Mrs. Smyth, through Louisa Henry, 17 March, an autotype of an engraving of the portrait, as well as a list of questions drawn up by Robert Scott Tait to try to determine the authenticity of the original portrait. Selina Smyth replied to Lady Derby, 21 March, confirming that TC’s autotype was “a true copy of the original.” She continued: “Mr Ralph Smyth is going next week to Gaybrook where the picture now hangs & will closely examine it and will reply as nearly as he can to the questions put by the Artist. … [I am] going to London next month and will be happy to take the picture over … for Mr Carlyle to see” (MS: NLS 1771.11). but I am sorry I must still trouble you with one message, which I hope will be the last on this subject.

Be still so good therefore as write to Mrs Smyth the brief assurance of my lively and hearty thanks for all that she has done and proposes to do in this affair,Lady Derby replied to Selina Smyth, enclosing TC’s letter. and signify that Mr Smyth’s report (which may be as well addressed to myself?) will be eagerly looked for; and above all that if she will be so very kind as bring the picture itself with her to London for accurate examination, I shall consider it a very particular favour done to myself, and, in the long run perhaps, to all Scotland and even to the world at large or such part of it as still honours its Heroes.
I look hopefully for another little Visit before long.
docBody.closer: I am ever / yours faithfully, / T. Carlyle.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 25 March. MS: NLS 528.9. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Today I send you the £150.3/ for those ‘Artizan dwellings’;John A. Carlyle wrote, 22 March: “After due consideration I think we shd only double our number of Shares in the Artizans &c Dwellings Co & if you will send me a cheque for £150, I will at once order 15 more shares for you & 15 for myself, making 30 for each of us”; see TC to JAC, 21 March. there is added to it 6/6d for the Dumfries Courier people;Mary Aitken noted in TC’s checkbook: “22 March 1874 / Dr J. A. Carlyle (for Shares in ‘Artizans’ dwellings co’ & payment of Courier Newspaper (6/6)) / £150 .. 9 .. 6” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). Presumably TC had arranged for the Dumfries Courier to be sent to him; John sent him a “Receipt for the Courier newspaper,” 26 March. if you wd call or send there & get the enclosed little bill receipted and send it back to me, that also wd be finished.

Your autotype, and Jean’s, of John Knox have I doubt not come to hand. There is no scarcity of autotypes here, but a great difficulty in getting them from the slow German Autotypist, who has them on hand, and with the profoundest courtesy and opulence of promise, breaks every engagement he makes. The name of him is Praetorius,Charles B. Praetorius (1818–1900), Viennese born pioneer photographer, 14 Clareville Grove, Kensington. the man who has served Stirling Maxwell
all thro’ those two immense collections of prints about Charles V,TC presumably refers to Sir William Stirling Maxwell, The Chief Victories of the Emperor Charles the Fifth. Designed by Martin Heemskerck in M.D.LV., and now illustrated with portraits, prints, and notes (London and Edinburgh: privately printed for the Philobiblon Society, 1870), which Stirling Maxwell sent him, March 1870; see 46:177TC to WSM, 24 March 1870; and his Engraved Portraiture of the Sixteenth Century (London and Edinburgh, privately printed, 1872), of which Praetorius was one of the printers. which possibly you may have seen or heard of. I sent a Knox to Stirling-Maxwell, among others, and expressed a hope of seeing him soon, not specifying whether by his effort or my own. Today I mean to send off half a dozen to LaingSee TC to DL, 26 March. for distribution; I will be careful not to give him any spur or hint of such in regard to his Knox enterprise but will merely request him to distribute those five autotypes among the likely persons of his circle. I have made or have got to be made a good deal of investigation about the print compared with the other seven or eight prints extant of Knox, not one of which, not even the Torphichen one can make the least stand before it. This Somerville picture I find is now gone to the heart of Ireland to a place called Gaybrook in the neighbourhood of Mullingar; the last Somerville, it appears, died about 2 years ago, the Peerage becoming extinct; and a Sister of the last Lord’s became proprietress who had married an Irish Gentleman of the name of Smyth. This Lady undertakes in the most handsome manner to answer a set of queries drawn up by Tait, concerning the Picture; nay, what is still handsomer & quite unexpected, volunteers to bring the Picture itself with her to London in about a month, when it can be investigated to the very bottom, or as far as London’s best pictorial knowledge at the present time will go.See TC to DL, 30 Dec. 1873, and TC to LDE, 23 March. Selina Smyth was a sister of the last but one Lord Somerville, and a cousin of the last. Pray be sure to send me back this brave Lady’s note to Lady Derby when you write next. Forster’s to me you may also return. I will send Gordon a copy or two on getting his address.John Gordon, old friend of both TC and John A. Carlyle, who had been ill for some time; John A. Carlyle wrote, 23 March: “I am sure that one of them [Knox portrait autotypes] from you wd give great pleasure to poor John Gordon who is now in such frail health.” John replied, 26 March, with Gordon’s address.

Doctor Blakiston & his WifeDr. Peyton Blakiston (1801–78), and Bessy Blakiston, b. Barnet (ca. 1810–91), old friends of JWC and TC; see 43:267; they had looked after JWC in St. Leonards, March–July 1864. were here half an hour ago, of whom the latter especially sent infinite compliments to you and was as in fact she always is, full of zealous enthusiasm in all manner of retrospective directions. Both people seemed to be in tolerable health, much refreshed by the excellent
spring weather we have.— I send my heart’s love to Sister Jean, my heart’s blessings to you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-DL, 26 March. MS: EUL. Quot: Kaplan, Carlyle 515; Scotsman, 6 June 1932. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO DAVID LAING

docBody.p:
The Knox enterprize seems to be rather hanging fire, or indeed I can suppose you find the matter difficult and complex, and requiring much deliberation before it even can be got begun. Nor is it the the purpose of putting any spur on that matter, or at all interfering with it, that I now write. But occasionally, almost ever since you last heard of me, I have been investigating what Portraits of Knox I could fall in with, and consulting the best Artistic Authorities (some of them reckoned of the highest order here) in regard to them; the general result of which is a clear and unanimous preference given to the Somerville Portrait, concerning which you have often heard me speak. Some eight or nine Portraits of Knox exist in the world, but except this last, and probably the Torphichen one, and the Glasgow College one, there is none judged to have the least real likelihood or credibility. Beza’s Icon, which might seem to have a solid external authority turns out to have none whatever; Beza’s Book of Icones, as Stirling-Maxwell has taught us, and as you doubtless know, was translated into French at Geneva, and published there the very year after Beza first came out;William Stirling Maxwell, Examples of the Engraved Portraiture of the Sixteenth Century (London and Edinburgh: Privately Printed, 1872); he includes two pictures of Knox (94), one from Beza’s Icones, and one from the French translation by Simon Goulart (1543–1628), French reformer, Les vrais pourtraits des hommes illustres en piété et doctrine (Geneva, 1581), commenting: “It will be observed that these two portraits, published by the same publisher, within a year of each other, differ considerably from each other, both in features and expression” (Examples of the Engraved Portraiture xxii). and in that translation (done, we may conclude, by a neighbour and probably a friend of Beza’s, in free communication with him) Beza’s Icon of Knox is silently withdrawn altogether, and a fattish kind of figure, supposed to mean Tyndale, the first English Translator of the Bible, is substituted in its room!In Goulart’s translation the portrait of Knox has been mistakenly replaced by one of William Tyndale (ca. 1494–1536; ODNB), English reformer (Les vrais pourtraits 204); Tyndale is mentioned (Les vrais pourtraits 190), but with no picture. This it seems to me puts Beza quite out of
court, and closes his mouth as a witness on the point in question. The Glasgow Portrait,The portrait of Knox held by the University of Glasgow is engraved in John Pinkerton, The Scottish Gallery; or Portraits of Eminent Persons of Scotland (1799). John Pinkerton (1758–1826; ODNB), historian and poet, wrote: “This portrait in profile, from the painting in the university of Glasgow, corresponds with the common delineations, and with that in Beza’s Icones, who being the friend of this reformer, could hardly be misled” (The Scottish Gallery 73). and, perhaps in a higher degree, the Torphichen one, of which I have seen three different Engravings, might be conceived to mean the same man, Knox, at an earlier stage of his life; but in respect to artistic merit, likelihood of detail or liveliness of expression, cannot stand the least comparison with the Somerville portrait. By the way, my lively niece misled me into believing (by an example at Dumfries) that the Torphichen and the Somerville are identical, but it turned out, about eight and forty hours after;—indeed as fast as the railway could run to and fro,—to be entirely an error!See TC to DL, 30 Dec. 1873. The five or six or perhaps seven other portraits, not only have no resemblance to Knox, but most of them no resemblance to any human creature at all,—more than the Highlander at the doors of Snuff shops can pretend to; so that it appears on the whole that of external evidence there is none whatever, for any of the so-called portraits of Knox, the Somerville one included; but that for the Somerville one the internal evidence is as complete as it could be, and for all the others, Glasgow & Torphichen included, internal evidence is altogether, or as good as altogether wanting. My own firm persuasion is, as it has long been that as near as such a thing could or can ever be certain, it is certain & humanly credible that this Portrait, evidently by a first-rate Artist, is actually the Portrait of Knox.

As the Engravings seem to be very scarce, I have had 50 Autotypes of it executed, of which I now send you six, one for yourself,Laing wrote a draft reply, [late March]: “Thanks for the Portrait called John Knox. I know it well—not so the Papal attestation. I would rather have christened it T.C. indignant at D.L. for presuming in such a matter, to call in question his infallibility! … Now to come back to the … various oil-paintings with the Reformer’s name, no one has any feasible title to be held as genuine. I have met with nothing to change my opinion … that the woodcuts of Beza 1580 and the engraving of Hondius in Verherden 1602, must be held as the standards to judge of his likeness. Beza had no concern with the French translation 1583 which contains several additional, and by some unaccountable mistake, that of William Tyndale was inserted at p. 204 instead of its right place at p. 190.” Hendrick Hondius I (1573–1650), Flemish engraver; Jacobus Verheiden (ca. 1590–1618), Praestantium aliquot theologorum (1602). five to be given away to the most valued of your fellow labourers;—if you want more, I will willingly send you more: perhaps you know people in Glasgow, in Perth, Aberdeen or other towns and localities who take an interest in this matter, and would be
interested to have a copy from me; if so, I pray you, speak. Sir William Stirling Maxwell has got a copy. For behoof of Edinburgh I send today to John Gordon two, one for himself; ditto, ditto to MassonTC had asked David Masson to give one of the autotypes to the Edinburgh Philosophical Institution, and had written at the bottom of the picture: “The one portrait I could ever believe to be a likeness of John Knox” (see TC to RHO, 10 April). Masson wrote, 12 April: “All your directions in your welcome note of March 27 were at once attended to. Putting aside, after much inspection, the copy of the autotype you kindly meant for myself, I delivered the other, the very day it came, to Mr Bowie, the Secretary of the Philosophical Institution, with a note explaining the circumstances, and containing a sentence extracted from your letter. … I see that the portrait, neatly framed, has been hung up in the Library, where all may see it.” Henry Bowie (1812–85) secretary and treasurer of the Edinburgh Philosophical Institution; TC was elected president for life, 1868; see 45:163TC to HB, 10 Aug. 1868; his presidency was re-affirmed at their annual meeting, 31 March, together with their grateful acceptance of the portrait (Scotsman, 1 April). & as yet no more at all.— I ought to mention that the Picture has now gone to Ireland; the last Somerville having died two years ago, and a Sister married in that country, being now proprietress: this lady offers in the most generous manner, not only to send me an answer to various queries on the subject, but to bring up the picture itself in about a month to London, whither she is herself coming. It can then be investigated to the bottom, or as far as our utmost amount of artistic intelligence can go.

closer.salute:
Believe me / dear Laing
Yours always truly,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 1 April. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p:
Permit me to report that I have received Mr Smyth’s obliging Answers, everyone of them so lucidly perspicuous, complete and exact, to the various queries concerning the Knox Picture at Gaybrook;See TC to LDE, 23 March; Selina Smyth sent Ralph Smyth’s answers to TC, 28 March. and that I beg to return him many hearty thanks for the trouble he must have taken, as well as to yourself for having engaged him in that kind act of service to me. The crowning event will be the arrival in London of the Picture itself, which I eagerly expect now, in something like “a month hence.” The Portrait is universally accepted as genuine by all I have shown it to here (some of them, persons of high artistic
quality, and all of them experienced in such objects): but as there is little or no external evidence though the internal is so perfect, it will be highly interesting and expedient to have the Picture carefully examined and every detail of it scanned by the best skill that exists in England.

In Edinburgh, where, you may perhaps have heard there is or was some confused intention of a Monument to Knox, the feasibility or total downbreak of that pious intention, it seems to me will depend altogether upon the credibility or otherwise of this Picture now in your possession.

These two fresh Autotypes I venture to send, partly on the suspicion that your first Copy, the only one I then had, was of inferior quality; partly in the notion that perhaps there might be some friend of Gaybrook & of Knox to whom you might think of some time furnishing a copy.
With many respects and many thanks, I beg to remain,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-RH [RHO], 3 April. MS: NLS 3706.89. Pbd: Wilson, Carlyle 6:326 inc. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Robert Horn, Vice-Dean of the Faculty of Advocates.
bibl.head: TC TO ROBERT HORN

docBody.p:
I can with great readiness, as in gratitude and mere love of truth I am bound to do, give my clear testimony as to the public uses of the Advocates Library.Robert Horn wrote, 27 March: “Presuming on my acquaintance with your brother Dr Carlyle … I take the liberty of asking your attention to a Statement relative to the Advocates’ Library here. … Having been Senior Curator of the Library for four years past, I have done my best to get it put in as good working order as the resources of our body would admit. … Might I ask you to … drop me a few lines simply saying what your estimate is of our Library, and whether you found us willing to make its treasures available to those for whom it is mainly intended,—what I term ‘true workmen’?” John A. Carlyle wrote, 8 April: “The Mr Horn whose letter about the Advocates’ Library you forwarded to me, is an old acquaintance, a wealthy advocate in large practice, noted for punctilious accuracy in all matters, & very zealous for the interests of the Library about which he takes great pains & has always done.” I found it my one resource for serious reading while first attempting literature in Scotland,TC first used the Library in 1820; see 1:293TC to MAC, 6 Dec. 1820. and still remember with thankful pleasure, the free access and useful help afforded me there, while my claims on it, if any, were all in a prospective or incipient state. I was at once courteously admitted, I forget on what Member’s introduction, probably on the late Sir Wm Hamilton’s.Sir William Hamilton (1788–1856; ODNB); see Carlyle, Reminiscences 427–33. I had free admittance at all times afterwards, and the best accomodation for
silent study, and such helps, bibliographical and other as I have never met with elsewhere, and found the Library by very far the best I had ever been in, and indeed, putting all qualities together, one of the best I have ever since become acquainted with. It is incomparably the best of all the Libraries we have in Scotland, and in fact the only Library worth calling such, to which literary aspirants and known literary people, except connected with Colleges, have any practical admittance; an Institution which may to Scotland in that respect be called invaluable.

My clear testimony therefore is, that, essentially, it belongs to Scotland at large,—such the liberal practice of the Honourable Faculty whose property it especially is,—and that it fairly deserves all reasonable help and support from whatever calls itself a Government in that country.The Advocates’ Library was formally inaugurated in 1689 as the law library of the Faculty of Advocates. Under the terms of the Copyright Act, 1710, the Library was given the right to claim a copy of every book published in the United Kingdom. The Glasgow Herald, 10 Jan. 1874, summarized the financial predicament of the Library: “The funds of the incorporation had been all but exhausted upon buildings, and in the maintenance of a staff for the accommodation and use of the books given to them by the Legislature, with the view of carrying out the policy of the Copyright Acts. Not only had the available capital of the Faculty thus been expended, but its whole estimated prospective income had been forestalled for the future management of the library already accumulated.” The Faculty had recommended in a proposal to the government, 1 May 1873, that: “the Legislature should, 1st, provide to the Faculty the sum necessary for the erection of a hall (fronting George IV. Bridge Street) as a reading-room for the public. … The Faculty … were to provide the ground required for the purpose. … (2d) That the Legislature should provide an annual grant of say £2000 to assist in the maintenance of the increased staff that should thereby be rendered necessary, and otherwise for making the library more thoroughly available to persons engaged in literary pursuits than is now practicable” (Scotsman, 12 Jan. 1874). This proposal was rejected, 5 May 1873, by the then chancellor of the exchequer, Robert Lowe (1811–92; ODNB), partly on the grounds that this was a local matter for Edinburgh to finance. I think you have a solid right to bring your claims before the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and it will give me real pleasure to hear that they are supported, say, by Scotch M.P.s, seriously considered, and in fine acceded to by that high Functionary[.]The new chancellor of the exchequer (1874–80) was Sir Stafford Northcote (1818–87; ODNB). At the annual meeting of the Faculty of Advocates, 14 Jan., a report was presented with the results of the 1873 petition, with recommendations for a further petition; principally that “If … the House of Commons should prefer to have the principle already so long acted on still carried out—viz., of having a copy of every book published in the United Kingdom preserved for reference in the Advocates’ Library, then it was suggested that the Faculty were entitled to expect the Legislature to give them the means of doing so by a grant in aid of the expenditure which they had hitherto been in use to supply entirely from their own funds”; and that “The efficient maintenance of the Advocates’ Library is an object of importance to the nation at large, and not to the Faculty or to the city of Edinburgh only” (Scotsman, 12 Jan.). It was not until 1925 that the National Library of Scotland was established, incorporating all the Advocates’ Library’s non-law holdings.

Your privilege of having all the new Books sent to you under charge of putting and keeping them all in order and readiness seems to me a penalty rather, and even, considering what new Books usually now are, and tend ever more to become a very severe one;—I could almost venture to counsel that your “new Reading-Room, near Geo. IV. Bridge,” should be furnished exclusively with these, or what remain of these after your selection of the hundredth or thousandth new book for the main Library, which properly belongs to a far more serious class of readers.
docBody.closer:
Believe me, dear Sir,
Yours sincerely, / T. Carlyle.

postscript.p: Ps. The Two Knox Autotypes are intended one for yourself, the other for whatever person or public Institution, Reading-room, Club-room or the like you may think serviceablest for diffusing among Scotsmen some possible idea of what the real likeness of the greatest, truest and most Scotch of Scotsmen history knows of, was.— Mr Laing dissents rather fiercely from this Picture, his grounds seem to me surprisingly invalid, but don’t provoke him farther by showing him the print.Horn replied, 6 April: “Your most kind present of a copy of the ‘Knox’ you believe in would have been at any time highly prized, but it comes more than usually opportunely just at this time, when you and my delightful friend ‘old David’ as I profanely call him, are conspiring, now that the absurd ‘Knox Memorial’ bubble has burst in the hands of the Clergy, who got their fingers on it, to get up a simple Statue of glorious John, to be placed somewhere about St Giles!”

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 4 April. MS: NLS 528.11. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Most likely you would get the poor draggle of a Glasgow Newspaper with Hutchison Stirling’s Letter,James Hutchison Stirling (1820–1909; ODNB), Scottish philosopher, known to TC since 1840. which were enclosed for you in Jean’s parcel the other day. It appears Emerson has actually consented to stand candidate for the Glasgow Rectorship,Stirling was the honorary president of the Glasgow University Independent Students Club, who wished to invite Emerson to stand for the rectorship of the university. Stirling wrote to Emerson, 17 Feb., to declare his support for the invitation (Amelia Hutchison Stirling, James Hutchison Stirling: His Life and Work [1912] 261–66). Emerson telegraphed his agreement, following it with letters to both Stirling and the Student Club, 18 March, expressing his deep gratitude, and his pledge to the students that “if elected, I shall certainly endeavour to meet your wishes, and those of the University, as to the time and the duties which the office shall require” (Glasgow Herald, 8 April). College newspaper and Stirling’s letter untraced. and is contented to cross and re-cross the Atlantic
for the sole purpose of delivering an address to the poor gorbs of student creatures there; a fact I had vaguely heard of, but could only ascribe to Emerson’s great ignorance of the kind of phenomenon he wd actually encounter here. The matter had gone altogether out of my head when the Hutchison Letter and poor College newspaper reached me here the day they were sent away to you. The Hutchison request that I or any grown-up man should “speak the decisive word” or at all appear in such a water-gruel transaction appeared to me completely foolish, and so I spoke no word at all in the matter, nor shall,— as you wd already gather.

Laing’s Letter, on receipt of the Knox Autotypes,For the draft of Laing’s letter, see TC to DL, 26 March. along with which I had written a candid and altogether kindly report to Laing about the 8 or 9 Knox Portraits I had been examining, struck me with a kind of ludicrous surprise, mixed with pity, & accordingly has had no answer, nor, till some quite new opportunity occur, shall have any. Poor Laing must be getting into dotage or irritability, I almost think; otherwise the only feeling one could have would be something of the ludicrous and amusing. My Pope’s Bull, therefore, imposing upon Laing a necessity to believe my opinion instead of his own shall remain quietly what it is, the statement of an indubitable fact of a nature altogether personal to myself, and all Laing’s poor project of a “monument to Knox” or of any body’s “monument” at present shall drop quietly into the inane. I know not if you have Laing’s painful and praiseworthy edition of Knox upon your shelves; but the notion he persists in about Beza’s foolish blotch of a “picture” & supports, in this enclosed Letter, and at p. 8o vol I is amongst the feeblest and foolishest imaginable.See TC to DL, 10 Dec. 1873. In the prefatory “Advertisement” to The Works of John Knox, Laing wrote: “I was very desirous of obtaining a Portrait of the Reformer, to accompany this volume. Hitherto all my inquiries have failed to discover any undoubted original painting. … In the meantime, a tolerably accurate fac-simile is given of the wood-cut portrait of Knox, included by Theodore Beza, in his volume entitled ‘icones.’” He added in two footnotes: “That Lord Torphichen’s picture at Calder House is a portrait of Knox, cannot be doubted, and it may have been copied from an older painting; but at best it is a harsh and disagreeable likeness, painted at least a century after Knox’s death” and “A French translation of Beza’s volume appeared in 1581, with several additional portraits; but it is somewhat remarkable that a totally different portrait should have been substituted in place of that of Knox. … From its marked resemblance, I am convinced, that the portrait substituted was intended for William Tyndale.— When the engraved pseudo-portraits of Knox are brought together, it is quite ludicrous to compare the diversity of character which they exhibit” (The Works of John Knox 1:viii–ix). See that same p. VIII if you have it at hand: to what
Laing has there said there is only to be added, that Goulart, who the year after Beza’s Icones came out (1580), printed his translation of Beza into French in the same city of Geneva, with Beza’s Portrait of Knox quietly abstracted, and something like one of Tyndale clapped in instead,—was by no means a hungry pamphleteer, but a man of conspicuous dignity in the clerical office, Beza’s successor in fact, 20 years after,The Presidency of the Genevan Company of Pastors was held by Beza, 1564–80, and by Goulart (see TC to DL, 26 March), 1607–12; during the intervening 27 years the presidency was changed weekly. & a man in daily intercourse & communication with Beza, & that neither Beza nor he had ever seen Knox. But enough of Laing & his ignorant fatuity and total want of either skill or feeling in regard to portraits. You observe he is liquidating, at the rate of 10/ in the pound, the old funds collected in the Knox Fiasco of last year; and there his and my concern with any Knox monument may as well rest to the end of the chapter.The Knox Memorial Committee, 8 Dec. 1873, decided to hold a competition, open until May 1874, to create a marble statue of Knox; see TC to DL, 10 Dec. 1873. John A. Carlyle replied, 8 April: “The letter of David Laing about the Knox portrait is curious. I saw him after the first meeting about a monument to Knox. … He had been forced to take the chair as no one else wd take it. The meeting had been most noisy & disgraceful; & poor Laing looked excited & flushed in a high degree. … [T]he second meeting … turned out as bad as the first & as disorderly. I think he got his nerves shaken very much by those meetings, & must have been looking forward with some bitterness & anxiety to the settlement meeting of which he speaks when your letter with the portrait came to him, & took away all hope, I shd say, of getting any statue … wh would be another rather sore trial for him.” Laing’s remarks on the Knox Memorial committee are not included in the draft.

We went to dine, Mary and I, the night before last, with Forster and the famed and rather flagrant Earl of Shaftesbury:Anthony Ashley Cooper, 7th earl of Shaftesbury; he was famous for his philanthropic efforts, particularly around living and working conditions for the laboring poor; see 17:324–25TC to MAC, 30 March 1844. the dinner like all Forster’s was beautifully perfect quant au physique [as to appearance] was perfect but quant au moral [as to mood]— I found the Earl, whom I had not seen for many years a distinctly rather fluffy article & parted without the least ardour of wish to see him again, especially on similar terms. Worse still, as Mary and I were walking homewards, we were overtaken by a sharp front shower, took refuge in an accidental hansom (unfortunately of new fashion, with one great lid instead of the two little doors there used to be) and after a dirtyish progress to Cheyne Row, were there assaulted or at least I was by a violent smash from the new fashioned lid; driven by the high wind, and hitting me right on the nose, happily without farther damage except a little bleeding in that organ: avoid new fashioned hansoms again; that shall be a steady rule with me. — Mme VenturiEmilie Venturi. has come in for Mary & is waiting down stairs. I
must therefore end abruptly. With my blessing to one & all of you. Ever your affectionate,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 7 April. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: Many thanks for your highly welcome announcement. On Saturday afternoon, about half-past four, I hope to have the honour of waiting on you at Almond’s Hotel, and of settling about the invaluable Picture,Selina Smyth wrote, 5 April: “I hope to arrive in London early on Saturday next & remain until Monday Morn at Almond’s Hotel. … Will you kindly let me know at what hour you will call & see my picture of John Knox, as I shall then be able to make arrangements with you as to the lending of the portrait for inspection.” Almond’s Hotel, 6–7 Clifford Street, Piccadilly. which I am at last to see. Should I not find you arrived, I will call about the same hour next day, Sunday though it be,—for in truth it is a work of “necessity” this of examining the Picture, and almost of “mercy”Cf. Matt. 12:1–12. as well!— With many regards,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAF, 10 April. Pbd: Dunn, CLF III:595–96. Quot: Waldo H. Dunn, Froude and Carlyle (1930) 15. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature (Dunn, Froude and Carlyle 15).
bibl.head: TC TO J. A. FROUDE

docBody.p:
I am very much obliged by the kind little note you were so good as [to] write me the other day. Alas, alas, I understand too well the state of ‘torpor or half torpor’ you speak of; but you have chosen the one good method of meeting the Inexorable & Unalterable which has fallen upon you;Froude was mourning the death of his wife, Henrietta; see TC to JAC, 14 Feb. and by valiant patience, and the steady determination to work while it is called Today,Cf. Heb. 3:13. the silent flight of Time will gradually soothe into pious composure the thoughts
which are at present too painful to flesh and blood. The little bit of work you are at present engaged on is naturally above all others interesting to me:TC presumably refers to Froude’s work on the “Letters and Memorials of Jane Welsh Carlyle,” which TC had entrusted to him, June 1871; see 47:183TC to WILL, 6 Feb. 1873, 216–17TC to JA, 7 July 1871, and 227TC to JAF, 26 Sept. 1871. that also is according to all human calculation a thing you will soon have to do; and surely it is wise to be thinking of that withal while it is called Today.

The Longmans have never yet sent me the Irish Book;Froude’s The English in Ireland (see TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1873). vols. 2 and 3 were pbd. 2 April, advertised in the Athenaeum, 4 April: “The English in Ireland in the Eighteenth Century. By J. A. Froude, M.A. Vols II. and III. price 32s. completing the Work, in 3 vols. 8vo. price 48s.” whence I infer that you forgot to order them,—but that you will now at once do it. Brother John at Dumfries, according to the last post, is waiting in daily expectation of it,John A. Carlyle wrote, 8 April: “I see Froude’s book is out, & I have ordered the last two vols & expect them daily.” and probably at this moment sitting greedily in studious perusal of it. The Review in the Times,The Times critic wrote, 4 April: “The volumes that complete Mr. Froude’s history prolong the notes he struck in his first one. Their ‘argument’ is the absolute incapacity of the Irish for self-government. … No dispassionate man who has respect for the well-being either of the British Empire or of the Irish people can read the book carefully and continue to have the smallest belief in Home Rule. We do not pretend that Mr. Froude shows any of the serene impartiality of the Judge. … But we are bound to say that he proves his case in the main beyond a cavil, and generally justifies the honest vigour of his language.” which probably I should not have known of except for a hint by accident from Rector Blunt,Abel Gerald Wilson Blunt (1827–1902), rector of St. Luke’s, Chelsea. pleased me on the whole very well; except for some external editorial flourishes by way of hinting to the public the supreme impartiality & perfect freedom from intolerance in those puddle-dockPuddle-dock: place or state of corruption. quarters, the Able EditorJohn Thadeus Delane (1817–79; ODNB), ed. of the Times 1841–77. completely adopts, with due recognition of artistic skill on the Author’s part, the whole Narrative with the stern inferences drawn from it:—I welcomed this as a glad omen of what the general conclusion of solid & not quite stolid Englishmen on the subject will be. The only other review I have seen is the Newspaper slip here enclosed, due to my Brother’s scissors, is review from the Glasgow Herald,The Glasgow Herald critic declared, 6 April: “The essential proposition of Mr. Froude’s book is, that Ireland was in the eighteenth century and that she is still unfit for Parliamentary Government. … In the 18th [century] we had to govern Ireland by a mixture of military force and unblushing corruption, because by maintaining an Irish Parliament we gave the Irish members the opportunity of blocking the path of whatever policy we wished to follow. Often enough it was a bad and foolish policy—but good or bad it would, Mr. Froude believes, have been the same thing. The two countries differ essentially in many things, but they have got to rub on together, and the way to make it impossible is to re-establish an Irish Parliament, which could only end in a repetition of the Irish rebellion. These are the propositions sustained in this brilliant book.” reckoned the principal or all
but the principal of Scottish Newspapers at present: in this I have read an equally favourable omen of Scotland in regard to the Book. In fact it seems to me likely to have a great sale, to do a world of good & to be important soon & for all time coming in totally altering England’s hedious [hideous] manner of proceeding with her ever vexed “Bermoothes” of a Sister Island—hagridden, too, to a singular degree as BermoothesCf. The Tempest 1.2, Shakespeare’s name for the islands of Bermuda, which were “hagridden” by the witch Sycorax. used to be!

What you say about my coming to youFroude, with some of his children, was staying at Crogan House, near Corwen, Merionethshire, Wales. is full of kindness & you may depend on it I shall not forget it, but will on all sides earnestly consider it, & if there seem a feasibility, shall be right willing to embark in the adventure, but an adventure it certainly is, especially in the article of quiet sleep, which is at once so indispensable & so difficult a condition to fulfil. Meanwhile I think at least you might be on the outlook for a good Welsh pony or a pair of ponies suitable [for] philosophic riding;—or indeed they would be useful to the young ladies independent of philosophy. So far, I think you might safely go.

Mary saw Miss FroudeFroude’s eldest da., Georgina Margaret, had apparently remained in London, visiting relatives (Dunn, Froude 2:389). last week. We have not heard whether they are all gone to you, but think it likely they are. I have been much whirled about within the last week in regard to Edinburgh controversies about the Knox Portrait, and more especially about the arrival of the Somerville Picture itself, which is to come ipso corpore [the body itself] tomorrow and thereafter be scanned with all the pictorial science London can produce for us.

I need not say that I miss you much here & am like to do till we meet again. Do not forget how much I should like a little word from your own hand now and then. Write whatever comes uppermost & be sure always of a grateful welcome to it. I will reply whenever fairly possible, when impossible or quasi-impossible, as too often the case, never mind.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-RH [RHO], 10 April. MS: NLS 3706.91. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO ROBERT HORN

docBody.p: Your two Letters have been very amusing to me, and combined with his own Letter, give me a lively representation of the truly worthy and excellent Laing, & of his troubles in regard to the Knox Monument of the past & ditto of the future, which he still contemplates. I should be the farthest in the world from wishing to irritate his friendly mind for one moment; but there are two things evident to me: first, that to set up a false image and label it Knox the truest of men, would be a solecism beyond match; & second, that Laing’s notions as to the real Portrait of Knox are thoroughly dark and without basis.Robert Horn wrote, 7 April: “Since writing you yesterday I have had a chat with friend David on the vexed question of Knox portraits. I enjoy nothing more than poking him up a bit on any subject, the result being a never failing sense of his imperturbable good humour and the acquisition of an amount of ‘actual knowledge’ … to me at least quite astonishing.” He continued: “David believes that Beza, who knew Knox personally,—he says,—could not have published a head which was not a fair likeness of the man, at least. … With his usual spirit he threatens to get up a rival head to your favourite, which he says he will send you and me. It will be fun to have the two,—each with its testimonial from two such worshippers of Knox.” In regard to Knox’s writings and the leaving of a perennial picture of Knox’s mind, surely no man alive has equalled or been second to the magnanimous David, whose efforts have been so persevering, heroic, and at last victorious in this respect; for which all Scottish men of this and of the following generations are his debtors:—but as to his Beza Portrait of Knox (more like the figure-head of a ship than like Knox or any other Son of Adam) & as to his faith about the mystery of Beza’s Print & the silent withdrawal of it next year by Goulart, his translator into French (see Laing’s Works of Knox vol i p VIII), I must say it fills me with amazement. I add only, that Goulart was, in 1581, no hungry pamphleteer, but a man of high distinction at Geneva, & indeed over Europe, and Beza’s official Brother (who afterwards succeeded Beza in chief priestship) who must have been in daily intercourse with Beza, and that neither Beza nor he had ever seen the face of Knox. That Note at p. VIII of our friend David seems to me unspeakable;—though I would not for the world say a word to him about it in his present mood and predicament!—

figure.p:
Somerville portrait of John Knox with Thomas Carlyle’s annotations
Courtesy of the National Library of Scotland

Portrait of John Owen
Courtesy of the National Library of Scotland

docBody.p:
But the fact is, the Somerville Knox Picture, such the great kindness of its owner is on its road to London due tomorrow; when I expect to see it, and settle about having it examined to the bottom by the most perfect skill we can
muster round it in this country. With a view to that enterprise, I want very much from Laing, if you can gently borrow it, or from yourself (if you have a copy) the loan for a three weeks of a certain Penny’s Engraving of the Torphichen Portrait of Knox,Horn replied, 11 April: “The Torphichen portrait given by McCrie, and of which Penny’s is a fuller engraving [Laing] thinks is substantially the same in features & character with Beza’s wood-cut, and is the most likely to be near the truth of any of the oil pictures, from Knox’s intimacy with that family. Laing got only a few days ago, a copy of Penny’s engraving, which … he has with his wonted kindness offered to place under my care to take up with me to London next Thursday.” Laing noted: “It was engraved for Dr. M’Crie’s work; and, on a large scale, there is a most careful engraving of it, by a very ingenious and modest artist, Mr. William Penny of Mid-Calder” (The Works of John Knox 1:viii). William Penny (ca. 1788–1867), engraver. Thomas McCrie, D.D. (1772–1835; ODNB), secession minister and ecclesiastical historian, The Life of Knox (Edinburgh, 1811). which Laing describes as by far the best, & which is not to be found here. This is all I really wanted with the present Letter I have given you the trouble of reading. Solely farther, I will offer you the enclosed picture of John OwenJohn Owen (1616–83; ODNB), reforming minister, supporter of Oliver Cromwell. by way of silent answer to Laing’s opinion that the Autotype Knox with his tippet & small rational beard (Laing’s second Knox in his vol. VILaing includes two portraits of Knox, the first taken from Beza’s Icones and the second from Verheiden’s Praestantium aliquot theologorum, by Hondius (see TC to DL, 26 March), which Laing believed to be a copy of the first; see Laing, The Works of John Knox 1:xiii and 6:xiii. has a beard which unless he meant to tie it up every morning in a slip knot, seems to me an irrational); & by this engraving Laing, I hope, may begin to convince himself that the Cromwellian divine wore bands instead of tippet & had shaved away all beard, irrational or otherwise.Horn wrote, 7 April: “[Laing] thinks the dress in Lord Somerville’s Knox is of the time of Cromwell [a century later than Knox], and so could not have been done from life.” In the picture Owen wears clerical neck bands and is clean shaven, while the Somerville Knox wears a tippet and a modest beard. For the comparison of Knox and Owen’s dress, see TC to RHO, 10 April. If you care in the least to keep the print, be altogether certain that I shall think it well disposed of.
Believe me, dear Sir,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 April. MS: NLS 528.11. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I must not let the week pass without sending you a word, though the usual fact holds good that I have nothing particular to say. Last night I expected to have been at this hour in presence of the benificent Irish lady & the Knox picture;Selina Smyth; see TC to SCS, 7 April. but at 10 o’clock, by the last post of the evening, there came a letter from her husband, to announce that she had unluckily “sprained her wrist”Ralph Smyth wrote from Castle Bellingham, 9 April: “I am sorry to say that Mrs Smyth will not be in London on Saturday or I am afraid for a few days. She sprained her right wrist badly yesterday which detains us.” & that their journey & the picture’s was inevitably delayed for a few days. The disappointment was not great, so feeble was my humour and condition. I rather felt a kind of dull joy that the infinitesimally small transaction was postponed to hoffentlich [hopefully] “a better time.” Nothing particular ails me: I daily bathe, walk out a mile or more and swallow, not entirely with disgust, my poor porridge & weak milk. But I am very weak & idle, totally without energy for any real employment, except reading Books, for most part, if I hoped for any instruction from them altogether empty, too often disgustingly stupid: & in fact the only vestige of real work I can still be said to have on hand is this of the Irish Portrait of Knox; which is all I can contribute towards his “Monument”;— & truly this will be something, if by such simple means I can give the Scottish people a real knowledge instead of an imaginary & stupidly false of what Knox in his face & figure was actually like. The biggest Monument, “higher than Arthur’s Seat,”See TC to JAC, 1 Jan. could essentially do no more, & this, thanks to Tait & other Lieutenants I have is already I can reckon almost as good as done. I mean to have about three Artists,TC consulted primarily Joseph Edgar Boehm, Robert Scott Tait, Samuel Laurence (see TC to JAC, 25 Feb.), and Henry Merritt (1822–77; ODNB), picture conservator and artist; see Carlyle, Works 30:362–67. or men really skilled in the history of Art to say, after earnest survey, what the certain or probable approximate date of the Painting is & to set their names to two or three words of testimony accordingly. We will then, I am still uncertain by whom, have an honest photograph taken with these names at the bottom; & let the Photographer, who may fairly see a considerable sale ahead, shove it abroad into the world, especially the Scottish world & leave it there to whatever fate can gradually befal it. This is my small shot in regard to the enormous Knox Monument; shot
which as you see is nearly primed & loaded &, once fired off, I end. Laing’s infinitely meritorious Works of Knox afford to all mortals that care about it an imperishable or long enduring Monument of Knox’s mind, & the good Laings incredulity as to the picture of his body shall never be objected to him or ascribed to a cause in the least degree criminal.

You will be amused by your friend Horn’s two letters on this subject, which set me fairly laughing: I wrote again yesterday to Horn, asking from him the loan, for three weeks, of that Penny’s Engraving of the Torphichen Picture to be ready against the Irish arrival. I sent him also a copy of the excellent print (given in Cromwell, Library Ed.) of John Owen to convince Laing in an especially mild way that the Somerville Knox’s costume was by no means a Cromwellian one; Horn was also to see if he cd borrow from Laing (in case Horn’s own resources failed in that matter) Laing’s copy of the Penny article required here.See TC to RHO, 10 April. But in any & all cases he was charged to treat the excellent Laing with the most delicate forbearance, caution & softness, & avoid before all things irritating his honest & at present heavy-laden mind. I daresay yr interpretation of him & the humour he is in was perfectly just.See TC to JAC, 4 April. I avoid writing to him altogether on this sad topic. There is also a small note from poor Gordon,John Gordon; see TC to JAC, 25 March. which you need not take the trouble of returning to me. You may, if it is quite easy for you, send back all three of Horn’s;John A. Carlyle replied, 12 April: “I at once return Horn’s three notes. He is a solid punctual man, has the best collection of pictures I ever saw in Edinr, has considerable skill in painting himself, & is faithful & punctual in all he undertakes.” I am still interested about his Advocates’ Library-affair; & shall be really sorry if it do not succeed. Froude’s Letter also I beg you to return. The Glasgow Herald review of him was intended to be sent yesterday but got missed in the hurry;—small matter as it nearly altogether coincided with the view taken by The Times. Forster, whom I saw yesterday, is still poorly, & at times very dejected; but he keeps busy with some work about SwiftForster was working on The Life of Jonathan Swift. Volume the First. 1667–1711 (1875). which he has on hand; and certainly he slowly improves. Mary is just on the point of ending a successful little Article on ConstableUntraced. which she is completing, as if by miracle.— Our paper, as you see, is utterly done, & it is not worth while wasting more on such inania. I send my heart’s love to Jean whom I should like to hear from again though I have no right to ask such a thing. My poor blessing on you, one & all

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 17 April. MS: NLS 528.12. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Essentially I have nothing to say this Friday, but I write a word all the same. Our Irish Lady with the picture and sprained wrist has not yet made appearance or sent any sign, but as nothing but the wrist detains her we confidently look for her soon. Tait in the meanwhile has been busy making preparations, in particular, has collected four or five choice engravings of so-called portraits of Knox; has been providing pictorial experts &c for survey of the Somerville picture; & on the whole seems to me to have rather sound ideas about the probable work and authorship of that. Painted, he guesses as probable by one Porbus,Frans Pourbus, the elder (1545–81), Flemish painter, living in Antwerp. a famed Netherlands Artist who was in England (Tait asserts) in the last decade of Knox’s Life, and who painted an excellent BuchananGeorge Buchanan (1506–82; ODNB), Scottish poet, historian, and administrator; his portrait, attributed to Pourbus, belongs to the Royal Society. the style of which considerably resembles this of Knox and his Porbus’s name on the Engravings of it,—one of which I well know here for many years back. In short, I do rather hope for a good issue to this poor enterprise, but will trouble you no more on the subject—and only wind up by enclosing Horn’s last letter to me, which announces his advent hither in the end of next week and the worthy Laing’s distracted theories beliefs & scepticisms in regards to this the “one real likeness of Knox.”Horn wrote, 11 April, announcing his forthcoming visit to London, and listing in full Laing’s reasons for believing the Beza portrait to be the true one.

Maggie Welsh, you perhaps already know, is expected here tomorrow “to stay for a month.” Mary seems to intend being off very shortly after, though as I often explain to her, there is no need whatever of the least hurry; but she seems to be mainly done with her various literary enterprises, and has besides seemed to me and to herself and others in a rather weakly way of health: so that a spell of country air & rustic ways of living may really do her sensible good.—Long ago, I spoke something to you about your own coming hither; but you yourself have never since said anything practical about it. Nor do I wish to hurry or disturb you about the matter, but only wish you to know at all times that your apartment is ready for you here, & that our Spring weather seems to be getting more & more agreeable.John A. Carlyle replied, 21 April, reporting Mary’s safe arrival in Dumfries that morning; he continued: “I said before that I accept your kind invitation to Chelsea, but could not then fix any time. … I now propose starting on Monday next week 4th May if all goes well till then, & mean to go straight through by the usual Express train which leaves Dumfries about noon & should get to Euston a little before 9 p.m.” I am myself, sad to say, what
must be called entirely idle, doing nothing but read more or less disgustingly stupid books for most part, if they chance to be on any subject that has a vestige of interest to me: upon Toussaint L’ouverture, a singular nigger hero greatish Man & savage “Wütherich” [hot-tempered person] combined.François-Dominique Toussaint L’Ouverture (1743–1803), Afro-Caribbean, born into slavery in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (now Haiti); he became a politician and soldier, and leader of the Haitian Revolution, 1791–1802. You see, therefore, how the matter stands and that everything is open when you like.

Forster has just been here; still suffering much and really looking weak and worn: he contemplates going to the sea side, had the Summer once come, and seems rather to intend a long stay there. I suppose it is really his best chance. Froude’s Book I suppose is in your hands & getting itself read with eagerness.John wrote, 17 April, giving family news, and reported: “I got Froude’s ‘English in Ireland’ on Thursday last … & find it very interesting, & have nearly finished the 2nd volume.” Everybody is busy with it here & it seems to be almost universally applauded & agreed with. Poor fellow his sick daughterRose Mary Froude; she had been ill for some time; see 48:114TC to HFR, 5 Dec. 1872. I fear is in a dangerous way & too likely to bring a new sorrow on his heavy laden heart.— My paper is done, my subject too must end. Love and blessings to you all; especial recommending of me to Jean.

bibl.sourceNote: MW-JT [JTY], 23 April. MS: Royal Institution RI MS JT/1/W/20. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARGARET WELSH TO JOHN TYNDALL

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me thank you cordially for your kind offer to come to take him to the Deanery on Saturday. As yet Mr Carlyle has not heard anything of an invitation thither for that day;Presumably Westminster Deanery, home of Arthur Penryn Stanley; invitation untraced. & even should there be a proposal to that effect,—he says he fears he would not be able to accept. So he bids me say, he would not like you to have the trouble (solely on that account at least) of coming so far, unless you should hear further from him before Saturday.
docBody.closer: I am, / Dear Sir, / Yours truly, / Margaret Welsh

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 23 April. MS: Houghton. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p: For a good while back I have been expecting some word from you less or more, but none ever comes. Months ago soon after your last letter, & mention of Trübner & Co.See TC to CEN, 29 Jan. as your conveyance for books, Niece Mary carried over to the said Trübner, & personally delivered to him with all exactness, the third volume of Andrew Marvell’s Works; which I now begin to doubt you may never have received.See TC to CEN, 8 Dec. 1873. Norton replied, 7 May: “I have to thank you … for the third volume of Marvell’s Works which came safely to me through Trübner’s hands.” Mary I remember said she had, on summons to do so, valued at £ 1.1 this third volume of Marvell; but I myself suspected the value might be considerably in excess: so that if the poor volume never get to you at all, there is, now that you have had notice of it, little ill done.

My principal errand today was the inclosed Autotype likeness of John Knox, of which I have sent you three copies; one for yourself, another for Emerson if he don’t object, & the third for any well-affected soul you may please to pitch upon.Norton replied thanking TC for the portrait: “It is a very credible likeness, and a face that may well stand for that of the Reformer.” He said he would be seeing Emerson the following week, and would give him a copy then, and “The third copy … I shall take the liberty of presenting in your name to the Massachusetts Historical Society, which has the honour of counting you among its Honorary Members.” You said very justly last time we were upon this subject, that the one real utility there could be in a Public Monument to Knox was that of perpetuating or continuing to future ages the bodily lineaments of Knox;—to which end naturally first of all the inexorable preliminary is, that a credible resemblance of him should be clearly known to the Builders of any such Monument. The little engraving now sent you in Autotype has been beside me for some five & thirty yearsSee TC to JAC, 21 March. with growing affection & belief on my part; & as the poor little print appeared to be getting very scarce in the shops, & the current engravings of Knox were always incredible & inconceivable to me, I got fifty of these Autotypes carefully thrown off, & have been distributing them (chiefly in Scotland) among the chief lovers of Knox, hoping by the aid of Time, they might banish utterly the seven or eight other so-called “Portraits” of Knox, most of which are of no value at all, or of less than none,—David Laing’s Two being palpably imaginary, more like a Figurehead of a Ship than like Knox or
any human creature; & only one of the rest, a real portrait of a Man, but by far inferior Artist to ours, having some chance to be a real Portrait of Knox about the age of forty, & not of sixty odd as this Autotype is.

Not to tire you out altogether with this poor Knox business I will say only that to myself it appears there is as good as no external evidence whatever for any Portrait of Knox, & that for this alone of them all the internal evidence is as complete, or nearly so, as such evidence can in any case be: A man typically Scotch in every feature, with Knox’s character written on it throughout; a man of distinguished faculties in the Theological Costume of that period;—of whom one may justly ask, if not Knox Who on Earth is He?—— By way of winding up the matter I have got a promise to have the Original Painting brought hither to be examined by the best Experts extant among us, & finally to be correctly photographed, with signatures of said Experts appended, & set into circulation over the Photograph world, that whosoever cares, may come & examine & pass sentence for his own private behoof. The picture was to have been actually here ten days ago, but the benevolent lady whose it now is, has met with some little accident (“sprain of the wrist” it appears),See TC to JAC, 11 April. which prevents her coming up to Town for a few days:—the actual locality of the Picture I was struck to learn is now the heart of Ireland, six miles from Mullingar in the County of Westmeath! The Somerville peerage has died out two years ago, & this Lady, Sister of the last Peer, Hon. Mrs Ralph Smythe by name, has carried it over to one of her residencies in that perverse Sister Island. It is in good preservation the Husband reports, & “extremely like” what the Autotype indicates. Enough, & ten times more on this Knox topic.

The notablest bit of American news I lately hear is that of Emerson Candidate for the Rectorship, Glasgow University, which came upon us here as an unexpected event. The poor fellows at Glasgow are I hear extremely busy “Caucusing” with all their strength, & hopeful to succeed. It will really be an interesting & pretty little thing if they do; intrinsically you would say if you saw the poor young “Yellowbills” of Glasgow in their bits of red cloaks“Yellowbills” was originally a medieval term for first-year students; see Manuale Scholarium (Heidelberg, 1481), trans. Robert Francis Seybolt (Cambridge, MA, 1921) 18. In Scotland they were known as “bejants” from the French “bec jaunes”; red gowns were also traditionally worn by Scottish undergraduates. no very great thing, but a great looking always, & one which would be well taken on both sides of the Sea. A still more undoubted advantage to some of us, Me among the foremost, will be that we may once more behold the face of Emerson in this World.

Through Winter last I have had physically rather an indifferent time. Winter, especially a soft muddy one, being always unfriendly to me: but we have
now got into beautiful Summer, & the burden of Life is again more bearable. I have, as when you saw me, no special ailment whatever to complain of; but of course am wearing weaker every year & every day,— & should be a very foolish creature to complain of so doing. What is necessary is to creep closer & closer within one’s own little circuit; more & more avoiding extraneous interruptions, quietly contemplate the immense & forever unfathomable Change, which is hourly drawing nigh.— I read a great deal, & could I be supplied with good books, should be happier than ever I was in any other employment: but alas, alas it is very rare that one gets a good book; & of badness in books (even books that you are for some reason of curiosity of your own obliged to read) there has yet no limit been found. Toussaint l’Ouverture for example & his Haytian monstrosities, whom I was led into above a month ago by something I found in Madame Michelet’s Histoire d’une enfantAthénaïs Michelet, Mémoire d’un enfant (Paris, 1867), trans. as The Story of My Childhood by Mary Frazier Curtis (Boston, 1867). Athénaïs Michelet, b. Mialaret (1826–99), was the da. of Yves Louis Jacques Hypolite Mialaret (ca. 1777–ca. 1838), who had been secretary to Toussaint L’Ouverture, and tutor to his children. Her book relates her father’s stories of his life, including his time with L’Ouverture (Mémoire d’un enfant 307–20). —what a gulf of delirious balderdash in French & English by way of Picture to that amazing & as yet very inconceivable scene of Black persons & things! Some man of Genius & industry should really take up that subject, & bring it clearly home to mankind: to me it seems the most amazing phenomenon, or nearly so, to be met with in human history. The stupidest & intolerablest of all the books on Toussaint seem to be the latest, that of Dr Beard;Rev. John Relly Beard (1800–76; ODNB), English Unitarian minister and educational theorist; his The Life of Toussaint L’Ouverture (1853) was written partly to support the abolitionist movement in the U.S.: “A hope of affording some aid to the sacred cause of freedom, specially as involved in the extinction of slavery, and in the removal of the prejudices on which servitude mainly depends, has induced the author to prepare the present work for the press” (The Life of Toussaint L’Ouverture v). the baddish best that of La Croix,François-Joseph Pamphile de Lacroix (1774–1841), La révolution d’Haïti (1819). who was of the final thirty four thousand splendid soldiers,Lacroix served as chief of staff to Gen. Charles Victoire Emmanuel Leclerc (1772–1802), leader of an expeditionary force sent to Saint-Domingue by Napoleon, Dec. 1801, to restore slavery and the colonial authority of France. More than 31,000 troops landed on the island, including Spanish and Dutch soldiers as well as French. sent thither by the “Greatest of the Whites” to take captive, & fling into death & the Castle of Joux, the “Greatest” (& still more certainly I think the ugliest) of “the Blacks.”As Governor-General of Saint-Domingue, L’Ouverture framed a constitution which he sent to Napoleon, addressed from “The First among Blacks, to the First among Whites” (The Story of My Childhood 168) [“Le premier des noirs au premier des blancs” (Mémoire d’un enfant 318)]. Following his defeat by Leclerc, L’Ouverture was arrested, 6 May 1802, deported to France and imprisoned in the Château de Joux, in the Jura mountains, where he d. from illness, 7 April 1803. Soulouque,Faustin-Élie Soulouque (1782–1867), soldier and politician, born into slavery in Saint-Domingue; he fought in the Haitian revolution, 1803–4, stayed in the army until he became president of the Republic of Haiti, 1847–49, then made himself emperor, 1849–59. Following a revolution against him he abdicated, 1859, and fled to Jamaica, returning to Haiti in 1867. with his huge swine’s trough
of an Imperial hat, fled to Jamaica I think; but what became of him there I never heard.

Adieu, dear Norton—pardon me for babbling to you so long;— it was solely in the hope of getting a word from you in return.
