I send my kindest regards to every one at Shady Hill; especially my love to little Sally;Norton replied: “At this moment I hear my little Sally … practicing on her fiddle. … She is faithful in her devotion to you, & only a day or two since said to me, ‘Papa, what can I make for Mr. Carlyle that he would like? Shall I knit him a tippet for next winter?’” blessings on her bonnie face, poor little soul! Ever yours sincerely,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 27 April. MS: NLS 528.13. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:306–7. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: This day week then Monday 4th we expect you here. All is ready; Mrs Warren, the very day she heard of your advent, silently flitted Maggie, without consulting either her or me, downstairs to the room on this floor: I hope you will arrive in good heart, & find everything swept & garnished.

Your Friend HornRobert Horn; see TC to RHO, 3 April. called one morning, accompanied by a certain Moncrieff (sublime inventor of something they call the “Moncrieff gun”),Sir Alexander Moncrieff (1829–1906; ODNB), army officer and engineer, who conceived the idea of mounting guns on curved elevators, which would enable them to rise for firing and fall for loading. a decidedly solid & lively little man;—Horn himself I found inferior to his letters, a very honest-looking, but rather prosy, dim & in fact horny kind of man; who however did not stay long or do me the least harm. I could not show him the Irish Knox Picture, as you know: but that invaluable object, I now learn, is actually at hand; on Wednesday, the day after tomorrow I am actually to find the Lady with the Picture ready;Selina Smyth wrote, 24 April: “I hope to be in London on Wednesday morning next with my picture of John Knox and shall be happy to see you at any hour you may appoint.” I bring it down hither, if Tait & some of his
AdjutorsSee TC to JAC, 11 April. can set to work next day; & so the affair, following its due course, will be completed in due time. On Friday next, May Day, I am to give my first sitting for a statuette by Boehm,Joseph Edgar Boehm had been commissioned by Lady Ashburton to sculpt a statuette of TC. Boehm made two different versions, an example of the first, wearing coat and trousers, is at Carlyle’s House, Chelsea; see 98, and the second, wearing his camel hair dressing-gown, became the model for the life size statue on the Chelsea Embankment; see also Mark Stocker, “Joseph Edgar Boehm and Thomas Carlyle,” Carlyle Newsletter 6 (1985): 11–22. of whom Mary, if you ask her, will give a full account. He seems to me by far the cleverest sculptor or Artist I have ever seen; the statuette is for Lady Ashburton & at her urgent request; otherwise, in spite of my esteem for Boehm, I could hardly have consented at all to sit. He says he will complete the affair in four sittings; but that I fear will hardly be the case, & any way I must take my chance; only I resolve six shall be the absolute maximum, & that will not hurt me much.

figure.p:
Joseph Boehm’s statuette of Thomas Carlyle
Courtesy of Carlyle’s House, National Trust

docBody.p: Froude is coming tomorrow, & intends to stay about ten days; his Daughter seems not to be nearly so ill as some of the reports had borne; in ten days he expects she, like all the rest of them, will be able to return with him to Wales.Froude had been in North Wales; see TC to JAC, 10 April. This is pretty much all of news I had to tell you. Ruskin’s letter,Ruskin wrote a long letter to TC from Naples, 20 April, commenting: “Italy is in rapidly advancing decay;—this place was bad enough 30 years ago; but now!” John returned the letter, 28 April, writing: “The reading of it this morning amused us all.” See also TC to JRU, 13 May. which came the other night, will be a bit of curious reading for you: please return it by the very first opportunity there is.

I had two little notes from Mary, both of which are pretty little musical chirps, & gave me pleasure; tell her to write again without loss of time, & I, with little loss of ditto, will actually endeavour to reply. Give my kindest love to Jean & to all the rest.— Allingham is waiting for me downstairs — not a word more. Ever your affecte Brr,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 27 April. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: I am truly glad to hear that your painful little accidentSelina Smyth’s journey to London had been delayed because she had sprained her wrist; see TC to JAC, 17 April. has gone its way; & that I shall at last have the pleasure of seeing you & the valuable prize you are so kindly bringing over to me. The Experts are all in readiness, impatient to examine; & some hope of authenticating, what to me, on internal evidence, is so completely probable, is a general feeling among us. On Wednesday, between three & four P.M. I expect to have the honour of waiting on you & thanking you for your very great kindness in regard to this matter.
With many respects / I remain, / Dear Madam,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JTD, 29 April. MS transcription: Harry Ransom Lib., Univ. of Texas. Hitherto unpbd. John Thadeus Delane; see TC to JAF, 10 April.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN THADEUS DELANE

docBody.p: I have not read the enclosed paper, intended for the “Times”; but am able to testify with great clearness, that the writer of it, Mr. Lattimer,William Lattimer (ca. 1830–89), textile worker and then manager of Ferguson Brothers textile mill, Holme Head, Carlisle; he and TC had had some previous correspondence; see 28:340TC to WL, 15 Dec. 1853, and 33:186TC to WL, 3 March 1858. He was an advocate for land reform, but this article was apparently not pbd. in the Times. is a man of sound, clear & solid character, more or less worthy to be heard by every body on whatever practical question he has made up his mind about. I rather predict that your official Lieutenant will give his vote for insertion of the Lattimer discourse upon the Coal Question & the Agricultural Labourer’s do. In the Contrary event would you please have the paper returned to me here; in the other or favourable event I will beg of you to have the copy of the “Times” sent to me in which Lattimer appears. Inclosure no. 1 you can read, if perfectly at leisure, & then burn. The three half-pence stamps are Lattimer’s own contribution, & by strict right will belong to you!
Hoping I may have the pleasure still to meet you in this World. & that all in the meantime with you goes well.
I remain, / Always yours truly, / T. Carlyle.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Sir WSM [WSM], 3 May. MS: Glasgow City Archives. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SIR WILLIAM STIRLING MAXWELL

docBody.p: The Somerville Knox Picture is actually here; ready to be seen & examined by you whenever you will be so kind.Stirling Maxwell was a respected art collector; see TC to DL, 26 March. I am hardly ever out till 3½ P.M; but you yourself will be admitted at any hour. Pray come soon;—& My LadyAnna Maria Stirling Maxwell. with you if she will be so good. To her my kindest regards as well as to yourself.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-RS [RSM], 6 May. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO RALPH SMYTH

docBody.p:
The Knox Picture has been closely examined by several Artists,See TC to JAC, 11 April. Ralph Smyth wrote, 5 May: “When convenient to you we shall be obliged by your letting us know … the artist’s opinion of the picture of John Knox & whether he considers it an original.” some of whom are of the first eminence in their profession; especially one of whom, Mr Boehm the Sculptor, I consider for insight, sincerity & clearness of judgment in regard to pictures, by much the trustworthiest man to be found in this Country. By all of these visitors the excellency &c of the Portrait is cheerfully admitted;—for which indeed as our own eyes & physiognomical discernment may teach us, we are under little obligation to third parties. But I regret to add that all these judges, Boehm at the head of them, are clearly of opinion that the Picture is not an Original, nor belongs to the 16th Century at all, but to the middle part of the 18th. Boehm’s demonstration to myself, in view of the Picture, was painfully indisputable by symptoms & reasons clearly perceptible to me. I had to admit that this was a Copy, not older than the 18th Century; & had been done (so Boehm made it probable to me) from some
Original smaller in size than itself. That point therefore I consider to be completely fixed. And of course am very sorry for it; for, like Boehm himself, I greatly esteem its worth as a Portrait, & am not hitherto the least shaken in my belief that it is verily a likeness of Knox, & the only one hitherto discovered in the World.

The next question now rises, Can any indication, guess, or surmise of what the Original of it was be formed? This I fear will be of quite minor interest to you & to the dear Lady, who takes such interest in this Portrait: but the researches here, in a Historical sense, are still very important, & it is altogether desirable that, by this opportunity, these also should be pushed as far as they will go. I find a great wish extant to have for this object some accurate idea of what the Ranferly & the Torphichen Portraits actually are;For the Torphichen portrait of Knox, see TC to JAC, 9 Dec. 1873. The Ranfurly portrait was presumably in the possession of Thomas Granville Henry Stuart Knox (1849–75), 4th earl of Ranfurly, of Dungannon, Co. Tyrone, Ireland. In The Works of John Knox, David Laing had noted that the “name of Knox … is said to have been derived from the lands of Knoc or Knox, in Renfrewshire. The chief family was that of Ranfurly in the same county, some of whose descendants having settled at Dungannon, were raised to the peerage of Ireland.” However Laing goes on to say that “there is no evidence to prove the most distant connexion with that family; and as the name of Knox was not uncommon in other parts of the country, we might rather conjecture that his ancestors were related to the burgesses of Edinburgh” (Laing, The Works of John Knox 6:xiv). to both of which there seemed, through you, & the obliging Military gentleman, whom I found with you, to be easily possible access?Ralph Smyth replied, 8 May, thanking TC for his letter; he wrote: “I shall be only too happy to do all I can in getting a Photograph of Lord Ranfurlys picture & in getting Captain Bunbury to interest himself … in that of Lord Torphichen.” He then wrote, 13 May: “I have just heard … about Lord Ranfurly’s picture of John Knox that it is only an engraving of the painting in possession of Lord Torphichen— My friend Captain Bunbury … has heard from him that he will be happy to answer any enquiries from you in reference to his picture— It is I believe in a house only 12 miles from Edinburgh so could easily be inspected.” Captain Bunbury not further identified, although there was a prominent family of that name in Co. Tipperary, Ireland. If from both of the Gentlemen an exact photograph of their respective Pictures could be speedily got it would be a great furtherance in this inquiry;—& I should take it as a great kindness if you found it possible to accomplish this for me. A so-called Original Portrait of Knox, lately bequeathed to Aberdeen University by a Mr Thomson,Alexander Thomson (1798–1868), lawyer, agriculturalist, philanthropist, and traveler, of Banchory, Aberdeenshire. Thomson stipulated in his will that on the death of his wife, Jessie, b. Frazer (1799–1870), the contents of his library and museum would be bequeathed to the Free Church College at Aberdeen. The portrait of Knox is not further identified. who used to believe himself lineally descended from Knox’s Daughter,Thomson’s claim to be a descendant of Knox through one of Knox’s daughters was reported by Thomas M’Crie in The Life of John Knox (3d edn., Edinburgh, 1814) 2:451. Knox had three das.: Martha (1565–92), m. Alexander Fairlie (ca. 1550–1607), Margaret (1567–1625), m. Zachary Pont (1565–1618), and Elizabeth (1570–1625), m. John Welsh (ca. 1568–1622) of Ayr. —has
been confidently promised me since you saw me:Robert Horn had offered to procure this photograph; see TC to RHO, 12 July. with these three Photographs (I mean exact likenesses of the Pictures, however ugly) would, as I consider, be furnished all the data to complete what we already have upon that question.

A surmise exists that F. Pourbus a famous Netherlands Painter, whose Portrait of George Buchanan,For Pourbus and Buchanan, see TC to JAC, 17 April. a Friend & Contemporary of Knox is now an accredited picture of the Royal Society here, may also have been the Painter of Knox: this is a supposition, which seems to me of little validity; but happily it may be settled very soon, whether there is any likelihood (or none) in following it out beyond the Royal Society Buchanan in question.

Permit me to send many kind regards to the dear & beautiful Lady, who has been so kind in all these matters, & my true wish to hear that the ugly accident had indeed (as I rashly fancied), completely disappeared.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-HM [HMAR], 6 May. MS: Yale. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature. Helena Martin, b. Faucit (1814–98; ODNB), actress, m., 1851, Theodore Martin; see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1873.
bibl.head: TC TO HELENA MARTIN

docBody.p: Alas, dear Mrs Martin, during the last seven or eight years I have gradually been discovering that I was grown unfit for dining out; and, in effect, for the last two or three have altogether discontinued the practice;—altogether or only in cases of the most rigorous compulsion.TC and Mary Aitken had dined with Theodore and Helena Martin at Froude’s, 24 Nov. 1873, and TC had talked of seeing Helena Faucit play Desdemona to W. C. Macready’s Othello in 1843. In his memoir of his wife, Martin later recalled: “Lady Martin met Mr Carlyle one evening at Mr Froude’s in November 1873 … and in her Diary next day she writes: ‘It was a great pleasure to me, when, talking with Mr Carlyle about Mr Macready’s revivals, which he spoke of very warmly, he referred in glowing terms to my Desdemona. Amid much else, he said he had never felt the play so deeply before. One phrase especially struck me—‘It quite hurt me to see the fair, delicate creature so brutally used.’ Would that I could give an idea of his tone and accent, gentle and tremulous, as if a suffering living creature were there before him!’” (Sir Theodore Martin, Helena Faucit, Lady Martin [Edinburgh, 1900] 101). William C. Macready (1793–1873; ODNB), actor and theatre manager. By a singular chance one such case does occur on Saturday next, the very night you are so kind as invite me!TC had agreed to dine with Forster on Sat., 9 May, however Forster wrote, 7 May, saying he was too ill, and hoping that TC could come the following week (Kinser and Tarr, II, 73). So stands the matter; dismally exact as I now state.

With very many thanks for his merciful diligence in regard to the Menteath business;Theodore Martin wrote, 14 April: “I hear you wish to have some talk with me, & that you kindly offer to come to me at my Chambers,” and suggested that TC call the following day. He then wrote, 10 May: “I have just received a letter, from which I fear that the poor widow’s application to Sir Thomas Biddulph has come to nothing. Never did I read a more piteous story of disaster than was told in her letter. … Although the Queen has no power to help her towards a pension, I was in hopes that some present relief in the shape of a money grant might have been given.” The widow is unidentified; the Menteth family came from Closeburn, Dumfries, and both TC and JWC had known them for many years (see 9:32JWC to TC, [30 July 1836], and 14:59TC to JWC, 7 March 1842); however, they were a landed aristocratic family and it is unlikely that any of them needed financial help. Sir Thomas Myddleton Biddulph (1809–78; ODNB), courtier and army officer, had presumably been approached in his role as keeper of the Queen’s privy purse. Theodore Martin also had contact with Queen Victoria, having been commissioned by her to write a biography of Prince Albert. & with all manner of kind regards to yourself and Him,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 13 May. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: For weeks past I have not had a word or whisper of you; nor except through Forster at rare intervals have known so much as your approximate address. Please do tell me at once where you are, & what is the meaning of this “detention” at Oxford,Unexplained. whether of Mary or of yourself. I do very much desire to know; & indeed have often wondered why you did not, of your own accord, send me a little word; though knowing well at all times that it was not from unkindness that the omission came.

The good Forster, whom I have not seen above once a week latterly, & who let me in yesterday by altogether exceptional favour,—is in heavier suffering, & more continual misery than I ever saw him before. I do not myself reckon that there is anything absolutely dangerous in his present situation, which I impute almost solely to the grim weather, & perhaps to an imprudent sally he made to the late Academy dinner.The Royal Academy Anniversary Banquet, Sat., 2 May, at Burlington House, Piccadilly. But the sad fact now is he coughs continually day & night; & has not slept at all, or had not yesterday afternoon, for the
last successive six days & nights. No remedy, I fear, till the bitter weather go, which I hope & judge, will now be soon!

Boehm has had his four Sittings for the statuette;See TC to JAC, 27 April. Lady Ashburton wrote, 25 May: “I can’t go to bed without writing a line to tell you Mary & I drove to Mr Boehm’s today—& I must thank you for allowing me to possess that beautiful work of art—& delightful likeness—the only thing of you that gives any just representation it is indeed precious—& will become more & more so— Mary is quite as happy about it, as I am.” which has seemed to me decidedly promising all along. He has had the due supply of “old clothes”In the statuette that Boehm made for Lady Ashburton TC is dressed smartly in coat, trousers, and patent-leather shoes; however, Boehm planned to make a life-size statue as well, and for this Boehm wanted TC to wear clothes that would attract less attention; in the final statue TC is wearing his camel-hair dressing-gown. for the last five days past, & is to have by way of overplus, for which his “thanks” are great, a final go of me tomorrow at half past one. The Sittings have been almost really a pleasure to me, so ingenious, sincere, intelligent & amiable is the Man. I shall be sincerely obliged to you withal, or principally, if the dainty little article succeed. With all hearts wishes to Mary & yourself, especially to the sick one of you I am & remain always

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JR [JRU] 13 May. MS: Ruskin Lib. Collection. Pbd: Cate 181–83. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: Your Naples letter was a welcome appearance here, & all the more as testifying (I hope) the intention of promise fulfilled by performance, & that other letters from you will follow this! I well comprehend the incessant business you have, leaving you only minutes of leisure; so that no impatience is permitted me, though as much desire as I like. All I will say is, that I read this Naples letter with a pleasure & interest entirely unusual in these late years, & that it will be very charitable in you to write as often as you fairly can.

Your con-spectus of the Foreign nations is gloomy & mournful, & I doubt but too well-founded:Ruskin wrote, 20 April, a long letter from Naples complaining bitterly about the current state of France and Italy: “[E]very time I come abroad, I have a deeper sense of the advancing ruin of every country except your Germany,—nor do I believe that it will escape unpunished for its cruelty.” See also TC to JAC, 27 April. I suppose this long while they are all, like ourselves, got into the Niagara Rapids, & hastening towards a nameless doom. Not
towards absolute destruction, I always hope, but towards black centuries of Anarchy & agony, & sordid tribulation, till a better spirit rise in them. Sometimes in late months I have been fancying the poor English Nation to be getting faintly sensible of this & the other long-continued delusion, & feebly preparing to get rid of it: but the curse of boundless wealth which they call “unexampled prosperity” lies heavy on them; giving such unbounded arena to the development of all their low desires & endeavours, that nothing of real spiritual health is likely to be possible for a long while yet. God help them, poor wretches,— us too ditto, ditto!

As is now, alas, nearly inevitable for me, I have been doing Nothing, merely reading mostly idle books (not one book in twenty can be called other than a bad book), & drowsily musing over them with many silent feelings; among which, willingness to close the Shop on signal given is constantly present,—mixed also with others still more inarticulate, unutterable glimpses of things that have a certain dignity & even blessedness, which would be lost by speaking of them.—Latterly I have lost my chief walking companion, Froude having gone to Wales for the Summer;See TC to JAF, 10 April. solitary walking, which is next-best, seldom falls to my share, though in general I rather do avoid what is clearly foolish, insincere & frivolous in my collocutors, peripatetic or other. In short I am grown very old, & have made, I notice, very rapid progress in that operation during the last year. If you did not so unjustly dislike the Germans, I would translate for you a beautiful “Zame Xenion” of Goethe’sPossibly Goethe’s verse, from Zahme Xenien II: “Wie das Gerstirn, / Ohne Hast, / Aber ohne Rast, / Drehe sich jeder / Um die eigne Last [Like as a Star, / That maketh not haste, / That taketh not rest, / Be each one fulfilling / His god-given Hest]” (TC’s trans., Carlyle, Works 27:432); see also 5:287TC to G, 10 June 1831. which is often privately in my mouth while contemplating this Finale of my affairs.

You appear to me to be clearly in the right in reference to your Architectural Society Medal.The Royal Institute of British Architects had awarded its annual Gold Medal to Ruskin, 9 March, with the approval of the Queen. Ruskin explained to TC that that he had decided “after a fortnights very careful thought—to refuse the gold medal of the Architect’s institute,” continuing “I cannot accept medals from people who let themselves out to build Gothic Advertisements for Railroads—Greek Advertisements for firms in the city … while they allow every beautiful building in France and Italy to be destroyed, for the ‘job’ of its restoration.” Ruskin wrote to the Institute from Rome, 20 May, declining the medal, and citing four examples of architectural neglect to explain his decision: the tomb of Cardinal Brancacci at Naples used as a “lumber-room”; the church of San Miniato at Florence converted into a cemetery; the destruction of the carved cross on the church of Santa Maria della Spina at Pisa; and the proximity of the railway to the Abbey at Furness in Cumbria. He concluded: “For the existence of this state of things we, the members … of the Institute of British Architects, are assuredly answerable, at least in England; and under these circumstances I cannot but feel that it is no time for us to play at adjudging medals to each other. … For we have none of us … any right remaining either to bestow or to receive honours” (Ruskin’s Works 34:514). The offer of it I find to be a decidedly pretty little thing;
but, for a name so clothed with lightning & quack-devouring Fire, it is at least equally becoming & imperative to decline speech or acceptance on any terms which exist at present in that quarter. Achitecture, down to the very art of making bricks, has fallen fatuous at present, fatuous & false, to be shunned by every one who is sane, & not under clear compulsion to it.

One thing will perhaps seem curious to you; the real excellency, in a kindred province, of our Chelsea Embankment, which was at last opened the other day.The Chelsea section of the Thames Embankment, opened 9 May; see 48:145TC to JAC, 14 Jan. 1873, and 146TC to JAC, 14 Jan. 1873. It was done by our Board of Works; essentially, so far as I can find, by one Bazalgette;Sir Joseph William Bazalgette (1819–91; ODNB), civil engineer, responsible for major sewage works and the embanking of the Thames in central London. —& my testimony is that it entirely surprises me. Miles of the noblest Promenade. The Thames rushing grandly past you, & even at low-water leaving a foot or two of pure gravel; a labarynthic flower-garden, with all manner of planted young trees, green spaces, subsidiary walks, & grand pavements; Cheyne Walk looking altogether royal on you through the old umbrage & the new; I was obliged to say, & still repeat, I have never seen anything, of any description whatever, nearly so well done in this monstrous City since I knew it first. I long to shew it you, & hear your judgment of it. To me it will be a great resource for the rest of my appointed days here. In another 50 years, were the shrubs & saplings all grown, I think it will be admitted universally that there is no other such pretty region in all London & its environs. This Bazalgette I have heard the name of before, but will henceforth attach a meaning to it, such as to that of few others in any line of business like his.

Your ‘Fors,’ two numbers of it at once,Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera, letter 40, “The Scottish Fireside” (April 1874), and letter 41, “Bernard the Happy” (May 1874). came punctually on May 1st, & were, as always, eagerly read. Winged Words, tipped with empyrean fire. not in my time has the dark weltering, blind & base mass of things been visited by such showers & torrents of an element altogether amazing to it. Euge, Euge [Well done, Well done].

Adieu dear Ruskin. Do not forget me, in your Grotto, or other Italian Studies;—& write a line or two when you have a minute of leisure. Mary, you see, is gone from me; on a visit of some few weeks to her Mother; I am sitting (by compulsion) for a statuette to one Boehm, who is worth your knowing, if I do not altogether mistake his artistic talent. The one sitting more will set free [me] from him. All good be with you dear R.—Yours Ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JEB, 18 May. MS: Yale. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOSEPH EDGAR BOEHM

docBody.p: There will come to you, I hope, on Wednesday morning from Birmingham, an authentic cast of the skull of Burns;Robert Burns (1759–96; ODNB), poet; his mausoleum in St. Michael’s Graveyard, Dumfries, was opened, 31 March 1834, for the burial of Burns’s widow, Jean, b. Armour (1765–1834; ODNB). While the tomb was open a plaster cast of his skull was made by James Fraser, plasterer, under the supervision of Archibald Blacklock (ca. 1791–1875), former surgeon in the Royal Navy (Mark Fraser, “The Phrenologists and Robert Burns,” Robert Burns World Federation Chronicle (1996): 215–221). TC apparently acquired a copy, now untraced. —for which, as for an inestimable document, I have no doubt you will wait.

I find also that there is in the National Gallery, accessible to you at any moment, a Picture of Burns by Raeburn,Oil painting of Burns, ascribed to Sir Henry Raeburn (1756–1823; ODNB), portrait painter, now in the Burns Birthplace Museum, South Ayrshire. as well as the Original by Nasmyth,Half-length oil painting of Burns (1787), by Alexander Nasmyth (1758–1840; ODNB), artist and engineer, now in the Scottish National Portrait Gallery. of which you possess only the engraving.

Permit me to send back the invaluable Schiller,Possibly a copy of the death-mask of Johann Christoph Friedrich von Schiller (1759–1805) by Johann Christian Ludwig Klauer (1782–1815), German sculptor, now at Carlyle’s House, Chelsea (Carlyle’s House 102). with the petition to have the dust washed off him; which one of your men can alone do to perfection.

On Wednesday I hope to call, with a most extraordinary Report upon the Knox Picture from one who in himself transcends all authority!Possibly George Scharf (1820–95; ODNB), artist and gallery director, sec. of the National Portrait Gallery 1857–95; he drew a sketch of TC, 16 May; see frontis. TC discussed the Knox portrait with him later in the year; see TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug.

postscript.p: Lady Ashburton’s address is, I find,
and her Ladyship seems to be expected today or tomorrow.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady D [LDE], 18 May. MS: V&A. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY DERBY

docBody.p: Unfortunately, as you anticipated, I must forbid myself to come.Lady Derby wrote, 17 May: “The Emperor of Russia is coming to the Foreign Office on Wednesday evening next the 20th—& I am to try to collect all the distinguished literary & scientific men that he may look at them.” For Alexander II, emperor of Russia, see TC to JAC, 8 Jan. In the first place I have no “Uniform”;Lady Derby continued: “I cannot possibly omit to ask you, altho’ I much fear nothing would induce you to come, more especially as it is necessary to appear in some sort of uniform or full dress. … Perhaps you will think me quite mad to ask you.” & in the second, what is still more important, I am constantly from 9 o’clockLady Derby enclosed a formal invitation card, giving the appointed time of arrival as 9:45 p.m. onwards a being incapable of nothing, except of silence & gloomy musing,—alleviated only by reading some wise or half wise Book, when I can procure such; & in the worst case, alas, by reading some unwise Book with silent patience, though not without abhorrence, till the clock strike one, when I disappear into the realm of Somnus, the beneficent Brother of Death. Judge how unfit to look on the face of Czars!—
I do regret my inability very much, both for your sake & for His Czarish Majesty’s, whom, & whose grand, deep & potent Nation, I have always held in true respect.

Perhaps when all these Mighty Sceneries & Ceremonials are well over, you will look in upon me again, your own quiet Self & give me an hour’s pleasant dialogue.Lady Derby wrote, 25 May: “I breathe freely once more now that I am in the country, & hope next week I may be able to go to see you. I was very happy to have the honour of receiving the Mighty Czar—he interested me & has filled my thoughts.”

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], [30] May. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Maggie Welsh’s hand, with TC’s signature. Conjecturally dated by Boehm’s letter to TC, 29 May.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p:
Mr Boehm is sorry to inform me that his Princess Louise or her Marquis of Lorne rather seemed to hang fire in regard to that matter, the Marquis of
Bute’s pictures, two or three of which now in Eccleston Square Boehm wished to examine on my behalf & the Reformer Knox’s.Joseph Boehm had apparently asked for help from his friend Princess Louise Caroline Alberta (1848–1939; ODNB), da. of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, and her husband, m. 1871, John George Edward Henry Douglas Sutherland Campbell (1845–1914; ODNB), marquis of Lorne; Boehm wrote, 29 May: “I did not receive … a reply to my request about the Bute Gallery. Would it not be better to get access to the Porbuses through Lady Ashburton?” John Patrick Crichton-Stuart (1847–1900; ODNB), 3d marquis of Bute, philanthropist and patron of architecture; his London home was at 38 Eccleston Sq. The pictures in question are by F Porbus,Frans Pourbus; see TC to JAC, 17 April. whose works seem to be rather scarce in London. Boehm counsels me as our time is uncertain, & may be rather short, to apply to your Ladyship for assistance; who I had happened to tell him, could, if necessary, make the due request to the Marquis Proprietor. If this be really the case, & will not be disagreeable to you, & does not involve any considerable degree of trouble, I will say, Pray do it for my sake. If it be in reality any way troublesome or disagreeable I will, on the contrary, forbid you; & bid Boehm be more patient with his Princess & Marquis and wait quietly on their good pleasure.

Poor Forster was reported yesterday & the day before visible improved; today we have not yet heard. I trust you got happily to MelchetLady Ashburton left London for her house at Melchet Court, Hampshire, 27 May. Friends unidentified further. & have your Friends still with you,—to whom, if so, my best respects. A hearty salute to the Darling Mary in her new sea-element.

postscript.p: P.S. I asked leave to add my own kind & respectful regards

bibl.sourceNote: TC-TW [TWO], 10 June. Pbd: Amy Woolner, Thomas Woolner, R. A. His Life in Letters (1917) 295.
bibl.head: TC TO THOMAS WOOLNER

docBody.p:
The enclosed letter came to me this morning in the inside of one from your old friend ParkesHenry Parkes (1815–96; ODNB), premier of New South Wales 1872–75, 1877, 1878–83, and 1887–89. Parkes and TC met Oct. 1861; see 37:241TC to HP, 2 Oct. 1861; Parkes and Woolner met in 1854 when Woolner was visiting Australia. —who I believe is still what they call Premier at Sydney. He only seems to fear you may not be able to undertake the Captain CookParkes wrote, 11 April: “The Legislature of this colony has voted a sum of £2000 for a statue to Captain Cook. I have written the enclosed note to Mr Woolner on this subject, and, as I do not know that gentleman’s address, I take the liberty of asking you to deliver it to him.” James Cook (1728–79; ODNB), British explorer, who had claimed the east coast of Australia as a British possession, 1770. for
£2000; in which sad case he asks me to “advise” who should be next applied to.Parkes wrote: “This Government is desirous of having the work executed in the best style of art and I shall be indeed very glad if you can yourself advise as to the sculptor to whom it may be most safely entrusted. I can easily understand that it may not suit Mr Woolner himself.” I think it would be an excellent subject & well worthy of you, if you found the money offer sufficient.Woolner received the official commission, Aug. 1876, for a bronze statue, 13 ft. (4 m.) high; it was finished in 1878 and displayed in London before being shipped to Australia; it was unveiled in Sydney, Feb. 1879.
In any case please communicate with Parkes as soon as possible, and let me know what you have decided on.

It is a long time since I have seen you and I myself, as is natural, go out less and less; but I hear always from time to time that everything is going well with you in your art & otherwise. Best success to you, now and ever.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAF, 20 June. Pbd: Dunn, CLF IV:241–42.
bibl.head: TC TO J. A. FROUDE

docBody.p:
I ought to have written to you weeks ago and would have done it had my own hands been at my service or the incubus of old age pressing upon a poor back now nearly broken permitted any exertion beyond that of plunging lazily day after day and night after night into idle reading and inarticulate contemplation of the past, present and future. I need not say how gratefully I recognise your beneficent persistence in the purpose of having me with you this summer; nor how gladly I would try if there were a fair likelihood (as I always try to hope there is) of its proving a successful adventure for parties concerned. My idle notion generally or always is that I certainly will lift anchor and make towards you on trial: but the truth is I am idle as a dry bone and hardly ever in my life felt as totally weak in soul and body, as hitherto in this summer. I reckon on the whole the likelihood to be that I shall crawl about here till the hot weather, which we still look for in July or August, render London plainly insupportable and force me to go somewhither; in which case
there seems no place within my whole horizon so probable as Merionethshire & Crogan.Froude had been in Wales for some months; see TC to JAC, 10 April. We must let it stand that way for the present. As you surmise, I can do nothing with OxfordFroude apparently had to visit Oxford and London for a few days before returning to Wales. or its celebrations nor can you therefore charitably take me in tow:—leave me half asleep on the strand lazily dreaming of departure; that is all we can make of the thing at present.

I have read all your BookFroude’s The English in Ireland; see TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1873. carefully over again, and continue to think of it not less but rather more favourably than ever: a few little phrases and touches you might perhaps alter with advantage; and the want of a copious carefully-weighed concluding Chapter is more sensible to me than ever; but the substance of the book is genuine truth and the utterance of it is clear, sharp, smiting and decisive like a shining Damascus sabre; I never doubted or doubt but its effect will be great and lasting. No criticism have I seen since you went away that was worth notice. Poor Lecky is weak as water,—bilge-water with a drop of formic acid in it; unfortunate Lecky, he is wedded to his Irish Idols;For William Lecky’s review of Froude’s first vol. of The English in Ireland in Macmillan’s Magazine 27 (Jan. 1873), see 48:135TC to JAC, 4 Jan. 1873. In his review of Froude’s second and third vols., Macmillan’s Magazine 30 (June 1874) 166–184, Lecky continued his attack on the author’s apparent disdain for the Irish people: “[Froude] describes Ireland in the palmy days of the penal laws and of Protestant ascendancy as an absolute Pandemonium. If we accept his judgment, we must believe that murder and riot, and the ravishing of women, the houghing of cattle, the mutilation of Protestant clergymen, the ‘carding’ of tithe-proctors, were the habitual employments of the people” (Macmillan’s 183). Lecky also wrote: “[Froude] is a complete disciple of Mr. Carlyle, whose influence, inspiration and peculiar antipathies may be traced in every page of this book, and who, as is well known, is of opinion that despotism is the ideal government” (Macmillan’s 167). let him alone. An amazing piece of block-headism came three days ago; a lecture by some reverend Presbyterian somebody;TC probably refers to Rev. Isaac Nelson (1809–88; ODNB), minister of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, anti-revivalist, abolitionist, and proponent of Irish home rule, although at 65 years old he was hardly “a young Gentleman.” probably, like a Prayer I have heard of, the stupidest ever addressed to a Belfast audience. The Presbyterian somebody is a young Gentleman conscious of being developed into an Apostle of Progress, Liberalism &c &c, your bitter enemy, tho’ from a lofty stand point; and for ignorance, insolence & natural grossness & baseness of mind excels any Lecturer I have almost ever seen. Avoid his Pamphlet,Nelson’s pamphlet was The Present Importance of Irish History. A Lecture delivered in the Presbyterian Meeting House, Donegall St., 16th April 1874 (Belfast, 1874). The Belfast Weekly News, 18 April, reported that “Mr. Nelson having dealt with certain statements in Froude’s history … went on to observe it was often said that whatever wrongs Ireland suffered in the past she had no grievance now; but his reply was that never had dissatisfaction been more widely diffused than at present … and never had Ireland been more wretched than at present.” if it
have not already fallen to you; except its own dirty self and maker’s self it can throw no light on anything in Heaven or earth.

Poor Forster has had a very sore fit of increased illness, almost ever since you went; at one time his doctors looked so grave, and he himself was in such spirits, I was for two or three days in serious alarm; but he is now considerably mended out of all that. His week at Hastings, of which you no doubt heard, is ended today or Monday, and has been favourable & successful in spite of the noxious East winds; I have long believed that a silent summer by the sea-side, such as he now proposes after a week or two, will do him more good than all the doctors could ever do. He is already so far recovered, it appears, as to have decided on a dinner for next Friday;Forster wrote, 16 June, from the Royal Victoria Hotel, St. Leonards-on-Sea, nr. Hastings: “Notwithstanding the relentless North East wind which has blown ever since the night of our arrival, the change has certainly strengthened me, and I have been steadily better than when in London. / I had been saying to the Small One [Eliza] here that the first thing I should do at our return would be to get you to fix our long deferred little dinner at Palace Gate. And here comes a letter from Froude saying he shall be in London from the 23d to the 27th … that his time is so limited that he must dispose of it beforehand, and asking me to give him an evening with you at Palace Gate” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 73–74). amazing result, and almost terrible to me, though you also are to be there & the noble Forster is a hexcellent cove no less than a harbitary.See TC to JAC, 4 Feb.
Adieu, dear Froude, I feel to be the stupidest of mankind, but also

closer.salute:
Very positively and sincerely
Yours ever
closer.note: Forster also wrote: “The only other book (excepting Frederick) I have been reading much in, is Mary’s Collection of Songs. … Certainly a more Choice selection was never made. The ring of good is in them all. But oh how far beyond every one else is Burns—and what a writer he was!” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 74). Mary’s book was pbd. in May; see TC to JAC, 21 March.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JR [JRU], 20 June. MS: Ruskin Lib. Collection. Pbd: Cate 189–190. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p:
That was an excellent scheme you had of writing to me dailyRuskin wrote from Rome, 19 May: “I am going to write for a little while to you, as I used to my own father,—who had his letter every day, whether there was anything in it or not.” He wrote again, 20, 21, 24, and 27 May, addressing TC as “Dearest Papa.” a detached bit of thought observation or experience,—excellent, had you but been able
to continue. The three or four you sent came duly each of them a blazing fire flake, or direct photograph of the minute passing over Rome and you; altogether strengthening and pleasant to the mind of the recipient. But alas, it could not continue; with that wildly touching, and as if tragic disinterment of the poor old Christian Church of “the third century”Ruskin wrote, 1 June: “Dearest Papa / I haven’t written for a day or two because I had nothing to tell you—but yesterday I saw what may interest you—a buried—or (properly), dug church of the 2nd or 3rd century.” The church had been partially buried, and was therefore untouched by the restorers who Ruskin felt had ruined so many ancient churches. into the closing epoch of Pio NonoPope Pius IX; see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. 1873. and company, your fire flakes or quasi-living photographs suddenly ceased; and I have remained ever since, not from that cause alone (though doubtless that helped), one of the most indolent, torpid and useless souls now extant on this Planet. In sad truth, except walking every morning to the end of our embankment and back, on the finest sleekest most undisturbed and soothing promenade I ever had, nothing has been done by me but another rather longer walk or crawl, latish in the afternoon, into one or other of the Parks and idle reading or slumber and sleep all day and all night. I say to myself, but not too angrily, Is this what they call euthanasia? euthanasia? Well, well! In fact there is no end to the cloudy musings I have,—especially on that benificent Chelsea embankment;See TC to JRU, 13 May. unluckily until Death itself come there is no escaping the dismal necessity to eat food and the still more dismal & almost impossible ditto to digest the same. Patience patience; Hope, too, a little; and thanks always and loyal reverence to the Almighty Builder. Amen.

About a week ago, I got from Aylesbury the promised first proof sheet of your Book on Botany,Ruskin’s printers, Watson and Hazell, of London and Aylesbury, sent TC advance copies of his works; see TC to JRU, 31 Oct. 1873. Parts 1 and 2 of Proserpina. Studies of Wayside Flowers, while the Air Was Yet Pure (1875–1886) were pbd. 1875; see Ruskin’s Works 25:188–569. which, to judge from this first sample, will be a most welcome Book to me, such as I have never met with before in my struggles, completely fruitless hitherto, to get any insight into the “Science of Botany”Ruskin advised his readers: “[E]ven if you only ascertain the history of one plant, so that you know that accurately, you will have helped to lay the foundation of a true science of botany, from which the mass of useless nomenclature, now mistaken for science, will fall away, as the husk of a poppy falls from the bursting flower” (Ruskin’s Works 25:228). or those strange and beautiful fellow creatures of ours that make lovely every year the face of this “rugged all-supporting Earth.”Quotation from Sophocles; see Carlyle, Sartor 118 and 344, and Last Words 121. What a long-eared people that Guild of scientific gentlemen is and has been here below!—

Your Architect Gold Medal, left stranded on the waste beach,See TC to JRU, 13 May. had an immense rumour for some days in London; and I doubt not is still standing like a fateful Sphinx-riddle in the minds of many men. The blame I think was not laid heavily on you, but the astonishment, the mocking pity for the Medal and its authors was large and loud. I continue to discern that in your situation and in that of Architecture there could nothing else be done. I have heard a great deal also about your volunteer young gentlemen, delvers & diggers, now busy about Oxford; really an almost miraculous thing; proof such as was not seen for long ages of the influence of an earnest man upon earnest youths; at which even the penny-a-liner pauses for a moment, uncertain what to say or do.When Ruskin took up the position of Slade Professor of Art at Oxford, he often walked through the nearby village of Ferry Hinksey, which was very dilapidated owing to regular flooding and poor sanitation. He persuaded a group of undergraduates to work to improve the drainage and the roadway. The Daily News reported, 29 May: “[The undergraduates] are restoring the road to its old course, and securing it against future collapse by making a substantial cutting, three or four feet deep, whose sides may be expected to remain in statu quo for any reasonable period.” The project was widely ridiculed in the British Press. However, Ruskin’s friend Henry Acland (1815–1900; ODNB), physician, regius professor of medicine at Oxford 1857–94, was very encouraging of schemes for public health; he wrote to the Times, 20 May: “An ‘Oxford Correspondent’ has addressed … an attack on the undergraduates who have been induced by Mr. Ruskin to take to ‘digging at Hincksey.’. … Surely, in an age of liberty and philanthropy well-meaning men might be allowed to mend the muddy approaches of some humble dwellings of the poor without being held up to the public as persons meet only for the neighbouring asylum? … Mr. Ruskin, a man of no narrow sympathies, has known Oxford for 40 years. He is as interested in the greatness of the educated youth of England as he is in the well-doing of the poor. He is loved by both. To the high-spirited youth of Oxford he has said, ‘Will none of you out of the abundance of your strength and of your leisure do anything for the poor? The poor ye have always with you. Drain a single cottage, repair a single village by-way, make good a single garden wall, make pleasant with flowers one widow’s plot. … Is he wrong? Are the hearty, kindly men who obeyed him, wrong? … Is Mr. Ruskin unpractical in thus harmlessly evoking the sympathies and energies of the unspoiled minds about him?” See also Tim Hilton, John Ruskin: The Later Years (New Haven and London, 2000) 265–66. Ruskin replied from Assisi, 24 June: “The Oxford movement was … long since planned by me; but I did not intend to begin it till [later]. … But one or two of the men themselves asked me to begin now—so I let them— And truly, I think it will grow.— Next October, I go out myself with them, and hope to get other tutors to join.” In fact it becomes clearer to the world than ever that there is but one Ruskin in the world; an unguidable man, but with quantities of lightning in the interior of him, which are strange and probably dangerous to behold. Well, well; unguidable to outsiders you surely are; and you justly may pretend to spend your own lightning in the way you find suitablest to this wildly anarchic condition of affairs. Continue only for a quarter of a century yet as you may fairly hope to do; there will be something of result visible, something of combustion,
kindling here and there in the dark, boundless belly of our Chaos; and meanwhile the clang of the silver bows will be cheering to all the select of men.

I wish you would write to me at once again, and say clearly what your address is, and is to be in the now current weeks,Ruskin continued to write at least once or twice a week, from Assisi, Florence and Lucca. what your describable employments are and when we may look for you home. Adieu, dear Ruskin; you know well enough what my thoughts towards you are. With my whole soul I wish you noble victory and success.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 27 June. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: I have written at great length to Lord Torphichen, but not at all requesting, rather forbidding the trouble of sending his picture up hither for a thorough examination. Since you last heard of me, an actual Photograph of the Torphichen Picture (taken here two or three years ago by the Portrait Exhibition people)The Torphichen portrait of John Knox had apparently been displayed in a Portrait Exhibition in 1869; see Carlyle, Works 30:330. TC had also recently seen a copy of Penny’s engraving of the portrait; see TC to RHO, 10 April. has come into my hands and indicated sufficiently what the origin of that production may be. There was no other question I had except as to the time when this Picture came into the family and that I already concluded was quite unanswerable. Perhaps it is still possible Lord Torphichen in some mood of enthusiasm for Knox and his country may yet send us a look of the Picture itself for thorough examination; but if so, we are innocent of the adventure.

Your own beautiful Portrait of Knox, which I continue to believe in as the one extant Portrait of that Hero, has gone through a great deal of miscellaneous & continually diligent investigation, which is now about as good as completed. Some clear report of which I expect to have the pleasure of presenting when the Picture itself comes into your possession again.— The writing at the top of the Book in Knox’s hand is now found to be the Heading of the page & the Book itself the Geneva Bible.The Geneva Bible (Geneva, 1560) was one of the earliest English translations of the Bible; it was widely printed, and became the primary bible of English-speaking protestants. Which is a pretty fact surely.

It would give me real pleasure to be assured that a certain beautiful little hand and wrist were now quite themselves again.Selina Smyth had sprained her wrist in April; see TC to JAC, 11 April. Yours, dear Madam, with many thanks and regards / T. Carlyle

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 3 July. MS: FC. Quot: Brent E. Kinser and Clayton Carlyle Tarr, “‘How all goes with me here’: The Letters of John Forster to Thomas Carlyle, Part II,” CSA 32 (2017): 77. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: I was greatly vexed to have missed you on Tuesday; I intended fully both that day & the day before to have been at your house myself, but both days was driven aside by interruptions; and here was the last chance missed, and not to return for at least a week. I had to thank you for that fine Gift of the Dickens in noble green morocco (a most munificent and ornamental superfluity);Forster’s Life of Charles Dickens. Forster wrote, 28 June: “I know that you will give this book a place on your shelves for my sake and his who is gone. With how many grateful thoughts and earnest wishes it goes to you I may not even attempt to say” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 75). and still more especially I wanted to ascertain a little for myself how you really were and what your prospects in the improving weather[.] Pray send me a word in regard to this;Forster replied, 4 July: “To your kindest of enquiries I have more favourable answer to give than has been possible to me for (I might almost say!) years past. I tremble to think how soon the picture may be overshadowed, but all is fair for the present. Even my cough has been bearable, and my health otherwise, and above all, sleep, very good” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 76). it is the one purpose of my writing today. If you write tomorrow by your first post I shall get the note that night; instead of not till Monday morning at soonest. One line, if you please, and can.

Froude had gone his way that Tuesday morning. I have heard nothing from him since; but understood he had been in treaty with Lord Caernarvon about some considerable work to be done by F. in the Colonies and first of all in the Cape of Good Hope;Froude had been appointed by the colonial secretary, Henry Howard Molyneux Herbert, 4th earl of Carnarvon, to go to South Africa “and give the Government what help he could to understand the condition of affairs there” (Dunn, Froude 2:390), with a view to determining whether a confederation of the South African states could be achieved. —which I hoped and hope much will take effect & prove an excellent and useful labour for both parties. More about this when we meet.

Sunday last Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, Knt came down to me hither: a solid, grizzled sexagenarian, in excellent spirits and preservation; he asked specially
& anxiously about you;Duffy visited Europe 1874–76. Forster wrote to Duffy, 27 June: “My health is completely broken. I cannot speak of it. Carlyle, whom you are to see to-morrow, as I hear, will tell you something of it” (Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, Conversations with Carlyle [1892] 249). is naturally looking out all the old friends he can come upon; does not yet decide positively where to settle nor will completely for a year yet when wife and family are first to be home from Melbourne. He seemed hearty & hopeful; though out of health for some time before starting on his late voyage round the world.

For several days back I have been looking into Swift;Jonathan Swift (1667–1745; ODNB), writer, dean of St. Patrick’s Cathedral, Dublin, 1713–45. re-reading after some sixty years, his Tale of a Tub, Battle of the Books &c, (reserving Gulliver for a dainty apart); and today and yester-night have been busy with his Letters,—continually thinking of you, as was natural on such a task.TC owned Swift’s Works, 13 vols. (Edinburgh, 1768); see Sotheby’s (1932) 127. Forster was currently working on a Life of Swift; see TC to JAC, 11 April. Both Bolingbroke’s and Pope’sHenry St. John (1678–1751; ODNB), 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, politician, diplomatist and author; Alexander Pope (1688–1744; ODNB), poet; both friends and correspondents of Swift. Letters, especially the former’s, pleased me less than Jonathan’s; those final letters of his in the last months of his life were strange & tragical one of the grimmest sunsets to a strong and manful human life I have ever met with!—

Mary and I send our united loves to Mrs F., with all hopes to hear that she is prospering in the country.Forster wrote, 5 July: “I continue to go on well, and my poor little wife is getting back some of the strength lost in my service” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 77). Please remember me withal to Lord Lytton (whom Froude has fallen in love with, as I have some thoughts of doing also); if at any time he were passing this way & cared to look in, I hope he already knows how welcome he would be.Edward Robert Bulwer-Lytton, known as Robert Lytton, with whom Forster was staying at Knebworth Park; Forster replied, 5 July: “Great was [Lytton’s] pleasure at that kindly hint of yours, and he bids me tell you that he will most certainly be heard of in Chelsea next time he goes to London” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 77). Ever yours, dear Forster, and hoping good news,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-RH [RHO], 12 July. MS: NLS 3706.105. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO ROBERT HORN

docBody.p: Your kind and entertaining letter, which I read with thanks and instruction, has not been answered sooner solely because I was in expectation of the Banchory photographHorn wrote, 22 June: “Doubtless you have been wondering what has become of the photograph of Mr Thomson of Banchory’s ‘John Knox’”; see TC to RSM, 6 May. Horn continued: “My friend … instead of having the portrait photographed in Aberdeen, very considerately sent it down to me here, where I have had the verdict of James Drummond, the Curator of our S. National Gallery upon it. When the picture was taken out of the frame the canvass, he said, proved that it could not be more than a century & a half old, but that it seemed about that age. So to all appearances it was painted about the beginning of last Century. Then he objects that the cap is not round a-top, as a Geneva one should be. Burton, however, says it is like the French cap of Knox’s time.” James Drummond (1816–77; ODNB), artist, curator of the National Gallery of Scotland 1868–77; John Hill Burton (1809–81; ODNB), historian and political economist, historiographer-royal of Scotland 1867–81; see 45:77TC to WBCH, 18 Dec. 1867. TC had apparently been in touch with Burton about Knox, as Burton wrote, 7 June, with some historical notes, ending: “If I can find out anything touching the portrait I shall be sure to let you know.” which you were taking such obliging pains about. I conclude now that your photographer finds difficulties or almost impossibilities in the dark state of the Picture: indeed there is usually in such cases no method of obtaining a good photograph, but by first making, on thin transparent paper, a correct tracing of the Picture (a thing not difficult to do by a skilful hand), and then making a Photograph of that. Such a tracing of the Somerville Knox I have got done here, and intend to have it photographed, perhaps autotyped, and sent circulating through the Scottish population, as far as it will go, by some active dealer in such things. If you can find no expert Tracer in Edinburgh, or cannot without much difficulty find one, pray give up the Banchory adventure; and let it stand where it is, with many thanks from me for the trouble you have already taken.

The worthy Laing’s discovery of that record in 1581 of a payment to some foreign Artist for two Pictures, one of Knox, one of the young King himself, sent to Beza, is very interesting and even illuminative; and we shall all be much indebted if he will at once get us an exact copy with name of the Artist, sum of money paid him and whatever other particulars there are.Horn wrote: “Friend ‘David’ has found in the Treasurer’s Accounts for 1581,—what a dreadful fellow he is for poking!—the entry of a payment to an Artist (with some foreign name) for portraits of James VI and John Knox ‘sent to Mr Beza of Geneva.’ And he points triumphantly to Beza’s ‘Icones’ in which you find the young King given as the Frontispiece and ‘Joannes Knoxius’ as the only other Scotch helper of the Reformation, of whom a portrait is given.” Laing wrote, 20 Aug.: “[T]he payment you wished to have a note of from the Treasurer’s Accounts … is as follows: — ‘Junij 1581 / Itim, To Adrianc Vaensoun, Fleming painter, for twa picturis painted be him, and send to Theodorus Besa, conforme to ane precept as the samin producit upon compt beris. £8 .. 10 .. 0.’” Adrian Vanson (d. ca. 1602), Flemish painter, court painter (1584–1602) to James VI (1566–1625; ODNB), king of Scotland, England and Ireland. See also Carlyle, Works 30:323. Especially
interesting it would be were there any indication of the exact or approximate time when the work was done. Beza’s Letter to BuchananFor Beza’s letter to Buchanan, see David Irving, Memoirs of the Life and Writings of George Buchanan (Edinburgh, 1807) 184–85, and Carlyle, Works 30:322. , accompanying the Gift of his Icones to the King, is of date March 1580, and makes not the least allusion to his likeness either of Knox himself or of the King;—both these illustrious “Icons,” neither of which has the least vestige of resemblance, must have been cut in 1579 at latest; and the only conjecture I can form on the subject is that, in March 1580, or still more in Goulart’s rejection of the Beza Knox in 1581,For Goulart’s translation of Beza’s Icones, in which he replaces Beza’s portrait of Knox with one of William Tyndale, see TC to DL, 26 March, and Carlyle, Works 30:325–26. they must have given such a shock to the Court at Edinburgh that a resolution was formed to send poor Beza a pair of actual attempts at likeness; which Beza, one hopes with some slight pang of repentance, would put into his drawer, out of which drawer they would gradually go into utter darkness again by what steps no man can specify!— Please let us have the Note at any rate, as exactly as you can; and the sooner the better.

There has been a good deal of examination going on about the Somerville Picture here, chiefly in the way of strict search for all the F. Porbus Portraits, starting from that of Buchanan in the Royal Society here;See TC to JAC, 17 April. not altogether without success, but Portraits by the elder Porbus are not frequent in the Galleries here; and some five, mostly of Guise Frenchmen,The House of Guise was a French noble family; Mary of Guise (1515–60; ODNB), married James V (1512–42; ODNB), king of Scotland, and was the mother of Mary (1542–87; ODNB), queen of Scots. now in Hatfield House;Hatfield House, Hertfordshire, was the home of Robert Gascoyne Cecil (1830–1903; ODNB), 3d marquess of Salisbury, stepson of Lady Derby. Lady Derby wrote, 29 June: “I have ascertained that there are four pictures at Hatfield nominally by F. Pourbus, the Duc d’Aumale used to tell me that he doubted their being genuine, & I believed till yesterday that my successors at Hatfield had thrown still greater doubts upon them. / However there they are … & if you wish to commission any friends of yours to go & look at the pictures, the enclosed letter to the housekeeper will enable them to be admitted.” Henri Eugène Philippe d’Orléans (1822–97), duc d’Aumale, French collector of books and manuscripts, who lived in England for many years. are to be overhauled on Tuesday next,Boehm wrote, 15 July: “[I] saw the four portraits by Porbus there—that is to say three, as one of them is a wretched nameless daub. … [One] I could well imagine to be done by the Author of the original of that portrait of John Knox which you have shown me. … [I] believe that Porbus be the most likely painter who may have made a likeness of John Knox the size of the head of Buchanan from which the copy in the possession of Lord Somerville now at your House has been done.” and will terminate the quest
in that direction. I think I have already told you that the Book in Knox’s right hand fairly appears to be the Geneva Bible, with its margins, headings &c. The first folio Bible printed in Roman letters, which is another point to be remembered. For the rest, I am about to return the Picture to its owner; and conclude, for ever and a day, my enquiries into it; the end of which is little more than what the beginning of it was, That either this represents John Knox, done by some excellent Portrait-Painter (Porbus or another now lost or hidden), copied by some skilful, but much less careful and delicate master of the brush; probably not earlier than 1750 or else that it is entirely a mystery to me, its meaning inconceivable as to who or what it can possibly be.

The last thing I have to tell you is that I am in hopes the Torphichen Picture itself will arrive here shortly for examination;Horn wrote: “I should like much to have a look some day of the Torphichen portrait at Calder House, to have it subjected to the same critical inspection.” that I have seen the an excellent Copy of the Penny’s Engraving, and still farther a Photograph of the Picture itself, (what photograph they could get when the Picture was here two or three years ago in the Portrait Exhibition then held);—and that I already seem to myself to discern pretty clearly that this famed Torphichen Picture is simply a copy of the Hondius (or Verheiden)For Hondius and Verheiden, see TC to DL, 26 March. big, blusterous-looking beardie, whom you know, second edition of that incredible Figure-head set forth by Beza in 1580 & withdrawn by Goulart next year; from which Torphichen Original all the so-called Family Knoxes, your Banchory among others, are probably derived! Lord forbid, that I should utter this in Laing’s presence, but such I believe is the sad fact. Believe me, dear Sir

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAF, 13 July. Pbd: Dunn, CLF IV:243–44.
bibl.head: TC TO J. A. FROUDE

docBody.p:
Your letter leaves an impression on me such as I seldom have from any Letter: impression of solemnity, sorrow and thoughts that go into Eternity; deducting from it all the immense exaggeration of your kindness to me, I
accept and will for ever remember it with a sacred thankfulness full of blessed sorrow and something better than any joy.Froude wrote from Crogan, 10 July, hoping he and TC could meet before he left for South Africa (see TC to JF, 3 July): “I do not know whether I shall find you on my arrival still in Cheyne Row. The risks of Life increase in a long journey like that which I have before me— I should like to hear something of your plans that I may see you again before I go— You must give me directions about the sacred letters & Papers which you have trusted to my charge—whether you wish them to be returned to your custody during my absence—or whether they shall be locked up in a sealed parcel in Onslow Gardens, with instructions in case I never come back, to be placed in such hands as you desire. … [N]o words of mine will ever convey the obligation which I feel. … To me, you & you only have appeared to see your way in the Labyrinth of modern confusion—you have made it possible for me still to believe in truth & righteousness and the spiritual significance of life which creeds & systems have been felling to pieces. … Now when I am about to part with you on this long & uncertain journey I feel compelled to tell you in words what hitherto however I have tried to shew you silently.”

On awakening on Saturday my first determination was, to write to you that day, the day your Letter came; and certainly I should have done so, had not a series of practical errands and then a ditto of importunate interruptions spent all my time,—so that nothing remained at last but Mary’s hasty word and a dreary twenty minutes of American Bancroft’sGeorge Bancroft (1800–91), American historian and diplomat, U.S. minister to Prussia, 1867–71, and to the German Empire, 1871–74. Bancroft wrote in his diary: “On [11 July 1874] as I was in London, on my way home from Berlin, I remember Carlyle, with whom, in the years which I passed in England, I was intimately acquainted. So very often both he and his wife visited together in our family. … I found him cordial and pleasant; he spoke to me of himself without any words introducing it from me, of his own improved condition in point of fortune. It seemed to be strongly present to his mind that it was but a melancholy enjoyment to him; and he said of it: ‘Ah, if she were but here to enjoy it’. … I never heard a man in conversation seem more sincerely moved by grief at the thought of having been bereaved of his wife” (M. A. DeWolfe Howe, The Life and Letters of George Bancroft [New York, 1908] 2:275–76). conversation, whose “Fly”A light horse-drawn passenger vehicle. I noticed, with a shudder, waiting for me in the rain; evidently some human soul determined on an interview, the outcome of which was Bancroft after an absence of five and twenty years,TC first met Bancroft 18 Dec. 1846, soon after his arrival in London as U.S. minister to Britain, 1846–49; see 21:161JWC to HW, [17 Feb. 1847]; see also 22:156TC to RWE, 13 Nov. 1847. not at first recognizable at all, amid his wrinkles and huge grizly beard, nor supremely welcome when recognized. Poor fellow, he was very good too in his Extinct-Socinian way; and speaking well of some whom I liked well.

You are quite right in judging that the heat is horrible to me, and has roused all the remnants of energy I had, to get my affairs concluded here quàm primùm [as soon as possible] and rush out into the open air. Essentially I have
only three things to do: settle finally about the Knox Picture (to have the tracing of it photographed, which I hope will be done two days hence), secondly to have a glance at the Torphichen Picture (which has not yet come but is expected this week & of which I think I have already discovered the mystery) and thirdly to transact in some way that sublimity of an interview with the Prussian Imperialities,TC had been asked to meet Frederick William (1831–88), crown prince of Germany, and his wife, m. 1858, Victoria Adelaide Mary Louisa (1840–1901; ODNB), eldest child of Queen Victoria, who visited England 4 July–26 Aug.; see TC to JAC, 18 July. or see whether it can be transacted at all: I have not seen Lady Derby at all since you went; yesterday I found her fled to the country; but today, I am to have a little errand at the Athenaeum and propose to try in St. James’s Square again. This is how matters stand in London with me.

Furthermore on Wednesday last my Brother sailed for Lerwick,Lerwick, main town and port of the Shetland Islands. via Aberdeen. We hope to hear tomorrow that he is safe in Lerwick, diligently looking out for some bathing possibility there, — which I doubt, such are my sleep difficulties, will turn out impracticable. On the whole therefore, what I can say is that in ten days hence I purpose to set out towards Crogan and you; there to stay till your departure thence. After that, should Lerwick be possible at all, we will look to the sea, from Liverpool, by Glasgow and the Western Isles; or in some other way endeavour to dispose of ourselves. This is all that I yet see clearly or need report at present.

Everybody here warmly approves of the enterprize Lord Caernarvon and you have ahead; nothing could be wiser on his Lordship’s part, says everybody, nor could any appointment be so suitable as that of Froude. In fact I look forward to a new field of adventure & endeavour for you in which the good you may hope to do is practically immense, and which will probably be far more solid & wholesome, especially in your present mood than any other could be. I fausto pede.See Horace, Epistles 2.2.37: “With fortunate feet.”
I am called Athenaeum way but will leave this open to add a word concerning my Imperial affair before closing.

I have come home from my various errands, mostly re infecta [unfinished business], and utterly tired. Lady Derby is still in the country till tomorrow noon; will probably call here for a moment after that when the Prussian affair will be prophecied to me. Not a word more at present, dear Froude.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-BB, 14 July. MS: NLS 3278.166. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO BETTY BRAID

docBody.p: Here has a day come round againJWC’s birthday, 14 July. which awakens many thoughts in both of us. To me it must be for ever sacred and memorable beyond all other days of the year,—one other day alone excepted.The day of JWC’s death, 21 April 1866. You will allow me to send you the poor enclosed tokenMary Aitken recorded in TC’s checkbook: “14 July 1874 / Mrs Braid (Betty) / £5 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). TC sent Betty Braid a gift every year to commemorate JWC’s birthday. of my feelings towards you, who nearly alone of all the earth can fully sympathize with me in all my feelings on this occasion.

It would give me satisfaction to hear that you are not specially failing (which I think is not the case or else I should have heard from my Aunts);JWC’s aunts Ann and Elizabeth Welsh living at Craigen Villa, Morningside, in Edinburgh. but that your poor share of health like my own is still mercifully continued. I cannot well ask you to write in reply to this. Pray send me an old newspaper addressed in your own hand, and that shall suffice till you feel perhaps more disposed to write. I pray God to be with you, dear Betty, and to conduct us both to the rest appointed for all the weary[.]

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JR [JRU], 15 July. MS: Ruskin Lib. Collection. Pbd: Cate 202–5. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p:
We have been bountifully furnished with these precious little showers of manna which fall [word illegible] on us day after day with a wonderful continuity on your part. They are really strange and charming to me, wonderfully annihilating time and space between us, bringing you and your whereabout vividly home to us as in a magic glass.Ruskin was writing regularly to TC from Italy (see TC to JRU, 20 June), his letters full of descriptions of his surroundings, sometimes including architectural drawings. It is little to say of them that I have had
no such epistolary pleasure for the last eight years.TC means since he used to get letters from JWC. If I could command or expect such a thing, I should say Encore, encore, do not cease while I live! but, alas, that is not in my power; and while the reciprocity is all on one sideCoterie speech; see 19:196JWC to CGD, [1845]. such a thing in nature is not to be expected. Go on at any rate, so long as it is not a bother to you, and know always that nothing you can do is more certain of a grateful welcome. I think we have had eight Letters since I wrote to you last, and now that you are going or gone to Perugia and we are soon to be driven out of London by the fervent heat, I write again to apprize you as far as possible when we are going and whitherward, both of which points, especially the latter, are still somewhat involved in haze.

As to the time, it seems certain enough that we are still to be here for ten days; so that there is still room for a Letter or two, if you will stand good, not to say for three or four wh. could be safely and immediately forwarded to Froude’s in Wales (J. A. Froude, Esq., Crogan, Corwen, Merionethshire);—and should we even sail to Lerwick, where we suppose my Brother John to be, diligently looking out for bathing quarters, there is a daily post to that Scandinavian locality with only an addition of two days or perhaps of only one to the distance between Cheyne Row and you. Go on therefore for at least ten days hitherward and for ten more Froude-ward, Before the latter period expire you shall have another dispatch concerning our ulterior movements; and so enough, on that poor time-table head.

Mary and I turned up and punctually perused, I with great attention, all the chapters and passages of Scripture appointed you in childhood, by one now sacred to you;Ruskin wrote in Fors Clavigera, letter 42, “Misericordia” (June 1874), that he had been looking at his oldest Bible: “My mother’s list of the chapters, with which, learned every syllable accurately, she established my soul in life, has just fallen out of it. … And truly, though I have picked up the elements of a little further knowledge … this maternal installation of my mind in that property of chapters, I count very confidently the most precious, and, on the whole, the one essential part, of all my education” (Ruskin’s Works 28:101–2). nor did we omit the recent passage of Jeremiah’s Lamentations; but cannot any more than yourself ascertain who the “them” and “they” especially are.Ruskin wrote, 30 June: “I’ve been reading Lamentations IV and thinking that I’m a precious son of Zion comparable to fine gold, but I can’t make out who ‘they’ is, and who ‘them’ is in the 15th and 16th verses.” See Lam. 4:2 and 15–16. As to the rest, I found them one and all beautifully significant and maternally fit; indeed in nearly all of then I was struck by a kind of divineness of piety, intensity, and perfect sincerity not to be found in any other Book; ever wonderful old Jews! In three or four of the pieces, I forget now which, there was speech about Wisdom, of its dwelling with the Lord before anything else existed, of its being the essence and foundation
of all that does or ever will exist; nay, of its being almost the Lord himself,Of Ruskin’s list of chapters from the Bible, TC probably refers to Proverbs chaps. 2 and 8, and Psalm 90. which struck me very forcibly and with a light quite new, as words springing from the very deepest region of man’s soul, and being eternally the truth for the soul of man,—for me at this day as for the ancient Hebrew that penned them in his remote wilderness, thousands of years ago, thrice wonderful old Hebrews, sunk now to Baron Grant and his scoundrel Resuscitations of the Fine Arts in Leicester Square!Albert Grant, born Abraham Gottheimer (1831–99; ODNB), financier and company promoter, regularly accused of fraud and corruption; he was awarded the title of Baron in the Italian nobility, 1868. He purchased the derelict land in the middle of Leicester Square and converted it into a public garden, installing statues of eminent former residents, Joshua Reynolds (1723–92; ODNB), painter, Isaac Newton (1642–1727, ODNB), natural philosopher and mathematician, William Hogarth (1697–1764; ODNB), painter and engraver, and John Hunter (1728–93; ODNB), surgeon and anatomist, and a white marble fountain surmounted with a statue of Shakespeare in the centre. He donated it to the city, 2 July 1874. — Under this head too, I may as well mention that your earnest and eager enquiry twice repeated, 24th & 27th June, about my notions on Abbot Samson’s religion, on King Friedrick’s. Cromwell’s, and my Mother’s,Ruskin wrote, 24 June: “None of your readers, I believe,—none even of the most careful, know precisely, or in anything like practical approximation—what sympathy you have with the faith of Abbot Samson, or St Adalbert.—— I don’t know myself; To me the question of their faith is a fearful mystery, but one which I am sure is to be solved. … But I don’t know what your own inner thoughts are of the faith—such as you told me of in your mother—and such as so many noble souls have had in Scotland.” TC writes about Abbot Samson (1135–1211; ODNB) in Past and Present, and St. Adalbert of Prague (956–997) in Frederick. Ruskin then wrote, 27 June: “You have perfectly shown the value of sincerity in any faith moderately concurrent with the laws of nature and humanity. … You have also shown the power of living without any faith—in charity and utility—as Frederick.
