And what you say of Friedrich’s sorrowful surroundings and impossibilities of believing anything is to me the most precious passage of the whole book. … But you don’t say what you would have had Frederick be?— You don’t say what a Master ought now to teach his pupils to believe—or at least wish them to believe. And this, remember, is now a quite vital and practical question for me at Oxford.” He does not apparently mention Cromwell. have been often present to me; and at first gave me some surprize at finding you think I had still something more to tell you on that subject; though of late the surprize has gone, for I can now bethink me of almost nothing I have ever hinted, even in the obscurest way, on that point, if it be not one transient, but to myself significant allusion in Past and Present apropos of that duel Apud Radingas where a sinful caitiff, desperately fighting for his life,For the duel that took place near Reading, 1156, between Henry of Essex (d. ca. 1170; ODNB), administrator and royal constable (TC’s “sinful caitiff”), and Robert de Montfort, a relative of Henry’s second wife, Alice, see Carlyle, Past and Present 109–11. “Apud Radingas” means named for the Radingas, the Saxon people who lived near Reading. sees the gigantic figure of St. Edmund,St. Edmund (d. 869; ODNB), king of the East Angles, venerated as a martyr. looking doomful and
minatory upon him in the splendour of the evening sun, and falls down as if dead, but is brought to life again by the monks and lives as a monk many years afterwards abstracted from the world. There followed that a little word or two which had much much meaning to myself;For “the little word,” see Carlyle, Past and Present 118–19. but I now see can have had none to anybody else. I would gladly write on that subject, were there left in me, without fingers, the smallest power of writing, but it will be better that we first talk of it, as you propose, which I shall long for an opportunity of doing.

Froude is bound for the Cape of Good Hope and generally for the Colonies on an earnest mission from Lord Caernarvon and the Government to look into that colonial problem with his own eyes, and to advise what, in his own best judgement, can by a wise Government be done or attempted. He is to leave Southampton for Cape Town on the 23rd August; to be away many months, so that, probably, I shall never see him again. But the whole world, and all British men in the first place, may fairly expect to get some good of it, and in the end a boundless quantity of good by this adventure; and to himself in his silent sorrow it seems to me of all enterprises the most promising and wholesome. Everybody that I hear speaking of it warmly approves of the project & of the man selected for it. For my own part I feel well enough what I shall lose by the affair and how sad and solemn the adieu is. Of course I must see him on whatever terms for a few days before we part.

I had much to say about the last ForsRuskin wrote, 2 July: “I wonder what you’ll say to the July Fors! And the French and German bits!” Ruskin had long disagreed with TC over the relative merits of France and Germany; see TC to JRU 13 May. In Fors Clavigera, letter 43, “The Chateau Rouge. French Freedom” (July 1874), Ruskin discusses the word “frank,” which he defines as openness of heart: “But at last comes a nation called the Franks; and they are so inherently free and noble in their natures, that their name becomes the word for the virtue” (Ruskin’s Works 28:113); he contrasts it with “The frightfullest thing of all, to my mind, was the German temper, in its naive selfishness” (Ruskin’s Works 28:111). and things relating to yourself but my unfortunate ethereal part is so crushed down into the foul mire by this intolerable heat and feebleness of nerve and muscle that I must forbear it all till a better time. I tell you only two things; first, that I think and have long thought that you are dreadfully in error as to the German people and the genius of Germany; which (including England & its Shakespeares, wh. are radically German) I place far above the genius and character of any other people ancient or modern; very specially above whatever can be called French; and truly I wish you could get to understand how poor an affair, if you deducted those Franks out of it who are purely German every fibre of them, and not the best of Germans, la belle France, with all its boundless self-conceit, and even its pretty tailoring and cooking and ingeniously filigreeing talent, would be.

The second thing I had to say is but a repetition, namely of the dreadful shock
you have given to the Fine Arts here, especially to the Architectural, by your refusal of the GoldmedalSee TC to JRU, 13 May. to be presented by the Queen & the tittering and teeheeing of many sober minded and ingenious people by your dreadful offer to sit willingly in sackcloth and ashes with any respectable body of Fine-Artists that will invite you for such a purpose. Oh joy! Was there ever such cruelty heard of! How well deserved, I and the ingenious people do not now say.
Adieu, dear Ruskin, many kind adieus. Mary adds her kind regards and best wishes to mine.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAF, 18 July. Pbd: Dunn, CLF IV:244–45.
bibl.head: TC TO J. A. FROUDE

docBody.p: We have at length had tidings of my Brother’s movements & intentions,—yesterday by a telegram from the Isle of Skye,Isle of Skye, largest island in the Inner Hebrides. & today by a Letter from StromnessStromness, town on Orkney. John A. Carlyle wrote from Lerwick, Shetland, 13 July: “There are great crowds of tourists here just now, & every inn & lodging is crowded. There is no pleasant place for bathing in the sea, bottom being everywhere of rough rocks; &, after full consideration I find that neither you nor I could get any good of trying to bathe under such circumstances.” He then wrote from Stromness, 14 July: “This place so far as I have seen is the most agreeable I have been at since leaving London, & I shall halt to rest myself tomorrow as the little inn seems to be the best I have met with in the islands.” (of prior date & in the way home from Lerwick) his purpose is now to wait in Skye at glorious bathing in Kyle Akin (the Kyle of Hakon, after being beaten in the Battle of Largs)Kyleakin [Strait of Haakon], village on the E coast of Skye, where the Norwegian King Haakon IV (1204–63), was said to have rested after the battle of Largs, 1263, against Alexander III (1241–86; ODNB), king of Scots 1249–86. & thence to return direct to Dumfries; so that now he is out of the Welsh project altogether, and I, on seriously considering the matter this day have, with regret, but clearly, come to the conclusion that I must give up the hope of seeing you in Wales; and wait with patience, diligently knitting up the ravelled sleeveCf. Macbeth 2:2. of my pitiful employments & engagements here, so as to fly somewhither (uncertain yet as to the special whither) from the Nebuchadnezzar furnace,See Dan. 3:6. which grows more & more oppressive to me here.

The night before last I unexpectedly got done with my principal engagement,—that of the Prussian Imperialities: early in the day Lady Augusta sent from the Deanery positive order to appear there at 6 p.m.;See TC to JAF, 13 July. Lady Augusta Stanley wrote, 16 July: “The Crown Princess of Germany is most anxious to see you and wishes to do so here at six o’clock this afternoon.— Pray make this your afternoon walk, and give us the great pleasure of seeing you here to meet this interesting Lady.” not for years had I been in worse case, but what remedy!— I had to promise, & to go. The interview, quite in unceremonious shape was pleasant beyond all expectation. I found the Prince a gallant, noble-looking man tall, perpendicular, with a pair of royal eyes & a fine manful countenance, completely kind & civil to me; & the Princess Imperial one of the gracefullest, most intelligent & lovable of young ladies; and the whole interview was transacted in few minutes more than an hour. For the rest, we were but a dimmish party, Matthew Arnold, Motley, W. E. ForsterMatthew Arnold (1822–88; ODNB), poet, writer, and inspector of schools; John Lothrop Motley, American historian and diplomat; William Edward Forster (1818–86; ODNB), politician, philanthropist, and Liberal M.P. for Bradford 1861–86; known to TC since 1843; see 47:153TC to JAC, 10 Feb. 1871. & self of the man kind & a certain ancient, extremely wrinkly but good humoured Madame Moll,Mary Elizabeth Mohl, b. Clarke (1793–1883; ODNB), salon hostess and author; she mainly lived in Paris. the only female stranger. The Princess seemed to have some Dame d’Atours [Lady-in-Waiting]Unidentified further. with her, to whom I was not introduced & who did not speak at all. We sat throughout, shook hands at parting like common Christian people & went each his several way. Lady Derby had been here that morning (properly afternoon) & had taught me to expect that the Imperial interview, at least on the Prince’s part, lay farther ahead; but I was right glad to find it more succinctly arranged by the judicious Lady of the Deanery & all done before the sun went down.

I have now only the dreary puzzle of the Knox Portrait to clear my hands of; which in all practical respects is now finished—my own opinion being made up, & no farther elucidation to be had anywhere, tho’ many paltry enough outer details are still incumbent; which ended, I quit the subject for ever & a day.

Tell me so soon as you can what day you are to be expected here. I will meet you or be feebler & worse bested than I have almost ever been. God bless you, dear Froude; I think you have great things ahead and none wishes you more luck in fulfilling them.

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-RH [RHO], 20 July. MS: NLS 3706.109. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO ROBERT HORN

docBody.p: My Uncle, Mr Carlyle, desires me to send you his best thanks for your Letter and the two Photographs of the Banchory Knox.See TC to RHO, 12 July. Horn wrote, 22 June: “I hope in a few days now to send you a photograph of this ‘Banchory Knox,’ which may at all events afford you some fun in your back garden at Chelsea, where you told me you sunned yourself occasionally at this season. Only I much fear you may be apt to lit your pipe with it when you see the beard!” The latter he finds very interesting, & he is surprised at the clearness of the photography.

He would be extremely obliged if you would have the kindness to get for him an exact copy of the note respecting the payment of Beza’s woodcut which you said Mr David Laing had lately found.See TC to RHO, 12 July.
With my Uncle’s best thanks and regards I am / Yours very truly

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JR [JRU], 30 July. MS: Yale. Pbd: Cate 208–10. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: Thanks again and again for these little showers of manna immediate from the skies, which do not wholly cease but still come to us now & then,—last night from Florence, for example, and some nights before from Perugia: wonderful things for us amid the dusty tumults of London in our little cell at Chelsea here.

The gorgeous splendour of your room at Florence,Ruskin wrote from Florence, 26 July: “There’s … only one room in the inn, not under ‘restoration.’ That room is twelve of my paces by thirteen and a half … it has three tall windows—and six tall doors—over every door is a chandelier with five candles in it, and in the middle of the ceiling a chandelier with 62 candles in it … the furniture is scarlet & gold—the paper green and gold—the doors, all double folding, hidden by crimson curtains—a landscape good enough to sell to an American for a Salvator hangs opposite the windows—& the marble chimneypiece is finely sculptured with vine leaves and a nymph going to sacrifice a goat.” and, alas, your own wild gloom of mind while lodged in it, as if it were the blackest nook of Malebolge;Ruskin wrote that he felt “all black & damp like a bad walnut with biliousness and sulkiness.” After describing his room he wrote: “The general sense of being in one of the deepest holes of Dante’s inferno which this room produces on me … is very unpleasant.” For Malebolge, see TC to CEN, 3 Nov. 1873. that is a strange but not unaccountable phenomenon, such as easily
occurs in this wicked perversity of a world! But we can expect a still more emphatic and scorching Fors from you on that account, which is some benefit of good out of evil.

On the whole, is it not evident for one thing, that the Italian summer is getting far too hot for you; that in practical truth you ought to bundle up your notebooks and come home, or nearer home? I really think so, but must not take upon me to advise. If at the “tomb of Simon de Montfort,” in more tolerable air (in France, as that may well be), you could pick up for us any vestige of clearer evidence or intelligability about that notable and to me inconceivable man, it would beyond doubt be a welcome thing. But wasn’t he clearly cut down and chopped into mince meat, flesh and bones, at Eavesham;Ruskin wrote from Perugia, 13 July: “The heat has come heavy at last and I begin to think of home. I want to see the ‘Mont’ of Simon de Montfort, by Seine side—as I come back, and if France is pleasant may linger there.” Simon de Montfort (1208–65; ODNB), 8th earl of Leicester, was killed in battle at Evesham, Worcestershire, 4 Aug. 1265. His remains were buried in Evesham Abbey. His family came from Montfort l’Amaury in the Île-de-France, about 31 mi. (50 km.) W of Paris. how then can he have got buried near Paris? Furthermore, have you not heard that his Son was “The blind Beggar of Bethnal-Green”?TC refers to the legend that Sir Henry de Montfort (1238–65; ODNB), eldest son of Simon de Montfort, was not killed at Evesham as had been supposed, but was blinded, and became the “blind beggar of Bethnal-Green,” celebrated in the Elizabethan ballad, “The Beggar’s Daughter of Bednall-Green,” printed by Thomas Percy (1729–1811; ODNB), writer and cleric, in Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765) 2:155–69. It was also the subject of several plays, including one by James Sheridan Knowles (1784–1862; ODNB), in 1828. What a Dark-LanternDark-lantern, lantern with a slide to hide the light. is history, or worse, even, a Lantern of darkness; absolutely tenebrific, instead of illuminative!

The one real object of this Letter is to tell you that we are still here, & likely to be so for at least a fortnight longer, hungry therefore for your immediate missives if you will have the charity still to send such. Froude is expect[ed] here Saturday (the day after tomorrow); stays for three weeks, and in the course of the first, must settle many small but important things with me in case we should not meet again in this world.See TC to JAF, 13 July. I am confident he will do real good in his colonial expedition; good, even in the emigration line, in spite of the pot boiling over. These things go on at an inconceivably slow rate; a century, nay ten centuries, representing what would actually be but a minute in the real pot, dashing its fat into the fire. Patience, my Friend, patience; we must have patience.

Before leaving Florence I must ask you to take another look at Michael Angelo’s Statue of David and explain to me a little (on your return) how it is that the gigantic plaster cast of this Figure (in our Brompton BoilersA plaster cast of Michelangelo’s “David” by Clemente Papi (1803–75), Italian sculptor, was given to Queen Victoria, 1856, who gave it to the South Kensington Museum; it was installed in the boilerhouse and opened to the public 20 June 1857; see “View of the interior of South Kensington Museum, Boilerhouse, featuring the Statue of David. Photograph. London, England, c. 1860s” at vandaimages.com/preview.asp?image=2006BG7754. For the “Brompton Boilers” see 35:91TC to FMB, 10 May 1859. here) is more impressive to me than any statue I have ever seen.
Not a word more— there is an intrusion jingling at the door, peremptorily saying Cease. Mary sends her love.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JHW, 3 Aug. Addr: 1 Briant’s Villas / North Finchley / N. MS: NLS Acc. 9681. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. John Hunter Watts (1853–1923), socialist activist.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN HUNTER WATTS

docBody.p: I suppose the transient utterance you have found in Friedrich on the world old question, of “Fate, Freewill, Foreknowledge absolute”Cf. Milton, Paradise Lost 2:560. has been introduced [by] way of mocking at the endless puddle that poor mortals have in all times created for themselves on that entirely insoluble and practically useless question. It is a question that to me for my own part, was early disposed of, as utterly useless for practical business, which is all we have to do or care for in this world; and I would recommend you and your friends to dismiss it on the same terms, as lying beyond the limits of the human faculty, practically unknowable and of little use were it even known.
Believe me,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 3 and 4 Aug. MS: NLS 528.14. Quot: Wilson, Carlyle 6: 335. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your letter of this morning; we had got no tidings from Scotland at all through the week and were glad to hear your specific accounts of everything.

I have been very weak & useless all this while, though with nothing particular to complain of, except perhaps the multifarious interruptions and empty intrusions of people who for most part have no real business with me, or at least none that, to myself that could be of either pleasure or profit.

At this point yesterday enter a new interruption, Samuel Laurence Painter to see the Knox Picture &c &c; which completely cut off all the time and possibility I had left. So let us peaceably proceed swallowing down the disgust of the inevitable.

Froude was expected at home last nightFroude had been in Wales for several months; see TC to JAF, 20 June. within an hour or less he will probably be here. Let us be speedy therefore. He is to continue between here and RamsgateFroude was to visit Caroline Warre, b. Grenfell (1809–86), Henrietta Froude’s widowed step-mother, at Westcliff House, Ramsgate. Froude was also friendly with Henrietta’s brother John Henry Warre (1825–94); for the Warre family, see 46:235. for three weeks; sails by appointment Aug. 23rdFroude sailed from Dartmouth on the Walmer Castle, 23 Aug. 1874. for the Cape of Good Hope & other colonies; is to be absent some ten months; so that our meeting again is uncertain enough, and there are various, to me, important little thingsSee TC to JAF, 13 July. that have to be settled with him in case we meet no more.

My other real business here, if business it may be called is all included in the Somerville Knox Picture and the winding up of that for ever and a day. About a week ago, after tedious & insipid negotiation, the Torphichen Picture of Knox has also arrived and there are photographings &c to be gone into; & then as some succinct & clear record of the results arrived (at which will not be a very long story will have to be put on paper, & so my hands washed of that poor affair for evermore. I do not grudge the manifold fasheries I have had in regard to that affair. My hope is that there is at last a fair chance given to Scotland for recognising what the veritable likeness of John Knox was in this world; if they choose still to hold by the Beza figure-head & the unhappy Laing absurdities, they can freely do so & I am guiltless. The Torphichen
Picture, now in the hands of the Hon. Mrs Ramsay of Barnton, Aunt of the young Lord Torphichen,Hon. Mary Ramsay, b. Sandilands (d. 1891), widow (m. 1828) of William-Ramsay Ramsay of Barnton (1809–50), great-aunt of James Walter Sandilands, 12th Lord Torphichen. She lived in Edinburgh but was visiting in London and had apparently brought the portrait with her; she wrote, 17 Aug., thanking TC for its return. who has been very civil in the matter I have already been to see, & made up my own mind about it, as being a worthless & totally incredible piece of “portraiture” done from the primitive Beza figure-head, which you know so well instead vice-versa. But Boehm is not here for the next four or five days, and till then nothing must be decided. Scharf isGeorge Scharf; see TC to JEB, 18 May. likely to go with me today and look at it. Tait, I rather think, has already been: nobody I think will be able to guess the Painter, for he is evidently a man of no character or mark. Tait, who is helping me a little, saw Laing the other day at the British Museum; reports him to be busy on a pamphlet in regard to this subjectLaing did not publish the pamphlet, but apparently passed his notes to James Drummond (see TC to RHO, 12 July), who delivered a paper based on the notes to the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, 10 May 1875 (privately printed as The Portraits of John Knox and George Buchanan [Edinburgh, 1875]), in which he sharply criticized TC’s claims in favor of the authenticity of the Somerville portrait; see Marinell Ash, “David Laing and Carlyle,” Carlyle Newsletter 4 (1983): 27–31. (pamphlet much unlikely to be elucidative to me). Laing himself has not been here, nor do I know where he is. One thing is clear, I will have no controversy with LaingLaing did visit TC while in London; he wrote to Robert Horn, 22 Aug.: “I was glad to have an opportunity of seeing the original Somerville portrait, then at Chelsea. I also accompanied Mr C. and Mr Scharf of the National Portrait Gallery to see the Torphichen portrait which had been sent to Lord T’s Aunt (Mrs Ramsay of Barnton) to gratify Mr Carlyle’s curiosity. They both were of opinion very much that which I had asserted thirty years ago it was a bad copy from Beza’s woodcut” (MS: NLS 3706.117). or with anybody; but simply after putting down the little I have ascertained in my own sphere of enquiry, glide silently out of the affair.

The town, as you will guess, has now vomited forth all its quality at once & is, or is fast becoming, one of the most silent places in England. The heat, too, ceases to annoy, though as yet we can get no real welting of rain. Almost every day, at some period of it, promises deluges, but in result nothing but driblets come. There is great want of rain; the grass about Chelsea Hospital I found, this morning, all withered into snuff & even Hyde Park is dusty in some parts. Doubtless there will be rain & deluges of it, most likely till we are all tired of that too.

Forster who came back from Lord Lytton’sForster had been staying with the Lyttons since late June; see TC to JF, 3 July. wonderfully improved has returned thither, but only for a little while. What he is to do next remains still a little doubtful to him, the sea-side most probable, but he seems evidently
gravitating towards a warmer climate for the winter. Allingham has at last got what he feels to be secured in the Editorship of Fraser;Froude had been editor of Fraser’s Magazine since 1860; he had recently resigned and Allingham had been appointed. and still more astonishing is straightway going to be married. His intended, whom he suddenly brought here one day & trailed me through the woods of Kensington Gardens along with, is a reasonable enough young woman kind of artist in wood cutting or drawing for wood cutters; modest, rational & miraculously content with her Allingham;Allingham m., 22 Aug., Helen Mary Elizabeth Paterson, watercolor painter and illustrator. to whom, poor soul, one cordially wishes all possible good. Duffy seems to have vanished towards Dublin, thence to Aix-le-bain & a winter in Provence. I had several walks with him; avoiding carefully his Irish heterodoxiesDuffy had spent some time in London during 1865–66, and later wrote: “In all our intercourse for more than a generation I had only one quarrel with Carlyle, which occurred about this time, and I wish to record it because, in my opinion, he behaved generously and even magnanimously. … I spoke with indignation of the treatment of Ireland by her stronger sister. Carlyle replied that … it was his opinion that Ireland had brought all her misfortunes on herself” (Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, Conversations with Carlyle [1892] 223). but strongly counselling him to abjure the same, if he meant to prosper in London, or do good in God’s world. Poor Brookfield died suddenly,Rev. William Henry Brookfield, friend of the Carlyles since 1846, d. 12 July at his home, 16 Hereford Sq., London. as perhaps you know, & has left Miss Bromley,Caroline Davenport Bromley. a fifteen years friend of his, in great sorrow; which truly & the death of Brookfield, too, awakens many sympathies in me. Dugald ChristieWilliam Dougal Christie d. 27 July at his home, 32 Dorset Sq., Marylebone, London. He was TC’s chief aide in the setting up of the London Library, and remained a committee member until his death; see 48:206TC to WDC, 18 June 1873, and 208TC to JF, 24 June 1873. too, is dead: neither Forster nor I had heard the least intimation of his illness, but Forster thinks it was mainly a kind of heart-break, or kind of depression of mind, after so many failures to recover his lost position in Politics or diplomatizing or any other directing that had gradually worn him away. He was a tough, stubborn creature; but of dull, stiff, pig-like nature & has ended this. Ay de mi.Coterie speech, see 6:241TC to JSM, 16 Oct. 1832.

I am diligently reading Boswell’s Life of Johnson, new edition;James Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D. together with a Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, 3 vols., ed. Percy Hetherington Fitzgerald (1874); see TC to JAC, 4 Feb. purged from all the Crokerisms MaloneismsTC reviewed Boswell’s Life of Johnson, ed. John Wilson Croker (1780–1857; ODNB), politician and essayist (1831) for Fraser’s Magazine (1832); see 6:72TC to JAC, 20 Dec. 1831. Edmund Malone (1741–1812; ODNB), Irish literary scholar and biographer, encouraged and assisted Boswell with writing A Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785) and The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D. (1791), and subsequently ed. several further edns. of both. & other intrusive rubbish; printed spelt
&c exactly as Boswell himself did it; & really I think the most eligible Boswell. It is above forty years since I read any part of it; & the view I get of the things & persons now is in curious & various contrast to what they yielded me before. Every night for two or two & a half hours I sit quietly sunk in this Book; Mary eagerly learning to draw beside me (wonderful to see); and these in spite of fatal Indigestion & whatever it can do are commonly the best hours of my day.

Write to me again, dear Brother; do not plague poor Jean with writing to me, but let her understand that her writings are always welcome. I send my love & blessing to one & all of you; would that it could do you any good! And so adieu for this time. Ever your affectionate Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 4 Aug. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: Our multifarious investigations of the Knox Picture are now altogether completed, I mean of your Knox Picture,—for by the kindness of Lord Torphichen his Picture also of the Great Reformer has now come to town, and got under examination, but that, I expect, will not be a difficult problem, and indeed the secret of it, or every way probable secret, is; to some of us, already discernible. But as to the Somerville Knox, I clearly think there is now nothing further discoverable at present; & the precious Picture itself is now ready to be delivered to its benificent Lady owner, directly on notice given. I am not certain to be in London above a ten days longer, & indeed was under risk of leaving it weeks ago: but I hoped, and still hope, to have the pleasure of delivering it to you in person,Selina Smyth replied, 7 Aug., that she had returned to Ireland. and of seeing once again one whom I shall always remember as a signally polite and amiable benefactress to me (and in a sense to all Scotland as well as me) in regard to this matter.

Our conclusion arrived at here is, 1o, That this Knox Picture is by a Limner of eminent talent; a portrait of very great felicity, and, in the highest degree, characteristic of John Knox, the most memorable of Scotsmen. 2o, That what we have of it is a Copy, not earlier than the middle of the last century; copy of excellent swift execution and singularly faithful in result; though probably of much inferior delicacy to the original it was taken from. 3o (after manifold examination and enquiry), That it has discernibly probable features of the style
of Francois Porbus, painter of George Buchanan, at or about the same time, and of Six other distinguished Portraits, accesible in this neighbourhood; all of which have been minutely examined by what I think the highest authority and best judge discoverable in England, I mean the German Sculptor Mr J. E. Boehm, whose candour & veracity in regard to this, as to all matters is also much to be relied on.TC and Boehm had been to see the portrait of Buchanan at the Royal Society; see TC to JAC, 17 April, and several other Pourbus portraits; see TC to LLA, [30] May; for Boehm’s visit to see the Pourbus portraits at Hatfield House; see TC to RHO, 12 July. Lastly, It is the opinion of all competent inspectors of this Picture, and remains my own as emphatically as ever that this Picture is either verily the likeness of John Knox or else a thing totally unintelligible and at present inconceivable. If at a future day, what is possible, though, alas, not very probable, the original Porbus, hidden in some dim, unexpected corner, do turn up, all this hypothesis may change itself into clear fact,Boehm visited Bruges, Ghent, Brussels, and Antwerp in Sept., and wrote to TC, 30 Sept., that his findings “left no doubt whatever in my mind that the portrait of John Knox which you had in your House … is a copy after a smaller portrait of John Knox by Porbus. There are 2 pictures at Brüges in each of which are 16 portrait heads, carefully painted & somewhat smaller than the head of Buchanan … and I can most vividly figure to myself that the original from which the said head was done—must have been like that & not otherwise. The costumes in some of them being also very similar to John Knox’s garments and collar. … if I had found the original in a corner of a gallery my astonishment would have been as small as my pleasure would have been great, in apprising you of the find. … I saw no less than 40 portraits by [Pourbus], and they all bear the same traces in drawing, arrangement of light & shadow conception of character, and all those qualities which can never quite be drowned in a reproduction.” but, if otherwise, of course it must rest always deniable withal, & the likeness of your Picture to Knox be a matter depending on internal evidence not on external,—which indeed is wanting in perhaps a still higher degree to most of the other supposed Pictures of him. Of all this I intend to put on paper a more explicit statement and contrast with the Torphichen Picture, were that once thoroughly examined (but unluckily Boehm is absent for a few days & that latter cannot be settled at once): of this Paper you shall have a copy, you who best of all deserve one.

One point I must not omit; for there may be something of haste in it. In one of the early notes, written by your Sister the Hon. Mrs Henry, which Lady Derby shewed me,For the correspondence between Louisa Henry and Lady Derby, see TC to LDE, 23 March. it was stated, dubitatively, that there had existed in the family a tradition connecting this Picture in some way with James 13th Baron Somerville your and your Sister’s Great-great-grand father, who died in 1765 (?).Lord Somerville is a title in the Scottish peerage, and after the union of the Scottish and English crowns the numbers ascribed to each Lord differ according to different authorities. The Lord Somerville referred to here is James Somerville (1698–1765), usually now known as 12th Lord Somerville, Selina and Louisa’s great-grandfather. I could wish much that you examined into this matter before
leaving England. It seems to me that whenever the Somerville Papers become accessible,Selina Smyth replied: “I regret to say that we know nothing concerning this picture … & fear any trace of as to how it came into our family will be almost impossible to discover, as all the Somerville M.SSs & papers, deeds &c were destroyed by fire some years ago.” this 13th is the Lord Somerville, whose correspondence, accounts &c are by far the most likely to contain some hint of the Knox Picture. He appears to have been a man of much culture, widely known in society for his accomplishments; had been acquainted with Pope &c &c. A few days ago I found, concerning him, a curious & interesting little notice by Boswell in the Life of Johnson which I will by no means fail to send you by the next opportunity.See TC to SCS, 19 Aug.

But the thing practically most pressing today, relates to an external detail, namely the having a Copy of the Knox Picture taken before it leave for Ireland. We did try photographing with our best skill, but that proved entirely a failure; nothing realized, but a dim spectre, seen in hairy outline, as of a shadow drowned in London fog. But yesterday there came to me an old acquaintance, one Lawrence, well skilled in painting, who greatly admiring the pictorial talent displayed in this Knox, was extremely anxious to take a copy of it in oil; and would engage to have it done in one week (adding only two days of law). I answered that it was impossible without your permission, but that I would immediately write, and beg you to give the speediest answer you could.Selina Smyth replied: “I am making arrangements for the placing of it in the S. Kensington Museum as a loan, but before doing so will, with pleasure, allow Mr. Lawrence to take a copy of it in oils.” This Lawrence has a great deal of sound sense and feeling about painting, though he has never risen into the eminence, once anticipated for him: I am not certain he will make a perfect or first rate Copy, but it will most likely be something respectable; and to have, in case of accident to this invaluable Knox, even a tolerable copy in existence would surely be a desirable thing. Please answer me on this point, dear Lady so soon as my question reaches you.
With many regards to yourself and to Mr Ralph Smyth, I remain

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 7 Aug. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Many thanks for the kind little Note so full of benificent intention and friendly feelings towards me; of which I at no time have any doubt whatever, though the renewed assurance of them bring always a new pleasure[.] I am very glad also to have the good accounts of MaryMary Florence, Lady Ashburton’s da. and yourself and of the happy combination of play and work in which you spend your last BuxtonBuxton, spa town in Derbyshire; for Lady Ashburton’s visit there, Sept. 1872, see 48:90TC to JF, 4 Sept. 1872. days. Are you very sure these Buxton baths do yield you new strength? The immediate result you describe as quite the contrary. But let me not interfere with medicalities. The fresh breezes of Ross-shireKinlochluichart, Lady Ashburton’s Highland estate in Ross-shire. I calculate will at any rate blow away all these “enervations.”

Thanks many and many for your bountiful offers about Seaforth.Seaforth Lodge, Lady Ashburton’s house in Devonshire; TC and JWC had been there together, March 1865 (see 41:182TC to JAC, 9 March 1865–202JWC to SWA, 30 March [1865]), and TC had only visited once since, in Aug. 1872; see 48:71TC to JCA, 20 June 1872. I do wish I were there, and had a good pony to ride & the sea to swash into: but, alas, the inevitable fash, uncertainty and sadness of recollection that all this involves, stand threatening in the way and forbid any resolution of such magnitude. Seldom in my life have I felt so weak & utterly useless as now in these last months[.] It cannot be the hot weather either, for now the weather is grown dark, and at times even coldish. On the whole it seems as if should the rain come, as come it surely must before long, I may as well loiter languidly and sorrowfully here as anywhere else. The town is growing quiet as a desert, & I am at least surer of a nightly spell of some kind of sleep & welcome oblivion of all terrestrial things here in my own poor Chelsea den than anywhere else in the world. We shall see. Froude at any rate is here since Tuesday last, bound for the Cape of Good Hope on August 23d for long months to come; I have many things to settle with him on the chance of his not finding me when he comes back: that and the final winding-up of the much petty botheration about the Somerville & Torphichen Pictures of Knox wh. I am just getting rid of seem to me the only vestiges of real business I have on hand; & the scene for these lies in Chelsea withal. The immediate question is, Will it rain today, or will it keep fair!—

Adieu, dear Lady; do not fail, I beg of you to write again, at latest when you
get to L. Luichart or again change your locality. My best blessing upon dear,Word repeated with a line over it at turn of page. good Mary and you.

bibl.sourceNote: MA-SCS, 12 Aug. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me say, with his kind regards and thanks for your and Mr Ralph Smyth’s notes, that I have written to tell Mr McLeod that of course Mr Carlyle will be most happy if he will come here and inspect the Knox Picture.Ralph Smyth wrote, 9 Aug.: “I have received a letter from the Director [of the South Kensington Museum] saying that it is not usual to accept pictures … on loan without their first being seen by an officer of the Museum and asking where it could be inspected. I have therefore taken the liberty of directing him to your home, and hope it will not be inconvenient to you allowing it to be seen there.” Norman Macleod (b. 1803), sec. of the South Kensington Museum. I am,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 19 Aug. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p:
A week ago the Knox Picture was sent up to Mr Laurence (6 Well St., Oxford St.),Laurence lived in Camden Rd., his studio was at 6 Wells St., Oxford St. who is now busy copying it,—I know not yet with what success. Some two days afterwards I was called upon by Mr WallisGeorge Wallis (1811–91; ODNB), museum curator and art teacher, senior Keeper of the art collections at the South Kensington Museum 1863–91. of the S. Kensington Museum from whom I received this morning the enclosed Letter; intimating that all is settled as to Laurence and the Museum and that the Picture is to go to its place on Monday coming. I suppose you have already had, at Castle Bellingham a notice of this result now arrived at; but fancied a word
from myself over and above would do no harm. I hope to see the Picture well hung in Kensington Museum on my return to town, and under interesting scrutiny of many people who are anxious about Knox and his real likeness. To yourself they and, in the first place, I are under deep obligation for the prompt and very great kindness you have throughout manifested in the matter

There will be, I hope, before long some distinct account drawn up and put in print of the rival claims (if rival they can be called) of this Somerville Knox & the Torphichen one, which latter seem to me to border on nothing: of this you shall according to promise have the earliest copy. Meanwhile, what also was promised, I send you the extract from Boswell’s Johnson concerning your Ancestor the probable introducer of this Picture into the Somerville family; a pleasant little piece of reading if you dont know it already.
Apropos of Johnson’s assertion that PopeAlexander Pope; see TC to JF, 3 July. was somewhat deficient in conversational brilliancy Boswell remarks:

‘The late Lord Somerville, who saw much both of great & brilliant life, told me that he had dined in company with Pope & that after dinner the “little man,” as he called him, drank his bottle of Burgundy, & was exceedingly gay & entertaining.’ And Boswell adds in a footnote:

‘Let me here express my grateful remembrance of Lord Somerville’s kindness to me, at a very early period. He was the first person of high rank that took particular notice of me in the way most flattering to a young man, fondly ambitious of being distinguished for his literary talents; & by the honour of his encouragement made me think well of myself & aspire to deserve it better. He had a happy art of communicating his varied knowledge of the world in short remarks & anecdotes with a quiet pleasant gravity, that was exceedingly engaging. Never shall I forget the hours which I enjoyed with him at his apartments in the Royal Palace of Holyrood House, & at his seat near Edinburgh, which he himself had formed with an elegant taste.’ (Boswell’s Life of Johnson, Vol II p.)TC omitted the page no.; the reference is to the Fitzgerald edn. of Boswell (2:434) that he was currently reading; see TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug. See also Boswell’s Life of Johnson, ed. G. Birkbeck Hill; 2d edn. ed. L. F. Powell, 6 vols. (Oxford, 1964–71) 4:50.

Boswell wrote his Book in 1789 so that “the late Lord Somerville” must be James 13th Baron who died in 1765, the Ancestor alluded to by your Sister in reference to this Picture of Knox. If in writing to that Lady, any time soon, you could ask on my behalf for the precisest form she can give to this recollection of her childhood,Selina Smyth wrote, 24 Aug., thanking TC for the extract from Boswell’s Johnson; she continued: “My sister Mrs Henry … says she remembers only to have quoted what my Aunt (Lady Head) says in reference to the Knox portrait—viz. that she concluded it was one of the old family paintings in possession of my great grandfather James 13th Lord Somerville.” Selina Smyth’s aunt was Julia Valenza, b. Somerville (1792–1879), Lady Head. —if indeed there is any more precise form than the one I
already have,—it would be a new obligation to me. I am leaving town at the end of this week, but dont expect to be absent many days, and a note directed hither will follow me at any time
I beg to offer many kind regards to Mr Ralph Smyth; and am ever, with the kindest wishes I can form, dear Madam,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 27 Aug. MS: NLS 528.15. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your letter of this morning. I am doing pretty well here,TC and Mary Aitken left Chelsea, 22 Aug., and traveled by steamer to Edinburgh. They were staying in lodgings with Agnes Orrock (b. 1817) and her sister Elizabeth (b. 1819), 73 George St., where John A. Carlyle always stayed when in Edinburgh; see 48:116TC to JAC, 7 Dec. 1872. that is as well as could be expected after such violent revolutions, breakages of sleep &c &c. This morning in particular I feel better considerably than since leaving Chelsea the rather perhaps as yesterday, after a sleepless night produced by many intricate confusions of my own poor inner man, was one of my worst days.

We have daily had a punctual swash in salt water, yesterday at PortobelloPortobello, coastal suburb 3 mi. (5 km.) from the center of Edinburgh. for the first time and by a mere bathing machine which seemed to be rather the elligiblest plan. I have seen Laing, who indeed had come to me in London, all in the old humour as he again was in his angular little room in Parliament Square.Laing’s office in the Signet Library, Parliament Sq., Edinburgh. Stirling of Kier unexpectedly stept in while Mary & I were there & was very blithe and taking, but I made no engagement as to Keir, nor held out much likelihood of any.Sir William Stirling Maxwell. In fact we are perfectly incognito here; attend only to our own bits of affairs & have not hitherto seen even Masson,David Masson. tho’ more than once intending to do so,—were it only for the purpose of borrowing a Book or two for perusal in the evenings.

Of course there could not be any objection to your coming hither, except this only that we have put you out of house and home here; and if you came
you would have to find a new lodging place, or else we should!— Probably it will be better to leave things lying for a day or two; at all events till a new week, by which time the view ahead will be a little clearer. Since we began writing there has come the letter now enclosed from Peter Swan;Patrick Don Swan, known to his friends as Peter; he lived at St. Brycedale House, Kirkcaldy, and Springfield House, nr. Cupar, Fife. the one chief or sole objection to his offer of Springfield is that there will be no sea-bathing there for me and I think he said before his Kirkcaldy house was at present under the painter’s hand. But we shall see, we shall see.
My kindest love to Sister Jean and the rest, my mournfully affectionate blessing to you all.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SCS, 27 Aug. MS: British Lib. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SELINA C. SMYTH

docBody.p: On Friday last, the day before leaving London, I called at Laurence’s and found his copy of the Somerville Knox very promising indeed and not far from completion: he was himself to leave town on Tuesday (now two days ago); so that I suppose by this time the Knox is fairly in its place in the S. Kensington Museum, and Laurence’s copy finished, or only requiring a few supplementary touches. He admires the picture very much; finds that the original Limner (F. Porbus or another) must have been an Artist of eminent talent;—and on the other hand that the person who “lined” the picture, perhaps not very many years ago, must have produced most of the superficial cracks & also have “mended” the picture by various little touches of paint, by no means to its advantage. I for my own share continue to believe that there is some real probability that Porbus did the Original along with his contemporary Portrait of Buchanan and that for the rest whoever painted it, it either means the actual John Knox or else nothing that I can form the least idea of. By & by I design to put on record with all brevity what little clear light is proved attainable in this otherwise inscrutable subject,—on which next to nothing of external evidence exists at present and in which the internal speaks wholly as above.

Almost from early boyhood I remember the “Memorie of the Somervilles,” but do not ever remember to have seen the Book itself. For your sake & your
worthy great grandfathers I will now look into it with pleasure & am greatly obliged by your offer to send it me. But before actually putting you to such trouble let me try in the London LibrarySelina Smyth wrote, 24 Aug.: “We have 2 or 3 editions in our family of the ‘Memorië of the Somervilles’ by James 11th Lord & edited by Sir Walter Scott. If you would care to glance thro’ the 2 vol: book I will with pleasure send it to you.” James, Eleventh Lord Somerville, Memorie of the Somervilles; Being a History of the Baronial House of Somerville, 2 vols. (Edinburgh, 1815). The book is listed in the Catalogue of the London Library (1865). whether it is not there attainable on my return home. If otherwise I will then have the honour of applying as you permit.

closer.salute: Always, dear Madam, / Yours, with many thanks & regards,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 Sept. MS: NLS 528.16. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:307–8. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
St. Brycedale, Kirkcaldy, N. B
1 Sep. 1874
docBody.p:
We packed up vigorously yesterday morning; cleared away into the Burntisland railway & were swept across the sunny breezy Firth in perfectly propitious circumstances;Burntisland, town on the N shore of the Firth of Forth, 5 mi. (8 km.) across from Granton. Passenger services of the Edinburgh and North Railway connected with the ferry on both sides of the firth; see 35:112TC to JAC, 13 June 1859. —& found here hospitably waiting us at the Kirkcaldy Station our excellent host P. Swan with every appointment & equipment for the exercise of perfect human hospitality, as perfect I believe as I could experience in this world He had called on Friday afternoon in our absence & reappeared for a hasty moment towards evening intent to chase away all remnants of Painters & encumbrances & have us all across safe on the Monday succeeding.Swan’s home, St. Brycedale House in Kirkcaldy, had been being repainted; see TC to JAC, 27 Aug.; TC and Mary arrived on Mon. 31 Aug. His prognostics hitherto have all proved more than verified: this is an excellent, solid, shady silent & convenient human habitation close behind Kirkcaldy yet quiet as if many leagues from it; in brief I seldom or never in my days had a lodging so much to my mind or that promised to be fitter for me so long as it will last. I have excellent sea-bathing within few minutes walk; had yesterday afternoon one of the finest plunges (much superior to Portobello in clearness of water tho’, alas, there is no bathing machine & I believe I must undress & dress in a boat, or on the sand itself as we used to do on the
Devonshire gravel two years ago).TC and John A. Carlyle stayed at Seaforth Lodge, Devon, in Aug. 1872; see TC to LLA, 7 Aug. For the rest, there is absolute composure to be found in this house & the most complete & practical liberty conceded & impressed upon you to do your own way; & as practical sum hitherto I feel myself better today than I have been not only since leaving Chelsea, but for many months before that.

figure.p:
Thomas Carlyle, John A. Carlyle, Mary Aitken, and Patrick Don Swan
on the steps of St. Brycedale House, Kirkcaldy, 1874
Courtesy of The Carlyle Society

docBody.p: I find P. Swan really one of the most honest hearted simple & genuinely kind of men; a man of real natural munificence fidelity simplicity & human worth: & I really think you will find it a delightful place to pay a visit in, as I believe you had promised, whenever time suits. I have not yet written to Stirling Maxwell, but am privately clear that it will not answer to me to meThus in MS. to go thither; that in short I can do nothing so reasonable as stay where I am till the time for returning is at hand.

Swan has said nothing about your coming hither during our stay; nor can I of course speak of it myself till he speak again but the matter evidently stands open;John A. Carlyle did go and stay there; he wrote to Janet Hanning, 8 Oct., with details of TC’s time in Scotland; TC and Mary “staid one week in my old Edinburgh quarters, & then went to Kirkcaldy in Fifeshire, & spent more than a month with an old friend there. … I was with them too for the last ten days of their stay. Then we all came to Dumfries, & they staid here till Tuesday last [6 Oct.]. … During his stay here, Tom went to the Gill to see Mary & her family, & also to Scotsbrig and Thornhill” (MS: Yale). For a photograph of TC, John, Mary, and Patrick Don Swan taken on the steps of St. Brycedale House, see opp. & even though I should miss you while here on this occasion (which will be a real regret to me) I feel a real pleasure to think how well you may be here now & then when you take any notion of a jaunt, the pleasantest I do believe that now exists for any of us.

Since the middle of last week the weather has become a little broken. There had fallen last night, as I found on sallying out this morning a great deal of rain & since breakfast time there has again been a vigorous shower, but all is now sunshine again & I hope by good study of the opportunities to get a favourable plunge in the sea two hours before dinner after which there is nothing to hinder my loitering over books &c within doors independant of the weather. Meanwhile all is green & leafy here, as if three or four weeks in fair preferability & superior youth to London where above half the leaves in the park were already strewed brown on the ground & the grass itself was fast verging towards that bad hue.

I will write no more dear Brother but go out into the sunshine which you yourself would rather have me do. Write to us as speedily as possible & with all the detail you can. Many & many are the loving mournful thoughts I send towards you all; but they are practically, alas, of little or no use & not to be
expressed in words with precision at all. God’s blessing be upon you from eldest to youngest. Assure Sister Jean of my unalterable regard

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 1 Sept. MS: FC. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.dateline:
Care of Patrick D. Swan Esq.,
St. Brycedale, Kirkcaldy, N. B.
1 Sep. 1874.
docBody.p: Ever since the frightful disruption & disrooting of self and affairs on Saturday morning gone a week I have had nothing but a series of convulsions & confusions multum jactati terris et altoCf. Virgil, Aeneid 1.3: “much buffeted on land and sea.” which did not cease but only begin in new forms when our steam ship moored at Granton Pier about 2. a. m. & set us afloat on the new elemental tumults of Edinburgh which lasted day & night for a week more: so that only since yesterday about 3. p. m. when we landed in this blessed haven,—peaceful, kindly beautifully silent & pathetic as Hades or Elysium, have I had leisure to write you a word. I wanted much to hear were it only in the most succinct manner how you yourself were faring since we left, & of that kindness I hope you will not delay me for one post after this gets to hand.

I kept entirely incognito in Edinr; but there as in the steamer itself was very soon found out; so that the incognito amounted to nothing more than the silent precept, faithfully obeyed of Don’t speak to me or meddle with me, good Christian souls. In our beautiful steamer we had no crowd or avoidable disturbance—only hostile Eastern breezes, which kept us far away from sight of the beautiful coast, nothing but the revolving or other light-houses all the way from Flamboro’ Head,Flamborough Head, promontory on the Yorkshire coast with two lighthouses; there are several more between there and Edinburgh. visible along that beautiful coast. In Edinburgh, which was swarming with mere tourists from the four quarters of the earth I did nothing but silently visit all the old localities of vanished loved ones & events; Comley BankComely Bank, street in Edinburgh where TC and JWC had their first home, 1826–28; see 4:112JBW to TC, 28 June [1826], and 42:186TC to JWC, 11 Aug. 1865. to begin with & I daresay you guess where ending.JWC’s grave at Haddington. A kind of sacred or even religious operation which far surpassed any conversation or connection with secularities the world now holds in it for me. In fact
I spoke to nobody except to honest David Laing & Masson (deep sunk in his inexpressible Milton);For David Masson and his book on Milton, see TC to JAC, 1 Jan. both of whom were sworn to secrecy had it much availed.TC’s activities in Scotland were widely reported in the Scottish press: “Thomas Carlyle paid a visit to Edinburgh last week. … During his stay Mr. Carlyle enjoyed sea bathing at Portobello; and in the course of the week he spent a day at Haddington, in the ruined abbey of which quiet county town Mrs. Carlyle is buried. His friends and admirers will be pleased to learn that Carlyle is in the enjoyment of excellent health, but desirous of quiet and retirement” (Scotsman, 2 Sept.). In fine, yesterday we lifted anchor & came gloriously thro’ the sunny breezes to this desirable haven where I mean now to continue safe & silent for the rest of my appointed time in Scotland. Never in my life was I lodged so well. Last night, too, there was vouchsafed such a sleep as I have not had for six months before; item in the afternoon the finest sea-bath procurable or imaginable which is to be repeated every day. God willing, I feel accordingly considerably better than on leaving Chelsea & am very thankful to have got under the broad & benificent shadow of my Provost here who really is one of the worthiest of opulent men & who has such a house & verdant umbrageous piece of ground about it in the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, within ten minutes of the beautifullest clear sea I have ever known & is my old loving pupil withal & gives me in all respects a profusion of silent laissez faire as is rarely to be met with in this world.The Dundee Courier reported, 18 Sept.: “A glimpse of the manner in which [TC] spends his time may not be uninteresting. Early in the morning, before most people are astir, he may be seen walking briskly along the shore in the direction of the picturesque ruins of Seafield Tower … for the purpose of having a bathe. On other mornings, to diversify this, he walks inland along one of the country roads. … After breakfast … is his smoking time, and armed with a long clay pipe, he saunters through the beautifully laid out grounds of St Brycedale. … Although he is thoroughly averse to company of any sort, a privileged few have had the honour and pleasure of a talk with Mr. Carlyle. … His mien is decidedly peculiar, for he adopts the sensible plan of putting comfort before appearance. In common he wears a felt or straw hat with a brim of unusual dimensions, a light greatcoat reaching to his feet, and the costume is completed by a pair of comfortable slippers.”
But in brief lest I weary you with the detail of my unexampled blessing (only twenty hours old yet) let me at once give you his & my address
“Care of Patrick D. Swan Esq
St. Brycedale, Kirkcaldy N.B.”

— pressing request to let me know how you & the dear little lady both are since I left & what farther projects have risen or are rising in you for the ulterior weeks or months & so Good be ever with you & her, dear Forster, & a happy meeting to us all before long. Yours always

bibl.sourceNote: TC-FA [FAL], 5 Sept. MS: Nigel Althaus. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Friedrich Althaus (1829–97), German writer and historian living in England; he wrote a biographical study of TC for the German periodical Unsere Zeit (July 1866); see TC to FAL, 12 July 1866, and completed Joseph Neuberg’s German translation of Frederick, 1867; see MAI to FAL, 12 Feb. 1869.
bibl.head: TC TO FREDERICK ALTHAUS

docBody.p: I retain with as much force as ever, and permit you to repeat wherever necessary, all the opinions expressed by me as to your merits and qualifications on former occasions of this kind; and on the present occasion will only add that I think you well qualified for the post you now aspire to of Teaching Professor of German Literature in an English UniversityAlthaus wrote, 1 Sept., asking for a letter of recommendation from TC: “As you were kind enough, when I saw you last, to offer me your help in cases of this kind, I venture to ask whether … you would kindly promote the success of my present undertaking.” Althaus was applying for the professorship of German at University College, London; he wrote, 10 Nov., thanking TC, and saying that he had been appointed to the post; he held it until his death in 1897. TC and Althaus last met in Oct. 1870; see Wilson, Carlyle 6:215–18.
Believe me, dear Sir, / Yours always truly / T. Carlyle.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Sir WSM [WSM], 16 Sept. MS: Glasgow City Archives. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO SIR WILLIAM STIRLING MAXWELL

docBody.p: Many times have I been thinking of you since that morning in Edinburgh;See TC to JAC, 27 Aug. indeed almost day by day the question has risen on me whether I could undertake the beautiful adventure of seeing Keir and its gracious inhabitants again, or must decline it as too hazardous and difficult for me. Sorry I am to say that at last the evident fact is, I am too old, worn-out and weak for any visit to the bright circle at such a house as Keir or indeed to any great house whatever,—except it were a Convalescent Hospital which might be “great” in another sense. My regret is vivid and great; but such really is the too evident fact.

With my kindest thanks and grateful regards to Lady Anna and yourself;
and hoping soon to see you both again in London whitherward the anchor is now “apeak”Nautical term meaning the ship is directly over the anchor, presumably as a prelude to raising it. (may the wind prove fair for as frail a vessel) I remain always

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-GA, 7 Oct. MS: NLS 9654. Hitherto unpbd. George Atkin (1822–1907), son of Peter Atkin (1798–1876) and Alice, b. Hope (1790–1854), sister of TC’s old friends David Hope (1786–1857; see 29:biographical notes) and William J. Hope (1788–1853; see TC to DH, 11 June 1835).
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO GEORGE ATKIN

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle, who remembers his old friends, your Uncles, very well bids me thank you cordially for your kind letter which, but for a mistake on my part, would have been answered at once. It was forwarded after some little delay to Dumfries where he was for some time and there lost sight of until an hour ago.

It would have given him pleasure to visit you at Liverpool on his way back from Scotland, but he shrinks from new places however kind they may be and it was very difficult to keep him away from Chelsea even for six weeks this autumn. The change, has, however, done him good, I think.

He begs to be most kindly remembered to Mrs Atkin,Atkin and Emily, b. Tweedale (1831–1911), m. 1855, lived at Egerton Park, Liverpool. to whom and yourself he sends his cordial thanks for your kind invitation; and I am, with his best wishes,

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-BB, 16 Oct. MS: NLS 3278.168. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO BETTY BRAID

docBody.p:
We are very sorry indeed to hear, by Mr Brodie’sDavid Brodie (1822–88), M.D., medical superintendent of the Home School for Invalid and Imbecile Youth, Edinburgh; see 35:44TC to THE, 25 Feb. 1859, and 25335:biographical notes. He wrote, 15 Sept. [Oct.]: “Mrs Braid has given me permission to express to you her concern to know whether you have safely returned to your home, her regret that she had not had the pleasure of seeing you when you were in Scotland, & also to inform you of the state of her husband. Some days ago his staff had failed him & he fell on the floor of the cold unused room where he lay for some hours before any one could be got to help him. There was only the slightest abrasion of the skin but he has been unable again to get out of bed & he is now today unconscious & not likely to survive beyond one or two days— She is herself in a very frail state but her sister is now with her & her immediate cares are thus lightened.” Brodie then wrote, 16 Sept. [Oct.], to say that Alexander had died the previous afternoon. Brodie misdated both letters Sept. rather than Oct. Betty’s sister was probably Isabella Bickerton, b. Pringle (b. 1798). Letter, that your poor Husband is so ill; and sorry to think of all the anxiety you must have about
him. I have asked Mr Brodie to let us know again how your Husband is and how you yourself are; and if there is anything that you would like to say to my Uncle you know how glad he will be to hear it.

We were at Morningside when we were in Edinburgh and were fully intending to go on to Green End to see you; but we could not possibly manage it before the train for Dumfries left and we had to hurry back to the station instead, much to our regret. But Miss Anne WelshAnn Welsh; see TC to BB, 14 July. promised to go and see you the first time she could and explain this to you.

My Uncle is I hope rather better for his visit to Scotland. We got back here only last week and are going to settle down for the winter. He would have written to you himself, dear Betty; but his hand shakes so much that he never uses the pen except to sign his name and even then as seldom as possible. But you may be sure that there will never be any change in his affectionate feelings for you.
God bless you, dear Betty; with sincere sympathy for you in your trouble from us both[.]

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 17 Oct. MS: NLS 528.17. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:308–9. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
This is the first you have heard of me since our parting in Dumfries—all that was essential you have no doubt heard from Mary and John;Their nephew John Aitken. and the reason of my not writing sooner, which indeed still subsists and would be readily guessed by you was that I had nothing especially to say & that my langour dispiritment and utter weakness always rather advised me to shut myself up
in solitude rather than attempt to speak or communicate the poor humour I was in. Seldom in my days have I been more utterly inactive solitary & in a word idle than since we parted on the flags of Dumfries. Within the last day or two I seem to have been acquiring a little more sense of being still alive; and indeed have got all my multifarious paltrinesses of what may be called business & rearrangement, including that paltriest but inevitable concern of the sanitary “drain”“Introduction of a system of drainage, from the garden to the street, passing under No. 5 Cheyne Row” (A. Carlyle’s note in NL 2:308). & the clipping of my hair, fairly off my hands; and am looking forward to the actual beginning of that thing about Knox’s Picture (which it is possible or probable I may have to shift from Fraser’s Magazine to some GraphicTC’s “The Portraits of John Knox” was pbd. in Fraser’s Magazine, April 1875. The Graphic (1869–1932) was a weekly illustrated newspaper. or other newspaper, owing to the difficulties about the Prints needed in it); and as to employments, heaven knows, the only one I have, that of reading Spedding’s Bacon,James Spedding, The Letters and the Life of Francis Bacon; see TC to JAC, 15 Nov. 1873. TC described the book to Allingham: “a most admirable work, has brought together every fact with the utmost diligence, honesty, and good judgement, and produced a book of great value, which is almost unreadable from its flatness and prolixity” (Allingham Diary 234). is far from a seductive one! The illustrious business of the drain about which we had such sputtering & fussing has turned out to be a most undeniable improvement in the department concerned with it and I now find is and was all along considered by the Vestry & InspectorMuch of the district of Chelsea was owned by Chelsea parish, and administered by the vestry. to be a work of benificence & of homage done to merit on their part—and in whole does satisfy me as a real benefit, now that it is completely done, & well done. The price of it too I now learn is to be mainly borne not by me but by the Proprietor,—unless I privately decide to help her a little, as she is a Widow,The current owner of 5 Cheyne Row was Ann Elizabeth Oldridge (1847–85), widow of Cyrus Albert Oldridge (1848–74); TC’s checkbook recorded: “26 Dec. 1873 / C. A. Oldridge Esq. (Rent) / £33 .. 14 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). it appears; and not in an opulent condition.

The Town is as empty, all this while as I have almost ever seen it; & is only now beginning to show its luggage cabs, in sign that it will be full enough again, and to spare in another week or two. My loss in FroudeFroude had left Britain 23 Aug.; see TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug. I find is likely to be very sensible; no other walking comrade that I am likely to have in the least comparable to him. For the rest, there are still left walking figures enough; and I must do the best I can with them. Forster went to Seton Lodge, where we were two years ago the very morning after we arrived here.Forster wrote, 6 Oct.: “It is a sad disappointment to me, dear Carlyle, to go away without seeing you. … I have had a hard time since you left London— I have made two persevering attempts to get to Brighton—could not manage rooms anywhere! … Then came kind intimation that Seaton was still available—pressed with such generous urging that I resolved to make the trial!” He concluded the letter the following morning, 7 Oct.: “Just as I sit down to finish my letter this morning, comes your kind message with your nephew— Oh how I regret my inability to see you” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 84—85). Forster was going to stay at Lady Ashburton’s cottage, Seaforth Lodge, Seaton, Devonshire; TC and JAC stayed there in Aug. 1872; see TC to LLA, 7 Aug. I was
ready to go to Palace Gate House as I understood he expected, that morning; but he sent an express to regretfully forbid. I have since heard from him and written to him: I believe he is doing tolerably well there, and privately my persuasion is that he is considerably better though liable to unreasonable terror when any of his old sad symptoms even partially return upon him. Poor Mrs Forster had slipt or stumbled somewhere in “The Chine” (which you well remember of) & had slightly hurt her side.“The Chine,” a steep-sided gorge with a path leading down to the beach. Forster wrote, 10 Oct.: “We left town safely, and the house of course is full of comforts. … My failure here … has been in matter of sleeping. … And the little Wife … slipped footing in trying to get down to the beach, and but for the gardner would have rolled to the bottom! As it is, a little strain and stiffness … is all” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 86). Nothing else of sinister there. DarwinErasmus Darwin. one day picked us up one day on the embankment and drove me about a good while, not unpleasantly. He had never quitted town again after we left him there. TaitRobert Scott Tait. came down the day before yesterday, as dry a biscuit as usual, but happily TrevillyanPresumably George Otto Trevelyan (1838–1928; ODNB), politician and author (see 43:105JWC to LT, 16 Jan. [1866]), rather than his father, Sir Charles Edward Trevelyan (1807–86; ODNB). joined us just as we stept out and he is a fellow that never wants for talk. Allingham, also, is at hand in abundance, if we do not reckon him superabundant: he is at present in the top gallant“Topgallant” is the highest sail on a ship. of human felicity; having wedded & got not only an editorship but a wholesome, honest & promising young wife above 20 years his junior;See TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug. far better probably than he could have expected or deserved.— With a considerable shock I learnt from Darwin that poor TwisletonEdward Twisleton d. at Boulogne, 5 Oct. was dead three or four days before; but where or how Darwin could not tell me nor could anybody I have yet seen. It is a true sadness to me, this sudden loss of poor Twisleton. He was a thoroughly honest man, of accurate, intelligent & courteous nature; always well affected to me; long ago with the beautiful little wife he had, much a favourite here.Twisleton’s wife, Ellen, had been a close friend of JWC’s. Brookfield, too, I feel to be a loss in this impoverished condition of the field, and now left to my own reflections more than I did when the event happened.
Poor Miss Bromley is deeply distressed by the loss of him,See TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug. —as you may see by this Letter of hers, which pray return to me.

Mary was out yesterday collecting serious ammunition, easels, palettes, brushes, colours &c &c, for assault upon the Art of Painting upon which the whole endeavour of the little wretch is strenuously set. From various Artists and the like there are good omens as to her possibilities; and I myself, though very dark about such things, do partly believe that there are traces of real talent in her for that object; certainly for one thing she is completely determined to persist with her best strength & try. Next week she begins a course of lessons with Mme VenturiEmilie Venturi. every alternate forenoon to be her own for that purpose; and I doubt not there will be report of progress from time to time before very long.— This morning there has come a letter of young Alick of Canada with a photograph of his Father here enclosed, wh. I was quite surprised at, and could hardly recognise till Mary pointed out that the eyes had been meddled with, & “mended” & made quite unrecognizable. You can give it to Jean if she care to accept. Give at any rate to her & to every one the warmest expression of my gratitude for theirWords repeated at turn of page with a line over them. goodness to me, & of my love & perpetual regard. Ever your affectionate

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 23 Oct. MS: NLS 528.18. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Since I wrote last there have two letters come from you; the first before mine had fairly got out of the house: such diligence and kindness on your part would compel me to write a short word today were there no other reason,—very short it must be, for Mary is just going out to her painting, I finishing my breakfast; and by bad accident, or by a set of such yesterday, the duty was neglected until too late.

We have no news whatever, except of the status quo, which is good news at all times rather than bad. I have not yet got my poor Knox problem begun; certainly after what you say and show by specimen I shall be slow to apply to the Graphic;John A. Carlyle wrote, 19 Oct.: “I sent a copy of the Graphic to Mary … it is a shallow, ostentatious thing that one never gets any good of. It is quite unworthy of having anything about Knox inserted in it.” & as for Allingham, the dreary mortal has not got any clearly
definite deliverance to give me as to Fraser and the Longmans:Allingham was now the editor of Fraser’s Magazine (see TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug.), which had been owned since 1863 by Thomas Longman (1804–79; ODNB) and his brother, William Longman (1813–77; ODNB), publishers. See also TC to TCON, 25 Feb. but this day, if I prosper it is my intention to wring one out of him yea or no. Did we tell you that this New Editor has got himself married; & for some weeks past has been the happiest of men; no cloud in his sky except that of dilatory workmen, especially of late a dilatory smith, who will not put his kitchen range in order, but plays the truant & the fibber; keeping poor A. still in lodging, out of port.William and Helen Allingham moved in Oct. to 12 Trafalgar Sq., Chelsea, where they lived until 1881. Such a case demands the sympathy of neighbours. On the whole I see but little of A.; hardly once a week. You know him an innocent, ingenious creature, but without any depth or compass; on the whole, tho’ perfectly honest & well disposed, very far inferior to Froude. Froude is evidently as I anticipated turning out to be a great loss to me, but the only recipe is make the best & most of what remains.

Forster writes hopefully from Seaforth,—still hopeful, but complaining somewhat of possible bad influences on his liver: I have heard nothing for above a week & a note to him which should have been written yesterday fell overboard like your own in the environing troubles. Did you in the Daily News see — or elsewhere hear of, a paper upon poor ProctorBryan Waller Procter (“Barry Cornwall”) (1787–1874; ODNB; see 33:279ss:biographical notes), poet and lawyer; known to TC since 1824; see 3:84–85TC to JBW, 23 June 1824, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 290–91. He d. 4 Oct. Forster wrote, 6 and 7 Oct.: “The dear good Procter is gone. He died on Sunday afternoon at ½ past 4—very quietly; had, indeed, been sleeping since Friday evening. He had a slight attack of paralysis a week before. A kinder heart never beat” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 85). which, it seems, was by Forster? I meant to ask him for that yesterday, for I cannot get it elsewhere nor I suppose can you.For the Daily News obituary, see TC to JF, 26 Oct.
Adieu, dear Brother, I must not detain Mary any longer. I will write, I hope, with more deliberation soon. My blessings & hearts love to one and all of you
Ever your affectionate Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 26 Oct. MS: FC. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: Your Letter of this morning was very welcome, and very kindly significant of your constant goodwill in this direction. The news about your health is not so good as could be wished, but it is by no means bad either, considering the weather and other bad influences; and the important item of the good effects which the place produces in your dear Better-Half (who, Heaven knows, has had enough of sorrowful & bad laid to her share this long while is an altogether joyful particular.Forster wrote, 24 Oct.: “[M]y week has been very indifferent; but the good wife profits much and that is comfort. … I cannot get sleep; and, though my cough does not positively increase, other incidents of my malady are very distressing” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 87). Your violent Sou-wester’sForster added a postscript the following morning: “Last night (Saturday) a terrible tempest—torrents of rain and a fearful Sou Wester” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 88). are not unknown on other parts of the island: in Scotland, especially about Dumfries and neighbourhood, we hear of desperate tempests; uprooting of trees and the like, reminding observant people of January 1839.Britain, particularly the north-west of the country, was hit by a terrible storm, 6–7 Jan. 1839. Over several days, 9–14 Jan., the Times carried reports of destruction and deaths from various towns, and also of many ships that were wrecked; see 11:3–4TC to MAC, 13 Jan. 1839. One morning here was very loud and blusterous; but only one that I heard in my den here which indeed is in general nearly the stillest place I know in the world, and constitutes the chief element of human prosperity that I now have. A very great blessing indeed to lay down one’s weary old head, and thank God, in spite of John Mill and Co,TC presumably refers to John Stuart Mill’s views on the nature of God, as expressed in his Three Essays on Religion: Nature, Utility of Religion, Theism (1874), pbd. 26 Oct. for the heavenly blessing of pure and absolute silence all round!—

I was on the edge of writing last week, but interruptions always drove me off, about some notice in the Daily News concerning poor Proctor which a straggling Newspaper told me was yours. I cannot get a copy of the Daily News in question from any of my neighbours; and so had to decide on applying at the Fountain Head: please, therefore, send me at once a little newspaper clippingSee TC to JAC, 23 Oct. Forster replied, 27 Oct.: “The Daily News article is not mine, but was written by our old friend Harriet Martineau” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 89). Harriet Martineau (1802–76; ODNB), writer and journalist, known to the Carlyles since 1836; see 9:88TC to MAC, 20 Nov. 1836. Her article “Death of ‘Barry Cornwall,’” was pbd. Daily News, 7 Oct. Forster sent a copy of the article to TC. or get it sent to me. I will be punctual in getting it sent back. If you write anything in Macmillan on the same subject, I shall be certain to see
it. You did not say if you had complied with the Macmillan Editor’sGeorge Grove (1820–1900; ODNB), musicologist and lexicographer, ed. of Macmillan’s Magazine 1868–83. request, but I clearly feel as if it were a pious duty on your part; as if the good Proctor really deserved some outline of his aspect and pilgrimage through this world; and as if you of all men were the best qualified to give it.
