He was a very gentle, gracefully lucid & humane Son of Adam, our poor Proctor that is now gone after so long a struggle to get his discharge. I remember him personally, in 1824; and I at once liked and recognized him, as what he all his life proved to be. Do not forget this precept I have just laid upon you.Forster replied, 27 Oct.: “[T]hough I know no law that would claim such compliant obedience from me as any injunction laid on me by you, I needs fear that I cannot comply in this matter of our poor dear old Procter” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 89).

It is such an alleviation to your heavy, physical miseries, dear Foster, that you are still able to write, & work some result out of every painful day,—such an alleviation as you yourself can make no just estimate of till once (which Heaven forbid) you are deprived of it. The ugliest day is brightened up by some bit of right work done, and does not count as a miserable zero among days. In fact among the days of this world I have found little else that would brighten them at all. Courage courage; and stand always to your arms. As for me, after the utter idleness and emptiness of so many months I know not whether there will ever return a few hours of spiritual effort and feeling that this is still life and not disgraceful lethargy and death: but, at least, I often enough feel what the latter branch of the alternative is.

Hitherto as usual, I do nothing but lazily read; lazily & painfully; all the books I can get for a long time back being bad & not good. With good Books one could hold out a long while; but alas, alas, where are they? For the last week, I have held on steadily by an innocent, feebly reasonable and honest old French Book, of 1764, called Dictionnaire d’Anecdotes de Traits &c;Honoré Lacombe de Prezel (1725–90), Dictionnaire d’anecdotes de traits singuliers et caractéristiques, 2 vols. (Paris, 1766). which contrasts mournfully in its style, both of writing and of thinking with the rabid howlings and revellings, scarcely human, of the France that now is. Possibly enough I may do the other volume as well, tho’ the misery is there is no remembering of the endless miscellany of objects presented, except of those already known which had no need to be offered one again. Among other notabilia of this book, I find the old Fonblanque article of Stone Broth (which no doubt you remember in the Examiner);For the fairy tale “Soupe de Caillou,” see Dictionnaire d’anecdotes 1:181–83. Albany William Fonblanque (1793–1872; ODNB), political journalist, ed. of the Examiner, 1830–47, when the editorship passed to Forster; the metaphor of the stone broth is used several times in articles in the Examiner, notably 14 Feb. 1841, 19 April 1845, and 20 Dec. 1856. and here I must say it is decidedly better done than in F.’s case; two hungry Monks being the operators who
come into a substantial cottage with nothing but two or three children in it, who, in their wonder & hope of a miracle, cheerfully furnish both the stone (caillou, which passes for a chicken to the children, but is left till tomorrow for them, as being still too tough and hard), and the other successive ingredients. In another place I found, put into the mouth of a vagrant City-Arab, delivering his Autobiography, Goldsmith’s proemFor the reference to the wandering player, see Dictionnaire d’anecdotes 1:153. Oliver Goldsmith (ca. 1728–74; ODNB), author; for his “Proem,” see “Adventures of a Strolling Player,” The Miscellaneous Works of Oliver Goldsmith, 4 vols. (1834) 2:198. “My Parents made considerable noise in the world, Sir, my Mother called oysters & my Father beat a drum.”— John Mill’s Book on what he calls Religion is come, but I have already seen what you saw in the NewspaperJohn Stuart Mill, Three Essays on Religion: Nature, Utility of Religion, Theism (1874); extracts were printed widely in journals and newspapers. Forster wrote, 24 Oct.: “Mill … I have been reading—in newspaper extracts, without much … edification. The mark of a hopeless kind of weakness … seems to lie on the whole of that display” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 87). & it has completely satisfied me that probably never since the world began was there heard any feebler or more futile gasp of utterance on that subject, comparable to the last mew of a drowning kitten; worthy of being forgotten by all creatures. Poor M’s notion of a proper God Almighty wd be that of an indulgent Nurse, male or female, giving his children perpetual lollipops by way of building them up to heroic action in this world of his. Adieu, dear Forster. Good be with you & with your dear Partner always.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-MW, 29 Oct. MS: NLS 8992.149. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Margaret Welsh, b. Kissock (1803–88; see 43:biographical notes), widow of JWC’s paternal uncle George Welsh (1799–1835), living at 19 St. John’s Grove, Richmond; TC’s last recorded contact with her was in May 1870; see TC to JAC, 26 May 1870.
bibl.head: TC TO MARGARET WELSH

docBody.p: Please to accept from me the enclosed little gift,TC signed a check: “29 Oct. 1874 / Mrs George Welsh / £50” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20752). which is meant to signify how well I always wish you and how much I respect your excellent management and fine quietly blameless demeanour in a world, where you are becoming, like myself, so solitary in. I wish all manner of good to you; and am ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-BB, 30 Oct. MS: NLS 3278.171. Pbd: Wilson, Carlyle 6:340. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO BETTY BRAID

docBody.p: Ever since the sad event that fell upon your household and parted a long companionship, carrying one away and laying the other on a sick-bed you have been daily in my thoughts.The death of Betty’s husband, Alexander; see MAI to BB, 16 Oct. It was very sad and mournful the manner of your good Husband’s sudden death; but in the essence it was surely merciful withal; a blessed deliverance of him from a load becoming too heavy to be borne longer. He is now gone to the silent home appointed for us all where earthly sin and misery cannot reach him any more. In this sense I was well pleased to hear as I anticipated that you took the matter up and thankfully accepted what the Eternal Father had sent.

I am sad of heart to hear how weak you are in bodily respects, but it is the greatest comfort that the spirit is as clear and bright as ever retaining all its calmness and looking forward with the immortal hopes that lie beyond this afflicted earth. It touches me to the very heart what you say this morning of those that were and are dearest to me in this world, and whom, for above three score years, you always so faithfully loved.Betty Braid wrote (by dictation to David Brodie), 29 Oct.: “I am laid here with perfect weakness & waiting for the change when the Lord is pleased to send it—& I look forward—I’m sure that I’ll meet with my Master & Mistress & their daughter Jeanie Welsh your dear Wife & many other kind friends on the shores of Glory—& oh my dear Mr Carlyle I do humbly thank you for all your kindness to me & may God keep you to the end is my best wish.” For David Brodie, see MAI to BB, 16 Oct. I know the honest tenderness of your heart, the noble piety, fidelity and continual integrity with which you have always lived; and to say truth there has been, for years back, no living creature whom I thought more venerable than yourself. “Submitted to the will of the Most High” in all things great & small; that surely is the wisdom that cometh from above.

God bless you and be with you, dear Betty, through what remains of Time and through the Eternity that never ends.Betty Braid d. 19 March 1875. If there were anything in which I could help you, I hope you know well it would be at once at your command. But I doubt there is nothing. Your good SisterProbably Isabella Bickerton; see MAI to BB, 16 Oct. I hope and trust will not leave you till you are better. Thank Dr Brodie much for me, and Mr BickertonGeorge Bickerton (ca. 1823–1901), Betty Braid’s nephew, English teacher living at 12 Arniston Pl., Edinburgh. too,
for the punctual news they send; & beg them to continue.
With my best blessings and a respect & sympathy which will last while I live, I remain

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JEB, 4 Nov. MS: Duke. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOSEPH EDGAR BOEHM

docBody.p: I want very much to see you, as soon as possible. I have received, out of Cheshire,Caroline Davenport Bromley sent TC a portrait of Knox from the house of her brother, William Bromley Davenport (1821–84), of Capesthorne Hall, Cheshire; see TC to JAC, 6 Nov. a very surprizing little Picture (like the ghost of an old Holbein) with “John Knox, Ano 1565” printed on the side of it; upon which I, above all things, want your commentary & elucidation. So soon as your work is done pray let me see you if possible. I shall be at home till ½ past 3

bibl.sourceNote: TC-UC, 4 Nov. Pbd. as facsimile: A. Carlyle, NL 1:310 inc. Apparently written by TC, in his own hand, as an autograph; recipient unidentified. Lines taken from Carlyle, Sartor 70. See 160.
bibl.head: TC TO AN UNIDENTIFIED CORRESPONDENT

docBody.p: ‘Sleep on, thou fair Child, for thy long rough journey is at hand! A little while, and thou too shalt sleep no more, but thy very dreams shall be mimic battles; thou too, with old Arnauld, wilt have to say, in stern patience, “Rest? Rest? Shall I not have all Eternity to rest in?”’

figure.p:
Thomas Carlyle’s handwritten autograph, 4 November 1874
Alexander Carlyle, New Letters of Thomas Carlyle (1904)

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 6 Nov. MS: NLS 528.19. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your three letters came punctually, and I am much obliged for the clear details you gave me about that lamentable event.John A. Carlyle wrote two letters, 29 Oct.; in the first he gave TC the news of the sudden death, 27 Oct., of their niece Margaret Stewart: “[S]he was seized with a violent pain in the upper part of the spine which soon produced paralysis of all the lower part of the body, & ended fatally next morning. One may say it was a mercy for her, as such diseases are beyond the reach of medicine.” He wrote again later that day with more details, after he and Jean had been to the Gill to see Margaret’s parents, Mary and James Austin, who had been with her when she died. It has been ever since a melancholy thought to me, that of the new-made grave in Mouswald Kirkyard,Mouswald Parish Church, nr. Dumfries; John wrote, 2 Nov.: “On Saturday [31 Oct.] we had excellent weather, & there was a large attendance at dear Margaret’s funeral. All the relations of her deceased husband were there, & our brother Jamie with his sons John & James from Annandale. Jean & James & I were there too in good time & staid till all was over.” with the poor bits of bairns, suddenly cut bare of a Mother’s protection.Margaret had a da. and three sons, all under fourteen. I am sorriest of all for poor MaryTheir sister Mary Austin, Margaret’s mother. whose heart I know will be filled with the tenderest grief; to her I would write; but except what she already knows, my sympathy with her, I could say nothing. Poor soul, in what heaviness of heart she will have to live for the months that are running!— It seems a very feasible arrangement that of Austin Junior going to take charge of the farming & Marianne of the children and the dairy department; but it does depend a little on Austin Junior's skill & other qualities;—Jamie Carlyle Junior,Margaret had been managing her farm, Ernhirst, since her husband’s death, 20 April 1869; see 46:42TC to JAC, 28 April 1869, and 48:184–85TC to JAC, 29 March 1873. It was now suggested that Margaret’s brother, James Austin Jr., should run the farm, and their sister Marianne take care of the children; John wrote: “The lease of the farm lasts for two years longer. … The farm, after what has been done for it, is now cheap at the old rent; & if the two coming years be favourable it should have considerable profit.” Their nephew James Carlyle Jr. had already been to the farm to offer help. as an Uncle to the children might naturally be of help and take some charge. You will let me know what is decided on so soon as there is any decision & how it is like to go on.

Poor old Betty at GreenEnd has lost her Husband, if it can be called a loss rather than a deliverance. The poor old man who for years back has been utterly hebetated had gone into the back room to walk; his stick caught upon
something or broke & he fell down & lay unnoticed for several hours, unable to make himself heard & on being found & laid in bed proved to be so injured by the chill, the fright & agitation he had got that the Dr pronounced him hopeless & even close upon death. He died accordingly, I think, within twenty four hours; and poor old Betty, who at any rate had got sore throat, was soon after the funeral obliged to take to bed, to send for a Sister who is still with her. Betty still in bed, so weak in body that the Doctors think she will never rise though she is clear & beautiful in mind as in her best days. The Doctor sends us punctual news & the other morning there came from him, under Betty’s dictation a touching little note, full of quiet piety resignation & immortal hope which was beautiful to read.See TC to BB, 30 Oct. Poor old Betty she is the last frail relic of Haddington things, & you can easily fancy the many thoughts that dwell for me round that innocent & venerable deathbed.

For myself here I am not worse in health than usual, I might rather almost say a little better; still miserably idle, reading books for most part of little worth & in spite of my abundance of Visitors a little more solitary than I was before. Nobody supplies the want of Froude; of whom I yet hear nothing, not even of his arrival at the Cape. Il faut se ranger [one must compose oneself]; & indeed one’s own melancholy musings & memories & outlooks into the, inevitable, near Unknown are perhaps as good as any conversation one could get. I have read Charles Greville’s Journal;Charles Cavendish Fulke Greville (1794–1865; ODNB), political and social diarist, The Greville Memoirs. A Journal of the Reigns of King George IV. and King William IV., ed. Henry Reeve, 3 vols. (1874). three moderate octavos, without much interest; indeed often with a tendency to skip; though with a feeling, too, that “Punch Greville”Known as “Punch Greville” as he had a long, pointed chin and a prominent nose like the traditional puppet Punch. was really a more earnest, discerning & worthy kind of man than I had ever thought him before.For TC’s first impression of Greville in 1844, see 18:207TC to JWC, 14 Sept. 1844. Except for the interest one always has in having the faithful records of one’s own time set forth, & the continual comparison of them with one’s own contemporary doings & endeavourings, I dont much think this Book will be worth your reading; but if it turn up you may fairly try; the resource of skipping is always in one’s power. The editing by Reeve is not good, but is evidently what Reeve thinks good.Henry Reeve (1813–95), journalist and editor, edited out many of the more indiscreet parts of Greville’s Memoirs, but even so many people found the book deeply scandalous. Greville’s few months in Italy will be almost sure to interest you more or less;Greville spent March–June 1830 traveling through Italy; John A. Carlyle traveled in Italy during 1831–38 as physician to Lady Elizabeth Julia Georgiana Clare, b. Burrell (1793–1879); see 5:343TC to AC, 18 Aug. 1831. and indeed, tho’ trivial enough, is the best part of the book.

Ruskin has been here twice & is to come again tomorrow; the first of the series of weekly visits from Oxford which he promises:Ruskin had returned from Italy mid-Oct., and wrote, 28 Oct.: “I find it must be Saturday, not Friday, when I come to see you: my lecture is, (to my own surprise) on Friday instead of Thursday. … I want to get into the way of coming to see you every week, if I can.” As Slade Professor of Fine Art at Oxford, Ruskin was delivering a series of lectures on “Aesthetic and Mathematic Schools of Art in Florence.” I do not get much good of him, so high-flown is his strain of flattery, springing doubtless from the nervous nature of his being, which is never to be got rid of in dialogue with him & much spoils all practical communication. Forster continues at Seaforth Lodge, complaining, but I always hope, improving. His purpose was & I suppose still at bottom is, to continue till Xmas after which, London, or he knew not what. I suppose you knew Twisleton a little & wd read of his death in the Newspapers.See TC to JAC, 17 Oct.; an obituary of Edward Twisleton was pbd. in the Pall Mall Gazette, 9 Oct., and repeated in the Times, 10 Oct. A secret circumstance in it, namely, suicide is not to me as to the world horrible but pathetic & even noble,—though for obvious reasons (for in fact it was deliberate suicide) I keep strict silence.

The Knox Picture business is fully before me; & I have now settled with Fraser’s people & engaged that it shall appear by & by;See TC to JAC, 17 Oct. but Heaven knows absolutely, when; such is my lethargic habit, my “work-arm” too literally broken & all vigorous exertion grown so foreign to me, but it must & shall be done, if I live for a month or two more.—— Jean sent me a short but very excellent Letter, which feat I truly wish she could repeat, without urgency of mine! Tell her, however, I will not fail to answer by & by. There came this morning a longish letter from Horne,Robert Horn. containing nothing at all, except of his own six weeks’ sickness in the neighbourhood of Killiecranky,Killiecrankie, village in Perthshire, about 31 mi. (50 km.) N of Perth. while we were in Scotland.Words repeated with a line over them at turn of page. A new Knox Picture has come from Miss Bromley out of her Brothers house Boehm very urgent to have it operated upon by spirits of wine & other solvents; Non mei refert [It matters not to me]. My kindest love to you all

bibl.sourceNote: TC-EF, 6 Nov. MS: Trinity. Pbd: FitzGerald’s Letters 3:522–24. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO EDWARD FITZGERALD

docBody.p: Thanks for your kind little Letter. I am very glad to learn that you are so cheerful & well, entering the winter under such favourable omens. I lingered in Scotland, latterly against my will, for about six weeks: the scenes there never can cease to be impressive to me indeed as natural in late visits they are far too impressive, and I have to wander there like solitary Ghost among the graves of those that are gone from me; sad, sad & I always think while there, ought not this visit to be the last?

But surely I am well pleased with your kind affection for the Land, especially for Edinburgh & the scenes about it.FitzGerald wrote, 3 Nov.: “Well: I was only three whole days in Scotland: but I find myself wishing to see Edinburgh again, as I scarce every felt for any strange Place. And little as you may idolize (!) Scott, you would like his Eildon Hills, Melrose, and Dryburgh, if you have never cared to visit them. … Then there was a Hill between Melrose and Dryburgh which Scott often went to, looking over the Border; and the man who drove me said that Scott’s Carriage horses, who also drew his Hearse, would stop there, and could only be got on with much coaxing, etc.” For Sir Walter Scott, see TC to MMH-S, 2 Dec. 1873. By all means go again to Edinburgh (tho’ the old city is so shorn of its old grim beauty & is become a place of Highland shawls & railway shriekeries); worship Scott, withal, as vastly superior to the common run of authors,FitzGerald wrote: “Oh, I know you think Scott a brave, honest, good-natured man, and a good Story-teller, only not a Hero at all.” See TC’s review of John Gibson Lockhart, Memoirs of the Life of Sir Walter Scott, bart., 7 vols. (1837–38), London and Westminster Review (Jan. 1838), and Carlyle, Works 29:22–87. and indeed grown now an affectingly tragic man. Dont forget Burns either & Ayrshire & the WestRobert Burns lived most of his life in Ayrshire. next time you go; there are admirable antiquities & sceneries in those parts, leading back (Whithorn for example; Whitterne or Candida Casa) to the days of St. Cuthbert,Whithorn, town 10 mi. (16 km.) S of Wigtown, Dumfriesshire, named for Candida Casa [White House], the first recorded Christian church in Scotland, built, ca. 397, by St. Ninian (d. 432). St. Cuthbert (ca. 635–87; ODNB), is more usually associated with sites in SE Scotland and NE England, but as a wandering missionary he traveled throughout southern Scotland, and there are various sites named for him, including a well in Middlebie, Dumfriesshire, about 2 mi. (3 km.) NE of Ecclefechan; see 26:123TC to MAC, 8 Aug. 1851. not to speak of Dumfries with Sweetheart AbbeyNew Abbey, Dumfriesshire, about 8 mi. (13 km.) S of Dumfries, a Cistercian monastery founded 1273, often called Sweetheart Abbey (Cor Dulce), after its founder Dervorguilla (d. 1290; ODNB), lady of Galloway, widow of John Balliol (d. 1268; ODNB), who was buried there holding a casket containing her husband’s heart; see 44:216TC to JF, 16 June 1867. For TC’s account of his visit to the New Abbey with JWC in 1828, see Carlyle, Reminiscences 131 and 443; see also Carlyle, “The Wisdom of our Ancestors,” ed. William Baker, Carlyle Newsletter 3 (1982): 2–7. & the brooks
and hills a certain Friend of yours first opened his eyes to in this astonishing world.

I am what is called very well here, after my return, worn weak as a cobweb, but without bodily ailment except the yearly increasing inability to digest food; my mind, too, if usually mournful instead of joyful is seldom or never to be called miserable & the steady gazing into the great Unknown which is near & comes nearer every day, ought to furnish abundant employment to the serious soul. I read, too; that is my happiest state, when I can get good books, which indeed I more & more rarely can.

Like yourself I have gone through Spedding, 7 long long voll. not skipping except where I had got the sense with me & generally reading all of Bacon’s own that was there: I confess to you I found it a most creditable & even surprizing Book, offering the most perfect & complete image both of Bacon & of Spedding, & distinguished as the hugest & faithfullest bit of literary Navvywork I have ever met with in this generation.FitzGerald wrote, 3 Nov.: “Come; [Scott] is at least as good as old Bacon, whom Spedding has consumed near forty years in whitewashing. I declare that is a Tragedy: the more so, as I cannot help thinking that Spedding is himself a little more doubtful at the end of his Labours than he was before.” For Spedding’s, The Letters and the Life of Francis Bacon, see TC to JAC, 17 Oct., where TC is less admiring of Spedding’s work. Bacon is washed clean, down to the natural skin; & truly he is not nor ever was unlovely to me; a man of no culpability to speak of: of an opulent & even magnificent intellect, but all in the magnificent prose vein. Nothing or almost nothing of the “melodies eternal” to be traced in him. Spedding’s Book will last as long as there is any earnest memory held of Bacon, or of the age of James VI upon whom as upon every stirring man in his epoch Spedding has shed new veritable illumination; in almost the whole of which I perfectly coincided with Spedding.FitzGerald replied, 20 Nov.: “I rejoice in what you say of Spedding’s work, which will console him … for the Apathy of the World at large. I admire his work as much, if not so wisely, as you do: but I still think Spedding might have done much more with the forty years of Life he has employed upon it.” In effect I walked up to the worthy man’s house,Spedding lived at Westbourne Grove, London. whom I see but little to tell him all this; & that being a miss I drove up, Spedding having by request called here & missed me, but hitherto we have not met; & Spedding I doubt not could contrive to dispense with my eulogy. There is a grim strength in Spedding, quietly, very quietly invincible, which I did not quite know of till this Book; and in all ways I could congratulate the indefatigably patient, placidly invincible & victorious Spedding.
Adieu, dear F. I wish you a right quiet & healthy winter & beg to be kept in memory as now probably your oldest Friend,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-RH [RHO], 11 Nov. MS: NLS 3706.132. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO ROBERT HORN

docBody.p: Thanks for your letter and your kind remembrance of me. I am glad to hear of you again, especially after your late fit of sickness,See TC to JAC, 6 Nov. from which I hope you are now almost completely restored. Pray be careful about venturing out, & keep clear of all chances of a relapse, which is apt to be more dangerous than the disease itself.

Soon after your leaving Edinr I received from Laing an exact copy of the Extract from the old Scotch Treasury Book concerning the “twa Pictures” sent to Theodorus Beza, of date June 1581;See TC to RHO, 12 July; Laing sent the extract from the Treasurer’s Accounts to TC, 20 Aug. this as I reported, you had bargained for on my behalf & he not knowing your then Highland address had dispatched direct to myself. Many thanks to you and to him; and now I think this ought to be the last trouble I gave you in regard to Knox and his pictorial affairs. The Banchory Picture I retain here among my curiosities or valuables. The pains you and your photographer bestowed on this picture must have been great,See MAI to RHO, 20 July. and they have resulted in a success far transcending anything we could do here by the respectable & faithful photographerBoth photographers unidentified further. whom I trusted with the Somerville Knox reading over to him the ingenious resources you had employed in the Banchory do was able to produce nothing but a miserable blotch, mainly black, with here & there faint traces of a feature or two in ghastly grey white. The like happened with his attempt upon the Torphichen Picture which indeed was judged by everybody a very miserable Picture, done from Beza’s “Figure Head” & totally unworthy to have been the Father of so many discrepant engravings, “improved” according to the fancy of every new engraver, as have been circulating ever since. I staid in Edinr only a week entirely hidden, except to Laing & Profr Masson, who faithfully kept their
secret;See TC to JAC, 27 Aug. Edinr as natural was very beautiful to me & also very mournful a city of remembrances, some of which must be sacred to me forever.
Believe me, dear Sir, / Yours, with many thanks and regards,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 17 Nov. MS: NLS 528.20. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 309–10. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: There is nothing new here which is much worth speaking of, but I will write you a few words in this small interval left of today; having been so often disappointed in the days that have passed since your letter arrived. Thanks for the details that you give us there. I am glad especially of your dialogue with Austin Junior & of the hopes you entertain of him in reference to Ernhirst.John A. Carlyle wrote, 12 Nov.: “Young James [Austin] & I took an hour’s walking down the river, & had a good deal of talk about the management of Ernhirst. He seems to think it will not be difficult for him to manage the farm, with Marianne indoors to take care of the cheesemaking &c. I was much pleased with the way in which he spoke on the subject, & think he has plenty of talent & information to undertake the task. … Young James Carlyle was here last Saturday, to settle with the lawyers about getting the necessary valuation of stock &c at Ernhirst; but he will not have anything farther to do with the farm, except giving any advice that may be asked of him.” A letter of Jean’s, concerning poor Margaret’s last hours took me by the very heart, & brought the whole scene vividly before me. It is her last letter but one; give her most impressively my thanks for it. I wrote to poor Mary a poor note yesterdayMary Austin replied, [16 Dec.]: “I would thank you heartily for your kind and sympathising letter. I never for a moment doubted of your brotherly love I well knew your kind heart would be so sorry for my dear Margarets death and for my sorrow.” which, alas, can do her no good but was a kind of satisfaction to myself.

The enclosed letters may be worth your reading, especially Froude’s letter & also Forster’s two. Hornes you can burn the other three please return to me when read. The only event here, if event it can be called is the actual beginning or rather attempt at beginning that pitiful thing on Knox’s picture; which, with fingers & eyes of my own, I could finish almost within a week but which with fingers & eyes of Mary only, both she & I will have a sad tussle with; lasting, let us say a month. Probably the last thing I shall write in this
world; comfortable solely, if even so, by the pious intention of it, if it can have any result at all.

What you say about coming to Chelsea is naturally very interesting to me & I have been thinking often about it, ever since the announcement.John wrote: “If at any time you wish me to come to London to be near you, I shall be ready to do so, as I daresay you already know. I might get some lodging near Cheyne Row.” Certainly it well deserves consideration from both of us, & I hope it may turn to something of good. If you do think of coming to Chelsea there can be none in the world that can expect such comfort from your being near me as I: but I fear you wd be uncomfortable & forlorn in a lodging here & the very thought of it makes me so already. You know well enough how matters stand here, & that this door is ever open to you, but also what the weak estate of things domestic here is apt to be: I must therefore leave the affair to your own mature consideration & content myself with dreaming of what good possibilities there may be in it if well dealt with.

I have seen Ruskin these three Saturdays in punctual sequence at 2 p.m. who promises to come weekly at the same day and hour by way of holiday at London, between his Oxford lectures. I get but little real insight out of him, though he is full of friendliness & is aiming as if at the very stars but his sensitive, flighty nature disqualifies him for earnest conversation and frank communication of his secret thoughts. Allingham is at all times very obliging; but in this thrice glorious Honeymoon time so overwhelmed in worldly happiness and joy over his Helen that there is little to be got from him that is interesting to third parties; in fact good conversation with one’s fellow creatures seems to have vanished very much from this scene of things for me.

The November fogs you heard of had been much exaggerated in the newspapers. There has been in fact less fog hereabout than in common years, & as yet nothing of “London fog” at all. In good part, too, the weather has been dry; drought ended; there came three sharp days of clean frost, upon which I gave up my morning cold bath, but on the third day our frost broke & gradually there has been considerable rain since; which however, up to this date, has done me no ill. I really feel not worse at all than usual; dare not clearly say better.— — Give my love to Jean to James & all the household. Good be ever with you all

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 19 Nov. MS: FC. Quot: Carlyle Encyclopedia 165. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: Many thanks for your kind punctuality in writing those bright & pleasant little Notes, regardless of my stupid looking silence, which indeed you know to be involuntary.Since TC’s last letter to him, 26 Oct., Forster had written four letters, 27 Oct., 31 Oct., 7 Nov., and 14 Nov.; see Kinser and Tarr, II, 89–97. They come dropping in, each of them like a little brief break of sunbeams, suddenly falling in through the dim mists, external & internal & are very welcome to me.

In spite of your many sufferings & incumbrances at Seaforth, I always struggle to persuade myself that you are intrinsically gathering strength, as indeed you have long been doing, & are better off there in this bad season than you could be anywhere else.Forster wrote, 14 Nov.: “Bitter cold has set in here, and for the present, I am altogether a prisoner. I have also had other than my ordinary and most liberal allowance of misery during the past week—the trouble of what Iago calls a raging tooth” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 95). Cf. Othello 3.3. Much, therefore, as I wish to see you again, after so long an absence, I am almost reluctant to think of your coming back to London, which is generally so unfriendly to you!Forster wrote, 14 Nov.: “We determine to return to London at the end of this month—if my condition does not drive us back earlier to the Doctors. Therefore I do not, you see, make brilliant report; but the days here have had a brightness they could not have had in London, and I am grateful for the rest” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 95–96). For one thing I am certain you need have no uneasiness as to Lady Ashburton’s intention to be there. It is evident she does not yet in the least know what to decide upon for the winter & I should think is likelier to make for Italy with her young Marigold than any whither else. Advise you, alas, I cannot in the least pretend to do; but somehow it seems to me as if you wd be safer continuing where you are than anywhere within these four seas.

I myself am very feeble; no more feckless man, as the Scotch term it, to be met with anywhere; & in mind can only brood over a world, which has nothing grand for me, except the universal Shadow of Death upon which, with a something of divinely mournful, boundless & sometimes unspeakably tender I daily muse & meditate. I can do no work or none that deserves the name; & yet, singular to say I am upon a little Narrative concerning Knox’s Picture & feel bound to finish it, in spite of what continually seems its impossibility on the terms allowed, namely want of hands, & of eyes, were there nothing else. We must try, we must try, nevertheless.

Of my reading, which wraps up my thorny evenings into a kind of grim &
only prickly composure, I can say nothing latterly that is comfortable: I have omitted “People’s William’s” onslaught on Cardinal Cullenism; thankful only to perceive by it that People’s William has at least cut loose from thatForster wrote, 7 Nov.: “I see we have the frightful prospect of another [pamphlet] from Gladstone upon papistical matters” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 94). Gladstone’s pamphlet, The Vatican Decrees in Their Bearing on Civil Allegiance: Political Expostulation (1874), was pbd. 7 Nov. Paul Cullen (1803–78; ODNB), Roman Catholic archbishop of Dublin, was a leading advocate of papal infallibility and a vigorous opponent of Gladstone’s Irish Universities Bill; see 48:171–72TC to JAC, 7 March 1873. Forster wrote, 14 Nov.: “How astounding all this about Gladstone that I see in the papers! That he should have lived all these years before he found out what Popery really means!” (Kinser and Tarr, II, 96). & that among the sad things we are like to see that ugliest can no longer be one. Punch Greville I got through some time ago; P. appeared to my surprise to have more shrewdness & sense than I had before given him credit for; but on the whole except the kind of Interest one has always in comparing any contemporary stupidest accord of the years we ourselves have lived through, there is little of interesting to be got from P. G. His occasional details about the two Kings,See TC to JAC, 6 Nov.; the three volumes of Greville’s Memoirs pbd. so far covered the reigns of George IV (1762–1830); ODNB), king of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland 1820–30, and his brother William IV (1765–1837; ODNB), king of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland 1830–37. which are abundantly cynical & credible, are curious to read, & almost nothing else is. I also finished Spedding’s Book on Bacon a good few weeks ago & found it wonderful; nay in some respects admirable; the most solid & complete investigation of a chaos to the very bottom that I have ever seen in this generation & a perfect picture both of Bacon & of Spedding; truly in its way a magnum opus—intolerably wearisome to read, indeed impossible without considerable skipping. Poor Spedding, I have been twice at his door to congratulate him on getting out of such a chaos so creditably. But the night has fallen—Mary is writing by candlelight & why should I bore you any farther.
Adieu, dear Forster; I shall hear from, shan’t I in a day or two. With loving regards to you and the dear little Lady

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 30 Nov. MS: NLS 528.21. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
There was a Letter on the point of being written to you last week, had not Mary anxious only to save me time & the embarrassments of writing which at
that time were considerable, maintained (mistaken little wretch that she was) that it was I who had written last!— which I did not till almost yesterday discover to be the reverse of fact. Never mind, I can assure you clearly enough, you lost little, for last week, all through it was nearly out of my power to have written anything either useful or agreeable even to a Brother.

Here as at Dumfries the weather for weeks past especially for the last two weeks has been eminently unfriendly to the old and feckless; nothing but frozen fogs, bitterly cold even when windless,The Times reported, 25 Nov.: “At 9 o’clock yesterday morning a dense fog enveloped the metropolis. … The severe frost … continued yesterday, the thermometer remaining below freezing point.” forced cessation of one’s morning bath; in short general pinching harrying & paltry wretchedness of the physical kind;—till on Tuesday night last there occurred a fair strike on the part of sleep, and, from about 3 a.m., abating only about daybreak such a revolt & insurrectionary revolution on the part of nature, that is to say, dyspeptic muscular & nervous do, as I have not experienced for many months before. The insurrection did indeed prove triumphant and a reinstatement of the status quo became probable next morning; & has, tho’ with difficulty, been proceeding ever since, especially since the weather changed to windy & muddy wet, admitting one at least to freely wash oneself & rush out for a walk, thro’ whatever weather. It appears to me the liver has suddenly, by that explosion, taken a new tack; perhaps not so much a worse one & today in spite of the universal moisture I walked rapidly along to the very end of the embankment & rather circuitously back; feeling to have slightly improved, tho’ still needing much to do more in that direction. This was nearly all the news you could have had, even had Mary been favourable, as the little genius, to her credit be it spoken, today fairly is.

After the despicablest efforts, fruitless for most part, I have got the poor Knox paper actually begun, some two pages of it actually put down; the prints all ready or handsomely progressing; complete emancipation from constraint on the part of Allingham;Allingham in his role as editor of Fraser’s Magazine; see TC to JAC, 23 Oct. nay ready help where his help is possible and a clear determination on my own part that the thing is to be done, if the gee of life do not go out altogether. This on the whole tho’ at first perhaps you will reckon it, an unnecessary trouble and sorrow is a real comfort of its kind; the only use I can get out of my heavy-laden existence & redeeming every day I can work at it some infinitesimal particle of good out of what would otherwise be altogether worthless & bad. Thank Heaven for small mercies; in my remorseful mind I often think we deserve none great, hardly any even small.

This morning I was truly grieved to learn by Maggie’s letter to Mary that she thought you had been very ill with these old established biliary
disorders;Maggie Aitken, Mary’s sister. John A. Carlyle wrote, 1 Dec.: “I have recovered from my fit of dyspepsia which was very severe for two days.” Like TC he attributed it to being unable to get outside for his usual walks due to the bad weather. alas, alas, there is no need to either of us of increase in that particular. My first notion wh. still continues with me, was that perhaps now would be the time when you could resolve on a sally out to London, which I also thought might prove beneficial.John wrote: “Thanks for your most kind invitation to Chelsea. I may perhaps start for London … but I could hardly hope to do you much good, or any good to myself there at present, until you get the Knox article off your hands.” If your own mind inclines that way, I can only say at once decide on trying it; try it, let us see you here. That of going into lodgings is far too sad to be for a moment contemplated; this house ought surely, while I live, to be your home-house for London & the door of No 5 to stand wide open for you. You know the condition of affairs here & no doubt have been considering the enterprize. Come therefore & let us try it. Your room upstairs shall be ready for you on a two days’ warning & another meeting take place between us two old Brothers once again before the end quite come. Write about that next time you write & it will need no more discussion. I have no news of the least importance beyond this; & indeed no time at all, being appointed to be whirled up to Lady Ashburton’s who is bedrid with bronchitis & her daughter, too, confined with cold; neither of whom have I seen or heard of for above a week past till this morning. With dispatch therefore I must pack my wrappages & clothes about me, & be off. Forster’s last letter is of this morning; nothing of improvement, but also little or nothing of injury from the wild weather at Seaforth;—& at the end of the week he is coming home. I have not got his letter fairly read yet nor shall till the evening, but will then send it on to you, ohne weiteres [without more ado].
Give my kindest love to Jean & the lassies & their Father & believe me ever your affectionate Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 Dec. MS: NLS 528.22. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your letter came this afternoon while Mary & I were busy on that miserable draggle of a paper on Knox. Tomorrow is her painting dayMary was taking lessons with Emilie Venturi; see TC to JAC, 17 Oct. and there will be no opportunity to write; so please to accept this little word of assurance that
nothing is wrong, as dictated before going down stairs to walk preparatory to supper and sleep.

We have as bad weather as you or little better; nothing can exceed its changefulness, and sometimes nothing its violence at least so far as rain goes and tempest; we have had frost too, ice, two days ago half an inch thick; but our frosts are usually bright & calm and break down at latest, hitherto, on the third day. On the frosty days I avoid cold bathing; of the two sorts the wet sort, which comes usually in deluges and high winds and is very warm for the season seems to me the more enervating and depressive; but both sorts are heavy enough upon a weak old body, though every morning hitherto I take the most vigorous walk that is possible to me; & get on without notable disaster in the night, since the bad scene noted in my last bulletin to you. On the whole I notice nothing more than the natural increase of burden due to a new year of time in the case of all mortal creatures, especially of the age of 80 going. The miserable waliedreg of a Knox’s Portraits goes on constantly, though miserably slow & not like amounting to anything in the least considerable; but I stand to it doggedly & will have it done, please Heaven by about the end of this month. Allingham is highly assiduous about it, poor soul & has settled all the outside preliminaries. He has also this very day, for finale, obtained from me, after much solicitation liberty to publish in three successive Magazine articles,TC’s “Early Kings of Norway,” chap. 1–7, Fraser’s Magazine 61 (Jan. 1875): 1–26; chap. 8–10, Fraser’s Magazine 62 (Feb. 1875): 135–55; and chap. 11–16, Fraser’s Magazine 63 (March 1875): 273–88. under his own editing that miserable scribble of Norse history which you know so well. He covenants to give me no trouble about it, except reading of it over when ready for the press & to be absolutely silent on the subject. He has read your Notes carefully along with the rest & engages to incorporate your corrections accurately in the text; so that you also will have no further trouble with it. I cannot but own to myself I regret having given him this permission; but the poor soul seemed to be so intent upon the matter & really to need so much some impetus given at New-year’s day to his all-important editorial efforts that I could not master cruelty enough to say No. Of society, tho by no means of interesting society I have enough & to spare; & the importance of my “work” (save the mark!)Coterie speech; cf. Merchant of Venice 2.1 and Othello 1.1. you may yourself judge.

Forster did not come till Tuesday evening in a day of tempestuous rain, wh. he considered himself to have stood wonderfully well when I saw him on Wednesday afternoon last. But, poor soul, it is too evident to me since that evening that he is no better for his Devonshire month or more; he has a regular fit of coughing from 5 till ½ pt 7 every evening, a daily headache, too, has superadded itself with fits of neuralgia which go the length or once went the
length of having a perfectly sound tooth torn out of his jaw, with the toothache merely flying to the other side of his face. The one strong point I can notice about him is that he still has power of eating; all else seems to indicate confused misery, for which no doctor can do anything. His best outlook clearly seems to me that of getting to Lisbon, whither his great Friend young Lytton is appointed Ambassador,Edward Robert Bulwer-Lytton was appointed British minister in Lisbon, Nov. 1874. who unluckily cannot yet receive him for about a month coming.

Along with this, is posted a book for Jean, wh. I hope she will be able to read, tho’ it is but a poor extract of the Abbe de Sade’s entertaining work:Jacques François Paul Alphonse (1705–78), Abbé de Sade, Mémoires pour la vie de François Pétrarque, 3 vols. (Amsterdam, 1764–67); for TC’s early reading of this work, see 2:212TC to JBW, [Early Dec. 1822]. probably it will not arrive by Saturday’s post, but in the meanwhile pray thank her for her letter, wh. was very welcome & assure her & all the rest of my continual love. Adieu, dear Brother. Ever yr affectionate

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 19 Dec. MS: NLS 528.23. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Today I have to confine myself to a little bit of business, the smallest in the world; we being both of us in a great press of business here, working at our Knox, poor feckless souls, with very little progress!

About two years ago I remember sending you a London Library Book of small size, called Errinnerungen der lustige Zeit of Geothe at WeimarJ. A. Diezmann, Goethe und die lustige Zeit in Weimar; TC sent the book to John in Nov. 1873; see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1873; Mary misspelled Goethe. (or some equivalent title) which also I remember your reporting to have liked; perhaps you returned this Book to the Lon. Library, perhaps not; certain it is they demanded it and another of me, Dahlmann’s Life of HerodotusFriedrich Christoph Dahlmann (1785–1860), The Life of Herodotus Drawn Out from his Book, trans. G. V. Cox (1846); this is listed in the Catalogue of the London Library (1865). There is no record of TC mentioning this book. , a very small book also, which I think you never had: to both of these demands, being able to remember nothing of them, and having been assured repeatedly on returning books that these were all we had I returned a positive denial that either of them was in my hands. The Dahlmann I have not yet got the least
trace of & believe it to be lost in some corner of their chaos but the other night it came into my mind that the Errinerungen was probably now in your hands shoved away in some by corner in your shelves. Please look for it if you cannot remember to have sent it & at once dispatch it, if discoverable, to the Lon. Library.John replied, 20 Dec., that he remembered reading the Diezmann book, (see TC to JAC, 29 Nov. 1873), but thought it had been in Chelsea; however he promised to look for it; he then wrote, 23 Dec., that he had “looked carefully for the German book … & can find no trace of it. If I ever had it here at all, it must have been punctually returned—as has been my habit in all similar cases.” This is all the bit of business & with this I must end; people having come in for Mary & waiting down stairs.

We keep in usual health, perhaps almost a shade better for my part in spite of this dismal weather & its snows & paltry frosts & slippery sleets wh I daily front with success & am no longer so terrified at as I seem to be. Ruskin was here yesterday & left a quantity of Italian drawings, especially the History of Moses by Botticelli: his Zipporah his burning bush &c &c.Ruskin was in Rome in May 1874; he wrote, 20 May: “I’m drawing in the Sistine Chapel … on Sandro Botticelli’s maid—Zipporah.” His studies of Botticelli’s fresco, “The Life of Moses” (1481–82), included “Zipporah,” Moses’s wife (see Exod. 2:21), “Gershom’s Dog,” Gershom was the son of Moses and Zipporah (see Exod. 2:22), and God appearing to Moses in a burning bush (see Exod. 3:2–4); see Ruskin’s Works 38:234. Sandro Botticelli (ca. 1445–1510), Italian Renaissance painter. It is to see these that the visitors down stairs have come. R. was in gt spirits has been here about 4 times once a week, but is now off to Oxford, Coniston &c & far enough away from this. Poor Forster is not a bit better. I send my lovingest farewell. My blessing to one & all of you

bibl.sourceNote: TC-BD [BDI], 29 Dec. Pbd: Froude, Carlyle 4:430–31; Wilson, Carlyle 6:344–45 inc; K. J. Fielding and Rodger L. Tarr, Carlyle Past and Present (1976) 234–35 inc.
bibl.head: TC TO BENJAMIN DISRAELI

docBody.p:
Yesterday, to my great surprise, I had the honour to receive your letter containing a magnificent proposal for my benefit,Benjamin Disraeli wrote, 27 Dec.: “A Government should recognise intellect. It elevates and sustains the tone of a nation. … When I consider the literary world, I see only two living names which, I would fain believe will be remembered, and they stand out in uncontested superiority. One is that of a poet [Tennyson] … and the other is your own. … I have, therefore, made up my mind, if agreeable to yourself, to recommend to Her Majesty to confer on you the highest distinction for merit at her command … and that is the Grand Cross of the Bath. … It is not well that in the sunset of your life you should be disturbed by common cares. I see no reason why a great author should not receive from the nation a pension. … Have the goodness to let me know your feelings on these subjects.” which will be memorable
to me for the rest of my life. Allow me to say that the letter, both in purport and expression, is worthy to be called magnanimous and noble, that it is without example in my own poor history; and I think it is unexampled, too, in the history of governing persons towards men of letters at the present, as at any time; and that I will carefully preserve it as one of the things precious to memory and heart. A real treasure or benefit it, independent of all results from it.

This said to yourself and reposited with many feelings in my own grateful mind, I have only to add that your splendid and generous proposals for my practical behoof, must not any of them take effect; that titles of honour are, in all degrees of them, out of keeping with the tenour of my own poor existence hitherto in this epoch of the world, and would be an encumbrance, not a furtherance to me; that as to money, it has, after long years of rigorous and frugal, but also (thank God, and those that are gone before me) not degrading poverty, become in this latter time amply abundant, even superabundant; more of it, too, now a hindrance, not a help to me; so that royal or other bounty would be more than thrown away in my case; and in brief, that except the feeling of your fine and noble conduct on this occasion, which is a real and permanent possession, there cannot anything be done that would not now be a sorrow rather than a pleasure.
With thanks more than usually sincere,

closer.salute:
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obliged and obedient servant,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady D [LDE], 30 Dec. Pbd: Froude Carlyle 4:431–32 inc. Quot: Carlyle Encyclopedia 128–29; John Nichol, Thomas Carlyle (1892) 143.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY DERBY

docBody.p:
Dear Lady,—As I believe you to have been the originator, contriver, and architect of this beautiful air mansion intended for my honour and benefit,See TC to BDI, 29 Dec. Disraeli had been encouraged to this offer by Lord Derby, apparently at the behest of Lady Derby; Lord Derby wrote to Disraeli, 28 Nov., urging him to award a knighthood to TC, who was “for whatever reason, most vehement against Gladstone. … Anything that could be done for him would be a really good political investment” (George Earle Buckle, The Life of Benjamin Disraeli, 6 vols. [1920] 5:355). Disraeli then wrote to Queen Victoria, 12 Dec., suggesting bestowing honors on distinguished literary figures: “Eminent literary men are so few, that there would be no trouble as to choice. … Mr. Disraeli knows only of two authors, who are especially conspicuous at the moment: Tennyson and Carlyle. He has no personal knowledge of either, and their political views are, he apprehends, opposed to those of your Majesty’s Government, but that is not to be considered for a moment. … Mr. Carlyle is old, and childless, and poor; but he is very popular and respected by the nation. … Would a G.C.B. [Grand Cross of the Order of Bath] be too much? It might be combined with a pension, perhaps” (Buckle, Disraeli 5:355–56). and
as the Premier’s letter appears to me very beautiful on his part, I venture directly to send you a correct copy of that and of my answer to it,Lady Derby replied, 6 Jan. 1875: “I wish I could thank you as warmly as I feel for your letter & enclosures. … I do like to think that the Queen thro’ her Ministers has done what she could to recognise that we have a great man amongst us.” which I really had a regret in feeling obliged to write; that is to say, in reducing so splendid an edifice of the generous mind to inexorable nothing; though I do say still, and will say it, the generous intention, brought ready for fulfilment from such a quarter, will ever remain a beautiful and precious possession for me.

Mr. Disraeli’s letter is really what I called it, magnanimous and noble on his part. It reveals to me, after all the hard things I have said of him, a new and unexpected stratum of genial dignity and manliness of character which I had by no means given him credit for. It is, as my penitent heart admonishes me, a kind of ‘heaping coals of fire on my head;’See Prov. 25:22. and I do truly repent and promise to amend. For the rest, I naturally wish there should be as little as possible said about this transaction, though almost inevitably the secret will ooze out at last. In the meanwhile silence from us all. . . .Lady Derby replied: “I will not let out the secret, but you must remember, please, that all the Cabinet know it, & Cabinet Ministers have wives!” Ellipsis in pbd. source.

Forgive this loose rambling letter. Write no answer to it till your own time come, and on the whole forgive me my sins generally, or think of me as mercifully as you can. With my respectful compliments to Lord Derby, and most loyal wishes that all good may be with you and yours,

closer.salute:
I remain, dear Lady,
Your attached and most obedient,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 Jan. MS: NLS 528.24. Pbd. A. Carlyle, NL 2:310–12 inc. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:432; John Nichol, Thomas Carlyle (1892) 143–44. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: The enclosed letter and copy of my answerSee TC to BDI, 29 Dec. 1874. ought to go to you as a family curiosity and secret: nobody whatever yet knows of it beyond our two selves here, except Lady Derby whom I believe to be the contriver of the whole affair. You would have been surprised all of you to have found unexpectedly your poor old Brother Tom converted into Sir Tom Bart., but alas there was no danger at any moment of such a catastrophe. I do however truly admire the magnaminity of Dizzy in regard to me: he is the only man I almost never spoke of except with contempt and if there is anything of scurrility anywhere chargeable against me, I am sorry to own he is the subject of it and yet see here he comes with a pan of hot coals for my guilty head. I am on the whole gratified a little within my own dark heart at this mark of the good will of high people, Dizzy by no means the chief of them, which has come to me now at the very end when I can have the additional pleasure of answering “Alas, friends, it is of no use to me, and I will not have it.” Enough, enough. Return me the official Letter, and say nothing about it beyond the walls of your own house.

The Knox (shame on us!) is never yet finished, but we are struggling forward with it, and it is really near done. Allingham, I believe,—or rather I was going to believe till Mary put me right, does not want it;—but the fact is he does want it,—before the Norse Kings is done. And, Oh me, Oh me, please the pigs,Coterie speech; see 9:376TC to MAC, 23 Dec. 1837. he shall have it!— But we do live under the grimmest circumstances here; frost, frost & fog. Yesterday was equal to midnight all day; a pair of candles burning from the time when it should have been noon. Today is much clearer and the frost considerably strengthened. This morning I noticed in my walk the Thames covered with tumbling blocks of white ice a new sight for many, many years back.TC last mentions blocks of ice in the Thames in Dec. 1860; see 37:76TC to JCA, 30 Dec. 1860. Happily we have had no more snow; but I live in fear of it every day. The streets, at least the thoroughfares, are wonderfully clear considering. I am afraid you are still worse off; & have got more snow. I hear of a new heavy fall at Edinburgh, in which Dumfries too probably participates.The Scotsman reported, 31 Dec. 1874: “Snow fell heavily throughout Scotland on Tuesday night and yesterday, the depth in some places reaching 7 or 8 inches. As there was scarcely any wind, no drifting took place. The severity of the frost relaxed very little during the snowstorm.”

The Christmas “festivities,” thank heaven, are all over. I rigorously declined everything, except Forsters inexorable Xmas dinner;Forster invited TC for Christmas dinner every year if he was able; see 48:122TC to JF, 20 Dec. 1872, and 141TC to LLA, 10 Jan. 1873. which in his present state of health and spirits, was very unpleasant to me; his spirits for the dinner being painfully hypocritical, with intent to deceive me on his part, poor fellow, with perception that I was not deceived. Heigh, ho. I send the current FraserFraser’s Magazine, Jan. 1875, containing the first chapter of TC’s “Early Kings of Norway.” straight off to Maggie Welsh, knowing you can easily get it at Dumfries, if you like. And really there are some good Articles in it; especially one by the “Author of Supernatural Religion”TC possibly refers to “Contrasts of Ancient and Modern History,” Fraser’s Magazine 61 (Jan. 1875): 110–20, by Francis W. Newman (1805–97; ODNB), scholar and philosopher, who was at one time thought to be the author of Supernatural Religion: An Inquiry into the Reality of Divine Revelation, 2 vols. (1874); that book had been pbd. anonymously, and is now believed to have been written by Walter Richard Cassels (1826–1907; ODNB), religious controversialist. The only other possible article is “Opinions of the Contemporaries of the Evangelists as to the Invisible World,” Fraser’s 61:100–9, which was by Francis Roubiliac Conder (1815–89), civil engineer, who contributed many articles to magazines on a variety of topics. (as I think) whose name it appears is not poor old Dr Muir of Edinburgh,John Muir (1810–82; ODNB), Scottish Sanskritist; see 43:62TC to JAC, 2 Dec. 1865. but one Pusey, Nephew of the Puseyite Oxford Pusey, & Son, I guess, of Philip Pusey,—an excellent gentleman whom I used to knowSidney Edward Bouverie-Pusey (1839–1911), nephew of Edward Bouverie Pusey (1800–1882; ODNB), Oxford theologian, and only son of Philip Pusey (1799–1855; ODNB), agriculturalist, whom TC much admired; see 11:46TC to JAC, 11 March 1839, and 18:294–95TC to LHB, 22 Dec. 1844. Be it by whom it will the Article is worth your reading,—yours if perhaps no others in the house There is also a Yankee piece, the last in the No of a very cheering and hopeful complexion.Charles K. Landis, “The Settlement of Vineland in New Jersey,” Fraser’s Magazine 61: 121–134. John A. Carlyle replied, 3 Jan.: “I have got the Fraser from library here, but have not yet had time to read aught else in it than the Norse Kings.” The Fraser people are to keep me 6 copies of the Norse Kings. By mistake they have sent in an unsewed condition the first portion instead of waiting till all the three were there. On reflection I will send Jean her copy today, should any of you like to read it; and tell her to keep it carefully till the other two arrive. It can then be sewed up with them for her own keeping.

You see I have nothing but clatters to report. Why should I continue it farther? “Compliments of the season” if I had any I would willingly send you. All I can send is from the bottom of my heart best wishes to you all and silent prayer that God’s mercy may still attend us while our pilgrimage continues

postscript.p:
A wonderful Book by a German Dominie at Hildesheim; a very honest,
patient & extremely grammatical performance; carrying out a most elaborate comparative survey of Macaulay & me,Adolf Brennecke (1841–92), German historian and teacher, Thomas Carlyle and Thomas Babington Macaulay contrasted with each other in respect to the form and the contents of their works (Hildesheim, 1875). Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800–1859; ODNB), historian and poet. wh. I think is sure to interest you, would have come two days ago, but TaitRobert Scott Tait. picked it up for a reading to himself & probably to DarwinErasmus Darwin. withal; so that it will likeliest reach you tomorrow. Do with it what you like.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 Jan. MS: NLS 528.25. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Today I have been sitting to Boehm for a big statueIn Jan. 1875 Boehm was working on a life-size plaster statue of TC, based on the statuette he had made for Lady Ashburton; see TC to JAC, 27 April 1874. It was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1875; a marble version of it is now in the Scottish National Portrait Gallery in Edinburgh, and a bronze version stands in the Chelsea Embankment gardens. he is intent on doing for his own behoof; I am just come home, very cold & feckless; Mary has been out painting & there is absolutely no time, almost none at all. But happily I can tell you still that we are all well, & that nothing whatever has gone wrong with us hitherto—nay the very Knox is actually near done; in the language of flattery, I said two days ago it was as good as done; Mary having undertaken to write it fair & give the last part of it any cornering & trimming it may still need & thus it goes on steadily on alternate days;Mary took painting lessons with Emilie Venturi on alternate mornings; see TC to JAC, 17 Oct. 1874. but will yet I find involve various fasheries, so we will not yet halloo, or not halloo loud. The weather is beautiful & temperate as with you; frost quite gone & even the seas of mud swept away or almost dried. I read up & down in Laing’s Knox or steadily through in RobertsonWilliam Robertson (1721–93; ODNB), historian, History of Scotland, 2 vols. (1759). whom I find to be smooth, & tidy, but very shallow & even indistinct in parts; hardly any dates accurately allowed one: my notion is to recommend Knox’s own History as a book vague & impromptu but highly worth reading & affording the only real image there is of that great time in Scotland.In “The Portraits of John Knox,” TC recommends: “The Works of John Knox, collected and edited by David Laing (the first complete, and perfectly annotated Edition ever given: a highly meritorious, and, considering all the difficulties, intrinsic and accidental, even a heroic Performance; for which all Scotland, and in a sense all the world, is debtor to Mr. Laing)” (Carlyle, Works 30:335).

To Jean, whom I recommend to walk diligentlyJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 5 Jan.: “Jean has been staying too much in the house during the storm, & must take some walking if the weather continues at all favourable.” Jean Aitken wrote, 1 Jan.: “Your kindest & best of letters was so to speak my ‘first foot’ this morning! I will not attempt anything in the way of thanks however much I feel your generosity both to the lasses & myself. I shall keep our £10 and half the other equally between the wenches.” TC’s checkbook recorded: “30 December 1874 / Mrs Aitken / The Hill / £20 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). The lasses were her das. Anne and Margaret. & otherwise take care of herself I send a Newspaper that came this morning where she will find something to read that will please her a little. The Article on Ruskin’s last Fors in particular would be highly worth Ruskin’s perusal so soon as you have done with it, could you kindly send it on to Ruskin,TC sent a newspaper (unidentified) containing a review of his “Early Kings of Norway.” The paper also contained a review of Ruskin’s latest Fors Clavigera, letter 49, “From the Prophet even unto the Priest” (Jan. 1875). John wrote, 13 Jan.: “I sent the newspaper punctually to Ruskin … at least the portion which spoke of his last Fors & of the Norse Kings.” or cut the article out & send it without any writing at all except the address Corpus Christi College Oxford.

To yourself I intend to write soon & enclose for the day a letter from Lady DerbyFor Lady Derby’s letter, see TC to LDE, 30 Dec. 1874. wh. please return. We hope to hear again soon; indeed we now begin to hope we shall see you soon.
With my kindest love to you all, I here (intrusive parties having come in & be hanged to them!) conclude

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-JAC, 18 Jan. MS: NLS 528.26. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Uncle promised to our good neighbor Mrs De Morgan of 8 Cheyne Row (the Widow of Prof. De Morgan)Sophia De Morgan, b. Frend (1809–92), abolitionist, suffrage activist, and prison reformer; she m., 1837, Augustus De Morgan (1806–71; ODNB), mathematician and historian. After her husband’s death Sophia De Morgan moved to No. 8 Cheyne Row. She had met the Carlyles briefly some years previously, and later wrote: “It was pleasant to me to be introduced again to Mr. Carlyle, for he kindly said he was glad to see me, as he was indebted to my husband for a notice of his mathematical work. This work had been the subject of a correspondence between Mr. Carlyle and Mr. De Morgan some years before” (Threescore Years and Ten, Reminiscences of the late Sophia Elizabeth De Morgan, ed. Mary A. De Morgan [1895] 232); for their correspondence, see 44:218TC to ADM, 19 June 1867. that he would send you the enclosed
MemorialAfter the death of Augustus De Morgan, a Memorial Committee was set up to fund a De Morgan medal, to be awarded annually for the most original mathematical treatise; the design of the reverse was taken from a bust of De Morgan made by Thomas Woolner, now in the University of London Library. which as you will see he & a great many others have signed, to ask if you, too, will put your name to it. In any case will you kindly return it to me.

One evening about ten days [ago] Mr Arthur WattArthur Watt, stepson of John A. Carlyle, who worked for the civil service in India; he was on two-years leave in Britain; see TC to JAC, 24 April. came & staid for an hour or so. He was looking well; told a great many interesting things about India & was good company. I daresay he would tell you about poor Miss Kingham’sMrs. Thirza Kingham (ca. 1805–75), of 174 Brompton Rd. (previously 48 Brompton Row), with whom John A. Carlyle often lodged when in London; see 42:226TC to JAC, 29 Sept. 1865. troubles with Mr Dunford.Possibly Rev. William Dunford (ca. 1811–76), minister of Brompton Episcopal Chapel; troubles unexplained. I have not yet been able to go and see her; but mean to do so very soon.

The Knox Article is still a long way from being done—by a long way I mean that it will need Uncle to work at it for several days. He has been sitting to Boehm lately for a life sized statue. It was not like him when I saw it; but I believe it is much improved since
We are busy at Knox today & I have not a moment more

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-JAC, 23 Jan. MS: NLS 528.27. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I am to write & say that Uncle hopes you will kindly excuse him for not writing today. He has been hard at work at Knox all the morning & I only steal this 5 minutes from the task to send you a line to say that he is well — in case you should wonder at his silence.
I duly received the Memorial & carried it to Mrs De Morgan,See MAI to JAC, 18 Jan. after getting Dr Blakiston,Peyton Blakiston; see TC to JAC, 25 March 1874. too, to sign it.
Excuse the shortness & haste of this Note, dear Uncle. With love from Uncle & myself

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 30 Jan. MS: NLS 528.28. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:312–13; Froude, Carlyle 4:433–34; C. R. Sanders, Carlyle’s Friendships and Other Studies (Durham, NC, 1977) 220. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: You have written to me several times in a very kind & agreeable way, for which I am greatly obliged, though driven by various accidents to be silent all this while. I now set about the clear duty of writing a word to you in the top of the morning (which, alas, is not very early by the clock, according to our habits here!)—neither withal is there any thing beyond what you generally know already that I have to write. I have not been worse in health since you last heard; in fact usually rather better; & at times in the midst of my multifarious infirmities there come glimpses or bright reminiscences of what I might in the language of flattery call health,—very singular to me, now wearing out my 80th year. It is strange & wonderful to feel these glowings out again of intellectual & spiritual clearness, followed by base physical confusions of feeble old age; & indeed daily I am taught again the unfathomable mystery of what we call a soul radiant with heaven & yet capable of being overclouded & as it were being swallowed up by the bottomless mud it has to live in this world!—

We have never yet absolutely done with that unfortunate Knox, tho’ it seems to be hanging for weeks back on the very edge of finis & will surely be altogether ended in a day or two, & put fairly into the drawer in clear Ms. to be there & rest until it is wanted for final emandation with the printer waiting for it. All the three parts of the Norse affairAllingham noted in his Diary, 11 Jan.: “Helen and I call at Cheyne Row about half past ten in the evening—show [TC] proof of Early Kings of Norway, second article. (He is particular to the minutest point, and rages against printers. Mary copied out all the MS., with no small labour)” (Allingham Diary 235). are to be printed before Knox come. The Second of them Jean would get this morning; the paltry enough Third part, of which I now recollect very little will be for the March Number of Fraser then we wash our hands of it for ever & a day. Except for the encouragement or other benefit it may give to poor Allingham nothing cd have
induced me to bother with it farther; but the poor man was so passionately anxious I cd not find it in my heart to say No.

There has been again a friendly assault made upon me, DisrealiMary misspells Disraeli here and below. himself the instigator in regard to the celebrated “Baronetcy’ affair. There was first a letter from Lady Derby which I enclose & you may return then there duly came the interview of ‘Wednesday,’ with a great deal of earnest & friendly persuasion to accept some part or other of the Ministerial offer;Lady Derby wrote, 20 Jan.: “Mr Disraeli is gratified, as you may suppose, at the terms of your letter but regrets your refusal & has not yet reported it to the Queen. He is so anxious that you shd reconsider it that he has begged me in his letter today to see you on the subject; he hopes that you will not make your decision public, or treat it as final, until we have talked the matter over. He is I know jealous for the honour of literature & both he & Lord Derby think that the profession will lose by your refusal of a distinction which however personally indifferent you may be to it was offered to you—if I may venture to say so—as its most distinguished member. … [I]f you will allow me [I] will call upon you on Wednesday [27 Jan.].” then at last when all had to be steadfastly declined as an evident superfluity & impropriety a frank confession from Her Ladyship that in good truth I had done well to answer No in all particulars The interview was not painful to me but rather the contrary, tho I really was sorry to disappoint (as it appeared I should do) both Disreali & a much higher Personage—Queens Majesty herself namely.Lady Derby met with TC, 15 Jan.; she reported to Disraeli: “I saw old Mr. Carlyle to-day, and he scarcely knew how to be grateful enough for the mark of attention you had paid him. I assure you it was quite touching, to see and hear his high appreciation of the offer” (Buckle, Disraeli 5:358). Lady Derby had at once permission from me to break the secret of the matter; & to tell & publish whatever she pleased of the truth about it. And so we may hope now to have got done with it; that is to have flung it over to the Newspapers & their babble which we need not heed.News of TC’s rejection of the honour was widely reported in Feb. and March. Forster wrote, 2 Feb.: “How much to believe of what I see in the newspapers I do not know … but I did not need to know that whatever unearthly influence might move our strange government to volunteer a worthy offer to you, it would be met by a worthier and nobler Non Placet [it does not please]” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 10). Tennyson too, it appears had refused; & in a way much less clear than mine in respect of courtesy & otherwise: Gladstone, he rather proudly intimated had already offered him this Baronetcy; which Alfred had declined for his own person, but accepted for his eldest Son & Successor when himself should have disappeared;See TC to LDE, 30 Dec. 1874. Hallam Tennyson later wrote: “My father answered Mr Disraeli that Mr Gladstone had offered a baronetcy before, and that he would prefer to adhere to the decision to which he had then come: that he respectfully declined the honour himself but wished it might be conferred if possible after his death on his son. Mr. Disraeli replied that such a course as reserving a baronetcy for a son was contrary to all precedent” (Hallam Tennyson, Alfred Lord Tennyson: A Memoir by his Son [1897] 2:162–63). to which it had to be answered that if Gladstone or any other friendly
potentate were in office on the Poet Laureates decease he cd certainly make his Son a Baronet;Tennyson finally accepted a baronetcy from Gladstone in 1883, and his son Hallam succeeded him. but otherwise the British Constitution cd not at this stage effect such a thing! And now enough enough of all this.

I hear nothing at all of Froude nor indeed of any I care for; mere “autographs” & rubbish are mainly what my fellow-creatures let me hear of them. I mean to write to Froude (if I can) next week; the last I understood of him that he was still in the Cape among the Diamond Fields of Natal; but about his farther purposes nothing whatever.Froude was on his way back to England, having left South Africa, 10 Jan. He arrived on the passenger ship Walmer Castle at Dartmouth, 3 Feb.

Poor Forster I fear is very ill. He is sensitive to the weather like a differential thermometer; day before yesterday when I last called he was reported to be in bed coughing very much.Forster wrote, 2 Feb.: “It has been a great grief to me, dear Carlyle, not to see you when you have called. … I have been very ill, and so continue, though with some alleviation of suffering during the last three days. What is to become of me, I do not know; but I find it to be an ill sign that my courage is leaving me” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 10). Lady Ashburton, whom I also called on; & who has been away in the country for weeks I found to be completely overset by cold, lately caught; though hoping soon to be better. I in these circes went no farther than the Hall; but promised to call again.

We begin now to expect that you will soon tell us something about your own projected sally towards Chelsea. Our weather, broken & capricious as it is, appears to be better than yours;John A. Carlyle replied, 11 Feb.: “Many thanks for your kind repetition of the invitation to Cheyne Row. But I should be afraid to start in such weather as this is, for I might be more unwell at Cheyne Row than I am here in these short days, & be a source of disturbance in that room adjoining yours. … [W]hen the weather gets a little better … [I] hope to start for Chelsea with better hopes of success.” especially the walking here, the beautiful new embankmentSee TC to JRU, 13 May 1874. were it nothing more must be clearly preferable to that of Dumfries; all we can say is that whenever you do give signal we shall at once make ready to receive you, & you will find yourself in your old quarters & environment physical & spiritual.

This is all I will write today, dear Brother, for many things are lying ahead,—far more alas, than will be got done. I can only send my blessings & best love to Jean & to you all, big & little & remain Ever your affectionate,

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-UC, 8 Feb. MS: Hilles. Hitherto unpbd.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO AN UNIDENTIFIED CORRESPONDENT

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me say in answer to your letter, that the house in which Johnson lived is in Gough Square.Samuel Johnson; see TC to JF, 16 Feb. 1874; he lived at 17 Gough Square, ca. 1746–1759, while compiling his Dictionary. If you enter this square from Fleet street you will find it on your left hand the last house in north-west corner.

Mr Carlyle did not think it worth while to ask the name of the man who lived in the house in 1832.For TC’s visit to the house in 1832, while writing “Boswell’s Life of Johnson” (1832), see Carlyle, Works 28:114.
