But as the building itself is well known he is sure that you will experience no difficulty in finding it out.
With Mr Carlyle’s compliments

bibl.sourceNote: TC-SL, 10 Feb. Pbd: Francis Edwards Ltd. auction catalog inc.
bibl.head: TC TO SAMUEL LAURENCE

docBody.p: The enclosed is a poor acknowledgment of many good turns which you have done for me in years past and for which you never from me received anything but barren thanks.TC enclosed a check: “10 February 1875 / Samuel Lawrence Esq / One Hundred Pounds Stg / £100 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20752). Laurence had painted TC (1838–41); see 10:frontis., and JWC (1852) from sketches done in 1849; see 24:100JWC to TC, [5 July 1849]. He had recently completed a copy of the Somerville portrait of John Knox; see TC to JAC, 25 Feb. 1874. Allingham noted a visit to Laurence’s studio at 6 Wells St. in his diary, 15 Jan.: “The painter is gone for the day, but a civil pleasant woman shows us in, and we see L.’s copy of the picture which C. maintains to be of John Knox” (Allingham Diary 235). Laurence wrote to American stockbroker Charles Butler (1802–97; see 45:125–26TC to CBU, 6 May 1868, and 22345:biographical notes), 17 March: “Carlyle I have seen rather much of. He came to Wells Street not long since very full of interest in a Portrait of John Knox. I should say it must be the man. C. feels assured it is, & he is a good judge of Physiognomies[.] This one is full of careful weighing—vehemently enthusiastic. We cannot discover who the Original is by” (David Southern, “‘That unhappy War of yours’: Eight Letters from Samuel Laurence to Old Friends in New York City, 1861–1875,” CSA 24 [2008]: 26). I pray you to accept it now with as kind feelings as accompany the sending of it and wish and expect heartily that it may do us both a little good.Laurence replied, 11 Feb.: “Your very kind note and Cheque for One Hundred pounds are in my hands. It is a grand return for my small doings in the years that are gone—as you tenderly put it; your sudden question yesterday, recalled all my needs present, and fears for the future. … Be assured— This is a Godsend to me just now—trebly acceptable, and serviceable, through the true kindliness, that prompted you to send it.”

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 13 Feb. MS: NLS 528.29 inc. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We received from NewfieldJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 6 Feb., from Newfield, Ecclefechan: “Last Wednesday afternoon I came over to Newfield to see Miss Mary Currie who has been unwell for some time … there is to be a consultation of two doctors about her care tomorrow & I have agreed to stay till then & hear what they have to say.” See also TC to AC, 4 March. this day gone a week your letter just when I was on the point of answering the foregoing one that had come from you: as you were not to be home for a couple of days I forbore writing; & now there is a third from you, & this poor scrawl must answer all the three together. I am much obliged by your punctual writing & paying no regard to my impediments & procrastinations,—which I hope wont go so far in the future for some time. A very little “work” fills up all my day; & from 4 oclock when I get out to walk, or should get, there is not the least good to be had of me, the sordid operation of dining with its preliminary & subsequent sleeps & etceteras hardly ceases till 10 p.m.; after which a dull bout of reading (generally very dull authors being mostly rather stupid), for about three hours or two & a half, finishes me off for the night. I have not been worse in health latterly; indeed in spite of the severe winter & though that has given me a great deal of paltry pain & annoyance, chiefly from cold, I have felt in general health almost rather better than in the two past winters; & to this day I take a most laudable & wonderfully rapid walk to the very end of the embankment & so return freshened for the first part of my breakfast, that is for a small basin of porridge & milk—the latter part of it an egg, a cup of coffee with some bread I do not like so well, but cant yet see how to change it.

Thank heaven we have at last got Knox done—that is to say it is nearly all clean on paper, will be Mary says this very night after wh. we wrap it close up & put it to bed for certain day & between this & the 1st of March I shall have it all trimmed out better or worse ready to go to press on April fools’ day;—which I hope is not ominous, though possibly it may be! Frederick Chapman who was here yesterday is clear for publishing both the Knox & Norse Kings; but first & foremost the Norse Kings, of which the last part went off last night in the shape of final revise not quite so bad as I had been figuring it. Jean will get a copy about March first. Chapman is pressingly in hurry to get that last
revise from me that he may send it off to Yankee Land upon some wild goose plan of having the Norse Kings printed by itself as a little book there!John Forster was negotiating with Frederic Chapman about publishing “Early Kings of Norway” and “Portraits of John Knox” in book form. It was pbd. in Britain in May 1875, and by Harper & Brothers in New York in June; see Tarr 209–12. Let him do his own way; can nowther do thee ill na’ gude.Coterie speech; see 4:369TC to MAC, 20 April 1828. — Did you hear of the Haddington peoples’ project of a sublime school there by way of monument to Knox?The Scotsman reported, 11 Feb., that Haddington wished to raise a memorial to John Knox, and had set up a subscription to assist the local School Board with the renovation of Knox’s former school, currently “in a state of utter collapse—without pupils, without teachers, with buildings ruinous and almost uninhabitable.” The plan “is to take up the work of the School Board when their powers of assessment are exhausted, and to add out of the funds collected such architectural ornamentation to the school building as shall give it a memorial character. The rest of the money is to be devoted to bursaries.” The medieval grammar school was founded in 1379. I rather discouraged it hitherto; tho’ within modest limits, it might perhaps do well enough but nobody connected with that I hear of is in the least likely for managing such a thing. I engaged to give them a subscription if the matter went on at all towards completion; but by no means intend, as they would wish me to set myself up as a signal post or flagstaff in the matter. Far far different is my intention & I do not yet see clearly what to answer them, if at present I answer at all.See TC to JB, 15 Feb.

figure.p:
Knox Academy, Haddington
Courtesy of Jane Roberts

docBody.p: Froude comes to me or I go to him every second day or oftener & is much better company than usual of late, tho’ his talk hitherto is mostly about the Cape colony & its astounding capabilities & do bewilderment under its Government of mere parliamentary palaver. Ld Carnarvon & the Government seem to have completely adopted his suggestions; & he is to go back in perhaps two months or so to continue [h]is operations farther there.See TC to JF, 3 July 1874; Lord Carnarvon wanted to establish a federation of the several British and Dutch colonial settlements in South Africa. Froude hoped that an intercolonial conference could be organized to resolve the outstanding disputes among the various constituencies, but on his return to South Africa in June his plans were thwarted by English officials in the Cape, who suspected him of siding with the Boers.

Forster, whom I saw some days ago seemed to be decidedly, in spite of the bad weather, a degree stronger; but his spirits I think are generally very bad, & sink deeply on a small discouragement of relapse. Froude, too, found him better much than expectation; & calculates along with me that with this years summer & Lisbon or CintraForster’s friend Robert Lytton was ambassador at Lisbon; see TC to JAC, 11 Dec. 1874; Sintra, town about 18 mi. (29 km.) NW of Lisbon. for next winter, he may fairly getMS ends here.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JB, 15 Feb. Pbd: Wylie 287 inc. Quot: Glasgow Herald, 6 March 1875. Text from Wylie, with the first sentence from the Glasgow Herald. John Brook (ca. 1827–1910), Haddington grocer and wine-merchant, and convener of the Knox Memorial Committee.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN BROOK

docBody.p:
It is desirable that there should be a memorial to Knox, and that the county town of so wealthy a shire as Haddington should have a school.See TC to JAC, 13 Feb. … If the site of the new school was on the ground on which Knox is known to have actually walked, it would beyond all things give the building a memorial character. In regard to ‘ornamentation,’ of which there was some mention in an article in the Scotsman, the best architect to be found anywhere ought to be employed;The architect chosen was John Starforth (1822–98), English-born architect living in Edinburgh; the building was finished, 1878, and dedicated to John Knox, 1879, and called the Knox Memorial Institute. It is now in private hands, on the same street as the modern Knox Academy. For a current photograph, see 189. —a man who would keep before his eyes the fact that Knox
never in his life said or did anything untrue or insincere;—and that the Parish School, or ‘National Monument’ (or whatever name it may be called), sacred to his memory, should be scrupulously preserved from every species of meaningless and unveracious ornamentation. … The people of Haddington would do a really good work by marking, by a simple obelisk and a good oak tree,TC’s request that a tree be planted on the site of Knox’s birthplace was later honored in a ceremony in Haddington, 29 March 1881, reported in the Glasgow Evening News, 30 March 1881. the site of the house in which Knox’s fatherWilliam Knox (ca. 1486–ca. 1525), merchant in Giffordgate, Haddington. lived, which Mr. Laing, in his Preface to Knox’s Work, says is discoverable.Laing wrote: “On lately visiting the locality, the question seems to me to admit of no dispute. Giffordgate is connected with Haddington by the old stone bridge across the Tyne, and the house was nearly opposite the eastern end of the Abbey Church. The accompanying view, which forms a portion of the “Prospect of Haddington,” [1693] may be considered a correct representation. The house itself no longer exists” (The Works of John Knox, ed. David Laing [Edinburgh, 1846–64] 6:xviii). For the illustration in Laing’s Works of Knox, see above.
John Knox’s father’s house in Haddington
Courtesy of Edinburgh University Library

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 3 March. Addr: Kent House / Knightsbridge / S.W. PM: London, 4 March 1875. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I have already made enquiries about the Sumner PhotographCharles Sumner (1811–74), American politician, Republican senator from Massachusetts 1851–74; TC had met him in London in 1838; see 10:98–99TC to CSU, 12 June 1838. His connection to Lady Ashburton is unexplained. TC borrowed the image of Sumner from George Frederick Samuel Robinson (1827–1909; ODNB; see 26:48–49TC to CK, 21 March 1851), 1st marquess of Ripon; see TC to LLA, 9 March. & hopes are held out that I shall have an actual copy of it tomorrow night. At lowest I am confident that the Photograph must be discoverable here; and you may take it for granted that I will not rest, till the Article is discovered and put into your hand.

I am delighted to hear that you are recovering, almost recovered out of these persecutions of winter weather: I expect to call between 4 and 5, perhaps with Mr Froude accompanying, tomorrow (Thursday) afternoon.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-AC, 4 March. MS: MUL. Pbd: Marrs 782–85. Where parts of MS are missing the text is taken from Marrs. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO ALEXANDER CARLYLE

docBody.p: For days & weeks past, I have been thinking of writing to you; but multitudes of trifling things & some bits of serious occupation have kept me more than usually occupied. All this added to my own inability to write, and my great distaste to dictation have held me silent. Often enough, I need not say, my thoughts are occupied with you; many, many times my thoughts fly across the wide ocean; & I ask myself what you are all about in your Canadian home. At length in an hour of absolute leisure I determine to write to you expressly once again.

We heard of you many months ago as suffering from asthma, which is a most grievous complaint; we heard again that it had a good deal left you; & that you were somewhat in your usual health; which for one now verging upon eighty can never be a high figure of health! But you keep quiet, no doubt; &
do the best & wisest you can, patiently waiting for the Almighty’s time, when earthly toils & sufferings are to be exchanged for the long repose. Your Alick & others of the boys write from time to time; & I had a direct letter once from Tom;The chief correspondent with their relatives in Canada was John A. Carlyle; for the last recorded letter to TC from Alick’s son Tom, Jan. 1873, see 48:136TC to AC, 7 Jan. 1873. thank him & thank them all for being so punctually mindful of us. My own health, considering everything has been wonderfully good this winter. It has been one of the coldest winters, now & then, we have ever heard of hereabouts; especially in Scotland they have had the fiercest colds & the deepest snows ever known there;See TC to JAC, 1 Jan. & few people have escaped throat disorders, rheumatisms & the other ills that flesh is heir to,Cf. Hamlet 3.1. in these circumstances. The Dr has had bits of cold once or twice, and Sister Jean we hear is still confined to the house, though now much better & only waiting for a sunny day or two to get into the air again, & be as before.See TC to JAC, 9 Jan. You heard no doubt of poor Margaret Stewart, Mary’s eldest daughter’s sudden death;Margaret Stewart d. 27 Oct. 1874; see TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1874. which naturally has been a sorrow to us all, and to her poor Mother a crushing calamity, coming with hardly a day’s warning; but she says nothing, poor Mary; keeps struggling about, & doing her appointed task as best she can. She is I think considerably the weakest of us all now; generally lame, sometimes lame of both knees,—owing to swollen veins & rheumatism,—poor soul, and yet is the cheerfullest & most unaffectedly kind of all the kindred. Her poor daughter, whom you & I both remember so dismally well was a skilful, active, resolute & clever woman; I think one of the best workers I ever saw; she had been left suddenly by the death of her husbandThomas Stewart d. 20 April 1869; see 46:42TC to JAC, 28 April 1869. in very difficult circumstances, & not one woman in a hundred could have managed so well as she had done & was doing, when all at once the end came; and her poor bairns, farm & everything they depended upon were left again, without guide of their own any farther. Jamie her one brother has been in management ever since, assisted by advice of those about him; & is said to do creditably well in his new position.James Austin Jr. was managing the farm, Ernhirst, with his sister Marianne helping with the dairy and the children; see TC to JAC, 17 Nov. 1874. The youngest of the four poor orphans a stirring kind of boy, of rather weak health has gone to his grandmother at the Gill,John wrote, 20 Dec. 1874: “I went down & saw poor Mary at the Gill. She looked composed & resigned, & in about as good health as usual. Margaret’s youngest boy [Thomas] is with her, & has a great likeness to his mother.” to whom I doubt not he is a consolation, not a burden. They are comparatively at their ease in regard to
economics far otherwise than you & I can remember of them & indeed of the whole kindred; which undoubtedly is a great comfort for the time being; but whether much an advantage in the long run one cannot always say. Brother Jamie has his two sons now both at hand. John he lives with mostly; but has over at Newlands near Kirtlebridge, Jamie always at hand too;James Carlyle’s son John lived with his father at Scotsbrig; his son James Jr. lived at Newlands farm near Kirtlebridge, about 3 mi. (5 km.) SE of Ecclefechan, as well as sharing the tenancy of Craigenputtoch with his father; see 44:196TC to JAC, 11 May 1867. with whom he stays a good deal. Jamie (Junior) as perhaps you have heard has seen good to quit Craigenputtock; & reduce it to the condition of “led farm”;A farm managed by servants, while the farmer lives elsewhere. which to me was rather unexpected, tho’ I have said nothing about it, nor will say: the place had got into a mournful state of degradation as a residence, the woods all cut away, our poor attempts at a hedge fallen altogether scraggy & ruinous &c &c: four or five years ago I spent a week there,TC spent five days at Craigenputtoch, July 1870; see 47:45TC to JF, 22 July 1870. driven thither by the noises of the railway at Dumfries. I wandered about in all directions; could scarcely find or recognize the “grave of the last sixpence,”TC’s name for a stretch of road near Craigenputtoch that marked some failed enterprise; see 6:433, 434TC to JWC, 7 Sept. 1833, and Ralph Waldo Emerson, English Traits (Boston, 1856) 21. the old cattle-shed you built behind the hill (nothing but the ruinous heaps of it); & in my life never spent six days more sad painful & solemnly mournful to heart & soul. My resolution then was that I must never go thither again.— Jamie Senior is always in puny health; & had, as you know, a great sorrow in the death of his only daughter, not long since;Jamie’s da., Jenny, d. 1 Feb. 1874; see TC to JAC, 4 Feb. 1874. but he is reported & I saw the fact myself last summer in visibly stronger health than formerly; has a better appetite, tho’ still very feeble & pecky; & takes a strict charge of sons & their farms, which are properly his; & they all live in good agreement together. Young John of Scotsbrig is a fine intelligent fellow, but is reported to have got a rather useless Wife, who brings him quantities of children.John Carlyle and his wife, Margaret, had five children by 1875; they were to have eight more. Jamie Junior is growing a monstrous bulk; but is very active, pushing & successful in business affairs, tho’ of weakish health now & then, like his brother John. Last Autumn as perhaps you heard I went to Fife on visit to Peter Swan,Patrick Don Swan, known as Peter; see TC to JAC, 27 Aug. 1874. now Provost Swan, for a good many years past, and a very worthy hospitable useful, human creature; who was very glad to see Niece Mary & me, when we came across to him, & Brother John, the Dr, who soon after followed.See TC to JAC, 1 Sept. 1874. Probably you remember Peter, a small, pretty, black-eyed boy, your school-fellow once for a while. He
is now grown an immense tower of a man, many feet in girth about the stomach part & with three chins, an altogether mountain of a man, but still active, very opulent & held in immense respect by Kirkcaldy & neighbourhood. He lost both his brothers years ago, who were busy & successful manufacturers in the steps of their Father;Peter’s father, William Swan (d. 1833), was a prosperous yarn merchant and shipowner; his sister, Sophia (b. 1810), and three youngest brothers, David (b. 1815), Robert (b. 1817), and James (b. 1819), all d. in childhood; his other brothers, Thomas (1811–40), William (1812–59), and Alexander (1814–67), were now also dead; see 46:194TC to JAC, 13 April 1870, and L. Macbean, Patrick Don Swan, Provost of Kirkcaldy, 1841–86 (Kirkcaldy, 1893). & Peter, left alone, has inherited them all; & has nothing to do with his great wealth, but lay it out, as he assiduously does, in works of benificence & general utility all round. Our old lodging in the KirkwyndKirk Wynd, Kirkcaldy (see 1:89TC to JJ, 10 Dec. 1816), where TC lodged, across the road from the school where he taught Nov. 1816–Nov. 1818; Alick attended the school for some months and lodged with TC; see 35:227TC to AC, 7 Oct. 1859, and A. Carlyle, NL 2:202. is standing precisely as it did, but nearly all the population of the place has vanished that were alive when we two knew it. I did not go inside our old lodging house, some subaltern respectable kind of man appeared to be living in it; but I recoiled at the many memories it would have called up in me. Kirkcaldy itself has grown twice as big but chiefly by widening itself & has still the old physiognomy. Far more manufacturing industry, perhaps double or treble what it had in our time. Peter drove us about at a great rate, far & wide at least as far as St. Andrews & Queensferry,St. Andrews, about 24½ mi. (39 km.) NE of Kirkcaldy; North Queensferry, about 15 mi. (24 km.) SW of Kirkcaldy. but to me as was natural at my age, it was a sorrow rather, at least what enjoyment it offered was drowned in sorrowful memories suggested. The people seemed exceedingly good to me, so far as we had any intercourse with them, & I did with difficulty get a little bathing of which I was in quest. On the whole I dont feel as if I could go again.— The other day I had a visit from James CurrieJohn wrote, 6 Feb.: “James Currie is here from Mauritius, & intends to go back this or next month. He is a very solid & worthy man, & often speaks of you. He knows that you have too many visitors, & on that account did not call again at Cheyne Row after I left London. I have told him that he may call between two & three o’clock any day when he gets back to London, & you will probably see him for a few minutes if not otherwise engaged. The connection between his Father & ours was very intimate in old times, & here in Annandale the connection has been kept up.” (Sandy Currie’s Son) who had been home on visit from the Isle of France [Mauritius]; chiefly for the sake of his eldest Sister, who is falling into loss of memory &, I think, of health otherwise;Mary Currie (see TC to JAC, 13 Feb.); her death certificate (1876) gave the cause of death as “softening of the brain.” & whom he wished to see once again in this world. He is a clever hardy fellow of 60; of much breeding & accomplishment,See 8:6TC to JSM, [ca. 10 January 1835]. compared
with any of the Curries we used to know. His brother John, whom doubtless you also recollect has been for many years, a peaceable nonentity at Newfield,John Irving Currie; see 25:182TC to JWC, 30 Aug. 1850. living with his SistersThe sisters were Mary, Helen, and George. there, quite under their control; a tall ladder of a fellow, I think an inch or two beyond his Father; not quite a fool to speak to, nor indeed perhaps internally a fool at all, but reduced to zero by the habit of drink he had got into;—& is now kept out of by rigorous tutorage in the nearly cutting off of the cash-supply altogether. I think they give him one glass divided into two at two different hours of the day, & he goes to bed at nine o’clock at night, and eats his meals in total silence. “Poor Currie, after all” as the Dr is in the habit of saying.Coterie speech; see 1:211TC to AC, 15 Dec. 1819.

But enough of all this clatter, dear Brother; which however I think you will not altogether dislike, tho’ the interest you take in it will have its mournful side withal. I have been printing some trifling things since New Year’s day of which you shall by & by have a copy. The chief portion of them relates to Knox & his Portrait, but really the whole affair is of no moment at all, & the use of it to myself is that it satisfies my mind a little & keeps me from utter idleness, which is unsuitable for all mortals so long as the gift of life is left at all.

Here has an interruption come, dear Brother & I must close more abruptly than I counted upon doing. My faithful & loving regards are with you all, from yourself downwards. Write me soon, some of you. God’s blessing be with you, one & all, now & forever more.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 7 [6] March. MS: NLS 528.30. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Letter misdated; Forster’s dinner was Fri. 5 March, and John A. Carlyle replied Sun. 7 March.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
This is merely to let you know that things are in the old state with us here, & that nothing material has gone wrong, while the week ends. I accomplished better or worse my dinner at Forster’s yesternight; & got no great harm of it, in spite apprehensions, except indeed that I never was sound asleep last
night; but lay steadily in half sleep for 7 or 8 hours; & found that this was not much worse. Today we have copious rains of a warmish temperature, with west wind, which I hope has reached Dumfries too as it least it will in few hours. Yesterday had quite the complexion of a March day, with an aim towards March dust, tho’ the wind was steady at east & had not got round till some time deep in the night. Froude & I went up together to our dinner & the rather flarey Earl,Lord Shaftesbury; see TC to JAC, 4 April 1874. wrong warned somehow, kept us 20 minutes waiting. He is a pleasant kind of man, with many considerable good qualities, but not to me at all edifying. The two topics he most insisted on were blackguard Kenealy’sEdward Vaughan Hyde Kenealy (1819–80; ODNB), Irish barrister, recently elected M.P. for Stoke-upon-Trent. Kenealy had served as counsel for the Tichborne claimant (see 48:41TC to JAC, 24 Feb. 1872) from April 1873, and was later expelled by the professional tribunals for his violent partisanship and unprofessional conduct both during and after the trial. exordium in the House of Commons, in which the Earl’s Son played so creditable a partIn the House of Commons, 4 March, Kenealy accused Anthony Evelyn Melbourne Ashley (1836–1907), Lord Shaftesbury’s son, barrister, and M.P. for Poole, of having breached parliamentary privilege by stating in a recent speech that Kenealy was morally unfit to serve as a Member of Parliament. Ashley argued that his speech did not constitute slander: “I own that I said these words hastily, and not without a certain underlying feeling and conviction that it is necessary in these days to speak out the truth now and then, even at the risk of encountering annoyance and trouble afterwards. … I can only state in that what I did say I spoke … from a keen sense and jealousy of the dignity of the House” (Hansard 222 [Feb. 1875–March 1875]: 1188). in the Earl’s own hearing; & secondly the advent of Moody & Sankey, with their fine spiritual revivals (& also Harmoniums)Dwight Lynam Moody (1837–99), preacher, and Ira David Sankey (1840–1903), gospel singer and composer, were American evangelicals, who toured Britain 1873–75, attracting large audiences. The Morning Post reported, 10 March: “The two American ‘revivalists,’ Messrs. D. L. Moody and Ira D. Sankey, who have obtained considerable celebrity in Ireland, and more recently in the north of England, appeared last night (for the first time) at the Agricultural Hall, Islington. Their London campaign has opened very successfully. … The whole work of preaching … is done by Mr. Moody, while Mr. Sankey sings and leads the choir and people, accompanying himself and them on a harmonium.” Shaftesbury was himself an evangelical Christian. For a cartoon of Moody and Sankey from a Glasgow newspaper, preaching and playing the harmonium, see opp. which were to kindle a flame of spiritual heat, much desiderated in England, sinking fast into muddy democracy, sansculottism & black Atheism for the time being. The harmoniums by the by he entirely denied when I suggested them, but without altering my belief in the matter.
Moody and Sankey Cartoon, 1874
© CSG CIC Glasgow Museums and Libraries Collection:
The Mitchell Library, Special Collections
Poor Forster was violently coughing when Froude & I came; but girt himself up into factitious shine & the stretch of hospitality, which to me had a distressing element in it. On the whole I hope it will be long before another dinner of the kind becomes imperative upon me. One thing we spoke about, that is Forster, the Earl & I did,
of a practical nature the investment of monies in these dwellings for the poor, which the Earl is busy with.Shaftesbury was the patron or president of many philanthropic organisations, including the Artizans, Labourers & General Dwellings Company, a philanthropic property company in which TC was already invested: see TC to JAC, 21 March 1874. Forster with emphasis, & he with some quiet assent, represented them as perfectly secure & of good or fair profit as to interest; Forster offering, with joy, to do the needful for me in investing. I have also heard for a good many months past indirectly from neighbour Laisné who is a stock-broker of credit, that the Russian Loan yielding good interest is an excellent investment;Mary Aitken later reported: “In June 1875, my uncle Thomas Carlyle bought seven £1000 1873 5% Russian Bonds from our next door-neighbour, Mr. Laisné, a stockbroker. On the 30th of June, 1875, these bonds were delivered to him, and as I sat writing in the dining-room at Cheyne Row after breakfast my uncle altogether unexpectedly brought me one of these bonds and gave it to me as a present” (Alexander Carlyle and Sir James Crichton-Browne, The Nemesis of Froude [1903]: 143–44). For Laisné and his sisters, see TC to JAC, 8 Jan. 1874. into which he has transferred a good portion of his Sisters’ income. I have long been tired of these £5 or 6,000 lying idle in the
drawer here; & I do think of putting some of them out in one or both of these ways but probably shall not do it till you come. Certainly at least not till you write to me on the subject a word or two.John A. Carlyle wrote, 7 March: “I do not know how it is, but I no longer have any zeal for new investments … more especially foreign investments. … I have got a great many copies of the proposed Russian loan at 5 per cent … & dont see my way to taking any part in them.” He continued: “As to the proposed investment of money for the dwellings of the poor which Shaftesbury & Forster approve of, I should be ready to make some investment beyond what we have already made. You & I have only £300 each in it; & it seems to be well managed so far as I am able to judge. The dividends have been six per cent hitherto, & if you wish to have more shares I could at once apply for them.” — Poor Mrs Forster has been very poorly, confined to her room for a month past. We did not see her yesternight at all. Forster himself works daily I believe at some kind of edition of SwiftForster, The Life of Jonathan Swift; see TC to JAC, 11 April 1874. & is clearly a good deal better, though still very far from well.

The Knox proofs are now daily expected; in the course of next week, I do expect to have that dreary business fairly off my hands. Chapman insists on making the Norse Kings & it, into “a handsome little volume” indeed has sent the former piece off to his American CorrespondentSee TC to JAC, 13 Feb. to start with it there forthwith in assurance of getting the Knox before he can be complete. As RobsonCharles Robson, TC’s printer. is to print here I should have no trouble with the matter; & indeed will let it go ahead, with indifference nearly complete, in the way proposed. Chapman too is about to print I know not how many copies of the Library Edition for his American agent; there was an unintelligible entry in his last a/c with me; wh., on being submitted to Forster, Chapman being immediately summoned, was discovered to be a mistake on Chapmans part;Forster wrote, 9 March: “If you could manage to call tomorrow afternoon I should be glad—having now cleared up the Chapman affair, and having a statement to show you.” & has ended in this triumphant result, worth to me I know not how many hundreds of pounds,—were these, alas, of almost any worth to me at this time of day!

Here has Miss BromleyCaroline Davenport Bromley. suddenly come in, after many weeks of complete absence; & I must abruptly end. I saw James Currie the day before he went. Froude & I called at his private hotel in the St James’s region & sat a good while with him. Froude he had before met when here Currie is a clever looking, handy & accomplished man. He seemed to be very grateful to you in respect to your kindness to his poor Sister.John wrote, 7 March: “I had heard from James Currie that you & Froude had called & seen him. … He had been much gratified by the talk he had with you at Cheyne Row. … His brother John & sister Georgie were here last Friday & staid for dinner. They reported their sister Mary considerably better that when I last saw her.” For his visit to Mary at Newfield, see TC to JAC, 13 Feb. Send me word punctually to tell
me how Jean is; & say I do design to write to her so soon as I have done the proof of Knox.

closer.salute: Love & blessings on you all. Ever your affectionate Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 9 March. Addr: Kent House / Knightsbridge / S.W. PM: London, 9 March 1875. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I send this one word to ask you if you will kindly warn your Photographer to return to me Lord Ripon’s Copy of SumnerSee TC to LLA, 3 March. by tonights post; so that I may keep my promise to Lord Ripon’s servant & not lead the poor man into trouble.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 14 [15] March. MS: NLS 528.31. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Letter misdated; Lady Derby visits Tues. 16 March.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your welcome letter came on Saturday. Many thanks to you for it. I could not well write that day being over head & ears in the correction of the Knox proof, which had itself been belated. It was not got ready till yesterday afternoon, but then, we hope, was reduced to completeness. The prints had not been introduced, but were lying ready (rather dim blotchy-looking prints) & will be duly introduced into their places, & give us no trouble at all except reading a final proof merely with the eye, as we hope. There is a phrase in Laing’s Knox i. 146, Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, which I wanted to consult you on, not myself seeing the force of it, or applicability on the occasion. Nor is it necessary that I should; only I want your explanation. Were the Bishop’s Crozier men in the habit of flinging money to the poor, on occasion of such procession & of using those words? or what meaning, if any, lies in them?Knox describes a skirmish, ca. 1545, between Gavin Dunbar (ca. 1490–1547; ODNB), archbishop of Glasgow, whom Knox labels “the glorious foole,” and Cardinal David Beaton (ca. 1494–1546; ODNB), archbishop of St. Andrews, whom Knox calls “the proude cardinall,” as to who should take precedence at Glasgow Kirk, resulting in them beating each other with their croziers. John A. Carlyle replied, 17 March: “That phrase … is from the CXI psalm of the Vulgate which I copy, as you may not have the Vulgate at hand. Dispersit, dedit pauperibus: justitia ejus manet in seculum seculi: cornu ejus exaltabitur in gloria [He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name (cf. Ps. 111.9)]. … My own idea is that Knox uses the words to indicate what a contemptible employment of scripture might be made in the case he speaks of.”
The Knox Article is of feeble character throughout & bad rather than good; but it is felt as a blessing by me to have my hands completely washed of it & to have done with it forever & a day. It was a kind of small pious service to the memory of Knox & all the miserable botheration I have had with it first & last shall be abolished out of my mind. My profane little Mary who also has suffered much, has been repeating “KNOX is geendet, Freude den Sterblichen!”“Knox is finished, Joy to the Mortals!” Cf. “Christ is arisen! / Joy to the mortal” (Goethe, Faust pt.1 lines 737–38). Chapman purposes within a few weeks to have ready a neat little vol. of the Norse Kings & it: I will then send a copy to each of the kindred; of the Norse Kings there is at present, no copy in my hands that does not want part I. Wait awee;—and so enough of all that.

Our weather is getting to be very tolerable; sometimes even nice & cheery,—as today for instance, though the wind is still gently to the eastward. Furthermore people are busy new papering your room, thoroughly cleaning it out. Mrs WarrenSarah Warren, TC’s housekeeper. also seems nearly on foot again (never ailed anything but a rheumatic knee): so that all now is ready when you like to give signal. I can say farther that the embankment is except in furiously east winds by far the best morning promenade I ever had; & has really been a benefit to me instead of a bother & impediment, which I long reckoned it would merely prove.

Forster continues working at his Swift; & is evidently considerably better, though his poor wife I fear is still a prisoner, being very weak about the throat & lungs. Froude has had unexpectedly an offer from the Whipper-in of the LiberalsWilliam Patrick Adam (1823–81; ODNB), politician, M.P. for Clackmannan and Kinross 1859–80, chief whip of the Liberal Party 1874–80. to become M.P. for the Glasgow & Aberdeen Universities;—this of course is a dead secret; but I think the issue will be that he will have nothing to do with the offer; & will persist in his Colonial operations.TC was right; Froude wrote to Lady Derby, 3 April: “[T]he Liberal Whip (Mr. Adam) asked me to stand for the Glasgow and Aberdeen Universities on very easy terms to myself. I declined, because I should have had to commit myself to the Liberal party, which I did not choose to do. … I was neither Conservative nor Liberal per se, but would not oppose Mr. D’Israeli. … I am too old to begin Parliamentary life, and infinitely prefer making myself of use to the Conservative side in some other way. … I am at Lord Carnarvon’s service if he wishes me to go on with his Colonial affairs” (Herbert Paul, The Life of Froude [1905] 277–78). See TC to JF, 3 July 1874. He was here
on Saturday & seemed to be gradually settling towards that fixed resolution which to me also seemed the advisable one. I hear nothing of Duffy all this while; & suppose he is still Aix-le-Bain, preparing to get his family across from the Antipodes & settle here in London.Duffy spent Sept. 1874 in Aix-les-Bains, spa town in Savoie; see TC to JAC, 3 Aug. and 4 Aug. 1874; he spent the winter in France, and the summer of 1875 between England and Ireland; TC does not mention seeing him. Duffy returned to France for the winter and from there returned to Australia, Jan. 1876; see Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, My Life in Two Hemispheres (1898) 2:347–69. He did not return to Europe for good until 1880. Taliter qualiter [one way or another]. He is by no means a bad fellow, nor without good intellect; though still with a tincture of O’ConnelismDaniel O’Connell (1775–1847; ODNB), Irish nationalist leader; Duffy attended the O’Connell centenary celebrations in Dublin, Aug. 1875. & Irish blarney which he will never get quit of.

The Princess Imperial of PrussiaCrown Princess Victoria, wife of Frederick William, crown prince of Germany; see TC to JAF, 13 July. TC had been invited to meet her, 16 July 1874, by Lady Augusta Stanley. has sent, through Dean Stanley, a request to have from me a list of the books I used in the History of Friedich [sic],—I cannot well see on what ground, since all the books I used are mentioned in the Friedrich itself: however in obedience to an order from such a quarter, I have set Mary to make out a list of what she can find in the Fried. section of the Harvard Catalogue, which is so well-known to you too;TC had arranged for the books he used when writing Frederick and Cromwell to be bequeathed to Harvard College at his death, and had sent John a list of these books so he could oversee the bequest; see 48:153TC to WILL, 6 Feb. 1873. See also 46:163–64TC to CEN, 2 March 1870, and 174TC to JAC, 19 March 1870. this she will speedily finish; & so end that poor problem also. Tomorrow at home Lady Derby announces herself. This is all the news great or small that I have.— —
I am truly gratified to hear that Jean is out again; & Annie too rid of her cold. Tell Jean I still remember my debt. I wrote a long letter to poor Alick several days ago. I send you all my kindest love I am & remain ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-WEF, 30 March. MS: Strouse. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. For W. E. Forster, see TC to JAF, 18 July 1874.
bibl.head: TC TO W. E. FORSTER

docBody.p: Mrs Frankau, widowed Sister of our good old friend Neuberg,Rosetta Frankau was the widowed sister of TC’s friend Joseph Neuberg. Both Neuberg and Forster had been partners in textile factories in the midlands in the 1840s, and both were active in social reform particularly around education for the working classes. Possibly these papers had some connection with this; otherwise unidentified. wishes you, for his sake, to look over these bits of Papers & consider if there is anything you can do to forward the object they aim at.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 1 April. Addr: Sandy Hill / Cambridge / Massachusetts. Via Cork. PM: 1 April 1875. MS: Houghton. Quot: Norton’s Letters 2:49; Kaplan 517. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p: Several weeks ago without delay on the postman’s part, I received your Letter wh. was very welcome after so long a silence.Norton wrote 21 Jan. I hope you have now got mainly done with your University enterpriseNorton had written, 7 May 1874, that he had undertaken for the University, “to take a class of elder students to instruct in the history of the Fine Arts and their relations to Literature.” and that we shall hear oftener from you while time yet is. My Niece Mary regrets in the meanwhile to bid me say for her that the letter you promised to post “next day” to her address never yet cameNorton wrote, 21 Jan., saying how pleased he was to get a letter from Mary Aitken and saying: “I will not trouble you with my thanks to her for her good deed. I shall offer them to her directly,—if not tonight, then tomorrow.” and that if there were any order or request for her in it, it is not she but the anterior parties that must be blamed.

I should myself at once have attended to your Whistler etching;Norton wrote that he had heard that Whistler had painted a portrait of TC, and that he had written to Whistler “to ask him to make for me, with your consent, an etching from the portrait,—the plate to be altogether private and only fifty impressions to be taken from it.” James Abbott McNeill Whistler (1834–1903; ODNB), “Arrangement in Grey and Black, No. 2: Portrait of Thomas Carlyle”; see 48:215TC to JAF, 30 July 1873. but that
this also was not feasible. Whistler has vanished from my eyes & from every body’s that I hear of for a long while, labouring or lounging somewhere about Liverpool in some Armidas Castle there,Armida was a sorceress in Torquato Tasso’s epic poem Jerusalem Delivered (1581), who created an enchanted garden in which to keep prisoner a Christian knight. Whistler was actually staying at Speke Hall, near Liverpool, painting family portraits for Frederick Richards Leyland (1832–92; ODNB), ship-owner and art collector. who knows? Besides which the full-length Portrait you had put your hopes in seemed to me little other than a fatuity; was considered to be unfinished after many weary sittings, and to be a Portrait not of my poor features, but of the clothes I had on; which & not the face seemed to occupy the strenuous attention & vigorous activity of my singular Artist all the while. He made a solemn enough “Exhibition” of this & other paintings and etchings;Whistler exhibited at the Flemish Gallery, Pall Mall, June 1874. The York Herald reviewer commented, 9 June 1874: “The principal works in the Exhibition are seven life-sized portraits, of which the first to attract attention is the recently-executed portrait of Thomas Carlyle, who is represented seated on a wicker-bottomed chair, dressed in black, and a brown cloak or shawl thrown over his knees, on the top of which rests his black wide-awake hat, his right hand leaning on a staff. … The exhibition comprises about fifty splendid specimens of Mr. Whistler’s universally admired etchings and dry point engravings.” of all which the etchings only seemed to me to have any real excellence. Aus dem wird Nichts [They will amount to nothing], I am afraid. A Sculptor friend of his, a man of real eminence & excellence by any judgement I can form, a Mr Boehm, fast rising to be be our first man here has done a life-size statue of me; which I hear people of good skill praising; but do not myself know much about: he has just sent it to the R. A. ExhibitionFor Boehm’s statue of TC, see TC to JAC, 9 Jan.; it was exhibited at The Royal Academy 1875 Summer Exhibition, 3 May–2 Aug. from which as soon as it is free, I will get you a photograph taken, which may be a fair surrogate for any thing we could have got of Whistler.

For a long time back with miscellaneous and multifarious enquiries about the Portrait of Knox of which you had a copy from me above a year ago the finale was a very poor Paper upon this subject and upon Knox’s history in this world which appeared in this month’s Fraser. The Paper is worth little or nothing; but gave me infinite trouble and months of irritating jumble and bother in my present handless condition, instead of being finished in days had I possessed writing hands, as I don’t any longer.TC had been suffering from an increasingly shaky right hand since 1866; see 43:195TC to JAC, 16 April 1866, and TC to JAC, 5 Nov. 1873. It was a small act of piety to the memory of the noblest Scotsman I know of; and has cleared my conscience of a small obligation at least. It as well as another straggle of a thing called “Early Kings of Norway,” done a couple of years ago in sheer horror of idleness, three
bits of Papers easily enough read & with little or no other merit, all this was snatched up by Allingham who has succeeded Froude in the Fraser editorship; & wished to proclaim himself at the opening of the year; whence very unexpectedly has come my reappearance in public print. Publisher Chapman has decided to print the whole matter with all dispatch & send it out as a small vol; I believe it is coming out simultaneously in Philadelphia;The Philadelphia distributors of TC’s works were J. B. Lippincott & Co.; see MAI to UC, 14 Jan. 1874; for the first U.S. edn., see TC to JAC, 13 Feb. but you shall have a copy from the fountainhead, if you will accept it,—probably in the course of next month. There is another agitation about a monument to Knox,—a grand School in his native townSee TC to JAC, 13 Feb. this time on the very spot where Knox got his education,—but this too I suppose will come to nothing and I strictly refuse to take any hand in it except a subscription if it do go on.

We have had an unusually frosty winter; but I to my own surprise got no real damage from it; strong in the dally promenade which I execute the first thing on a really beautiful bit of public work called the Chelsea embankment,See TC to JRU, 13 May 1874. wh. has been a real Godsend to me, as perhaps I mentioned to you already.

My bits of reading have been miscellaneous & insignificant. I could still be happy over a good book; but, alas, good books are like angels’ visits. I will say nothing more about them to you just now. On the whole though sensibly growing weaker year by year & almost month by month, I am still, in what ought to be called good health for a man in his 80th year. Nor does the continual gaze into the dark Beyond which is daily coming nearer & daily becomes more earnest & intense give me pain; but rather becomes less painful, piously desirable & full at once of a kind of blessed sorrow & a love that nothing earthly can abolish. It is strange it is high & great, Allah Akbar; Allah kereem [God is most Good; God is most generous]!— I will add no more today; only my blessing to your little Sally, who may be sure she is justified by the laws of reciprocity in loving me as well as she can.Norton’s eldest da.; see see TC-CEN, 3 Nov. 1873. Norton wrote: “Sally (who is as sweet & as happy as I could wish, says, ‘Papa do you think I might send Mr Carlyle my very best love?’” I send my blessings were they good for anything, to you & yours. I remain ever dear Norton,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-EEF, 2 April. MS copy in Edith Forbes handwriting: NLS 528.32. Hitherto unpbd. Edith Emerson Forbes, da. of Ralph Waldo Emerson, whom TC met in London April 1872; see 48:51TC to JAC, 20 April 1872.
bibl.head: TC TO EDITH EMERSON FORBES

docBody.p: It is some days since I received your letter; the request contained in which was from the first moment granted;Edith Forbes wrote, 27 Feb. “I am going to ask a great favour of you, because you were so very kind to me when I was in London. … You must know that Father writes very few letters, and his children save carefully every one that comes to their hands. … We know that you are the only person with whom he has corresponded with equal regularity, and therefore believe you possess a greater number of his letters which have been written in the last forty years than anyone else. Now if you have saved them, I wish to ask if you are willing to bequeath those letters to his children—or if not the letters, might we be allowed to have copies of such as you will trust to us.” and only the consideration how that fact should be put on record, in my now want of useful hands, occasioned any delay. This morning the great fact has been accomplished, the record of it reposited in its due place; and you are now to consider that your Father’s letters are to be punctually transmitted to you as soon as my Executor have done with what little they may want with them.

A certain number of these letters, chiefly or altogether of later date, lie in a bundle accessible to me; but ever since the year 1833, he has been in the habit of writing to me, greatly to my comfort and profit, and I certainly never destroyed with my will any scrap of paper his hand had been on.

There is a strict search and examination to be gone into for these letters; and as above said, they are wholly to belong to you. Except therefore some little delay, that may occur after I am gone in finding and examining (for their own behoof on the part of my representatives) your Father’s letters to me, all of them now anywhere in my possession are as good as yours.
docBody.closer: Signed T. CarlyleEdith Forbes concluded: “Your gracious picture with my Ralph is a treasure I am always thanking you for.” For the picture of her son Ralph with TC, see 48:55TC to JAC, 27 April 1872, and frontispiece (found in the CLO on the table of contents page for volume 48 ).

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 9 April. Addr: Seaforth Lodge / Seaton / Axminster / South Devon. PM: 9 April 1875. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I am getting to be very much in need of some news from you. Three lines of a precise nature would be a real favour to me. Bonnie MaryMary Florence Baring, Lady Ashburton’s da. never came to the Dentist,Unidentified further. at least never to me; and the only tidings I have heard were from Miss Bromley about a week ago; and were rather of a troublesome complexion, that you had been under visitation of cold again, and perhaps were not yet quit of that bad visitor. I learned from Forster also that you had found your great and good dog again; which I am sure would be a real pleasure to you; and to the excellent quadruped himself a most joyful miracle. Mary, it appeared by the news last week, had not then been with her dentist, nor perhaps has yet; so that there is still a chance for me: but a written word would of course be very welcome whether or not.

Our weather has been generally of very grey complexion hardly twice a week a gleam of sunshine and no sunny day; but the temperature in general mild; & the buds getting visibly green, tho’ not anywhere that I have seen pushed into leaves. I had caught a cold before you went; but it seemed & indeed was of no depth or importance though it has kept me slightly below par ever since; and in fact I have been and am extremely weak contemptible and idle. My one attempt at work has been a languid tedious correcting of proofsheets (for the poor little Book you heard of, Knox & the Norse Kings which you will see, were May here); except this and idle reading I have been wholly occupied with what may be called nothing at all; being in reality mere inarticulate musings and dreamings, mostly but not quite always sad as well as useless.— Forster is evidently a good deal better, though slow to believe it; he is very busy too with a new BookForster was working on his Life of Jonathan Swift; see TC to JAC, 7 [6] March. and works at it all day; which is a blessed thing for him, amid whatever troubles.
Write me a word dear Lady, & I will not here add another Yours ever truly,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JH [JCHA], 12 April. Pbd: Copeland 248–50.
bibl.head: TC TO JANET HANNING

docBody.p: It is a long time since I have heard direct from you; and a good deal longer since I wrote myself. But we see all your letters to the Dr.,John A. Carlyle corresponded regularly with family members; see TC to AC, 4 March. John wrote, 1 April: “The enclosed letters from Hamilton have come tonight, & I think you may take some interest in the details of them & so forward them at once.” yours and your children’s; and I hope and indeed even know, that you never doubt of my brotherly remembrance and affectionate thoughts of you all. Silent my thoughts are obliged mostly to be, for my hand this long while back is quite useless for writing and indeed even by dictation I never do write except on absolute compulsion. This time I send you a small practical memorialTC’s checkbook recorded: “3 April 1875 / Mrs Hanning / Hamilton, C.W. / £50 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). of which you will see the nature from Adamson the Banker’sSamuel Adamson of the British Linen Bank, Dumfries. little note enclosed; which I hope you will have no difficulty in negotiating and turning into dollars. Pray accept it kindly, and lay it out in buying yourself any little thing you find useful or agreeable to you,—or lay it by if you like better, added to any little pose of your own against a rainy day. Do not trouble yourself with writing any answer; merely send me an old newspaper, addressed in your own hand with three strokes,The Carlyles sent newspapers (free of charge) marked to indicate all was well. which will be taken as a sure sign that you have got it all right.

I have grown very old (now getting fast forward with my 80th year) and am very weak and useless, as is natural; but by blessing from above, still wonderfully keep my health, what health I could expect to have; and have suffered little or nothing by the late severe winter, which also I find has been so severe with you. Take care of yourself in the bitter cold when it comes again; and above all provide yourself with effectual warm clothing. I read with interest your daughter Mary’s letter: and was glad after all that you had been so kind as to go to Bield on report of Billy Bobby,Billy Bob (George) Carruthers (b. 1805), originally from Haregills, farm about 4 mi. (6.5 km.) N of Ecclefechan, now living in Toronto; he had visited Jean Aitken and family in Dumfries in April 1871; see 47:192–94TC to JCA, 17 April 1871. Apparently on his return to Canada he had visited Alick and family at Bield, with whom he had been friendly ever since they moved to Canada. tho’ the reception there was not quite of the kind one could have wished. Alas, alas! Perversity is born with us all, and comes out in little touches, where we least expected it. The one remedy
is to crush it down each of us for himself, and in respect of others to forgive and forget. Our spring here is very tardy; the weather still damp, chill and disagreeable. I hope it may be much brighter with you, thanks to your deep, clear skies; not drowned in mist like ours, and that it may be shining summer when this arrives. This morning we had a letter from the Dr. who reports all the kindred well. He proposes to come up hither about the end of the month;John wrote, 11 April: “I think of moving to Chelsea to see you again about the end of this month, if all goes well till then.” he has been much more quiescent this season than I have often known him; but is about to move at last. God bless you always, dear Jenny, you and yours.

closer.salute: I am and remain / Ever your affectionate Brother

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 15 April. Addr: Seaforth Lodge / Seton / S. Devon. PM: London, 15 April 1875. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Except the kind and welcome little Note you sent me directly on your arrival at Seaforth I received no “long letter,” nor any letter at all till the last you were so good as send me two or three days ago.Lady Ashburton’s letter untraced. I am much gratified to learn that your cold is in abeyance; and that all things go well with you and yours in the fine clear sea-breezes of that wholesome Devonshire coast. Alas, I myself must not think of coming to join you at present in that cheery little Paradise: I have absolutely quiet sleep here, which is pretty much the one blessing I cannot now anywhere attain except here in my old customary den. I am weaker than usual too; and the paltry cold which I spoke of has not yet entirely gone. Happily my poor printing labours which were paltry botherations rather are now at an end; and I am now gathering myself for a fit of reading which, if good books were attainable would be the eligiblest kind of “rest” anyhow attainable. Truth is I am altogether useless for anything that can be called work in this world except that of adjusting myself to what is the end of all work & must lie now near at hand.

Poor Froude has a new sorrow as he thinks, now imminent. His poor Daughter RoseFroude’s da. Rose Mary had been ill for some time; see TC to JAC, 17 April 1874; she d. in Torquay, probably early May. has been for years, as you know, in a sad state of lungs; but
for the last good while has seemed out of immediate danger, principally subsisting by the great quantity of sleep she had: sleep has latterly has almost altogether left her & the DrUnidentified further. despairs. Yesterday Froude went off to Torquay where she is; and seemed to anticipate that in a few days all would be over. He was very quiet about it to me, but evidently felt deeply as was natural.

Forster I have not seen since you last heard from me; but am intending to call today & confidently hope notwithstanding the perpetual cold & fog we live in here to find that he is still holding out & having a bit of driving or even walking almost daily.

MaryMary Florence, Lady Ashburton’s da. is not to disappoint me this time; tell her she absolutely must not. At any rate, add that I have (as announced already) a pleasant bit of trifling reading in store for her with the earliest days of May, which surely will carry something of sunshine with them to our benighted element. Did you see Dean Stanley’s Lecture at St. Andrews & ditto at Dundee?Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, dean of Westminster, delivered two speeches in Scotland, firstly his rectorial address at St. Andrews University, 31 March, “Greatness in Institutions, Men, Books, Ideas, and Actions”; and then “The Mutual Relations of Theology, Science, and Literature” to the Dundee University Club, 2 April. The Scotsman printed both speeches, announcing, 1 April: “The installation of Dean Stanley as Rector of St. Andrews University took place yesterday, when the Very Rev. Dean delivered an address, in which he impressed upon the students the duties incumbent on the inheritors of a noble past. Great men in their lives and in their writings were pointed to as an all-important means of culture, and all were exhorted to cultivate that habit of mind which in religion as in other matters seeks to lay hold on essentials, and give no more than their due significance to secondary details.” The Scotsman, 3 April, printed the Dundee speech, in which Stanley said he had chosen to concentrate on Calvin, Galileo, and Shakespeare: “It is my intention to speak of these great men as the representatives of theology, science, and literature, but chiefly with the view of showing the relation in which all the three stand to the religious and moral advancement of mankind, which is the one bond that unites together these three great branches of thought.” very pleasant syllubub, sweet & soft to the tongue; but carrying I fear not very much nourishment to the more interior parts of the constitution. Good be always with you, dear Lady, & commend me in your kindliest way to Marigold; & tell her to shew face again the soonest possible.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 17 April. MS: NLS 528.33. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your second Letter came today at noon, just at the time I had determined to redeem my promise of this day gone a week and write again in completion of the poor little Note that was then choked in the birth.

Except the favourable change of weather in the last two days, during which the sun has restored his visits and the wind oftenest easterly with us is mostly fallen away altogether I have nothing happily either of bad news or of good to send you; only the old assurance that things go on in their usual course; and that if it were true, as Montesquieu phrases it, “happy the nations that have no history”TC attributes the aphorism to Charles-Louis de Secondat (1689–1755), Baron de La Brede et de Montesquieu, French political philosopher; see Frederick, Carlyle, Works 16:196. in regard to men as it is to nations we here are in that happy state. Your room I am assured will be this day to the last item finished,—bed rearranged curtains new-dyed walls new-papered, everything clean and in order; so that whatever day you announce we shall be ready to receive you & welcome the sight of you once more in this world. I still fancy our spring must be more advanced than yours, tho’ your description rather contradicts me. Nothing is yet here in leaf except the lilacs and nothing in flower but certain foreign trees called Almonds,John A. Carlyle wrote, 16 April: “We have very temperate weather here just now, with wind mostly from South or west, & every thing in fields & gardens is growing rapidly.” Almond trees blossom in early spring, but need a warmer climate to produce fruit. which show their blossoms first of all but on no occasion bear any fruit. No doubt however the summer is at hand; and possibly we may have enough of it too and to spare. Poor old worn-out creatures like me are in the case of that peccant soldier, under the lash of that Irish drummer, whose exclamation you know: “Oh, the devil, Burnet there’s no plasing of you, strike where one will!”Coterie speech; Mary wrote “Burnet” instead of “burn it”; see 12:347TC to JOST, 7 Dec. 1840.

I have been reading, with much skipping, my poor fluff of a French book; concerning which you had the little letter sent you:Book and letter both unidentified further. he proves to his country men, with endless petitions that their one way towards human liberty, perfect freedom of creed & the abolition of Capital Punishment is That they should all become orthodox Huguenots & do as the Dutch, the English & above all things the superlatively glorious Americans have done. Interspersed are
critical remarks, some of which at least of the French part of which, are humanly legible, though seldom or never attractive; those of other nations, especially English & Yankee have seldom almost any value whatever, except always the good intentions of the worthy man. I will not send you his thick book, judging clearly that you would not read it; a considerably better book I had finished just before; one Pattison, an Oxford Don’s Life of Casaubon,Mark Pattison (1813–84; ODNB), scholar, rector of Lincoln College, Oxford, 1861–84, Isaac Casaubon, 1559–1614 (1875); Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614; ODNB), classical scholar and ecclesiastical historian. the same kind of thing as Irving’s Life of Buchanan,For Irving’s Life of Buchanan, see TC to RHO, 12 July 1874. but done infinitely better & really elucidative, illustrative & worth reading at this day. You will see it, I hope, when you get hither, though the copy is Allingham’s, not mine.

Froude was called away early in the week to Torquay on a mournful errand, what seems to be the last illness of his second daughter who has been consumptive this long time & hanging between swift death and a painfully lingering life; but who has now suddenly lost her 12 hours daily of dull sleep; lies awake altogether & is judged by those about her to be hastening to the inevitable end. Poor little girl I am very sorry to think of her & of her Father, and what are the grim arrangements of life & of death for some of us! F. expected to be back in about 10 days; but of course could set no time, and I have yet heard nothing from him since he went. His idea at present is that he will soon be sent back to the Cape of Good Hope where great & difficult new arrangements are on the anvil,—very difficult but not less necessary. Lord Carnarveon, he seems to think, is the one Minister that has any serious resolution at present of trying to do some good; he reports from Lord C. that the great obstructive to all action is the Lord Derby,Lord Derby was foreign secretary 1874–78. who has the clearest insight of any; and discerns clearly both the necessity of improvement and also its difficulty,—&, weighing one against the other does nothing & will consent only to stand stock still.

The enclosed letter I had from poor MotleyJohn Lothrop Motley; TC had last met him at a reception in July 1874 for Crown Princess Victoria and Crown Prince Frederick William of Germany; see TC to JAF, 18 July 1874. this morning the first I ever had from him, & indeed I think we only had two dialogues; both of which within the last twelve month. I found he had very considerably more credit than I had given him credit for & was an honest ingenious & discerning man, though probably with various crotchets, maintained in a very vehement manner. Poor fellow he has lost his WifeMotley’s wife, Mary Elizabeth, d. 31 Dec. 1874. some months ago; was already in some kind of half-paralytic affection or menace of such; & is now as you will
perceive in a most mournful condition. I have been surprised at the tone of his letter,TC had apparently called at Motley’s house in London, as Motley wrote, 16 April: “[H]ow much I regret the loss of your visit & how deeply touched I was that you took the trouble to make it. It has pleased God to try me with the severest affliction that could befal me & I am sure that you came to me in kindness knowing of my misery.” He went on to say that reading TC’s essays had been a great comfort to him at this time. & wish there were again a chance of seeing more of him than I have ever yet done. Please return me his letter. The French Newspaper came this morning, quite mysterious to Mary’s sharp eyesight; & it was myself that discovered the Article on Aulan;Word hard to read, possibly Aulan, either Etienne, marquis d’Aulan (1804–78), or an area in SE France; or possibly Dulau (London bookseller of foreign books; see 28:18TC to CAH, 23 Jan. 1853); article and newspaper not further identified. that you need not return End of paper peremptorily warns me to have done.
I send my kindest love to Jean and to all. May good be with you now & always,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JLM [JLMO], 19 April. Pbd: J. L. Motley, The Correspondence of John Lothrop Motley, ed. G. W. Curtis (1889) 2:384–85.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN LOTHROP MOTLEY

docBody.p: Your letter of Saturday last touches me to the very heart; not for many years have I had any word addressed to me which stirs up so many deep and tender feelings. Alas! I know too well what depths of suffering you are struggling with; how dark and solitary is all the universe to you—suddenly eclipsed in this manner; and how vain is all human sympathy, how impossible all human help.Motley had written, 16 April, about the grief of losing his wife, continuing: “You who have likewise suffered the greatest of pangs will I think pardon my speaking to you with an intimacy which the measure of my personal acquaintance does not justify.” Courage, courage, nevertheless! Time and pious patience do bring relief by slow degrees. Oblivion can never come, should never come; but the piercing vehemency of these feelings will at length subside into composure, and only a voice of love, infinitely mournful, yet infinitely beautiful, be the requiem of those we have lost for this world. Immortality itself, with all its infinitudes of splendour, if there were to be no meeting again, would be worth nothing or even less to us. As Goethe says, “Wir heissen euch hoffen [We bid you hope].”See Goethe, “Symbolum” (1815), Werke (Stuttgart, 1828–33): 3:69–70; TC translates the line as “Work, and despair not,” in Past and Present 135.

It is a real regret to me that you are not to be in London “in a week or two,” that there is no chance of my seeing you for the present; I feel for my own behoof, too, as if there were no man with whom I might have so much of genial, profitable, and cordial discourse as even with yourself, when bodily illness permitted you. I was too procrastinative and inert while you were still in my neighbourhood; but it is a fixed purpose that should a new possibility be offered, I will make a far more effectual use of it. God bless you, help you, and be with you always.
Believe me ever, if it be the least comfort to you,

closer.salute: Yours, with deep sympathy, affection, and respect,
closer.note: Motley wrote, 14 May: “Let me … say a single word of earnest thanks for your most kind & affectionate letter. Every word of it sank deep into my heart & remains there. I have read the letter many times & each time it has done me good, & created deep but not unhealthy emotion.”

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 24 April. MS: NLS 528.34. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your Letter of today did not come till between 12 & 1 oclock; so that I am very punctual & prompt this time, tho’ except the usual bulletin of assurance that all is in statu quo (what a blessing of heaven given only to few, we have had in that particular!) I have nothing to say that is much worth writing. Our cold weather still continues, but for the last two or three days I seem to feel a little more independent of it & to be about as well as I was while the winter lasted. Very weak, very dowie, mournful of heart, but not to be called miserable, far from it indeed, often with a placid thankfulness & inward content which are the reverse of miserable.

Two days ago, Horn & the painter HerdmanRobert Herdman (1829–88; ODNB), painter, a graduate of the Trustees’ School of Design, with whose management Robert Horn was closely involved. came down upon me as by appointment: Horn was very innocent, but more than usually dreary torpid & long-winded; Herdman is a very clever looking fellow; and has about him the air of doing with some effect whatever he undertakes in Art or otherwise. While Horn & I sat prosing, he took up a bit of drawing paper told us to continue our prosing without regarding him at all and in effect at the end of 20 minutes produced a kind of sketch which had a real likeness to me.Horn had written, 22 June 1874: “Robert Herdman has just painted a most excellent portrait of our dear friend Laing for the Antiquarian Society (on occasion of his 50th anniversary of his membership). I do wish I saw as successful a portrait done of yourself!” For Herdman’s portrait of Laing, see opp. Horn had evidently written recently asking if Herdman could do a portrait of TC, as Mary Aitken replied, 9 April: “Mr Carlyle. … cannot promise to comply with your kind request in regard to sitting to Mr Herdman for his Portrait. He … very much dislikes sitting. … I think however that if Mr Herdman … along with his genius as a Painter has a persuasive manner, there will be no difficulty in getting him to sit … at least for a sketch, or for a crayon or chalk drawing” (MS: NLS 3706.145). Horn then wrote, 15 April: “I am not a bit surprised to learn from Miss Aitken … that you think you have done enough for your country already in the way of ‘sittings’! … Had Herdman not been a quick operator, I should not have thought of suggesting to you to give him a trial. However as I mean to be in London next week and Herdman also has engaged to go up … I trust you will forgive me if I take the liberty of bringing him with me some forenoon.” Mary Aitken wrote to Horn, 18 April, inviting him and Herdman for 22 April (MS: NLS 3706.149). See also Nineteenth Century Prose 23:1 (Spring 1996): 1–10. This he
said he would put on canvas with its incipient colours & accompaniments; after which some day next week, he would return for his first sitting; & he thought a second good sitting would finish the affair.Herdman wrote, 29 April: “I intend to avail myself of the permission … to present myself at your house tomorrow … bringing with me the canvass on which I have laid down the rude foundations of your portrait. I beg that you will give yourself as little concern as may be possible about the sittings. … I simply ask that you will sit in your chair … & that you will permit me to work away in your neighbourhood.” This is getting a likeness cheap, if he get it at all; so I willingly consented. My hopes, I own, are not high decidedly low rather, but the expense you see is not large.

figure.p:
Robert Herdman’s portrait of David Laing, 1874
© Scottish National Galleries

docBody.p: Lord NeavesCharles Neaves (1800–1876; ODNB), Lord Neaves, Scottish judge and writer. called here the other day; but unluckily I was out. If he were not so far away (i.e in Clarges St. which alas, has become a big distance to me)The distance from Cheyne Row to Clarges St., Piccadilly, is about 3 mi. (4.5 km.). I would certainly call again; and indeed have some thought of making the attempt this very day. Poor Forster has caught cold again & was very miserable when I saw him yesterday: he had punctually settled every item of my bargain with Chapman for the little book,—a real favour to me. The book is coming out, I suppose on or directly after May-dayThe Early Kings of Norway: also An Essay on the Portraits of John Knox, was listed as pbd., Athenaeum, 8 May; see TC to JAC, 13 Feb. I will have copies shot off to Dumfriesshire by the earliest conveyance. Poor Froude is still at Torquay at least so I judge by his perfect silence; the poor young girl, we can only imagine is painfully perishing under his eyes. I meant to write, asking for news; but have hoped always, every day, that there would arrive some news of him

I go daily down to the end of the embankment at a rapid pace, gathering heat again, out of my cold bath. It is really the wholesomest appliance I make the whole day. I have lost a front tooth since I saw you; it broke away without the slightest pain or warning & I judged it at first to be a mere bit of hard
perkin. But indeed the general furniture of my mouth has become entirely delapidated and the poor tongue (which truly has a bad lodging there) might declare the whole apparatus to be as good as worthless. What can you expect? it has served me faithfully for about 70 years and had various hard nuts to crack.

I ought to terminate, dear Brother, for the time of walking has come & I am saying nothing but what the Fife people fairly designate as havers. Tell Jean I should be very glad to hear a word from her, when she is in the humour. The Arundel note, which you enclose is really interesting to me.John A. Carlyle wrote, 23 April: “Yesternight I had the enclosed note from Dale Park about the death of an old pensioner of [Mrs. Fletcher’s] who had been a servant at Hitchill in old times, when we used to be there; & like all the other servants, who survived the death of Mrs Church, pensioners of Mrs Fletcher. They are all gone now, I think, & Kirsty was the last of the maid-servants. Poor Mrs F. feels the loss of her husband very much. I think I told you [he] died rather suddenly some two months ago. He was a very good-hearted man in his way, & most kind to all his family.” Elizabeth Fletcher, b. Church; her husband, John Charles Fletcher (1798–1875), had been ill for some time; see 48:42TC to JAC, 24 Feb. 1872. They were old friends of John’s, living at Dale Park, Arundel, W. Sussex; see 41:61TC to JAC, 6 Oct. 1864. I hope to see that interesting daughter of HitchillElizabeth was the da. of the Churches of Hitchill Farm, near Annan, Dumfriesshire; TC had become friendly with them when he was a schoolmaster in Annan, 1815–16; see 2:200–201TC to AC, 13 Nov. 1822, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 213 and 450. some time and somehow in the course of this summer Your room here has stood invitingly ready for a good while & still stands.John replied, 30 April: “I received your kind letter … in which you again told me that my room upstairs was quite ready. … I mean to go by our usual midday train on Wednesday next.” John then asked if he should delay coming for a few days “owing to poor little Lizzie’s leaving,” continuing “if there be any difficulty with you in regard to servants, I could take [Arthur Watt] on my way to Chelsea for a few days.” His stepson Arthur Watt was staying with his family at Clifton, near Bristol, before returning to India in Sept.; see MAI to JAC, 18 Jan. Lizzie, Cheyne Row servant, unidentified further. With love & blessings to you all

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JW, 5 May. MS: NLS 2883.246. Pbd: Scotsman 28 Oct. 1889; Pall Mall Gazette, 29 Oct. 1889. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Jeannie Welsh Chrystal, sister of Maggie Welsh, cousins of JWC.
bibl.head: TC TO JEAN WELSH CHRYSTAL

docBody.p:
I cannot express to you, nor is it needful, the sorrow, astonishment and depths of sad remembrances and thoughts, which this stroke that has fallen upon us, incessantly clouds me with ever since the sad certainty came to us
on Saturday morning last.The news of the death of Maggie Welsh, 29 April. The Liverpool Mercury announced, 1 May: “Welsh—April 29, at her brother’s residence, Sandown Park, Wavertree, Margaret, third daughter of the late John Welsh Esq., of this town.” I had somehow tried to believe it not possible all the day before, vainly fancied that your little NieceMaggie had been staying with her brother Alexander and his family in Liverpool; the niece was presumably one of their three das.: Isabella, Margaret, and Jean. or that the DoctorPossibly Dr. Peter Murray Braidwood (1842–1905), a Liverpool doctor whom TC’s family had consulted when Jean Aitken’s son Thomas was dying; see 46:86TC to MA, 10 Oct. 1869; otherwise unidentified. had overstated the matter and that there was still hope, nay, as it were assurance. Your note of next morning put a sudden end to all this; and when the end of my mournful, sad and manifold emotions and reflections on it will come, is not to be reckoned or foreseen.
