Alas, alas, I confidently trusted to have had her here, bright and cheerfully contented as ever, in these very days;Maggie regularly visited TC, the last time was during April and May 1874; see TC to JAC, 17 April 1874; she was apparently due to visit again soon. and now——! Ah me; ah me.

To you, and to both your BrothersJeannie had two brothers, Alexander in Liverpool, and Walter in Auchtertool, with whom Maggie usually lived. and all their households, it will be a still heavier, indeed incalculable loss: for she went about among you like a bright presence, helpful cheerful and every way good; and the blank she has left all on a sudden, what can ever remedy it? But what can we say or do, nothing, nothing at all except teach ourselves to say, as she did to you in her last day, “God’s Will be done.” Good is God’s will.

No life that I have witnessed in this world was more touchingly good, beneficent, modest, always helpful, quiet and useful than hers who is now gone. Really a most modest, peacefully humble and yet dignified & ever courteous walk of Life was hers. I have not in my time seen a more perfect example of silent wisdom, piety, native humility and native dignity among fellow creatures that I have known. Let that be a pacifying consideration and a silent precept and consolation to us all.

Thank Walter for his kind Letter of this morning; he knows without my mention of it, what my sympathy with him in particular is and must be. For yourself also the loss is great, and can never be forgotten in your heart or in your household. Indeed which of us can ever forget? My own tumultuous recollections go back for the last 49 yearsTC had known the Welsh cousins since his marriage to JWC, 17 Oct. 1826. & call up innumerable thoughts which are beautiful, yet painful. Tell Walter I will write to him by and by, and never will forget him while in this world. Do you also, please, remember that you are my Cousin & that from time you must write to me and keep alive the relationship which I mean only to quit with life.
God bless you and yours, dear Mrs Chrystal; and teach us all to be wise while it is called Today. I am ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-ÉM [EM], 15 May. MS: M. Dominique Sardin d’Enjoy, Limoges, France inc. Quot: Pierre-Alexis Meunier, “Lettres inédites de Carlyle et de George Eliot à Émile Montégut,” Revue de Littérature Comparée 5 (1925): 504. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Some of the MS is missing, and one sentence is taken from the pbd. text. Émile Montégut, old friend of TC’s.
bibl.head: TC TO ÉMILE MONTÉGUT

docBody.p: I was agreeably surprized the other morning by your marriage announcement,Montégut sent, 22 April, an announcement of his forthcoming wedding, 22 June, to Anne-Marie Jeanne Hortense de Lajoumard de Bellabre. which, with the date ‘près Limoges’ known to me long since for your Native place made an altogether pleasantly significant bit of news. For about ten years I had heard nothing specific of youTC’s last recorded contact with Montégut was in summer 1865; see 42:29–30TC to EM, 19 May 1865, and 90 TC to JWC, 29 June 1865. except incidentally through your contributions to the Revue des Deux Mondes,Revue des Deux Mondes, French monthly magazine for which Montégut wrote. which were, as all your former contributions, sure always to be pleasant reading to me; and had no fault except that they were few and far between. Latterly I observed with new interest that you seemed to have been wandering and promenading over [. … . . .] studying inscrutable and old edifices, curious old towns which became in your [. … . . .] manifoldly suggestive & were sure to take me along with them. And now I hear, with still livelier interest, that you have ceased your wanderings, & sat down with [an] amiable Lady-companion [in] some nice rural village (such I love to fancy it) in your country, there henceforth to hold a contemplative and quiet life,—notably more favourable to your fine literary industries than any former portion of your life has been. Quod bonum felix et fortunatum sit [good luck and fortune be with you].

I now request you farther to send me a specific bit of Letter to detail and describe in some measure and reduce to historical certainty all this, which [is] hitherto somewhat of a shadow in the friendly imagination merely. Do this, I pray you; it will be a [. … . . .] employment of some hours [. … . . .].

The enclosed photograph of Wootton (Wood-town) Lodge or Hall, Rousseau’s place of refuge while in England;Wootton Hall, Staffordshire, where Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–78), French philosopher, lived 1766–67; see 38:227–28. was got for your behalf five or six
years ago, not that I supposed you would greatly care for it, but that it was indisputably authentic, and did belong to a very wonderful Jean-Jacques and might be among your retenta [keepsakes]: however I never till now could ascertain your sure address; and so now I send it. There are many Woottons in England, but this the notablest of all is on the northeast border of Staffordshire five, or six miles to west of Ashbourne in Derbyshire; and the LadyCaroline Davenport Bromley. from whom I had it is great-great granddaughter to the DavenportRichard Davenport (ca. 1705–71), Cheshire merchant. who was so unspeakably patient a friend to the mad and miserable Jean Jacques. She herself was brought [up] as a child in the three upper rooms that had belonged to Rousseau. The sketch she has just drawn me of what Wootton was in R’s time & the copy of her Note are here enclosed.

closer.salute: Adieu, dear Montégut. With my kindest respects to Madame, Yours ever truly

bibl.sourceNote: TC-PdeL [PL], 20 May. MS: Göttingen. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature. Paul Anton de Lagarde (1827–91), Biblical scholar, prof. of oriental languages at the Univ. of Göttingen, and leading nationalist and anti-semite theorist.
bibl.head: TC TO PAUL DE LAGARDE

docBody.p:
Several months ago I received from you a kind & cheerful little Note, which it gave me pleasure to read.Lagarde wrote to TC, 5 Dec. 1874: “You take such a lively interest in Germany, that I feel sure, you will kindly accept and peruse my ‘politische Aufsätze [political essays]’. … I do not belong to any of the parties in existence, so I must fight my way … so, I apply to you, who knows that a warrior life is the best of all lives.” The pamphlet which accompanied it has also been long since read, and with an unusual satisfaction & recognition of ideas, which have long, in the spoken or unspoken state, been my own; & were welcome to a high degree in the mouth of another.The pamphlet was probably Über das Verhältnis des deutschen Staates zu Theologie, Kirche und Religion. Ein Versuch Nicht-Theologen zu orientieren [On the Relationship of the German States to Theology, Church and Religion: An Attempt at Orientation for Non-Theologians] (Göttingen, 1873), in which Lagarde argued for the abolition of denominational distinctions in the teaching of theology and the establishment of a German national religion. In short it is many years since I have met with so much of faithful independent thinking & real originality in any book, German or other, that has come before me. All this I have felt it fairly incumbent on me to let you know ever since. But, alas, I
have, for years past, had no fingers that would write for me; nor can I, after many trials, learn in the least effectually to write by dictation; so that being furthermore in my 80th year, & still involved in many trifling duties & highly unfit for labour of any kind I am at all times much averse to writing, and never do it except on absolute compulsion. From blame for this long idle delay I by no means acquit myself altogether; but I hope you will accept the above considerations as a kind of excuse.

I find at p. 11 a very weighty thought, which had long, in the unspoken state, been altogether present in me; this, namely, “Ich halte Religion im grunde für nichts anderes, als fur Sinn für Realität [I believe religion is fundamentally nothing other than sense and reality]” &c. Surely a deep & most true thing, which it would much illuminate the bewildered mind of many a poor creature to have & to hold before his own mind in these interminable enquiries! I also agree with you in your estimate of the now condition of Protestantism, &, with still more emphasis, in the advice you give us, all & sundry, to regard the miserable old Chimera of a Pope and his jargonings & sprawlings as now at length become plain zero to all sincere human creatures, a thing to be eliminated from one’s considerations on this unfathomable Universe & left to sprawl itself out & let the poor world have done with it at the long last. We have wonderful Papist developments in this poor prurient England; & yet one thing is always apparent, that he & his diligent satellites have not inveigled one single man of sense; the nearest approach to one such is Father Newman,John Henry Newman (1801–90; ODNB), theologian, fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, until he converted to Roman Catholicism, 1845. long an Oxford dignitary, & respected still for his piety of mind; though his poor intellect, never a very complete one, has gone wool gathering at such a rate. His last utterance I hear is, that the newly declared Infallibility of the PopeThe First Vatican Council, 1869–70, declared that Pope Pius IX (see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. 1873) could make infallible pronouncements on matters of faith and morals. realizes the Roman Tyrant’s wish that the Roman people had all one neck, which could be severed at one blowWords attributed to the Roman emperor Caligula (12–41) by Suetonius, The Twelve Caesars (121). as the Pope & Papists have now got;—to which one only adds, Thank God.Newman wrote Letter to the Duke of Norfolk (1875), in which he argued against strict adherence to papal infallibility, on the grounds that doctrinal pronouncements required interpretation, and that abstract definitions had to take account of concrete situations. Your notion of the Jews, which has a fine spice of satire in it, amused me considerably. But above all things I was interested by what you say toward the end of the Book, that there is no real gain to any nation, except by the restoration of some real religion to it, this is to me a truth of truths; and I am anxious in a high degree to hear what farther you may
please to utter upon this highest matter. So if anything farther come from you on that head, I shall very specially request you to send me notice of it, if I am still here.Lagarde replied, 1 June, thanking TC for his letter, and saying that his book had been withdrawn, because although “men like you will understand it: the general publick needs more explaining. I shall be most happy to send you the new edition.” Patristik [writings of early Christian theologians] &c I am much less interested in; but this latter point seems to me all-important.
Permit me, dear Sir, to wish you continued courage, force & sincerity in declaring the message you are trusted with among your fellows.

postscript.p: I take it for granted that you do not publish this Letter.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-WW [WWE], 26 [24] May. Addr: Auchtertool Manse / Kirkcaldy / N.B. PM: London, 24 May 1875. MS: NLS 2883.250. Pbd: Scotsman, 26 Oct. 1889; Pall Mall Gazette, 28 Oct. 1889. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature; “With a Book” was written on the top of the envelope; Mary misdated the letter.
bibl.head: TC TO WALTER WELSH

docBody.p: I send you today a little Book,Presumably The Early Kings of Norway: also An Essay on the Portraits of John Knox. which many sorrowful thoughts accompany from me: alas, alas you too well guess why; the little Book should not have been sent to you, but to Another, who is now for ever hidden from our bodily eyes.Maggie Welsh. Daily She is present to my thoughts, and you along with her, ever since the sad stroke which suddenly bereaved us of her. One of the gentlest, most amiable, prudent, kind and good human souls, mournfully beautiful, sad, and strange to think of now.

Pray do not send any acknowledgement of the poor Book’s arrival just now. I long to hear from you, you need not doubt; but let it be on some independent occasion and when perhaps, you have a little settled your domestic arrangements,Maggie had lived with Walter and organized his household. so sadly cut asunder, & can write with more composure than at present. We have all of us had a heavy loss and bereavement; but I think always there is none whom it must have fallen on so heavily as you. God be with you, dear Walter, and teach you to do and feel, now and at all times whatsoever is wisest & best. Amen.
I am ever your affectionate Cousin / T. Carlyle

bibl.sourceNote: TC-WW [WWE], 14 July. Pbd: Scotsman, 26 Oct. 1889; Pall Mall Gazette, 28 Oct. 1889.
bibl.head: TC TO WALTER WELSH

docBody.p: I have written nothing, but my thoughts are often with you. Indeed, there are few days in which “I do not expressly visit” Auchtertool, and mourn along with you the irreparable loss we have both sustained there. Alas, alas! I expected to have had her now with me, at this very time, cheering with her gentle presence, ever so quiet, kind, and unweariedly helpful, the friend and household which will now never behold her more.

This day in particular (Mrs. Carlyle’s birthday), which for reasons you can well comprehend, is always to me a sacred and mournfully memorable one, bringing to me a world of unspeakable thoughts and remembrances: on this rather than on another day, therefore, I will beg you to accept the enclosed little tokenTC’s checkbook recorded: “14 July 1875 / The Revd W. Welsh / Auchtertool / £250 .. 0 .. 0” (TC’s checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). from me of my continued regard for you and yours, and of my lasting gratitude to Heaven for having brought me connected with your family. The little gift, alas! is a most poor expression of my feeling as to that, which indeed no words could express; but I do beg of you to accept it as a wholly genuine one to myself. In the wide world of unutterable feelings and remembrances it will be a kind of relief and solacement. I know not whether I shall ever see Auchtertool again,TC had last visited Auchtertool with Mary Aitken, 1–5 Sept. 1873; see 48:220MW to SW, 9 Sept. 1873. but in any case let it be as a kind of parting pledge between me and that hospitable home, which I ever felt to be wide open to me. Do not trouble yourself with writing any letter to me, dear Walter, beyond a simple announcement that the bit of paper has come to hand. I will wait your own time for a fuller account of whatever you think best to tell me about the dear old manse and your own ever kind, friendly, and hospitable self.Walter Welsh wrote, 20 Aug., apologizing for not writing sooner: “As I said to Miss Mary, in my short acknowledgement to her of both letter & gift, most deeply do I feel your kindness both of word & deed.”

Please offer my affectionate regard to Mrs. Chrystal and household. Give my love also to your brother Alick and his wife. I pray cordially God bless you all, and am ever your affectionate cousin, / T. Carlyle.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 27 July. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: I received your Letter with great thankfulness; & was very glad to find that in your swift and somewhat reckless expedition you had escaped any essential damage & found everything well and to your mind on your arrival at Loch Leuchart.Mary misspelled “Luichart.” Lady Ashburton arrived at her Highland estate, Kinlochluichart, sometime in July. The Inverness Courier reported, 12 Aug.: “Her ladyship distributed a quantity of clothing amongst the poor last week, and gave a dance to her tenantry and work people at the Lodge. Lady Ashburton also presented a number of prizes to the deserving scholars at the school.” By a sidewind I find since that your little fit of illness has quite gone; that the weather is again bright and that all is temperate & sunshiny in your new locality; long may it so continue.

I have myself almost as good as nothing to offer in return no news, no action; utter idleness, except constant reading, and no increase or diminution of my paltry dyspeptic and continually overclouded existence,—of which, as it is natural and irremediable, the less said the better. On the Sunday after your departure, weather being fair for a walk, I called on Lady Marian,Lady Marian Alford. who received me in her choicest moodCoterie speech; see 4:424JWC to JCA, [Dec. 1828]. & also at the same moment a handsome pleasant-looking fine-lady of middle age, who was very civil to me, but whose name I did not catch when presented to her.Unidentified further. Our colloquy was mainly kept up by Lady Marian’s own sprightly resources; to whom I could make no return, except privately some exposition of a silver Dutch snuff-box, in commemoration of a sea-battle on the DoggerbankDogger Bank, a large sandbank in the North Sea about 62 mi. (100 km.) off the E coast of England; a naval battle took place there between the British and the Dutch, 5 Aug. 1781; both sides claimed victory. which I got put into writing for Lady M’s sake on my return home. The good Lady has had, I fear, a painful event since then in the loss of her Uncle:TC probably refers to Lady Marian’s brother-in-law, Charles Henry Cust (1813–75), who d. 23 May. —but I had better enclose you Lady M’s own Note, which you doubtless can read, & which there is no need for returning.

I have seen Forster once or twice, nay we dined last night with his Wife & him, an unexampled feat for one of us, which indeed I think ought to be the
last of its kind. Mrs Forster is fairly recovering & Forster himself is evidently very considerably better. He has decided on setting out for Melchet tomorrow, about which I had given him all the explanations & encouragements possible; & I have no doubt he will derive great benefit from the six weeks among the silent woods & beautiful greeneries out there.Lady Ashburton’s estate, Melchet Court, nr. Romsey, Hampshire.

This is no letter, dear Lady; but I hope you will take it for one; & continue for me the history of Loch Luichart which I shall wish for with true desire till you return within speaking distance. I send a thousand regards to the MarigoldLady Ashburton’s da., Mary Florence. & desire her to expedite the “Letter” she has on the stocks & to make it as like one to yourself as she can. I accidentally saw yesterday for two minutes Miss Bromley, who was coming hither & indeed had got into the street when Henry CowperHenry Frederick Cowper. & I encountered her carriage but could not afford to return, such the pressure of time. She engaged us to go out to BarnesCaroline Davenport Bromley apparently owned or rented a house in Barnes, SE London; see 48:212TC to LA, 6 July 1873. on Friday next. She looked pretty well & seemed to have given up all notion of shifting into town till after the season is quite over. Which indeed it essentially is already, so far as I can judge. Adieu, dear Lady, all good be with you and yours.
I remain ever

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-CHH, 4 Aug. MS: Duke. Hitherto unpbd. Charles Henry Hart (1847–1918), Philadelphia lawyer, art historian, and curator.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO CHARLES HENRY HART

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me say, with his compliments, that the small line on the top of the head in the Somerville Portrait is evidently intended to indicate a skull-cap.For the Somerville portrait of Knox, see TC to RHO, 10 April. It is a little more distinct in the oil-picture than in the Engraving & the Engraving naturally loses a little by being reproduced.

Mr Carlyle has not the honour of being descended from John Knox,JWC often claimed erroneously that she was descended from John Knox; see 34:137JWC to HL, [17 Aug. 1858], and 16:41JWC to JW, [2 Feb. 1843]. —there never was any tradition in his family to the effect that it was in any way connected with him.

Mr Carlyle bids me ask you to accept his thanks for the honour which your Society wish to confer upon him and which he naturally has much pleasure in acceptingProbably connected with the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Pennsylvania of which Hart was the historiographer; otherwise unexplained.
docBody.closer: I am, / Dear Sir, / Yours truly / Mary Carlyle Aitken

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 4 Aug. MS: FC. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: We greatly want from you some news of your posture of affairs at Melchet, especially of your own & your dear Wife’s health since you went thither. Let me have, I pray you, a line or two on those subjects without delay.Forster wrote from Melchet, 4 Aug.: “The house is on too big a scale for my notions of comfort and home. … [A]nd, of course, since the fire, which left only this wing we inhabit, the splendid galleries and passages, as well as the rooms themselves, are of disproportioned size. … But what a beautiful country! … The drives everywhere are delightful, the beautiful woodiness of Country reminding me much of Warwickshire. … The drawback from perfect enjoyment is that which we bring with us. The poor Wife is so dreadfully weak, and a persistent north wind having checked improvement in me. We go on hoping nevertheless” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 14–15). For the fire at Melchet Court, Aug. 1872, see 48:84–85TC to LA, 4 Aug. 1872.

The Swift volumeForster’s The Life of Jonathan Swift. I finished on the second evening after you went and have been thinking of it frequently ever since I can say in general that I found it interesting and entertaining to me to read, and that for one thing you convince me clearly that you know far better than any biographer that has ever tried Swift’s Life before what the real circumstances tenor and details of it are. Clear, brief, neat and precise is all that you yourself say of it. The only point of question with me is the plan you have adopted in so difficult a job, that of introducing repeatedly, in the body of the narrative what seems to be properly of the nature of preface or introduction. The only passages I haggled on & did not find rapid & comfortable reading were those about the “little language”TC refers to the private language that Swift used in his correspondence with his friend Esther Johnson (1681–1728; ODNB), known as “Stella.” Swift’s Journal to Stella (1784) contains 67 letters, almost all written 1710–13; her replies were destroyed. Forster wrote: “Of the little language used in their intercourse something must now be said. Upon a previous page has been expressed the desire Swift had for a ‘life by stealth’ between himself and her, or in other words for confidences the world was not to share; and … there may in this be some remote shadow … of the first intention with which they began to talk to each other in phrases special to themselves. Such was the ‘little,’ or childish, language to which allusion has been made as perhaps dating from her girlhood” (Forster, Life of Swift 1:292–93). They met in 1689, when Stella was eight and he was twenty-two. &c &c; concerning which I have no plan of improvement, but can
merely state my own difficulties with them. It has struck me generally that a paragraph of your own now & then, detailing with brief precision what the real state of matters Swift was in the middle of, what Harley & St. John were actually aiming at & doing & what their opponents were and had been aiming at & doing,Swift lived in London 1709–14, partly to campaign for the rights of the Church of Ireland with the British government; to this end he gained the support of the Tory politicians Robert Harley (1661–1724; ODNB), 1st earl of Oxford and Mortimer, and Henry St. John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke; see TC to JF, 3 July 1874. Britain was part of a European alliance against France in the War of the Spanish Succession, 1701–14, but by 1711 Harley was conducting secret peace negotiations with France, and Swift agreed to write a defence of this policy, The Conduct of the Allies (1711), which attacked the Whigs for unnecessarily prolonging the ruinously expensive war. with clear dates & a few significant details put down, would be a great help to the reader. Especially the dates, were it only of such things as Malplaquet & OudenardeThe battles of Malplaquet, 11 Sept. 1709, and Oudenarde, 11 July 1708, were critical battles during the war. and the like would be a great help towards clearness; after which the details in the “Little Language” would be much more luminous. The “Little Language” itself is certainly a wondrous thing in a man like Swift, and I cannot give to myself any clear notion of it; but merely admit that it is a most significant feature of him, though a dim and hardly intelligible one. This is all I have to say at present and I think I may as well wait till we meet for a fuller as well as much more explicit discussion of it when restored to a sight of you again. Meanwhile [a Letter, do] not deny me a Letter with details about Self & Madam.

There is a new scheme on foot in regard to my own poor weary existence for the next month or so. Lady Derby in the most generous manner offers me a beautiful little cottage they have near Bromley in Kent, Keston LodgeLady Derby wrote, 26 July: “Lord Derby & I want … to offer you our little house at Keston, close to Holwood, for a few weeks during the fine weather. It is quite a cottage & very quiet. … You & your niece would be quite comfortable, & you would have a pleasure ground of 100 acres to roam about in … the house is kept by a man & his wife who would do all that you require.” Keston Lodge, adjoining the Derby’s Holwood estate, about 13½ mi. (22 km.) SE of London. they call the place, some 14 miles away, silent as Sahara with all the fittings corresponding: about wh. we are in great tumult & haste at this very time having as good as decided to try it.— I will not add another word, dear Forster, to this miserable semi-articulate blotch, but merely say that I am not worse than when you left me.— Good be ever with you, dear F.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAF, 6 Aug. Pbd: Dunn, CLF IV:246.
bibl.head: TC TO J. A. FROUDE

docBody.p: I was very glad and thankful for your Letter, which was long looked for and arrived two or three days ago. I can only at present remind you that any Letter from you, when you have a moment’s leisure will find a similar reception here.

I am to go in a minute or two upstairs to try for a little fore-dinner sleep. I must restrict myself therefore to what is the essence of this communication, that is, to enclosing a Note just come from Lady Derby, which brings news that I wish I could send by Telegram or through the air. I read with entire approval the report of your speech at the grand preliminary Dinner,Froude had agreed to return to South Africa at the behest of Lord Carnarvon; see TC to JF, 3 July 1874, and TC to JAC, 13 Feb. He left England, 23 May, authorized to advocate the case for an Imperial confederation. The governor, Henry Barkly (1815–98; ODNB), and the prime minister, John Charles Molteno (1814–86; ODNB), of the Cape Colony, opposed Carnarvon’s plan, on the basis that any move for federation should originate in South Africa and not in England. At a banquet held in his honor at Cape Town, 26 June, which Molteno and Barkly refused to attend, Froude defended the Imperial government’s policy, insisting that Carnarvon respected the Cape Colony’s political autonomy: “If you look at [his] despatch you will see that he has not recommended confederation; he says only that if in the course of the discussions arising on all these difficult subjects any wish should be expressed to form a confederation on the part of the different communities of South Africa, the British Government would be exceedingly glad to forward it. … having experienced the impossibility of managing the internal affairs of [our other] colonies at all successfully from England, we confine ourselves to their external defence, leaving them the entire management of their own internal affairs, native matters and all else included” (London Evening Standard, 3 Aug.). —a wise, clear, prudent and manful speech, as indeed the dinner itself and the general sentiment of your South-African public seemed to me to be wholly of a welcome character and quite agreeing with the comfortable state of opinion universally prevalent here. I hope and pray and also in some good measure believe that you will accomplish something really good in your present expedition. For the rest, I wish with my whole heart you were here again, for I am very solitary without you. Write pray whenever you have a convenient moment to dispose of.
docBody.closer:
Yours ever faithfully
T. Carlyle
(X his mark,
M. C. Aitken)

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 19 Aug. MS: FC. Quot: Brent E. Kinser and Clayton Carlyle Tarr, “‘The end of a chapter in my life’: The Letters of John Forster to Thomas Carlyle,” CSA 33 (2018–19): 15–16. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: Many thanks for your kind & punctual letter which gives us great satisfaction, tho’ on point of your recovering health there is still much to be desired. You must be patient, my Friend, patient! A rooted sorrow of that kind is not to be removed in a day or in a few weeks. One thing meanwhile is certain the beneficent elements of earth & sky are all clearly in your favour and assiduously acting at every moment: courage, patience, steadfast hope! I think your finest drives will lie towards the New Forest; nevertheless I remember in the other direction not far from your issuing by the main gate on the Salisbury Road some high lying, open & very pleasant country, which I have ridden over several times, as my pleasantest outroad of all;For TC’s enjoyment of the New Forest and the countryside surrounding Melchet, see 47:201–2TC to JAC, 13 May 1871, and TC to JAC, 15 May 1871. and suppose to be fitted for wheels also, though on that latter point I have no experience or clear recollection. Perhaps, also, you will make a visit to your Friend Lord Shaftesbury if he is able to receive visits in the grief that has befallen him.Lord Shaftesbury was presumably at his estate, Wimborne St. Giles, in Dorset. His da.-in-law Frances Elizabeth, b. Hanbury-Leigh (1848–75), d. 2 Aug.; she m., 1868, his son Anthony Lionel George Ashley-Cooper (1838–1914). Wimborne is about 20 mi. (32 km.) W of Melchet. I saw in Boehms the day before leaving a Bust of him,Boehm’s bust of Shaftesbury (1875) is now in the National Portrait Gallery. apparently near finished, wh. appeared to me to be strictly speaking what might be called admirable.

We have been out here a week and a day: I may truly call it the strangest & most miraculous looking place I have ever been in, silence in and around it, which reminds you of eternity; a park only of a hundred acres which seems to one, threading its Daedalean paths,In Greek mythology Daedalus designed a vast labyrinth for King Minos of Crete to hold the Minotaur. to be of a thousand or more; nothing easier for me than to lose my way after all this experience; here one wanders at discretion with whatever power of meditation, reflection or remembrance may be in one all day & if one liked all night; the night especially surpasses in silence the desert of Sahara; a place where you would think the most fidgetty of souls might compose itself to sweet sleep; but, alas, hitherto, no or not quite, though I hope to actually get accustomed to my environment and enjoy the good provided so bounteously for me. For the rest we are fed & provided
for by two excellent people (a most serious, wise Butler & his ditto Wife)Probably William Porter (b. 1835), butler, and Mary A. Porter (b. 1838), housekeeper, and their sons, William (b. 1867), and Richard (b. 1869) (Keston Census, 1881). who live quite secluded from us & yet quite at hand no prophet Elijah could have ravensSee 1 Kings 17:4–6. more punctual & provident. I do hope, were the flurry of novelty surprise & strangeness once well laid, I shall gradually attain some real temporal benefit from this immersion for a few weeks into so pure an element.— In the form of “employment” I diligently continue my reading of Michelet’s France:Jules Michelet, Histoire de France, 19 vols. (Paris, 1833–67). a most strange ingenious questionable & wonderful book. Yesterday I had from it by far the best, or rather the one good, fairly credible & true history of the Maid of orleansMichelet wrote about Joan of Arc (ca. 1412–31), known as the Maid of Orleans, in his Histoire de France bk. 10 chaps. 3 and 4. He began her story: “The originality of the Maid, what made her success, was not so much her bravery or her visions, it was her common sense” (editor’s trans.). which I ever heard of elsewhere. A small, pure blessing to me, & possession withal.— But, alas,Word repeated with a line over it at top of first page. here the paper ends, dear Forster, & we fall as through one of the trap doors in Mirza’s visionSee Joseph Addison, “The Vision of Mirzah,” Spectator 159 (1711); the vision is of a valley of misery through which runs the river of eternity, crossed by a bridge representing human life, with concealed trap doors through which some must fall; see also 45:168TC to CDB, [8 Sept. 1868]. and are heard no more till next time. Write to us quàm primùm[.] With love to you both

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-GH [GHOG], 28 Aug. Pbd: Life of Frances Power Cobbe, As Told by Herself, 2 vols. (1894) 2:164–65. George Hoggan (1837–91), medical practitioner and anti-vivisection campaigner. He m., 1874, Frances Elizabeth, b. Morgan (1843–1927; ODNB), physician and social reformer; she was one of the first women to gain a medical degree, in Zurich, 1870. Together with Frances Power Cobbe (1822–1904; ODNB), writer and women’s rights campaigner, they founded the Victoria Street Society for the Protection of Animals Liable to Vivisection, Nov. 1875.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO GEORGE HOGGAN

docBody.p:
Mr. Carlyle has received your letter, and has read it carefully. He bids me say that, ever since he was a boy, when he read the account of Majendie’s atrocities,François Magendie (1783–1855), French physiologist, notorious experimenter on animals. TC had heard Magendie speak in Paris, 1824; see 3:188TC to JAC, 24 Nov. 1824. he has never thought of the practice of vivisecting animals but
with horror. I may mention that I have heard him speak of it in the strongest terms of disgust long before there was any speech about public agitation on the subject. He believes that the reports about the good results said to be obtained from the practice of vivisection to be immensely exaggerated; with the exception of certain experiments by HarveyWilliam Harvey (1578–1657; ODNB), physiologist, anatomist, physician, and discoverer of the circulation of the blood; he regularly used vivisection in his researches. and certain others by Sir Charles Bell,Sir Charles Bell (1774–1842; ODNB), Edinburgh physiologist, anatomist, and surgeon, specializing in the functioning of the brain. He rarely used vivisection, believing it often led to false conclusions as well as causing great suffering. he is not aware of any conspicuous good that has resulted from it. But even supposing the good results to be much greater than Mr. Carlyle believes they are, and apart too from the shocking pain inflicted on the helpless animals operated upon, he would still think the practice so brutalizing to the operators that he would earnestly wish the law on the subject to be altered, so as to make Vivisection even in Institutions like that with which you are connected a most rare occurrence, and when practised by private individuals an indictable offence.

You are not sure that the operators on living animals “can be counted on your fingers.” Mr. Carlyle with an equal share of certainty believes Vivisection and other kindred experiments on living animals to be much more largely practised, and that they are by no means uncommonly undertaken by doctors’ apprentices and “other miserable persons.”

You are mistaken if you look upon the Times as a mirror of virtue; on this very subject when it at first began to be publicly discussed last winter,There had been a considerable amount of agitation around vivisection since the beginning of the year. At the end of 1874 Cobbe had drafted a Memorial urging the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals to present an anti-vivisection bill to Parliament, which obtained over 600 signatures, including TC’s (Cobbe 255). The RSPCA refused however, and instead two private members’ bills were introduced in May; this led to a Royal Commission of Vivisection being set up, 22 June, with the report pbd. 8 Jan. 1876. it printed a letter from. . . .Probably Ernest Abraham Hart (1835–98; ODNB), surgeon, medical journalist, and ed. of the British Medical Journal 1867–98; he wrote to the Times, 28 Jan., challenging the statement made by the RSPCA that “the practice of vivisection has now become the every-day exercise of hundreds of physiologists and young students of physiology throughout Europe.” Hart wrote: “I deny that there is a grain of truth in this bold assertion. … Experiments on animals have been the point of departure of nearly every great addition to our knowledge in medical science.” This led to a lively interchange of letters between Hart and various anti-vivisectionists. Ellipsis in printed text. which your letter itself would prove to be altogether composed of falsehoods.
With Mr. Carlyle’s compliments and good wishes,
/ Mary Carlyle Aitken.

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-EPH, 30 Aug. MS: Sophie Dupré Autographs. Hitherto unpbd. Edwin Paxton Hood (1820–85; ODNB), Congregational minister and writer. He lived in Islington, North London.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO EDWIN PAXTON HOOD

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle, my Uncle, bids me ask you to accept his cordial thanks for your very kind letterHood wrote, 27 Aug.: “It is very likely you have never heard of me; I have for many years (as myself a Public Preacher) been in the habit of quoting You. … I know so well & understand why it should be, that the real man differs often so utterly from the man apparent—that I have been afraid to venture to attempt to see you. … And you dear & revered man are I am sorry to know eighty years of age & must soon leave us … & I confess it would be … painful joy to touch your hand & to look into your eyes before you go.” wh. has been forwarded hither to him, and also for the Book,Hood, Thomas Carlyle: Philosophic Thinker, Theologian, Historian and Poet (1875). Hood wrote: “But at length I have gathered up my impressions & notices into a volume,—& I enclose it to you.” which no doubt lies safe at Chelsea waiting his return. He bids me say, too, with his kindest wishes that when he gets back to London, it will give him much pleasure to make your acquaintance. We shall not be absent more than a week or two, or perhaps I ought to say two or three weeks. I will, however send you a word when we get settled again at Chelsea.TC and Mary returned to London 30 Sept.
docBody.closer: I remain / Reverend Sir / Yours very truly, / Mary Carlyle Aitken

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 1 Sept. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p:
I am sadly at a loss for your very address just now, not to speak of any news or tidings of your movements and adventures. Since Gold Mary’s dainty little letter,Mary Florence Baring; letter untraced. for which pray thank her, I have heard nothing whatever, except that you were to leave L. Luichart which indeed she told me; & that probably you would still be in the Highlands for a moderate while. Forster writes weekly or mostly so, though for this week I have had nothing yet: his only news of you was that you were really still in the Highlands, but intended to be with Miss Hossmer at Seaforth Lodge before the end of autumn,Forster wrote, 22 Aug.: “Of my lady I have heard nothing since I last wrote—except that she has been staying some days with Fowler the Engineer, in a house he has built in the cortication of an Eagle’s nest, and which I think you once told me you had visited. Early next month she goes to Seaton, where her friend ‘Hatty Hosmer’ joins her for sea-bathing” (KInser and Tarr, III, 17). John Fowler (1817–98; ODNB), civil engineer, specializing in railways, including the Forth Railway Bridge. He lived at Braemore House, built on a promontory near the Corrieshalloch Gorge in Ross-shire, NW Scotland; TC had visited him there with Lady Ashburton in 1871; see 47:223None to JF, 18 Aug. 1871. Harriet Hosmer, American sculptor, friend of Lady Ashburton; see 48:4TC to JCA, 13 Oct. 1871. a very melancholy
lack of news for certain. I do not even know where Miss Bromley is, whether in France or England; if you know where she is, be so bountiful the first time you write to her as a beg a note from her for me.Lady Ashburton replied, 4 Sept.: “Miss Bromley is still at Barnes I had a delightful letter from her yesty.”

For the last three weeks all has been revolutionary about Cheyne Row, and I had to fly hither to the strangest Goshen imaginable to find quiet from the din & tumult of universal cleansing, sweeping, painting, washing, uncarpeting and general noise and confusion. The good Lady Derby seeing the state we were in remembered that they had a perfectly quiet, clear & empty little “Lodge,” lately bought by them, with a woody park round it and certain rooms of it already furnished tho’ never occupied: thither she despatched me,See TC to JF, 4 Aug. and here I am ever since. Two excellent, steady servants, a man & his Wife with two children,See TC to JF, 19 Aug. have charge of the place & do for us in all practical respects. There is a pureness in the air unsurpassable and all round, by night and by day a silence that I never met before in any section of my travels. The county has all the beauty of Kent in its best time, a woody fresh & interesting little park full of Daedalean paths; and little villages all round, peaceable and pleasant when one wants again, which I seldom do as yet, the view of human life and human diligence encircling one. I have now at last learnt to sleep, too, in some measure I seem to myself to be gaining some little clearness of bodily health and have a world of silent memories, strangely awakening all around me. In fact I ought to conclude myself really happy, though earth and sky fill me with a strange sometimes half-celestial feeling which for the rest is of the sadness of death, but also has a blessedness in it.

In brief dear Lady, the thing I want is instantly were it possible some news of you. From nobody except Forster, as was said, do I get anything of personal that could interest you. He still complains, but I think is really getting better. Melchet & its environs are throughout lovely to him. My Brother is home to Dumfries a week ago and will probably stay there. I add no other word but that I am, as ever,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 2 Sept. MS: NLS 528.35. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:313–15 inc. Quot: Carlyle Encyclopedia 320. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I understand you are for Peebles “the end of the week”;John A. Carlyle was visiting his stepson Arthur Watt (see TC to JAC, 24 April), who was visiting his mother-in-law, Helen Hunter, in Peebles; see 48:197TC to JAC, 26 April 1873. John wrote, 3 Sept., that he had just returned from visiting Arthur and his family: “I found them all well—Arthur himself looking much better than when I last saw him in London.” Arthur and Henrietta had three children, two of whom were being left in England, while they took the baby (b. June 1875) back to India with them. John wrote: “Arthur has always conducted himself well, & I felt rather sad at parting, it being unlikely that I shall ever see him again.” this day therefore will be the last on which there will be any chance to catch you. I hope the poor packet will arrive before you go. Part of it you may notice is for Sister Jean, from whom I had three days ago or four a long and very pleasant letterJean Aitken wrote, [24 Aug.], a long letter about her recent holiday in Edinburgh and Burntisland (see TC to JAC, 1 Sept. 1874). which I fully mean to answer more deliberately.

We are fairly doing well here, not ill at all; and profitting what we can by the glorious element we have got dropped into. One of the strangest I ever had experience of. The silence day and night is the completest in the world, solitude too is without parallel: all manner of chances are given one for profitable thought if one were capable of it, profitable, though mournful and melancholy in a high degree. Mary has been up to Chelsea & reports that everything is nearly completeThe house in Cheyne Row was being comprehensively cleaned while TC and Mary were away; John wrote, 12 Aug.: “Please tell Mary that the carpets of the upmost room & yours & the drawing [room] were lifted duly & taken away for beating today.” John had intended going back to Scotland soon after TC left, 11 Aug., but in the event did not return until 19 Aug. & that from & after this week, we can gather ourselves & go home when we like I think it is likely we may continue still for perhaps a week more. The first seven or eight nights, I had a great deal of haggling with my sleep; some of it painful, even wretched, though I always did get a proportion of sleep, good or bad; but Mary at last took the thing in hand & one afternoon contrived me what is equivalent to a real four post bed without the roof & with only half a side; but complete in the bottom part against all inroad of light (big clothes horse with big red table cover, firmly fixed with luggage straps) really an admirable bed in which I every night since [sleep] pretty much as well as usually at Chelsea and find it an immense relief and comfort in comparison to what preceded. All forenoon I sit reading, sub Dio [under the sky], exactly at half past 2 we get into a little shell of a four wheeled carriage light as a peascod
& with an eminent little bay pony, quiet & swift dash out for a drive of 14 miles or more whithersoever seems good to us. We dine punctually at six and are in general making into bed about midnight. Except Darwin,Charles Darwin; he and his family lived in Down House, Kent, about 3½ mi. (5.5 km.) S of Keston. Emma Darwin recorded in her diary that TC and Mary had visited Down House, 26 Aug. (Emma Darwin’s Diary, CUL.DAR.242[.39], transcribed Christine Chua, ed. John van Wyhe, Darwin Online, http://darwin-online.org.uk/). The Darwins had since gone to visit their eldest son, William Erasmus Darwin, living in Bassett, nr. Southampton; they were away 28 Aug.–11 Sept. Allingham later noted in his diary, 5 Oct.: “C.—‘We had a successful stay at Keston. Saw … Charles Darwin several times. I had not seen him for twenty years. He is a pleasant jolly-minded man … with much observation and a clear way of expressing it. Has long been an invalid. I asked him if he thought there was a possibility of men turning into apes again. He laughed much at this, and came back to it over and over again’” (Allingham Diary 239). TC apparently also expressed this idea to Forster, who wrote, 6 Sept.: “That visit to Philosopher Darwin must have been very agreeable, and it is to be hoped he will handle in his next Essay the very slight modification you propose in his system of merely beginning at the other end. We shall every one of us profit by that” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 20). TC had no belief in Darwin’s theory of evolution; see for instance 48:73. who has gone to Southampton since, we have seen, as it were, absolutely nobody. Darwin & family pleased me very much & indeed it is a good while since I have seen any brother mortal that had more of true sociability and human attraction for me. Erasmus D.Erasmus Darwin, Charles’s brother. we understand to be still in London, but that there is a chance for his coming down hither before we quite go away. One day, too, we called at Sir John Lubbock’s, found his Lady LubbockSir John Lubbock (1834–1913; ODNB), banker, politician, and scientist, friend of Darwin’s; his wife, m. 1856, was Ellen Frances (Nelly), b. Hordern (d. 1879), and they lived at High Elms, nr. Down House. very civil & assiduously obliging, but did not much take to her, nor by symptoms, to her Husband either who is commonly almost all week about London & who has never yet called except with his first card; and to say truth is not in any lively sense a desideratum here. I have had a good deal of walking through the woods here; almost every morning I pass that tree stump at the bottom of our park here where you read to me that of Hermann’s 100 feet StatueThe Hermannsdenkmal (Hermann Monument), 82 ft. (29 m.) high, was built by Joseph Ernest von Bandel (1800–1876), German sculptor and architect, to honor Arminius’s victory over three Roman legions at the Battle of Teutoburg Forest, 9 CE, in North Rhine-Westphalia; it was subsequently treated as a symbol of Prussia’s victory in the Franco-Prussian War. John visited TC and Mary at Keston for the day, 14 Aug., and again 18 Aug. & were cut off too abruptly for the adjoining details. I generally a little repent of that & wish I had you there to continue the palaver! I have no doubt you forgive me.

We saw Ruskin’s AllanGeorge Allen (1832–1907; ODNB), engraver and publisher, who lived at Sunnyside Villa, Orpington, Kent. Allen had been Ruskin’s publisher since 1870. one day at Sunnyside Orpington & got from him the
Fors of this monthRuskin’s Fors Clavigera, letter 57, “Michal’s Scorn” (Sept. 1875); see Ruskin’s Works 28:402–16. (which is good for little) and a whole half dozen or more of other little & bigger books, which I find to be superior stuff & have begun to read with real interest. Michelet several days ago I finished out; a most wonderful Book, wonderful, not admirable for it goes all dancing to one like a chaos; many parts of it difficult to understand with all one’s previous knowledge of the subject & totally unintelligible without; and the general result not the victory of the Reformation and partial restoration of God’s truth, but what M. calls the Renaissance, meaning thereby restoration or invention of the ballot box & for culmination the outburst and performance of the French Revolution; a fine genial creature, too, this M., though so wayward & from oneself so diverse. I design to have his Voll. bound,See TC to JF, 19 Aug.; TC’s copy: “Michelet (J.) Histoire de France, 17 vol. in 9, a correction in Carlyle’s writing on p. 133 of vol. V. half calf. 8vo. Paris, 1871–4”; see Sotheby’s (1932) 95. TC also contributed to the “Michelet Memorial” in 1877 (A. Carlyle, NL 2:314). however; & you shall read them if you have a mind.

Adieu, dear Brother; there is no right room for more. Send back poor old Alick’s photographTheir brother Alexander in Canada. (very sad & very touching to me); the rest of the enclosures, even Masson’s too,David Masson and his wife, Emily, both wrote to TC thanking him for the bust he had sent them. Emily Masson wrote, 16 Aug.: “I now write to thank you in Mr Masson’s name and my own for the truly kind and valuable present you have made us. The bust … is to stand in a suitable position and good light in our hall. It is in many points an excellent likeness, and my little girl, whom once you called ‘star-faced,’ recognized it the moment it was lifted from the case … and gave it a warm welcome.” The bust was a plaster cast (1873), sculpted by J. D. Crittenden (fl. 1853–78), and exhibited at the Royal Academy, 1874; it now belongs to the Edinburgh Public Library; see Isaac W. Dyer, A Bibliography of Thomas Carlyle’s Writings and Ana (1928) 536. are hardly worth returning. My heartfelt love to Jean & all of you. Ever your affectionate

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 Sept. MS: NLS 528.36. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I have received all your Letters, in due succession, and am very much obliged by your punctuality in reporting all that concerns the kindred in your
region. The letter you enclosed from young Alick of CanadaTheir nephew Alexander Carlyle in Canada. is exactly the double of one he had written hither to Mary & which I designed to enclose in my last to you but did not manage to do it, and thereby cut-off, to my regret, the explanation of several things that must have been obscure to you until Alick’s letter to yourself arrived. The photograph of poor Alick is very touching to me. It is liker by far than any of the former photographs, & it is mournfully old & has a spasmodic character of feebleness and frailty which goes to my very heart. Poor fellow, seemingly he is weaker even than myself; & his asthma is a specific burden from the like of which I thus far am spared. May the good God be with us all, and guide us mercifully to the end!—

We are going on here altogether in the style you last heard of, not worse in any respect. The most perfect solitude, ditto silence, scrupulous accuracy of service in every particular; Sleep fully as good as at Chelsea. In a word, nothing but our own indwelling sins, indigestions and corruptions to produce any wrinkle of ill-fortune in our minds. A great deal of reading gets transacted by me; not all of which is of a perfectly satisfactory nature;—especially Ruskin’s books, when he launches out upon high Art, are very hard reading, abstruse & fine-spun, yielding me next to no spiritual nourishment when I sum them up. I spent three days in wading through that dumpy little redbook,Edwin Paxton Hood, Thomas Carlyle: Philosophic Thinker, Theologian, and Poet (1875); see MAI to EPH, 30 Aug. which bears for title my own poor name & which must have come to Jean a day or two ago, having left this on Saturday. I found it a most surprising & to me incredible kind of Book; surely by a most well-meaning, but abstruse, weakish, confused & more or less absurd bewildered & bewildering man. I understand he is some kind of preacher & public lecturer: there came from him some time before the book, a most reverential bit of letter; and the prophecy, alas, included in it, that I was to see him at Chelsea and shake hands on my return. I do not advise either Jean or you to go deeper into the book than you respectively find pleasant. Profit there seemed to me to be little in it for any of us.John A. Carlyle replied, 10 Sept.: “The ‘dumpy book’ of Mr Hood came to Jean some days ago. … I looked into it last night, & found it only indifferent reading, though Mr H. has evidently done his best with it.” A reviewer in the Athenaeum was less kind: “It is rarely, indeed, that we meet with anything in prose that … is so inane as the volume before us; and we are all the more sorry to find this is the case, because Mr. Paxton Hood is not a new offender. … We find in his new production the same unbounded pretentiousness, the same turgid rhetoric, the same absence of thought, the same lack of critical insight [as in his previous writings]” (Athenaeum, 12 June).

A superfluity of letters, sorrowful, not joyful follows us out hither, mostly from Autograph hunters beggars & impertinent fools; nearly the only thing of rational and cheerful are Forsters weekly little notes. The last of which, produced yesterday, I here enclose, if you can take the trouble to decipher
it. No news yet of Erasmus Darwin coming over to Down, nor of his brother and family returning from Southampton. We have made no other visit or acquaintance of any kind; nor, I think intend any. Lady Derby speaks of being here about this day week or before it; after which we are earnestly entreated to stay;Lady Derby wrote, 5 Sept.: “I … wish you could know how much pleasure it gives me to think of your comfort & enjoyment at Keston. Will you prove that you believe me by consenting to prolong your stay until the fine weather leaves us? … We are going into Hampshire this week, & I was wishing to propose coming to call upon you in next week.” She visited TC, Mon. 13 Sept.; she then wrote to Charles Darwin, 14 Sept.: “I went … to Keston to see Mr Carlyle. … I suspect he is getting rather dull, & is half sorry to have been so unsociable to his neighbours on his first arrival!” (Darwin Correspondence Project, https:www.darwinproject.ac.uk/letter/DCP-LETT-10157.xml). Emma Darwin recorded in her diary that TC visited them again, 12 and 19 Sept. (see TC to JAC, 2 Sept.). but I rather guess the end after that will not be far.— Meanwhile we have a daily drive of some 15 or more miles in all varieties of direction, oftenest Beckenham or Croyden way; one day we got to Croydon altogether, a place profoundly impressive to me, when it suddenly dawned again out of the chaos of memory.TC had first visited Lady Harriet Ashburton at the Ashburtons’ estate at Addiscombe Park, nr. Croydon, 22 April 1843; see 16:134TC to LHB, 21 April [1843]; he and JWC visited many times over the years, continuing after the deaths of both Lady Harriet and Lord Ashburton, when the estate passed to Lady Louisa Ashburton; TC’s last recorded visit was 22 May 1872; see 48:64TC to JAC, 29 May 1872. By far the prettiest place we have seen is the Village of Westerham about eight miles to the westward of this;Westerham, ancient market town about 8 mi. (13.5 km.) S of Keston. a beautiful and bright place, hanging on a conical hill, in the bottom of a splendid green valley: nothing so beautiful hitherto have we met with in beautiful Kent. Another day we drove down to Eltham, not very far from Shooters HillEltham and Shooter’s Hill, about 8 mi. (12.5 km.) N of Keston. & looked again at the old palace, built by King Henry the Third,Henry III (1207–72; ODNB), king of England 1216–72, apparently spent Christmas 1270 at Eltham Manor, although it was not until the reign of Edward II (1284–1327; ODNB), king of England 1307–27, that it was developed into a royal palace. nay one day we were down all the way to SevenoaksSevenoaks, market town about 12 mi. (19 km.) SE of Keston. & staid ¾ of an hour there but that was decidedly too far a drive between 11 & 12 miles thither & again back.

And now, dear Brother, I will step out again to my balmy, green arena and convenient reading buttWord unclear; possibly “butt,” a small sheltered structure traditionally used when shooting game; otherwise unexplained. at the back of the house, where I have a volume of Southey’s WesleyRobert Southey (1774–1843; ODNB), poet and reviewer, poet laureate 1813–43; see 8:63; see also Carlyle, Reminiscences 386–401. Southey, The Life of Wesley; and the Rise and Progress of Methodism, 2 vols. (1820). Charles Wesley (1707–88; ODNB). & a pipe of tobacco waiting me,—the latter, I am sorry to say, fallen altogether from its high estate in my estimation & now hanging to me by mere use & wont rather than otherwise Give my love to Sister Mary, to my
Sister Jean including both their families, Ah me, Ah me. I quite agree with what you say of Jean’s coming hither & have had it in my mind from time to time for a long while back, were we once again planted down in our old moorings, the thing must be practically taken into consideration.Jean arrived in London for a visit to her brother on 21 Oct.; see TC to JAC, 26 Oct. Adieu, dear Brother: I am ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-EF, 15 Sept. MS: Trinity. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO EDWARD FITZGERALD

docBody.p: I was happy to see your old handwriting again & to hear the old tone of honest sympathy and friendliness holding out invincible against the flight of time and circumstance.FitzGerald wrote, 12 Sept.: “I do not write often because I do not wish to trouble you to dictate an answer, in return for the nothing I have to tell. And some one or another has generally told me a word about you… but I have let you alone now even more than half a year.” It is often a matter of some surprise and of more regret that you will not for these many years once step down to Chelsea and let me see your face again before that become impossible; but what can I say? You are perhaps wiser than myself in this matter; and at any rate a wilful man must have his way.

I am beautifully situated out here for the last five weeks in the daintiest of little hermitages three or four miles south of Bromley, alone with my niece and the pure breezes and charming woodlands, green knolls and hollows of lovely Kent;—which came to me as if it had all fallen from the sky by the assiduous bounty of a Great Lady, Lady Derby, to wit, who has always been very good to me since we first met when she was Marchioness of Salisbury.Lady Derby was the widow of James Gascoyne-Cecil, 2d marquess of Salisbury (d. 1868); they had been introduced to TC by Froude, 24 Feb. 1868; see 45:96TC to LN, 18 Feb. 1868; she m. Edward Henry Stanley, 15th earl of Derby, 1870. Many thanks, silent for most part, and long life to her gracious Ladyship. We are master, clear as Alexr SelkirkAlexander Selkirk (1676–1721; ODNB), Scottish mariner who was supposedly cast away on a desert island. was, of this beautiful hermitage with the great improvement over Alexander that every want of ours is provided for and all attendance, punctual as time, is ministered to us by two excellent servants & no duty left us to do except read at discretion amid the breezy woods and drive out every afternoon a fifteen miles or so in a convenient little phaeton gig or four wheeled carriage, light as a dried peas-cod, drawn by a most brisk little pony probably of mongrel breed but who bears the name of Shenstone on account of his great
appetite (now pretty much subdued by discipline) of making the attempt to call at every Inn.William Shenstone (1714–63; ODNB), writer; his poem “Written at an Inn at Henley” (Poetical Works of William Shenstone [Edinburgh, 1771] 152), extols the many virtues of an inn; for TC’s copy of this edn., see Sotheby’s (1932) 123. The county seems to me ill cultivated in comparison with Suffolk or Norfolk, but it wants only for perfect loveliness a sufficiency of running brooks which indeed is generally wanting in less chalky counties of the south. We have been to see all manner of places in these environs; one day we drove to Eltham, an ancient palace of Henry the Third;For Eltham palace, see TC-JAC, 9 Sept. many years ago I was once there already I had gone thither with Godefroi CavaignacEléonore Louis Godefroy Cavaignac (1801-45), French revolutionary republican; see 7:53TC to JSM, 17 Dec. 1833. He lived in England 1835–41, where he became friendly with the Carlyles; see 8:361–62TC to JAC, [25 June 1836], and 9:56–57JWC to SS, 11 Sept. 1836; see also Carlyle, Reminiscences 95. to see poor Edgeworth, whom you well remember,Francis Beaufort Edgeworth (1809–46), old friend of FitzGerald’s. who had nestled himself snugly enough in some corner of that huge ruin & where we found duly with his little Spanish Wife, but unluckily no “Pupils.”Edgeworth m., 1831, Rosa Florentina, b. Eroles; he tried, unsuccessfully, to set up a school in Eltham in 1836 (see Letters and Literary Remains of Edward FitzGerald, ed. W. A. Wright [1889] 1:36). There is no record of TC visiting him there with Cavaignac, but for his visit there with John Sterling, spring 1836, see Carlyle, Works 11:130-32. I searched earnestly for some trace, however faint of poor Edgeworth and his nest, but, alas, could find nothing: that side of the palace had been all cobbled up and plastered over with mortar & paint for behoof of some gentleman who “did business in the City”;Unidentified further. and that Edgeworth visit, which is still wholly a picture to me, has fled forever from all other mortals.
We still design to be here for a little while longer, but are dependent for the weather breaking into rain; upon which we make for Chelsea again and there rest.

I am really glad to hear of your sympathy with “Tooley” and the wild poetry and even in a sort divinity of that fine Norway Saint.FitzGerald wrote: “Your Norway Kings were quite delightful to me. We have a Saint Olave’s Priory on the River Waveney: the People call it ‘Saint Tuler’s,’ I wonder if an old Gentleman of Ipswich be of that kingly Blood: an Inscription there runs: ‘In peaceful silence let great Tooley rest, / Whose charitable Deeds bespeak him best.’ Perhaps this will make you smile a very little; and, if so, my letter will be something better than a bore.” The inscription refers to Henry Tooley (ca. 1470–1551; ODNB), merchant adventurer and burgess of Ipswich, Suffolk, who left most of his wealth to charities in Ipswich, in a trust which became known as Tooley’s Foundation. In “Early Kings of Norway” TC notes: “Speaking of the London Olaf Churches, I should have added that from one of these the thrice-famous Tooley Street gets its name,—where those Three Tailors, addressing Parliament and the Universe, sublimely styled themselves, ‘We, the People of England.’ Saint Olave Street, Saint Oley Street, Stooley Street, Tooley Street; such are the metamorphoses of human fame in the world!” (Carlyle, Works 30:284). Tooley St. is an ancient London thoroughfare S of the Thames; it was also the site of a devasting fire, 22 June 1861; see 37:176–77TC to JAC, 24 June 1861. Saint Olaf was Olaf II (d. 1030), king of Norway 1015–28, canonized for bringing Christianity to Norway; see Carlyle, Works 30: 260–84. The history of him is to
me like a bar of unwrought but genuine gold; he & his cousin Olaf Tryggveson,Olaf Tryggveson (d. 1000), king of Norway 995–1000; see Carlyle, Works 30:230–47. especially Olaf Saint himself, are a pair of chosen heroes to me.—

But I must end here dear F.; and go out to my reading while there is still an hour or two before Shenstone & his warmest welcome at an InnCf. the last line of Shenstone’s poem. come round upon us. Good bye, dear old Friend; I will not forget you while I continue in this scene of things.

bibl.sourceNote: MAI-EDC [ECO], 16 Sept. MS: Columbia. Hitherto unpbd. Ellen Dana Conway, b. Davis-Dana (1833–97), abolitionist, feminist, and Unitarian, m., 1858, Moncure Daniel Conway (1832–1907), Virginian abolitionist and Unitarian, and minister at the South Place Chapel, N London, 1864–84; he was introduced to TC by Emerson; see TC to JAC, 29 April 1863, and TC to MCON, 3 May 1863.
bibl.head: MARY AITKEN TO ELLEN DANA CONWAY

docBody.p: Many thanks to you for your kind & prompt reply to my by no means modest request.Mary had apparently asked Ellen Conway for help in finding a servant to replace “poor Lizzie”; see TC to JAC, 24 April. I the day I received your note heard of a young woman the daughter of a very good person in Chelsea whom Mme VenturiEmilie Venturi. & I have known for a long time & after some small preliminary difficulties owing to my not being able to go and see her, I today engaged her; so for the present I am in that happy condition described by the term suited. This is why I did not answer at once, as indeed I ought in any case to have done.
Poor little orphan, I should have liked very much to have her, but I already have far more responsibility than I like or find easy to undertake.

This is a very pretty place which Lady Derby has lent to my Uncle “for as long as he likes”; we have been here for five weeks and the change has done him a great deal of good. At Chelsea all is confusion; out of which seems to come no glimmering of Cosmos: this chiefly because, as David no doubt found when he had to employ people in the building of his cedar Mansion, “all men are liars,”Cf. 2 Sam. 5.11. We shall probably be returning however in about ten days;—our
maids are to be changed the day before we arrive so that we may enjoy their awkwardnesses with the other discomforts that will be going at the time.
We hope you have good news from Mr ConwayMoncure Conway was in the U.S. visiting his family. No doubt you will have had at least a telegram ere this.
With kind regards & many sincere thanks for your kind willingness to help me in my difficulty

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JF, 17 Sept. MS: FC. Quot: Sanders, Carlyle’s Friendships and Other Studies 219. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN FORSTER

docBody.p: This is only a word to thank you for your exemplary punctuality and great kindness in writing us those pleasant little weekly Dispatches. They are literally the jewel of our week’s correspondence, indeed almost the only part of it we are sure to get pleasure byForster wrote, 13 Sept.: “Mary … tells me she thinks you might miss even this small scrawl, so infinitesimal are your literary resources” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 22). and not fret & annoyance for the sad & habitual truth is nine tenths or more of the letters that come to me are mere blotches of impertinence and insignificance the real treatment of which for years back has been generally that of crumpling them together and flinging them into the fire.

You do not tell me so punctually and with such candid minuteness as I should wish, how your health really goes on and whether there are not more definite promises of improvement than you have the faith to let me know. In my own case, though I also am one of little faith, I can fairly recognise some traces of actual improvement, though I suppose always they will be quickly swept away again when I return to the embankment, with the dead porpoisesThe Times reported, 6 Sept.: “Porpoises in the Thames.— During the past fortnight several porpoises have been seen disporting themselves below and above London-bridge. One has been shot near the Cherry Tree Garden landing stage, Rotherhithe, and another was captured near Waterloo-bridge, and the carcass has been exhibited in the neighbourhood of the New-cut. The body of a dead porpoise has for the past week been floating up and down the Thames, to the great annoyance of excursionists owing to the offensive smell.” and other phenomena that are waiting there. And indeed the prospect of the winter to me is as ugly as to you;—and I have often been thinking in past months that we
should both of us make fairly ready and fly off for a trial of CintraCintra (or Sintra), resort nr. Lisbon where Forster’s friend Robert Lytton was ambassador; see TC to JAC, 13 Feb. for the two dismal months, December-February, in the dark hollow of the year? To you for years back I have constantly believed it could not fail to be beneficial.

Meanwhile all goes on with perfect equability in our strange sojourning here. Silence, solitude clear skies and tolerable sleep with nothing whatever to do but read books and drive to and fro between two and three hours on ShenstoneSee TC to EF, 15 Sept. & his phantom gig, all furnished and supplied as if the miraculous “Ravens”For Elijah and the ravens, see TC to JF, 19 Aug. were actually doing it, a thing unexampled hitherto in one’s biography. We do not yet think quite of going away, but cannot now be long about it, one would fancy. The very rain will come were there nothing else and warn us to be off. Meanwhile vis inertiæ (force of laziness itself) keeps one dormant.

I have read a great many Volumes, none of them quite excellent, but the worst of them not quite intolerable. Michelet is a strange creature, for whose ways of thinking I have a real sympathy, especially for his detestation of the papist “religion” and its infernal procedures in the last four centuries; no man can say more sincerely than does Michelet, Damn all that forever more. In short my Michelet agrees with me in almost everything till we come to the conclusion where M. turns round upon me & asks, “And is not this, then, that we have arrived at the actual Millenium and actual gate of heaven for all and sundry?”— Though with more of petroleum in it surely than one expected, answer I! Since then I have got into another French History book, Edgar Quinet on the French Revolution,Edgar Quinet, La Révolution; see TC to JAC, 11 Oct. 1873. which has some ideas in it of a true nature, but not many and a damnable iteration carried on in a loud tone of voice, wh. I cannot stand at all without occasionally skipping. But by tomorrow night I shall have done with him. One of my Books, surprizing to say has been Southey’s History of John Wesley & English Methodism. The view of that latter in particular has awakened manifold reflections in me & I do think the Protoplasm and other tadpole philosophies are fearfully and wonderfully illuminated by the blaze of human spiritualism indisputably springing out there among the rudest multitudes,—a thing which I cannot but hope may prove didactic one day, far beyond what it seems at present.

Alfred Tennyson’s, so-called, Shakespearian TragedyTennyson, Queen Mary: A Drama (1875). I had read before leaving home. With little disappointment, but with a dismal inclination to
exclaim, Scene after scene, “Did you ever?”Coterie speech; see 30:210. Browning’s new dramaticsRobert Browning, Aristophanes’ Apology (1875). are I trust awaiting my return.

Adieu, dear Forster! Here is enough of such babble. Sometime ago I had a pleasant note from Lady Ashburton at Inverary.Lady Ashburton wrote, 4 Sept.: “I was indeed delighted to get your dear letter this morng. … Mary & I are here at this delicious place [Inverary] with these delightful people. … Princess Louise is here, & I am quite bewitched by her—so much intelligence, fun, high feeling and distinction in all ways—the Marquis must be proud of his Princess wife—all my life I have had a true affection & admiration for Duke & Duchess. I like their ways altogether.” Inverary Castle, Argyll, home of the duke and duchess of Argyll (see TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1873); their son John George Campbell (1845–1914; ODNB), marquess of Lorne, m., 1871, Princess Louise Caroline (1848–1939; ODNB), da. of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. If you know her present address, please send it me.Forster replied, 20 Sept. “Of my Lady’s movements, I speak with misgiving. After she left Inverary she went to a castle on the Border, ‘Castle Coldstream’ in Northumberland. … and I fancy your safest address will be Seaton” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 27). Forster means Ford Castle, Northumberland, about 4 mi. (6.5 km.) E of Coldstream in the Scottish Borders. With my kindest regards to your dear Wife & self, Ever yours

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 Sept. MS: NLS 528.37. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I must write you a few lines today before the week end,—though it is only to assure you that all remains in statu quo and that nothing has gone with us or with our still existence here, since you heard of us last.

Some neighbours here,Presumably John Farnaby and Julia Lennard, see note 4; otherwise unidentified. with whom Mary had gone to Lunch persuaded us to drive over to a grand “Harvest Home” at a place called Wickham Court,Wickham Court, West Wickham, Kent. some 4 or 5 miles west; we went accordingly; found a large tent in an extensive, green enclosure and 100 or 200 Sunday-clothed individuals, many of them persons of quality, traces of what appeared to have been an enormous dinner and little else going on, except idle strolling round the Tent and bottoms of brandy (or Mary says it was merely beer) going out in moderation by peasants kindly disposed to treat their wives & children The Harvest-Home was not interesting, but reminded me of Scotsbrig and other “kirns,” with
which it was in strong contrast, whether to its advantage or not. It seems there had been as is usual a religious service in a church hard by much festooned with wheat-ears &c but the church was locked before we came, and, rather to my comfort, not so much as the wheat-ears to be seen. The manor house, hard by, is a beautiful old place, dating from Edward IV, and once a possession of the Boleyns,Wickham Court was built during the reign of Edward IV (1442–83; ODNB), king of England 1461–70; it was the home of Sir Henry Heydon (d. 1503), who m. Anne Boleyn, great-aunt of Anne Boleyn (ca. 1501–36; ODNB), queen of England 1533–36. but now belonging to somebodyThe estate now belonged to John Farnaby Lennard (1816–99); it had been owned by the Lennard family for over 400 years, but the original baronetcy had lapsed when the last baronet’s illegitimate son succeeded to the estate, but not the title. Lennard’s birth name was Cator, having inherited the estate through the maternal line; he was made baronet in 1880. who is married to a daughter of Hallam’s,Lennard m., as his 2d wife, 1852, Julia Maria Frances, b. Hallam (1818–88), da. of Henry Hallam (1777–1859; ODNB), historian, known to TC since 1838 (see 10:66TC to JAC, 12 April 1838), and one of the initial supporters of the London Library; see 11:6–7TC to JF, 17 Jan. 1839. an innocent-looking elderly lady by whom and whose daughterLaura Lennard, da. of John Farnaby Lennard and his 1st wife, m. 1847, Laura, b. Golding (d. 1850). we were introduced into the house; and saw amongst other less memorable things a very fine picture of Raleigh,Portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh (1554–1618; ODNB), and his eldest son, Walter (1593–1618), dated 1602, artist unknown; now in the National Portrait Gallery, London. by far the best I have yet seen. A windy drive to AddingtonAddington, village in Surrey about 2 mi. (3 km.) SW of Wickham Court. & back brought us two home in time.

Yesterday, by express invitation, we made out our little invitation to the Lubbocks;Sir John and Lady Ellen Lubbock; see TC to JAC, 2 Sept. L. himself is a rational looking, not very distinguished man of Science, Politics and opulent Banking; tallish, thinnish with small brisk grey eyes and a bald crown surrounded by manifold drawers of imprisoned ants, wasps &c with whom he occupies himself. He has a sickly looking Lady Lubbock who is an ardent accompaniment in these pursuits; a great number of scientific or quasi-scientific people attend him on Saturdays and Sundays: last Sunday in coming home from Darwins we met in one of those lanes that pass through Lubbockdom Tyndall, home from Switzerland strolling there with SpottiswoodeJohn Tyndall and William Spottiswoode (1825–83; ODNB), mathematician and printer, were staying with the Lubbocks, and had walked over to visit TC at Keston Lodge; Tyndall recalled: “[TC] was absent; but as we returned we met him and his niece … driving home in a pony-carriage. I had often expressed to him the wish that he and Darwin might meet; for it could not be doubted that the nobly candid character of the great naturalist would make its due impression. The wish was fulfilled. He met us with the exclamation: ‘Well, I have been to see Darwin.’ He paused, and I expressed my delight. ‘Yes,’ he added, ‘I have been to see him, and a more charming man I have never met in my life’” (Tyndall, “Personal Recollections” 31). the big Printer, which latter brought a very sad reminiscence to me.William Spottiswoode and his wife, m. 1861, Eliza Taylor, b. Arbuthnot (1837–94), were to have been at the tea party JWC had planned for 21 April 1866, the day she died; see 43:208JWC to TC, [19 April 1866], and 212JWC to TC, [21 April 1866]. TC later wrote “Spottiswoodes King’s Printer people. I durst never see them since. … 1869” (TC’s note in Froude, LM 3:335); see also 43:211JWC to TC, [21 April 1866].
