I am reading extensively, have finished Michelet long since; gone through Southeys Wesley too with multifarious reflections and an interest which goes with me far beyond that of the origin of Species, and indeed has not been articulated yet. Today I am to finish off a certain Edgar Quinet on the French Revolution; not a very domineering man, though he thinks himself one, but really containing some ideas, which may be new in France and useful there. After him, I take up Lubbocks Prehistoric Times,Sir John Lubbock, Pre-Historic Times, as Illustrated by Ancient Remains (1865). but don’t expect much from it. After which, there is no book left, though plenty are procurable.

Lady Derby was here on Monday, beautifully urgent that we should not run away till the last of the good weather had come; every thing is ready for us at Chelsea it seems, but it is very likely the very force of indolence may keep us here for another week or more,—unless the weather do break which has been supremely good all along hitherto. Today we have in view to take Down & the Darwins in our excursion; tho’ nothing of Erasmus I fear still is visible there.

We were very glad to hear of all being well in the home country and that James of Newlands’ little infants were got out of danger again.James Carlyle Jr. wrote to John A. Carlyle from Newlands, 4 Sept.: “Here we have had Measles for the last three weeks. Our eldest girl is mending nicely; the next two are ‘past the worst’; Aitken is doing well but is still very sick, while Tom’s state is at present the cause of much anxiety to us” (MS: NLS 1775F.175). John then wrote to TC, 10 Sept.: “I had a note from Newlands in which young James tells me his children were recovering from the measles.” I hope you have written or will soon write I send my heart’s love to all of you, Jean & Mary especially included; and am ever

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 2 Oct. MS: NLS 528.38. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
We got prosperously home on Thursday lastTC and Mary arrived home Thurs. 30 Sept. and have been solitarily arranging and adjusting many little items in the new household ever since. All
is bright and splendidly clean, even in Mary’s judgement; the two women servantsAnn and Rose; see MAI to ECO, 16 Sept. Ann was the cook, Mrs Warren having left Cheyne Row, and Rose the general servant (see TC-JAC, 15 Dec. 1875; MS: NLS 528.46). are eligible effective looking creatures and it is piously hoped and expected that things will turn out well and the late revolution, which has cost me so much botheration and irritation and her so much incessant industry will turn out to have been a really prosperous adventure and well worth all the trouble. Heaven grant it may, for I am passionately desirous of being at rest again in my own premises and getting into my poor old habits and pitiful “employments” as I am obliged in the language of flattery still to name them. My health I do sometimes think is really a little improved by the late rustication. At all events I am certainly not worse and am very glad to have it handsomely done at any rate. In a little while we shall certainly need Jean here for a good quiet visit and unlimited conversation and I commission you to give her notice to that effect and to persuade her to the enterprise by all methods you have.John A. Carlyle replied, 3 Oct.: “I entirely agree with you in regard to our sister Jean’s going to spend a few weeks with you. It would do her & you & Mary good, & should not be put off much longer. We have wet weather here at present as you have in London, but before the end of October it will probably become more favourable; & it now takes only eight hours & a half to get to London from Dumfries.” Jean Aitken wrote, 10 Oct.: “I am very glad to hear there is a probability of our seeing each other once more before very long. I am really begun to gather myself together & hope to come to you in quite tolerable health. … I am very swear to come out of my shell or even go out at all but I hope the change may do us all good.” It is a thing I have had in my eye this long time, and it will give me great disappointment if it do not take effect. I will write to herself about it before long in fact so soon as the house is thoroughly quieted and I need not say that no furtherance on my part shall be wanting.

Forster and his belongings came up from Melchet the same day as we from Keston. The day was bright and sunny for us all; the only bright day there has since been; I called yesterday but did not find Forster at home, was only assured that the journey had been prosperous, and that both F. & his Wife were in favourable case: but I have yet seen or definitely heard from himself nothing whatever; and indeed the weather, today a pouring rain has not been favourable in any sense;Forster apparently visited TC later in the day; he wrote, 3 Oct.: “The rain and damp, alas! have put an extinguisher on my Kew hopes. … Even yesterday, on my return from you, I found the air colder than was well for me” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 29). and nobody, not even Darwin,Erasmus Darwin, living at 6 Queen Anne St. knows that we are yet returned.

I will send Jean’s MagazineMagazine unidentified. on Monday, though I doubt she will get little good of it. To yourself today, I send a miserable pluister of a thing called Contemporary Review which the foolish EditorJames Thomas Knowles (1831–1908; ODNB), architect, ed. of the Contemporary Review 1870–77. (whom you saw at Miss Bromley’s last time) insists on sending me. I glanced through it the first night here, but doubt if there is one article which you will bother yourself with reading. If you fancy Dr Russell could get any good of it, you might push it on to him.John replied, 4 Oct.: “I will send on the Review to Dr & Mrs Russell, as there is at least one article in it, on West Indian Superstitions which will interest them much. I read it aloud to Jean & James in the forenoon.” Dr. James and Mary Russell, old friends of the Carlyles; see 48:166TC to JAC, 19 Feb. 1873. I have been and still am occupied almost exclusively with this monthly garbage of magazinery, and shall perhaps next week have other specimens to send you. The Fraser has gone off to Walter Welsh. There is in it one excellent Article by Profr. Owen on the Oil Springs, chiefly of Pennsylvania,Richard Owen, “On Petroleum and Oil-Wells,” Fraser’s Magazine 12 (Oct. 1875): 437–49. which I found greatly superior to anything I had read in a magazine for long months or years. You would see by the Canada newspaper (which Mary thinks she sent) that Alick Carlyle is actually appointed to the Professorship of Natural Sciences, which he was in quest of.Their nephew Alexander Carlyle; he had worked as a headmaster in several schools, and then was approached “by a Commission from … Albert University … who asked me to give up my Headmastership and come to the College as their Professor of Natural Sciences [autumn 1875]. … The University seemed to have no endowment, was poorly equipt and it was very ill provided with money. I liked my duties there, but the salary was not paid with regularity, nor was it sure being of being paid at all. … For these and other reasons I left it and got another Headmastership [Sept. 1876], in the Port Rowan High School” (Ian Campbell, “Jottings on Alexander Carlyle’s Life and Work,” Carlyle Annual 11 [1990]: 69). There is no particle of news farther here or from any quarter; so I ought to terminate my raw material being fairly done. I brought with me a book Prehistoric Times,Presumably John Lubbock’s Pre-Historic Times; see TC to JAC, 18 Sept. which is not well written at all, but contains many details about kitchen-middens, Lake-Cities &c, which might perhaps be interesting to JamesJames Aitken, to whom TC sometimes sent books on historical matters; see for instance 42:225 and 46:3. or to you. With my kindest love to one and all,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 7 Oct. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: It was very kind of you to write to me at once from Inverary, and I felt it a great satisfaction, and deliverance to my thoughts. I meant to answer at once by a letter to wait at Norham;Norham, village in Northumberland, near Ford Castle where Lady Ashburton stayed on her way home from Inverary; see TC to JF, 17 Sept. but, alas, my weak and empty mode of existence betrayed me at that time; and, all along, as you too well know, my good intentions went all a bad road!—

I returned hither on Sep. 30, and the first sure news I had of you was from Forster or rather from your own servant Henry at Kent House,Lady Ashburton’s new home in Knightsbridge. who charmed me by the announcement that you were in town at that very time, still possible to be seen before going off for Melchet, if I were lucky. I was not lucky as you know. But I called again yesterday; and the almost frightened Housemaid (judging me perhaps a robber in disguise) informed me that you were now at Seaforth Lodge and intending to be here on Friday coming I have only in brief to beg that you will let me see you on that occasion. I will come there at any hour you appoint, or next day at any hour; and I do much wish to see you again, and hear freely of all that has come and gone since you went to Scotland and of what is like to come still when you go to Egypt!Lady Ashburton planned to visit Egypt at the end of the year.

Miss Bromley informs me this morning that she is at CreweCaroline Bromley wrote, 14 Oct.: “I look forward to seeing you at the end of the month when I return to Barnes. … I have had a peaceful month here in the old Home taking long walks with my brother’s children & painting most days.” Her brother was William Bromley Davenport, living at Capesthorne, Crewe; he had six children. with a party none of whom I know. It is the first word I have yet heard from her,—so vacant has my life at Keston &c been.
My kindest regards to dear Mary. I ever am

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 Oct. MS: NLS 528.39. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature in blue pencil.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: There is nothing whatever in the shape of news to treat you with; but a line or two from my hand testifying that little will be welcome to you on the Sunday morning.

Nobody has yet come to town whom I know about! DarwinErasmus Darwin. I called for one day, but found him gone out, and he has not yet got hither. Considerably better his housemaid reported him, wh. is so far comfortable. Allingham has been here twice: apparently all happiness; he is better than nobody to break the solitude of my walk; but indeed after all that is a small improvement. I called on TyndallJohn Tyndall, living in an apartment at the Royal Institution, Albemarle St. yesterday and on Lady Stanley, but the latter was gone to Cortachy (her daughter Airlie’s place)Henrietta Maria, Lady Stanley, living at 40 Dover St., London. Her da. Henrietta Blanche, 5th countess of Airlie, lived at Cortachy Castle, Angus, 32 mi. (51.5 km.) NE of Perth. & Tyndall was out to his clubs There has come a letter from Froude after so many months of delay; clear, cheerful and interesting, though only on the political topics of Cape Colony; about which he seems to be hopeful, especially if the Home Authorities will have courage to dismiss their present Governor and Parliament, and dare appoint Sir Garnet WolsleySir Garnet Joseph Wolseley (1833–1913; ODNB), army officer, appointed high commissioner of Natal, South Africa, by Lord Carnarvon, with the task of advancing the cause of federalism in southern Africa; see TC to JAC, 6 Aug. Froude advised Carnarvon to dismiss Barkly as governor of the Cape Colony and replace him with Wolseley. with full power instead. I will send you the letter and would have done so today, but it has gone to Lady Derby and has not yet returned.Lady Derby wrote, Oct. 9: “I am very grateful to you for having sent me Mr Froude’s interesting letter. I heard two days ago from Lord Carnarvon that ‘Sir H. Barkley has been compelled to summon the Cape Parliament to meet on the 10th of November which is likely to destroy his Govt. He would not have done it, could he possibly have avoided it.’ If Sir H.B. should lose his appointment in this way it would even be a greater triumph for Lord Carnarvon than if he recalled him.” The day before yesterday, I was surprised & somewhat cheered by a visit from Masson who has gone again today, after completing some small Miltonic researches here. He has still a Volume to doDavid Masson, The Life of John Milton; see TC to JAC, 1 Jan. 1874; see also 48:207TC to WDC, 18 June 1873. and is patiently doing it of that dismal Farrago, but seems heartily weary and less ambitious of any
result than of simply getting done. The wicked IcelanderFor the Icelander, unidentified further, see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. 1873. brought me a mournful but not mad or ill-given account of his dreary circumstances here but this also I detain, having some small vestige of attempt to make to help the poor devil;—which is to be tried I expect this very day

My sleep has been bad during the week past, but I have taken my medicament; and all hands are busy here sorting up the innumerable items at present locked aside into there [sic] accustomed habitats. I am daily reading a huge folio history of Henry VIII by Lord Herbert of Cherbury;Edward Herbert (ca. 1582–1648; ODNB), 1st Baron Herbert of Cherbury, The Life and Raigne of King Henry the Eighth (1649). I came upon it as if by mistake, seeking something else of little significance, and was struck by the many fine & solid qualities it shews, much to my surprise, and after Michelet do get some real good of it by dint of skipping extensively. Our two servants continue to seem praiseworthy creatures, especially the elder who is an excellent Cook & seems in every way a highly respectable servant. In a little while things will be all in their place again, and I shall be at rest in the former statu quo, which will be highly welcome to me. In the course of not many days we hope to write with fixed dates &c of Jean’s coming to us and trust in the meanwhile that she is getting everything in readiness for starting with due promptitude. Give my kindest love to her and accept the same yourself with all the other branches young & old. Today I send off a book to James, which no doubt he will let you see, sooner or later; both of you, I conceive, may be able in time to get through it.
Adieu, dear Brother,
I am and remain

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 Oct. MS: NLS 528.40. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
There is nothing here for you but one or two letters of little or no significance which ought to have been sent on Saturday had not the hurry been so great. It appears, at any rate you are away from homeJohn A. Carlyle wrote, Mon. 18 Oct., that he had been to Scotsbrig, Sat. – Mon., to visit their brother Jamie and his son John and family; he had also visited their nephew James and family at Newlands, and Miss Currie at Newfield; see TC to JAC, 13 Feb. & would not have got
them till today. Froude’s letter is the only one that can have any interest,—which will be rather increased by seeing from Lady Derby’s note that the victrix causa [victorious cause] has in this instance proved to be Froude’s and that the present worthless Governor is to be replaced by WolseleySee TC to JAC, 9 Oct. Henry Barkly in fact stayed in post till his retirement, 1877, and Wolseley returned to Britain in Oct. in whom, so far as I can judge there is real hope. You got the GreenwoodProbably Frederick Greenwood (1830–1909; ODNB), journalist and author, founder and editor of the Pall Mall Gazette. Letter about Emile Montégut & the ill-famed Icelander;For Émile Montégut, see TC to ÉM, 15 May. John wrote, 23 Aug.: “[Montégut’s] three projects … all seem questionable. He would surely be better … writing what he can for the Revue des Deux Mondes … than in making excursions in England, writing for English journals”; there is no record of him writing for the Pall Mall Gazette. Montégut was probably working on a review of both TC’s Early Kings of Norway and George Webbe Dasent (1817–96; ODNB; see 44:37–38TC to JAC, 16 Aug. 1866), Scandinavian scholar, The Vikings of the Baltic (1875), pbd. as “Les derniers Vikings et les premiers rois du Nord,” Revue de Deux Mondes 17 (1876): 342–86. Possibly the Icelander was to help Montégut with research in early Norse. which gave me real satisfaction, seeing some plausible hope for M’s behoof & at least a kind of possibility for the wretched Icelander. I enclose his Letter now, which at least testifies to the wonderful progress he has made in English & to the still more wonderful tenacity of heart he shews in his wrestle with misery. Perhaps the poor soul is not so wicked as rumour makes him; it appears Vigfusson does not know him personally at all, & to me the other witnesses are also unknown. I at least have without trouble managed to give him the one vestige of help that lay in my power;John wrote, 20 Oct.; “The Icelander’s [letter] I will keep. Let us hope that he may soon get some employment on your recommendation. He has plenty of talent, & does not seem to be at all a bad man, only proved obstinate & difficult to deal with; & it was only on that account that Vigfusson kept clear of him.” For John’s friend Gudbrand Vigfusson and his earlier remarks about the Icelander, see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. 1873. and so let him disappear into the fire or whither you like.

The most important bit of news I have yet altogether of a private nature is that I have actually been to a dentist & started on the adventure of having some approach to a new set of teeth. Mary took me up on Saturday, “Manchester Square” is the place.William R. Balland, M.D. surgeon dentist, 26 Manchester Sq. The man seemed to me to be a real artist in his business & has done me already a great deal of good by cutting out (which he did without the least pain) the half dozen or more of miserable scrags & snags of sharp bone that have kept my tongue miserable for above a year; I have in a humble way some actual hope to get an essential improvement accomplished in that department and a kind of ability to chew food restored to me. If I do succeed you shall have no rest till you also go and achieve a similar result. I have had great difficulty, though our new cook is excellent, to get
panada made for me in late days of a sort that I can really eat, simply and solely for want of teeth, the substance itself being generally savoury & wholesome enough so far as I could judge Darwin whom I visited on Saturday was looking miserably ill, suffering under vague ague fits, but still patient, quiet and almost cheerful: I am very sorry about him and have bad anticipations, especially when in bad spirits. Forster was dreadfully ill at Brighton for a week,Forster wrote from Brighton, 10 Oct.: “This is just a little line, dear Carlyle, to say that my poor enterprise here has been a disastrous failure. … Alas, I have been basically ill ever since I came—the acidity most terrible—as if my liver had struck work altogether. We are driven back—I think tomorrow. The only doubt is whether I may be well enough to travel” (Kinser and Tarr, III, 30). but the weather has mended here and yesterday I found him looking unusually well A difficulty of poor Allingham’s with some stupid translator set me into looking at Goethe’s 49th Vol.Allingham noted in his diary, 12 Oct.: “C.’s. Walk with him to Piccadilly. Goethe’s Sprüche [Sayings] very hard to translate. ‘I found, when I was translating from the German writers that each man has a tune: Goethe has his; Richter has his, and, when I got into it, all went on well. That was the pleasantest kind of work I ever did. I could do it in any mood—like basket-making. Goethe’s style is by far the most refined and most difficult to render’” (Allingham Diary 239). Allingham had commissioned “Maxims and Reflections from the German of Goethe,” translated by Mathilde Blind (1841–96), for Fraser’s Magazine (March 1876). Goethe, “Einzelnheiten, Maximen und Reflexionen,” Nachgelassene Werke [Posthumous Works], Werke, 54 vols. (Stuttgart, 1833) vol. 49. Jean Paul Richter (1763–1825); for TC’s translations of him, see Carlyle, Works 22:115–332. & I was dragged into reading nearly the whole of it again; naturally the best bit of reading I have had for many a day. We are delighted to hear that Jean means to come immediately.John wrote, 20 Oct.: “Jean is making preparations for starting by the midday train for London tomorrow.” Things are in perfect readiness or if improvments are still wanted Mary & she may, with added convenience, effect them in consort. The weather at present is decidedly good October weather, dry for most part & hardly ever very dismally wet
God bless you all I am ever & always

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 26 Oct. MS: NLS 528.41. Quot: Sanders, Carlyle’s Friendships and Other Studies 219. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Accept from me a hasty word, for I am considerably hurried & fussed about; but I wish at least to tell you that we are all well here, and that I have
got my dental operation finished and have since yesterday the new teeth in my head. They fit remarkably well & I think will need few modifications when I return to the artist tomorrow: on the whole if I am not much disappointed they will really be of use to me capable of eating meat unpounded;—in which case you may depend upon it, I will zealously urge you to go & do likewise; no doubt there are good dentists in Edinr, Jean’s man in particular seems to have been very skilful and expert;John A. Carlyle replied, 31 Oct.: “I was glad to hear that your operations with the Dentist had been so far successful. … I should like to have more particulars of what was done, for I myself too suffer much from want of teeth, & have not been successful with dentists hitherto.” Jean Aitken had got a new set of teeth in Aug.; she wrote, [24 Aug.]: “I had for some time been speculating on a journey to Edinburgh to try to get a set of teeth” and John had reported, 3 Sept.: “Jean finds her new teeth quite painless still, keeps them on at night.” week in Edinr at any time would do the job for you, or if you wait till next visit to London I can ensure you of by far the best dentist I have ever seen.

figure.p:
Jean and Mary Aitken, early 1870s
Thomas Carlyle Papers, Rare Book & Manuscript Library,
Columbia University in the City of New York

docBody.p:
Jean is pretty well; is taking kindly to her new lodging & fast getting accustomed to the new bits of conditions available to her here. She has had a long walk & sail in the steamboatsThe London Steamboat Company had recently reduced their fares; their advertisement in the London Standard announced, 8 Oct.: “Penny boats every ten minutes daily. … Chelsea to Lambeth, Lambeth to London Bridge … and vice versa. Two-penny Boats every Ten Minutes, Chelsea to London Bridge, Westminster to Tunnel … and vice versa. Three-penny Boats every Half-hour, London Bridge to Greenwich and vice-versa. Four-penny Boats every Half-hour, Westminster to Greenwich, London Bridge to Woolwich, and vice versa.” For a photograph of Jean and Mary, taken either this year or a year or two earlier, see 254. along with Mary She & I I hope are going out today for a turn in the Hyde Park region. She reads a great deal works diligently also with her knitting or her sewing needles & is very interesting company to me. I am farther, for myself, looking out strenuously as I can for some vestige of real work to try at. I have bethought me in the first place of some bits of translation from Goethe’s Nachgelassene WerkeSee TC to JAC, 18 Oct. which I by accident steered into the other day & found that I had never read completely or in part at all. Two hours a day at this would be the chief salve to all my sores for I find daily that if one can do no work whatever it is better not to have the trouble to live at all, however old you may be. The weather for three days after Jean came was wet itself & mud itself but the last three days have been perfectly dry & one of them, yesterday altogether sunny & bright;—on which occasion Jean surveyed the embankment & wandered extensively about by herself during our absence at the dentist’s. Darwin I have never seen again since the time I mentioned to you; I fear much he is still aguish & unwell & mean to go & see without delay. Forster has still a great deal of everything to transact every evening but is to me evidently stronger & livelier, doing a little work at
his SwiftSee TC to JF, 4 Aug.; Forster was now working on the second volume. & complaining only that it is so little: medicine, it is clear, can do him no good; in nothing but nature & her vis medicatrix [healing power] is there hope of throwing out the poison that is lodged in the poor bodily system; he has still a fair appetite for victuals & for a man of 63 or 64 has still good energies. Various other people are coming home & the town is beginning to be populous again; but I have seen nobody except twice or thrice poor Lady Ashburton who is suffering much from throat disorders threatening to become pulmonary & has resolved by the advice of all her drs. on a winter in Egypt, for which under many bothering disappointments she is daily & hourly making ready, goes on the 6th Nov. coming, straight for Marseilles & the French steamer; & has from that point all manner of boatmen, dragomans, couriers Nile boats preengaged for carrying her directly up to NubiaNubia, region of southern Egypt, now divided between Egypt and Sudan; Lord and Lady Louisa Ashburton had honeymooned in Egypt; see 35:15–16TC to LA, 30 Jan. 1859. there to continue for so many months, her house a splendid boat on the Nile to which her chief difficulties seem to consist in getting proper friends to attend her I am really sorry for the endless chaos of confusions in which the poor lady seems to be involved; & I cannot but think six months of locking up the whole of them in the Rumpelkammer [storeroom] may prove a salutary deliverance for her.

Jowett has sent me a copy of his new Plato;Benjamin Jowett (1817–93; ODNB; see 35:173TC to JAC, 22 Aug. 1859), master of Balliol Coll., Oxford, The Dialogues of Plato, translated into English with Analyses and Introductions, rev. edn., 5 vols. (1875). 5 bright looking volumes; but I must not begin upon them just now. Have you seen Alfred Tennyson’s sublime Tragedy?Tennyson, Queen Mary; see TC to JF, 17 Sept. — Mary says you read in while here, & I conjecture will not long to know more of it; but will have to read the newspaper comments on the acting of it,A correspondent to the Scotsman wrote, 18 Aug.: “I understand that before ‘Queen Mary’ can be compressed into the dimensions of an ordinary working play, it will have to be reduced by at least one half, for the play as it stands would take no fewer than six hours to act. … I need hardly add that Mr Tennyson has in the kindest manner recognised the necessity of curtailing his work in order to meet the exigencies of the London stage.” I suppose. To me it seems no more stone-dead, ineffectual “Tragedy” had ever come across my experience;—at all events for me it shall fight its own battle & do me neither ill n’a gudeCoterie speech. from this date. Ruskins last ForsRuskin’s Fors Clavigera, letter 58, “The Catholic Prayer” (Oct. 1875); see Ruskin’s Works 28:417–38. awoke in us here the dreadful idea that he was losing his wits but in a day’s time this horrid idea dissipated itself again & I could only perceive still with real regret what a mad & ruinous career he was running & like to run,
with such a splendid outfit of faculty and opportunity, one would have said, as few of his generation had been gifted with. He is at Oxford again I suppose; but there comes no vestige of notice from him for many weeks back. Jamie of NewlandsTheir nephew James Carlyle, Jr.; John replied, 31 Oct.: “James of Newlands sent some partridges & a rabbit to me also last week, & reported that his boys had got almost entirely clear of their severe measles.” has sent us a box of Game & MaryMary Austin, their sister. an excellent 3 doz. of Eggs; tell her by next opportunity how dear her lively affection, continued to the last always is to me. Tell me what you are doing, how you are getting on: I am, with affection increasing instead of diminishing, ever yours, dear Brother,

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 6 Nov. MS: NLS 528.42 Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:315–16. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We are going on here much as usual still in considerable confusion but with the continual hope that all things to the last item will be reduced to order and that we shall then have quiet use and wont only in an improved form.The house in Cheyne Row had been thoroughly cleaned in their absence, and two new servants had been employed; see TC to JAC, 2 Sept., and 2 Oct. The weather itself is a considerable confusion very irregular in its alternations of wet and dry that is of west & east; but on the whole generally admitting the possibility of a reasonable walk without Mackintoshes to any and all of us which the majority diligently take advantage of. Jean herself goes out most days and is a superior walker, much stronger than I, but with very little knowledge of localities and not fit or inclined to venture out alone She works a great deal besides reading within doors & professes to feel in better health. The only day of thorough wet we have lately had was yesterday and even yesterday between four and five p. m. cleared itself up into damp composure inviting a dyspeptic walker to go out.

A good number of people are by this time come to town indeed I think plenty or more than enough for my purposes for nobody’s “company” is of high interest to me but perhaps is advantageous sometimes by inducing reasonable talk instead of brooding silence. LeckyWilliam Edward Hartpole Lecky; see TC to JAC, 1 Jan. 1874. & Allingham are my most frequent visitors; American Motley, a man of more gifts & deeper character
than either is back in England, still very infirm and no doubt very sorrowful,—I called the other day; but only left a card & expect him here when things favour.John Lothrop Motley; he suffered from paralysis, and his wife had d. 31 Dec. 1874; see TC to JLM, 19 April. He wrote, 14 May: “We sail for America 19th June returning in October—
after wh. one of my first visits will with your permission be to you.” Forster never stirs out except to the covered walk in the Horticultural.The Horticultural Society’s gardens in South Kensington, which had a covered promenade; see TC to JAC, 8 Jan. 1874. I see him about once a week in his own room,—he is really in greater strength but his cough at 5 p. m is still punctual like a clock & keeps him in great distress till far in the night.

My dentist speculation involving a journey to Manchester Square,See TC to JAC, 18 Oct.; Manchester Sq. is in Marylebone, about 3 mi. (5.5 km.) N of Chelsea. with extremely punctual date has bothered me not a little since I last wrote & today at 3 sharp I am due there; the first time this week but my persuasion has been that after all the enterprise is lost & my multifarious fash & expense gone for nothing. The apparatus in my mouth is perfectly easy & even welcome there; but it will by no means fix itself; & at every meal for ten days past I have had on the most cautious trial to find it cant up & require to be immediately laid aside Today I mean to ascertain as credibly as possible whether the artist ever expects it to fix itself; and if so, when. If never I will cheerfully lay the article into some repository and wash my hands (and my three remaining teeth) of it for the rest of my life. You shall hear what the event is.

I have roughly translated that “spiritual” fraction of Goethe & enclose it for you today.Goethe, “Geistes epochen, nach Hermanns neusten Mitteilungen” [“Epochs of the Human Spirit, based on Hermann’s Latest Theories”], (Goethe, Werke 49:3–6). In this essay Goethe describes the development of the human mind as the result of reason and understanding, out of which emerges four epochs of the human spirit: the ages of poetry, theology, philosophy, and prose. Mary says nobody can read it; but I doubt not you, with help of the original will make it out; & I want your serious consideration of it; and any help you can give me in mending it. “Tohu wa bohu” for instance evidently means chaos come again; but where does the phrase come from“Tohu wa-bohu,” is a Hebrew phrase from Gen. 1.2 meaning desolate and formless, describing the condition of the earth immediately before the creation of light. will any of your dictionaries indicate? also what is “Herman”? & what are his “communications”?John A. Carlyle replied, 10 Nov.: “I … spent most of the day searching for information in regard to that little essay of Goethe’s which you have translated. The ‘Tohu wa Bohu’ in it remains dark to me in spite of all my Dictionaries, & I could not find it anywhere else in Goethe’s Werke. But the Hermann is mentioned frequently in them.” John then gives several examples of Goethe’s comments on Johann Gottfried Hermann (1772–1848), German scholar and philologist, prof. of Rhetoric and Poetry at Leipzig University. John continued: “On the whole it seems to me that Goethe’s little Essay sums up what he had learnt from Hermann about old Greek Mythology, & digested for himself.” The other little paper came two nights ago from Montégut &
merely informs us that Greenwood & he are (I fear still vaguely) in some kind of treaty but nothing yet fixed.See TC to JAC, 18 Oct. I of course have only in self defence to keep absolutely clear of it & await the issue zero or other. The poor little letter can be made out; but it is somewhat cramp & is not worth any considerable exertion. I was on the whole distressed and disgusted with the monthly periodicals till I got them all away. I am now fixed down to Thucydides by Dean SmithWilliam Smith (1711–87; ODNB), classical scholar, dean of Chester 1758–87, History of the Peloponnesian War, Translated from the Greek of Thucydides, 2 vols. (1753). TC’s copy; Carlyle’s House 77. a good translation, now about a hundred years old. It is not extremely interesting but it is wise, solid & human, in grand & noble contrast with almost anything that is written now. Ruskin has not sent the Fors Clavigera this month hitherto.Ruskin’s Fors Clavigera, letter 59, “School Books” (Nov. 1875); see Ruskin’s Works 28:439–59. Does that mean anything? I fear it does not mean that he has given it up altogether!— Jean and Mary send their affectionate regards to one and all of you, as do I with my whole heart.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 13 Nov. MS: NLS 528.43 inc. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 316–17. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand; the end of the MS is missing.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Unexpected stoppage of the clock, which has pointed always towards something about noon when it should have indicated half past one has cut me very short for time; but I will not omit writing altogether on this last day of the week. Mary & I are bound to the dentist,—I do understand now for the last time & I hope you will have a longer letter from me on some brighter day before long. This day which rained heavily in the morning is now a soak of dim mist and mud, very uncomfortable and untowardly.The Times reported, 15 Nov.: “[B]y half-past 2 o’clock this morning the Thames had risen to such a point as to flood some premises in Thames-street, and in some instances horses were found in water up to their knees.” We intend to go up to the dentist in a cab

It was very kind of you to take so much charge of the Geistes-epochen. I
turned up all your references in Goethe and carefully read them; I have found also marked in the Lon. Lib. Catalogue both the Herman book you mentionSee TC to JAC, 6 Nov. John A. Carlyle wrote, 10 Nov., that he had found seven vols. of Hermann’s minor works listed in an old London Library Catalogue. and several others; these, also, I ought to look into and will try; but, alas, the days are so dark and unfavourable just now. I gather in general that Goethe (whatever Herman might do) means by this little Piece a bird’s eye view of the whole history of human religious speculation; including Christian Theology as well as others, from the first origin of Man in this world onward to the times we have now got to, which are To hu wa bohu (Chaos thrice confounded), such a pluister of black stupidities, hypocricies and bottomless basenesses of mind as “even the spirit of God,” says Goethe, “could not reduce into a world worthy of him!”— I strive to believe that in the latter clause Goethe is mistaken and that the “spirit of God” is equal to all emergencies: but the passage as a feature of Goethe is very remarkable to me.— You need not by any means copy the foul sheet you have got; but merely in carefully reading it over help out or correct the translation with all your skill in particular words & phrases as you go along.John wrote, 10 Nov.: “I could copy the translation, tho’ written indistinctly, for with help of the original I can read it all. It would hardly be intelligible to any general readers unless there were some commentary added.” That will be trouble enough & far too much to have put you to in regard to such a matter Simply enclose the sheet in any letter you are sending.

After trial of my teeth for another week, I now decide to take no farther trouble with them to retain the apparatus for occasional service in the mouth in keeping the shape straight &c but to understand that it cannot in general be of almost any practical use,—& that now at last the necessary bother about it has been faithfully gone through & ended. My reading for the last week has been rather poor & unproductive, Brownings last Book, the Apology of AristophanesSee TC to JF, 17 Sept.

bibl.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 20 Nov. MS: NLS 528.44. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:317–18; Wilson, Carlyle 6:371; C. R. Sanders, “The Background of Carlyle’s Portrait of Coleridge in The Life of John Sterling,” Bulletin of the John Rylands Library 55 (1973): 457; Kaplan 520. Written in Mary Aitken’s hand, with TC’s signature.
bibl.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your letter, with its obliging enclosure, arrived this morning, & was cordially welcomed. I am really much obliged by the trouble you have taken
about that Goethe Geistes-Epochen,John A. Carlyle wrote, 19 Nov.: “I enclose the translation of Goethe’s Geistes-Epochen. I cannot say that I understand the original at all clearly. … The general result of the whole is distinctly expressed; but I think one would need to have Hermann’s own ‘Mittheilungen’ to understand it completely.” See TC to JAC, 6 Nov. which I design to have settled & copied fair by the first possibility; but I am very weak and languid, & the ever changeful weather prevents me getting out often enough at the time I would go. I doubt, also, whether Herman himself will throw much light on the thing; but it is clear enough I ought to try. Our weather seems to be a little less glaurry & splashy than yours: twice or thrice we have had intervals of dry; & today is perfectly clear, sunny; & though in the morning as I did my embankment, there was to the eye in the complete clearness & dryness an appearance of frost there was nothing of it to the feeling & no ice yet visible. It is possible enough, however, we may have a day or two of frost; which, also, to my poor old skin is still more unwelcome than the splashy deluges, though these latter I suppose, are really more unwholesome and certainly more inconvenient. Two or three days ago I finished my Thucydides with great esteem & here and there great admiration for the author’s spiritual qualities, though the History, such a distance intervening between the historian & us, is by no means altogether luminous to a modern reader, so many things unknown to him, which were commonplace & known to everybody while the author wrote. Kirkpatrick’s Letter about Dante & himJohn wrote: “I had a note this week from Mr Kirkpatrick. … He is the best Greek scholar I know of, & a great admirer of Thucydides, about whom we used often to speak in our walks some years ago.” He then quoted at length Kirkpatrick’s views on the similarity of Thucydides and Dante: he sees Dante as a poet steeped in history, and Thucydides as a dramatic historian. Edward Kirkpatrick (ca. 1821–1901), friend of John A. Carlyle’s, private tutor, artist, and scholar; see 48:176TC to JAC, 12 March 1873; see also 46:173TC to JAC, 19 March 1870; he lived at 5 Picardy Pl., Edinburgh. was also welcome & estimable to me. I do find points of notable similarity between the two men, especially their brevity seriousness & pregnant force of expression; but the wild wail of unutterable affection that runs through Dante has no expression or almost none in Thucydides, who indeed may be said to have no religion or none to speak of in comparison with Dante. In the last two days by way of elucidating dark points in Thucydides, I have taken to Plutarch (Clough’s excellent edition)Plutarch’s Lives: The Translation Called Dryden’s. Corrected from the Greek and Revised by A. H. Clough, 5 vols. (Boston, 1857); see 43:30TC to JAC, 7 Nov. 1865. Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–61; ODNB see 20:76TC to AHC, 17 Dec. 1845), poet, friend of TC’s; see 38:15–17TC to JAF, [Nov. 1861]. & find him, too, a very estimable man, though of a different type. Reading, alas, is a poor resource in comparison with writing & working; but of reading one should make the most; & the difference between a good author & a bad is literally immense.

We are all well here. Jean doing very well among us & both Mary & she very
busy; sorting everything into perfection. I myself have had no success in regard to teeth; no contrivance of my worthy artist enabling me to keep them in their place or to eat with them in any profitable or practicable way, but I keep the machine all day in my mouth as a welcome object, though a foreign;—& if the worthy man would send me his account which he has never yet done, I should gladly pay him & finish off the adventure, “Foreign teeth possible or not?” which I felt bound to try, with this clear solution “Impossible.” We are much obliged for your news from Scotsbrig & the Gill;John usually gave news of family at Scotsbrig and the Gill in his letters. He wrote, 31 Oct.: “Mary … told us that the dwelling house at Gill was all covered in again. The walls had been raised three or four feet, so that there are now two very nice bedrooms of a complete sort upstairs, with windows, fireplaces &c. No alteration had been made in the lower parts of the house.” —& it was especially welcome to me ten days ago to hear about the settlement at Ironhirst & how generously you had come forward on that occasion.Ernhirst (Ironhirst), farm which had belonged to their niece Margaret Stewart and her husband, Thomas; since their deaths (see TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1874) the farm had been run by her brother James Austin Jr., with his sister Marianne to help with the dairy and the children; see TC to JAC, 17 Nov. 1874. Margaret’s youngest child, Thomas, lived with Mary Austen; see TC to AC, 4 March. John wrote, 31 Oct., that Mary had asked him “about taking a new lease of Ernhirst, the old one ending this year. There is to be a new valuation of the farm this or next month. … I could not give her any decided advice, but said I thought some smaller farm in a healthier locality might suit better.” John had loaned Margaret the money to take over the farm after her husband’s death, 1859; see 46:102TC to JAC, 3 Nov. 1869, and 47:5TC to JAC, 10 May 1870; it is not known what the new settlement was. I am often thinking of poor old Mary, one of the kindest beings in the world; & am always meaning to write a few words to her; but, alas, without fingers of my own, writing becomes daily more of a sorrow to me. There has come a pleasant enough Note from Norton in America;Charles Eliot Norton wrote, 31 Oct: “If postal cards were not quite such ugly objects, they might have great use as means of brief cordial communication. Suppose instead of a walk with each other through the Park this winter, once a week we send each other a postal card … with two words of remembrance. For my part, I will do it, and I will take your part for granted if you prefer,—but there would be to me a certain happiness in the mere expression in this poor way of the part that the thought of you, and affection for you holds in my daily life.” which, as not yet answered, I do not enclose today; there has also arrived from Harvard University a big Doctor Diploma & sublime little Letter from the President of Harvard CollegeTC received an honorary degree of Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) from Harvard University, sent with a letter of congratulation from its president, Charles William Eliot; see TC to CWE, 23 Nov. with which I know not yet what to do; never having been consulted upon it,Norton wrote, 30 June: “This morning … the President [of Harvard] announced that the University proposed to confer upon you the degree of LL.D, honoris causa. … It is the best ‘Order of Merit’ that America can offer you.” & being resolute
resoluteWord repeated by mistake. never to accept such a title & yet reluctant to fling the whole affair irreverently in their faces,Ironically, a hoax letter, in which TC scornfully rejected the honor, had been widely pbd. in both the British and American press since at least early Oct. Among many others, the Edinburgh Evening News reported, 11 Nov.: “Sometime ago … a paragraph went the round of the papers giving what professed to be abstracts from a pungent and not overly polite letter, in which Mr Carlyle declined to accept the honorary degree of LL.D. from Harvard University. The American people were exceedingly indignant at the terms of the epistle, and some of them waxed wroth at Harvard for throwing away its honours upon one who had ‘shovelled violent abuse upon America during the war for the Union.’” good souls who meant to gratify me highly though succeeding only in giving me a paltry disturbance by their bounty!John replied, 25 Nov.: “I have thought of the Harvard diploma you speak of. Why not simply thank the good people for their intended honour & let the matter rest without further details. There wd be no necessity for taking the title of Doctor.” I have also two altogether paltry French Letters, one of them from a young man just coming out of the schools & all aflame to write a book on Coleridge,Letter writer unidentified further; for Samuel Taylor Coleridge, see TC to JAC, 29 Nov. 1873. as the Lamp of England & Trismegistus [Thrice greatest] of Men,—but wishing greatly, withal, that I would set him on his way. Which you may judge how altogether likely I am to do. His Letter I do not send because it has been written as if with the claw of a cat in the palest of ink & to me is utterly illegible,—not completely legible even to Mary with her keen eyesight. O Curas hominum [Oh the cares of Men]!— Poor Forster I am afraid is worse than usual this week; but have not seen him since Sunday last Yesterday I called on Darwin & was happy to find him gone to dine at the Club.Erasmus Darwin; presumably the Athenaeum Club of which they had both been members since 1842; see 14:34–35TC to RMM, 3 Feb. 1842. My paper being entirely done, I end here. With my kindest love & blessings to you all, Ever yr affecte

bibl.sourceNote: TC-CWE, 23 Nov. Pbd: Edinburgh Evening News, 22 Dec. 1875. Charles William Eliot (1834–1926), president of Harvard 1869–1909. TC had previously had dealings with him over his bequest of his books to Harvard; see , and .
bibl.head: TC TO CHARLES WILLIAM ELIOT

docBody.p:
Some days ago I received your courteous and obliging letter, and along with it the University diploma appointed, for me on the 30th of June last, which now lies safely deposited here. In return for all which I can only beg you to express to the governing boards of the University my lively sense of honour
they have done me, and my cordial thanks for this proof of their friendly regard, which I naturally wish may long continue on their part. Toward Harvard University I have long had a feeling of affection—in some respect, almost veneration; and to Harvard and to you, its distinguished president, I now cordially wish all manner of prosperity and good esteem from wise men on both sides of the ocean.

div1.p: Adamson, Samuel (1831–80), of British Linen Co. bank, Dumfries, where TC had an account; son of Robert Adamson (1787–1861; see 10:23TC to JA, 14 Feb. 1838, and 37:261).
Airlie; see Stanley.

Aitken, Jean (“Craw”) Carlyle (1810–88), TC’s sister; m., 1833, James Aitken (1809–87) from Troqueer, housepainter of English St., Dumfries; they moved from Assembly St., Dumfries, to The Hill, Lochmaben Rd., Dumfries, 1863. They had two sons who d. in infancy (1834–36 and 1855–56), both named Alexander; James Jr. (1836–71), worked in mercantile houses in London, 1858–ca. 1864 and 1866–67, and Liverpool, 1864–66, and 1867–71, he died during a visit to London; Thomas (1841–69), at an inst. for the deaf in Glasgow from 1854 (see 29:186TC to JAC, 4 Nov. 1854), then lived at home ca. 1864–69; and John (see below). Their das. were Anne (1839–1919), Margaret (1845–1932), and Mary (see below).
Aitken, John (1843–1911), Jean and James’s son, bank clerk at the Commercial Bank, Dumfries, then moved to London, Sept. 1871, working for Chapman & Hall.

Aitken, Mary (1848–95), Jean and James’s da.; she worked as a pupil-teacher in Peebles, March–Sept. 1867, then returned home. She accompanied TC to London, Sept. 1868, “for about three weeks,” but stayed more or less permanently. She worked as a teacher and secretary in London, Jan.–June/July 1873, and then returned to live with TC in Cheyne Row. She m., 1879, her cousin Alexander Carlyle.

Alford, Marianne Margaret Egerton, b. Compton (1817–88; ODNB), Viscountess Alford, known as Lady Marian Alford; art patron and writer on needlework; widow of John Hume Cust, later Egerton (1812–51), Viscount Alford; they had two sons, John William Spencer Brownlow Egerton-Cust (1842–67), 2d Earl Brownlow, and Adelbert Wellington Brownlow Cust (1844–1921), 3d Earl Brownlow, who m., 1868, Lady
Adelaide, b. Chetwynd-Talbot (1844–1917) (for her sisters, see Lothian, below). They lived at 11 Princes Gate, Kensington, Ashridge House, Hertfordshire, and Belton House, Grantham, Lincolnshire.

Allingham, William (1824–89; ODNB), Irish poet and editor; he worked in the Customs Service 1846–70; friendly with TC since early 1850s. He lived at 131 Piccadilly. He m., 22 Aug. 1874, Helen Mary Elizabeth, b. Paterson (1848–1926; ODNB), watercolorist; she later painted portraits of TC; she also compiled the list of pictures for Carlyle’s House Catalogue. After their marriage they moved to 12 Trafalgar Sq., Chelsea.

Ashburton, Lady Louisa Caroline, b. Stewart-Mackenzie (1827–1903), m., 1858, William Bingham Baring (1799–1864; ODNB; see 11:40TC to MAC, 8 March 1839, and later vols.), 2d Baron, politician, and partner in Baring Bros., bankers. They had one da., Mary Florence (1860–1902). Lady Louisa was the da. of Mary Elizabeth Frederica, b. Mackenzie (1783–1862; ODNB), chief of Clan Mackenzie, and James Alexander Stewart (1784–1843); on their marriage (1817) the name Mackenzie was added to that of Stewart. Lady Ashburton was building Kent House for herself in London; she also owned Melchet Court (see 38:8JWC to LA, [11 Nov. 1861]), a country house 6 mi. (9.5 km.) W of Romsey, Hampshire, on the border between Hampshire and Wiltshire, a farm at Addiscombe, near Croydon, and Seaforth Lodge, Seaton, Devon. Lord Ashburton’s first wife, m. 1823, was Harriet, b. Montagu (1805–57; ODNB; see 11:40TC to MAC, 8 March 1839, and 26:ix–xv26:introduction); they met the Carlyles in 1839 and became close friends. Where necessary for clarity, we refer in notes to Lord Ashburton’s first and second wives as Lady Harriet Ashburton and Lady Louisa Ashburton respectively, although these are not the correct forms.

Austin, Mary Carlyle (1808–88), TC’s sister, m., 1831, James Austin (1805–78), farmer of The Gill, 6 mi. (9.5 km.) SW of Ecclefechan. They had eight das.: Margaret (see Stewart); Grace (1833–1922), who m., 1856, William Yeoward (ca. 1824–1911), of Toronto, Ontario; Jessie (b. 1836), who m., 1859, George Grierson (b. 1835); Jane (b. 1840); Mary Anne (b. 1842); Catherine (see James Carlyle Jr.); Isabella (b. ca. 1846); and Mary Carlyle (b. 1851); and one surviving son, James Jr. (b. 1848).
Baring; see Ashburton.
Bismarck, Otto von (1815–98), chancellor of the German Empire 1871–90.
Blackie, John Stuart (1809–95; ODNB), classical and Scottish Gaelic scholar, prof. of Greek at Edinburgh Univ. from 1852; m., 1842, Eliza, b. Wyld (1819–1908).
Boehm, Joseph Edgar (1834–90; ODNB), sculptor. Originally from Vienna, he settled in London after his marriage, 1860, to Louisa Frances, b. Boteler (ca. 1835–90).

Braid, Betty, b. Pringle (1795–19 March 1875), Grace Welsh’s Haddington servant, close to JWC (see 21:82JWC to JW, [30 Oct. 1846], and 24:221JWC to TC, 25 [5 Sept. 1849]); b. in Prestonkirk, E. Lothian;
m. Alexander (1792–15 Oct. 1874), stonemason and shopkeeper. Three sons d. in infancy: Alexander (b. 1826), James (b. 1829), and James (b. 1831); George (1827–65) was the only child who survived into adulthood. They lived at Upper Stenhouse, Greenend, Liberton, S Edinburgh.

Bromley, Caroline Davenport (1820–91), da. of Rev. Walter Davenport Bromley (1787–1862) of Wootton Hall, Staffordshire, and his first wife, m., 1818, Caroline Barbara, b. Gooch (1791–1827). A friend of Lady Louisa Ashburton, she became a close friend of JWC’s; she was now friendly with TC. Her London home was at 32 Grosvenor St., and she also had a house in Barnes, Surrey. Her brother was William Bromley Davenport (1821–84), m. Augusta Elizabeth (d. 1916), they had six children: Alice (d. 1945), Evelyn Caroline (1859–1931), Walter Arthur (1863–1942), Elinor Lucy (1866–1943), Arthur Henry (1867–1946), and Hugh Richard (1870–1954); they lived at Capesthorne, Crewe, Cheshire.
Brookfield, William Henry (1809–12 July 1874; ODNB), clergyman and school inspector, known to TC since 1841.
Browning, Robert (1812–89; ODNB), poet; friend of the Carlyles since mid-1830s.

Carlyle, Alexander (Alick) (1797–1876), TC’s brother; he m., 1830, Janet, b. Clow (1809–91), and immigrated with his family to Canada, 1843. They settled at the Bield, 4½ mi. (7 km.) W of Brantford, Ontario. They had nine surviving children. Jane Welsh (1831–84), m., 1852, Robert Sims (1825–80); they had four children, Alexander (1855–1922), Thomas (1856–1934), Jessie (b. ca. 1859), and John (b. ca. 1862). Thomas (1833–1921), m., 1867, Margaret, b. MacVicar (1847–1917); they had at least seven children, including Thomas Alexander (1869–70), and Hellen (b. ca. Dec. 1870). Janet (Jessie) (1836–1916), m., 1864, William Apps (1834–1911), miller from Ontario; they had at least five children, including Jessie (b. ca. 1867), Alfred (b. ca. 1870), and a da. (b. ca. 1872). John (1839–1924), moved to Brantford and became a carpenter, 1870, m., 1871, Helen, b. McVicar (1851–1927). Alexander (see below). James (1846–1924). Margaret (1847–1935), m. Edward Marrs (d. 1927), widower from Okmulgee, Oklahoma; see 1:166TC to AC, 23 Feb. 1819. William (1849–1935). Robert (1851–1932). An unidentified son (1832–33), Margaret (1835–36), James (b. 1840), and Euphemia (1853–54) all d. in infancy; see 32:4TC to AC, 3 Oct. 1856.

Carlyle, Alexander (Alick) (1843–1931; see 16:153TC to AC, 4 May 1843), Alexander and Janet’s son, school headmaster; m., 1879, his cousin Mary Aitken; lived with TC from 1879 and ed. various collections of the Carlyles’ letters and TC’s writings. After Mary’s death he m. Lillias, b. MacVicar (d. 1929), sister of the wives of his brothers Thomas and John.

Carlyle, James (Jamie) (1805–90), TC’s brother, farmer at Scotsbrig; m., 1834, Isabella, b. Calvert (ca. 1813–59). Their children were James Jr.
(see below); John (see below); Thomas (1839–41); and Janet (Jenny) (see Scott).

Carlyle, James Jr. (1835–88 [mistakenly given as 1871 in previous vols.]), James and Isabella’s son, m., 1866, his cousin Catherine, b. Austin (1844–1908); see 44:64TC to JCA, 6 Oct. 1866. Their first child, James, d. at birth 1867; they had nine further children, including Isabella (1868–post 1901), Mary (b. 1871), James (1872–91), and twin sons John Aitken and Thomas (b. 9 July 1874). They lived at Newlands, near Eaglesfield, as well as sharing the tenancy of Craigenputtoch with his father; see 44:196TC to JAC, 11 May 1867.

Carlyle, John (ca. 1792–1872), TC’s half-brother; immigrated to the U.S. in 1837, then moved to Canada (see 12:228TC to AC, 15 Aug. 1840); he lived on a small farm at Mount Pleasant, nr. Brantford, Ontario. He m., 1817, Margaret (Peggy), b. Benn (1798–1867); they had six children: Janet (1818–89), m., 1844, John Randall Ellis (1810–1911), postmaster and carpenter; Mary (1821–50); John (1825–26); John (1827–97), m., ca. 1852, Mary Catherine, b. Smith (1835–79); James (1830–1900), qualified as a doctor but worked for most of his life as a teacher, m. Wilhelmina Deborah, b. Patten (1847–1926); and William (1833–1911), teacher and later a school inspector, m., 1860, Emily b. Youmans (1835–1912), their da. Florence Emily Carlyle (1864–1923), became a prominent Canadian artist. William visited TC in London, Aug. 1864.

Carlyle, John Aitken (Jack, “The Doctor”) (1801–79; ODNB), TC’s brother, physician, and translator. He m., 1852, Phoebe Elizabeth Hough Watt, b. Fowler (1810–54), wealthy widow of Fitzjames Watt (1809–48), from Leek in Staffordshire, with four sons; she d. in childbirth, the child was stillborn. John A. Carlyle assumed responsibility for his stepsons; see Watt.

Carlyle, John Calvert (1836–1901), James and Isabella’s son, m., 1868, Margaret Little, b. Murray (1848–92), of Blackwood Ridge, Middlebie; they lived at Scotsbrig with his father; they had 13 children, including Isabella Calvert (1869–1915), Elisabeth Carruthers (1870–1947), James (1872–1931), a son (b. Dec. 1873), and another da. by Oct. 1875.
Carlyle, Margaret, b. Aitken (1771–1853), TC’s mother, m., 1795, James Carlyle (1758–1832), TC’s father.
Carnarvon; see Herbert.

Chapman, Frederic (1823–95; ODNB), partner in Chapman & Hall, publishers, took over the management of the company 1864; he m., 1861, Clara, b. Woodin (1842–66), they had one surviving son, Frederic, and a baby who d. early 1866. He then m., 1870, Annie Marion, b. Harding (b. 1848), da. of Robert Palmer Harding (1821–93; ODNB), head of a London accounting firm.
Christie, William Dougal (1816–27 July 1874; ODNB), diplomat and author; known to TC since 1840; see 12:56TC to WDC, [26 Feb. 1840]; see also 44:67–68TC to JAC, 10 Oct. 1866.
Chrystal, Jeannie (Babbie), b. Welsh (1818–95), da. of JWC’s maternal uncle John, m., 1853, Andrew Chrystal (ca. 1811–83), wine merchant from Glasgow, they had a da., Mary (1857–1937); see 40:226–27.
Cooper; see Shaftesbury.
Cowper, Henry Frederick (1836–87), M.P. for Hertfordshire 1865–85, brother of Francis Cowper (1834–1905), 7th Earl Cowper.

Currie (Corrie), Alexander (Sandy) (b. ca. 1773), of Newfield farm, nr. Ecclefechan; his surviving sons were James (1815–96), sugar-planter in Mauritius, and John Irving (ca. 1810–79), and his das. were Mary (1812–76), Helen (ca. 1819–91), and George (ca. 1821–91); all old friends of the Carlyle family; see 42:156TC to JAC, 28 July 1865.

Darwin, Erasmus (1804–81), friendly with the Carlyles since 1835; his brother was Charles Darwin (1809–82; ODNB), naturalist and geologist, m., 1839, his cousin Emma, b. Wedgwood (1808–96). They had seven surviving children: William Erasmus Darwin (1839–1914; ODNB), banker; Henrietta Emma (1843–1927); George Howard (1845–1912; ODNB), mathematician and physicist; Elizabeth (1847–1926); Francis (1848–1925; ODNB), botanist; Leonard (1850–1943; ODNB), scientist; and Horace (1851–1928; ODNB), civil engineer.

Derby, Mary Catherine, b. Sackville-West (1824–1900; ODNB), countess of, political hostess; she m., first, 1847, (as his 2d wife) James Gascoyne-Cecil (1791–1868), 2d marquess of Salisbury; she m., second, 1870, Edward Henry Stanley (1826–93; ODNB), 15th earl of Derby, politician and diarist, foreign secretary 1874–78. They lived at 23 St. James’s Sq., London.

Dickens, Charles (1812–70; ODNB), novelist; friend of the Carlyles since the early 1840s; m., 1836, Catherine Thomson, b. Hogarth (1816–79), separated from her in 1858; see 33:233TC to RWE, 2 June 1858.
Disraeli, Benjamin (1804–81; ODNB), politician and author; prime minister 1868 and 1874–80.
Duffy, Charles Gavan (1816–1903; ODNB), Irish nationalist, lawyer, and politician, friend of TC’s since 1845. He m., 1847, Susan, b. Hughes (1826–78); they immigrated to Australia 1855.

Eichthal, Charles d’ (1813–80), baron, from a wealthy German Jewish banking family in Munich, whom John A. Carlyle met in 1827; see 5:277TC to GE, 17 May 1831; Charles first visited the Carlyles in Dec. 1835; see 8:277TC to MAC, [24 Dec. 1835]. His wife was Isabella, b. Khuen von Belasi (1826–88), and their only son was Karl (1845–1909).

Emerson, Ralph Waldo (1803–82; see 6:425TC to JAC, 27 Aug. 1833), philosopher, essayist, poet, and transcendentalist. He first met TC in Aug. 1833; in spite of their differences they had close ties; he introduced many Americans to TC and played a leading part in arranging the publication of TC’s works in the
U.S. Emerson m., 1835, as his second wife, Lydian, b. Jackson (1802–92); their children were Waldo (1836–42), Ellen Tucker (1839–1909), Edith (see Forbes), and Edward Waldo (1844–1930), m., 1874, Annie Shephard Keyes (1847–1928).

Erskine, Thomas (1788–1870; ODNB; see 10:18TC to JAC, 1 Feb. 1838), theologian and retired advocate, living at Linlathen, Dundee; known to the Carlyles since the mid-1830s. He had two sisters: Christian Stirling (1789–1866), m., 1817, Charles Stirling (d. 1830); and David Paterson (1791–1867), m., 1821, Capt. James Paterson (1795–1856), their son, James Erskine Paterson (1826–88), and his family lived at 8 Newbattle Terr., Morningside.
FitzGerald, Edward (1809–83; ODNB), writer and translator, TC’s friend since 1842; he lived in Woodbridge, Suffolk.

Forbes, Edith, b. Emerson (1841–1929), da. of Ralph Waldo Emerson, m., 1865, William Hathaway Forbes (1840–97), businessman; they were to have eight children, including Ralph Emerson (1866–1937), Edith (1867–1926), William Cameron (1870–1959), and John (1871–88).

Forster, John (“Fuz”) (1812–76; ODNB; see 6:118TC to JPE, 27 July 1832; 11:7TC to JF, 17 Jan. 1839; and TC to JF, [25? Jan. 1839]), historian, journalist, and biographer; ed. of the Examiner 1847–55; sec., 1855–61, and commissioner, 1861–72, of the Lunacy Commission, friend of the Carlyles since the late 1830s and TC’s literary adviser. He m., 1856, Eliza Ann, b. Crosbie (ca. 1819–94), widow of the publisher Henry Colburn (ca. 1784–1855; ODNB); from 1863 they lived at Palace Gate House, Kensington.
Frankau; see Neuberg.

Froude, James Anthony (1818–94; ODNB), journalist and historian, ed. of Fraser’s Magazine 1860–74; he m., first, 1849, Charlotte Maria, b. Grenfell (1812–60); they had two das., Georgina Margaret (1850–1935) and Rose Mary (1852–ca. May 1875), and a son, Pascoe Grenfell (1854–79). He m., second, 1861, Henrietta Elizabeth, b. Warre (1824–12 Feb. 1874); they had a son, Ashley Anthony (1863–1949), and a da., Mary Caroline (“May”) (1867–1906). They lived at 5 Onslow Gdns., Fulham Rd.
Gladstone, William Ewart (1809–98; ODNB), politician; leader of the liberal party 1867–94, prime minister 1868–74, 1880–85, 1886, 1892–94. He m., 1839, Catherine, b. Glynne (1812–1900; ODNB).
Gordon, John (1797–1882; see 43:44TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1865), inspector of schools, old friend of both TC and John A. Carlyle.

Hanning, Janet Carlyle (1813–97), TC’s sister; m., 1836, Robert Hanning (1796–1878), who had immigrated to Canada in mysterious disgrace in 1841; she joined him in Hamilton, Ontario, Aug. 1851, with their two das., Margaret (b. 1838), and Mary (b. 1840), who m., 1864, Charles Coates Holden (b. 1836) and had at least two das., Jenny (d. Dec. 1870) and Jane. Janet and Robert had two more das., b. in Canada: Catherine (b. ca. 1852), school teacher, and Jane.
Henry; see Smyth.
Herbert, Henry Howard Molyneux (1831–90; ODNB), 4th earl of Carnarvon, politician; colonial sec. 1866–67 and 1874–78.

Horn, Robert (1810–78), Edinburgh advocate, Vice-Dean, 1874, and Dean, 1876–78, of the Faculty of Advocates. He m., 1846, Jane, b. Millar (1820–86), and they had at least six children; they lived at 7 Randolph Crescent, Edinburgh.

Hosmer, Harriet (1830–1908), American sculptor. Lady Ashburton had first met her in Rome in 1867 (see Surtees, Ludovisi 130–31) and they became close friends. TC also met her in 1867; see 45:58TC to LAL, 31 Oct. 1867; for his view of her then, see 45:63TC to JAC, 4 Nov. 1867.

Houghton, Richard Monckton Milnes (1809–85; ODNB), 1st Baron, author and politician; friend of the Carlyles since the late 1830s; m., 1851, Annabella, b. Hungerford Crewe (1814–74), they had two das. and a son; see 37:270.

Hunter, Helen, b. Vary (1804–85), widow of John Hunter (1801–69; see 8:161JWC to SS, [June or July? 1835]), old friend of John A. Carlyle’s; she now lived at Kingsmuir House, Peebles, Scottish Borders. See also Watt.
Huxley, Thomas Henry (1825–95; ODNB), biologist and educational theorist.
Irving, Edward (1792–1834; ODNB; see 1:92TC to RM, 12 Feb. 1817, later vols., and Carlyle, Reminiscences), the Carlyles’ great friend; religious leader and preacher.

Jewsbury, Geraldine Endsor (1812–80; ODNB; see 12:103–4TC to GEJ, 12 April 1840), novelist, reviewer, and misc. writer; friend of the Carlyles, particularly of JWC’s, since 1841. She lived at 41 Markham Sq., Chelsea.

Laing, David (1793–1878; ODNB), antiquary, librarian of the Signet Lib., Edinburgh, 1837–78. When TC became rector of Edinburgh University, 1866, he chose Laing as his assessor on the Senatus Academicus. Laing’s youngest sister, Euphemia (1808–96), lived with him as his housekeeper after the death of their mother, Helen, b. Kirk (1767–1837); since 1845 they had lived in East Villa, 12 James St., Portobello (see 43:122TC to DL, 14 Feb. 1866).

Laurence, Samuel (1812–84; ODNB), artist; for his portrait of TC (1838–41), see 10:frontis. He also painted JWC (1852) from sketches done in 1849 (see 24:100JWC to TC, [5 July 1849]), as well as many other writers and thinkers of the time.

Lecky, William Edward Hartpole (1838–1903; ODNB; see 44:97TC to JAC, 28 Nov. 1866), historian, m., 1871, Catharina Elisabeth Boldewina, b. Baroness van Dedem (1842–1912), writer, historian, and suffragist.

Leighton, Baldwyn (1836–97), 8th bart.; m., 1864, Eleanor Leicester, b. Warren (1841–1914); they had four children: Catherine Barbara (1864–1952), Bryan (1868–1919), Meriel Gundrede (1872–1947), and Cuthbert (1877–1954).

Lothian, Constance Harriet Mahonesa, b. Chetwynd-Talbot (1836–1901), marchioness of, widow of William Schomberg Robert Kerr (1832–70), 8th
marquess of Lothian. She lived at Blickling Hall, Norfolk, and Newbattle Abbey, Midlothian. Both had been friends of the Carlyles; see 38:120–21JWC to LL, 21 Aug [July 1862]. Her sisters were Lady Adelaide Brownlow (see Alford, above) and Lady Gertrude Frances Chetwynd-Talbot (1840–1906); their mother, an invalid who usually lived with one of her das., was Lady Sarah Elizabeth Chetwynd-Talbot, b. Beresford (1807–84), countess of Shrewsbury, widow (m. 1828) of Henry John Chetwynd-Talbot (1803–68), 18th earl of Shrewsbury.

Lytton, Edward Robert Bulwer (1831–91; ODNB), 2d Baron, 1st earl of Lytton (1880), diplomat and poet, m., 1864, Edith, b. Villiers (1841–1936; ODNB). His parents were Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer Lytton (1803–18 Jan. 1873; ODNB), 1st Baron Lytton, writer and politician, m., 1827, Rosina Anne Doyle, b. Wheeler (180–82; ODNB); both father and son were close friends of Forster. The family home was Knebworth House, Hertfordshire.

Masson, David (1822–1907; ODNB; see 16:312JWC to TC, [24 July 1843]), writer and editor, prof. of rhetoric and English lit., Edinburgh Univ., 1865–95. He m., 1853, Emily Rosaline, b. Orme (1835–1915); they had a son, David Orme (1858–1937; ODNB), and three das, Flora (1856–1937), Helen (b. 1864), and Rosaline (1867–1947); they lived at 10 Regent Terr., Edinburgh.

Maxwell, Sir William Stirling (1818–78; ODNB), art historian, book collector, and politician; known to TC since 1848; he m., 1865, Anna Maria, b. Leslie-Melville (ca. 1825–8 Dec. 1874), da. of David Leslie-Melville (1785–1860), 10th earl of Leven, and Elizabeth Anne, b. Campbell (1804–63). They lived at Keir, 3 mi. (5 km.) NW of Stirling.

Mill, John Stuart (1806–7 May 1873; ODNB), utilitarian philosopher and economist; m., 1851, Harriet Taylor, b. Hardy (1807–58; ODNB), feminist and political radical, who strongly influenced his thinking. Mill met TC in Sept. 1831 (see 5:398TC to JWC, 4 Sept. 1831); they remained on friendly terms even after the MS of vol. 1 of The French Revolution was burned while in Mill’s keeping (see 8:66–68TC to JFR, 7 March 1835), but later became estranged because of many differences in temperament and attitudes to social questions; Mill also believed that TC and other friends disapproved of his marriage. His sister was Harriet Isabella Mill (1812–97).
Milnes; see Houghton.

Montégut, Jean-Baptiste Joseph Émile (1825–96), critic and translator; known to TC since 1851; see 26:234TC to FB, 17 Nov. 1851, and 298. He m., 22 June 1875, Anne-Marie Jeanne Hortense de Lajoumard de Bellabre (ca. 1822–90), widow of his cousin Gustave Duverger (1804–65).

Motley, John Lothrop (1814–77), American historian and diplomat; see 44:129TC to MD, 24 Jan. 1867. He m., 1837, Mary Elizabeth, b. Benjamin (1813–31 Dec. 1874). He
came to Britain as the U.S. minister, 1869–70, and returned to live in England, 1871.

Neuberg, Joseph (1806–67; see 11:231TC to JN, 21 Dec. 1839), a German Jewish businessman, naturalized British 1845, and retired 1849; m., 1841, Marian (d. 1848; see 23:77JWC to JN, 22 July 1848). He was introduced to TC, whom he had long admired, by Emerson, 1848; helped TC as an unpaid sec., translated his work into German, and twice accompanied him on visits to Germany (1852 and 1858). His widowed sister, Rosetta (or Rosette) Frankau (ca. 1816–98), and her children lived at Roslyn Park, Hampstead; see 45:227–28.

Norton, Charles Eliot (1827–1908), author, journalist, and Harvard Coll. prof. of Art 1875–98. He m., 1862, Susan Ridley, b. Sedgwick (1838–72), they had six children: Eliot (1863–1932), Sara (Sally) (1864–1922), Elizabeth Lily (b. 1866), Rupert (1867–1914), Margaret (1870–1947), and Richard (1872–1918). Norton’s mother was Catherine, b. Eliot (1793–1879), and his sisters were Louisa (b. 1823) (married by 1872), Catherine Jane (1824–79), and Grace (1834–1926). He and his family spent 1868–73 in Europe, mostly in London, staying at 33 Cleveland Square, where he became friendly with TC.

Oliphant, Margaret Oliphant, b. Wilson (1828–97; ODNB), prolific novelist, biographer, reviewer, and misc. writer; friend of JWC’s since 1860; see 37:62JWC to MO, [12 Dec. 1860]; she lived at 6 Clarence Cres., Windsor. She had two surviving children, Cyril Francis (Tids) (1856–90), and Francis Romano (Cecco) (1859–94).
Quain, Richard (1816–98; ODNB), physician; see 45:101TC to JF, [2 March 1868]. He had attended both Lord Ashburton and JWC.

Robson, Charles (1805–76), TC’s printer since 1837; initially of Robson, Levey, & Franklyn, printers, 23 Gt. New St., Fetter Lane, which went bankrupt early 1864. He then went into partnership with one or both sons John (b. ca. 1837) and Christopher (b. 1843), forming Robson & Son, Great Northern Printing Works, St. Pancras Rd.

Ruskin, John (1819–1900; ODNB), author, artist, and social reformer; Slade Professor of Art at Oxford Univ. 1870–79. He m., 1848, Euphemia Chalmers, b. Gray (1828–97); marriage annulled 1854 (she then m., 1855, John Everett Millais [1829–96; ODNB], artist). Ruskin lived in the family home at 163 Denmark Hill, S London, with his mother, Margaret, b. Cock (1781–1871), after her death he moved to Brantwood, Coniston, Cumberland, 1872. His father, John James Ruskin (1785–1864), was a wine merchant.

Russell, Mary, b. Dobbie (1802–17 Dec. 1875; see 6:145TC to AC, [7 April 1832]), close friend of JWC and her mother. She m., 1829, Dr. James Russell (ca. 1796–1878); they had moved to Holmhill, nr. Thornhill, by Oct. 1859.

Scott, Janet (Jenny), b. Carlyle (1843–1 Feb. 1874), youngest child of James and Isabella Carlyle; m., 1864, William Scott (b. ca. 1829), draper; they lived at 27 Bradford St., Birmingham; they had a son, John James Carlyle (b. 1865), and two das., Isabella (b. late 1860s) and Jessie Beattie (b. 1870).
Shaftesbury, Anthony Ashley Cooper (1801–85; ODNB), 7th earl of, politician, philanthropist, and social reformer; chairman of the Lunacy Commission 1833–85.

Smyth, Selina Constance, b. Somerville (1841–1910), m., 1861, Ralph Smyth (ca. 1830–90), army officer, they lived at Gaybrook, nr. Mullingar, Co. Westmeath, and Castle Bellingham, Co. Louth, Ireland. She was the da. of Kenelm Somerville (1787–1864), 16th Lord Somerville, and his wife, m., 1833, Frances Louisa, b. Hayman (d. 1885); her sister was Louisa Harriet Henry, b. Somerville (ca. 1836–1923), m., 1871, Col. Charles Stewart Henry. The Somerville title became extinct after the deaths of their brother Hugh Somerville (1839–68), 17th Lord Somerville, and their cousin Aubrey John Somerville (1838–70), 18th Lord Somerville.
Somerville; see Smyth.

Spedding, James (1808–81; ODNB; see 8:196JWC to JCA, [Mid-Aug. 1835], and 19:205TC to TSS, 20 Sept. 1845), literary editor and biographer, known as “Lord Bacon” for his life’s work on Francis Bacon; he lived in Westbourne Grove, London. His brother was Thomas Story Spedding (1800–1870; see 10:32TC to TSS, 17 Feb. 1838), m., 1839, Frances Elizabeth (previously called Emily in error), b. Headlam (1811–96); they lived at Mirehouse, nr. Keswick, Cumberland; a lawyer, he devoted his life to local interests in Cumberland. Both brothers had been friends of TC’s since the late 1830s.
Stanley, Arthur Penrhyn (1815–81; ODNB), dean of Westminster, m., 1863, Lady Augusta Elizabeth Frederica, b. Bruce (1822–76; ODNB), lady-in-waiting, secretary, and friend of Queen Victoria.

Stanley, Henrietta Maria, b. Dillon (1807–95; ODNB), m., 1826, Edward John (1802–1869; ODNB; see 12:59TC to JAC, 27 Feb. 1840), 2d Baron Stanley of Alderley, Whig politician; they lived at Alderley Park, Cheshire, and 40 Dover St., London. Both were friends of the Carlyles. They had nine surviving children including Henrietta Blanche (1829–1921), 5th countess of Airlie, and Maude (1833–1915; ODNB), women’s welfare activist; see 48:240.

Stephen, James Fitzjames (1829–94; ODNB; see 41:24TC to JWC, 14 Sept. 1864), judge and writer, m., 1855, Mary Richenda, b. Cunningham (1829–1912); they had eight children: Katharine (1856–1924; ODNB), Herbert (1857–1932), James Kenneth (1859–92), Harry Lushington (1860–1945), Helen (1862–1908), Margaret Emily (b. ca. 1862), Rosamond (1868–1951), and Dorothea (1872–1865). Their London home was at 24 Cornwall Gds., Queen’s
Gate. His brother Leslie Stephen (1832–1904; ODNB), author and critic, m. 1867, Harriet Marian, b. Thackeray (1840–28 Nov. 1875; ODNB).

Sterling, Sir Anthony Coningham (1805–71; ODNB; see 9:103TC to JAC, 2 Dec. 1836, and later vols.), soldier; m., 1829, Charlotte, b. Baird (d. 1863), who suffered attacks of insanity and was jealous of JWC (see 18:266–67JWC to HW, [12 Nov. 1844], and 19:9JWC to HW, [9 Jan. 1845]); his brother John (1806–44; ODNB), writer, had been a particular friend of TC’s; see CL vols. 8–18 and Carlyle’s Life of Sterling (1851); for John’s surviving children, see 48:241.

Stewart, Margaret, b. Austin (1831–27 Oct. 1874), da. of Mary and James Austin, m., 1859, Thomas Stewart (1832–69), farmer from Hollybush, living at Ernhirst (Ironhirst), about 5½ mi. (9 km.) SW of Dumfries; see 38:19TC to JAC, 1 Dec. 1861; they had a da., Mary (b. ca. 1861), and four sons, William (b. 1863), James (b. 1864), Hugh (b. 1866, dead by April 1868), and Thomas (b. 1869). After Margaret’s death her brother James and sister Mary Anne moved to Ernhirst to look after the farm and the children.

Swan, Patrick Don (1808–89; see 46:194TC to JAC, 13 April 1870), known to his friends as Peter, known to TC since 1818 when he was TC’s pupil; see 1:143. Prosperous shipowner and shipbuilder, provost of Kirkcaldy 1841–45 and 1853–86. He lived at St. Brycedale House, Kirkcaldy, and Springfield House, nr. Cupar, Fife.

Tait, Robert Scott (1816–97), portrait painter and pioneer photographer; friend of the Carlyles since 1853, he painted TC’s portrait (see 31:84TC to AG, 6 May 1856) and A Chelsea Interior (see 33:197JWC to MR, 29 March [1858]), as well as taking photographs of both Carlyles.

Tennyson, Alfred (1809–92; ODNB), poet; poet laureate 1850–92; m., 1850, Emily Sarah, b. Sellwood (1813–96); friends of the Carlyles since the early 1840s. They had two surviving sons, Hallam (1852–1928, ODNB), and Lionel (1854–86). They lived at Farringford, Isle of Wight, and Aldworth, near Haslemere, Sussex.
Torphichen, James Walter Sandilands (1846–1915), 12th Lord Torphichen, living at Calder House, Torphichen, Midlothian.
Turgenev, Ivan (1818–83), Russian novelist and dramatist, whom TC first met in 1857; see 32:157TC to HT, 4 June 1857.
Twisleton, Edward Turner Boyd (1809–5 Oct. 1874; ODNB), civil servant, longtime friend of the Carlyles; he m., 1852, Ellen, b. Dwight (1828–62), from Boston, Mass.; see 43:278.

Tyndall, John (1820–93; ODNB), physicist, prof. of natural philosophy at the Royal Institution, Albemarle St., London, from 1853; TC’s admirer and friend from the mid-1850s; see 31:1–2TC to JF, 2 Jan. 1856.

Venturi, Emilie (ca. 1819–93; ODNB), da. of William Henry Ashurst (ca. 1791–1855; ODNB; portrait painter), supporter of Italian independence
and campaigner for women’s rights; unhappily m. to Sydney Hawkes, whom she divorced 1861; see 30:215JWC’s Journal, 13 Nov. 1855, and 235. She m., 1861, Carlo Venturi (ca. 1830–66). A strong supporter of Giuseppe Mazzini and the Young Italy movement, she published various English editions of his writings and Joseph Mazzini: A Memoir (1875).
Victoria (1819–1901; ODNB), queen of Great Britain and Ireland 1837–1901; m., 1840, Albert (1819–61; ODNB), prince consort.
Vigfusson, Gudbrand (1827–89), prominent scholar of medieval Scandinavian history, friend of John A. Carlyle’s.
Ward, Charles Augustus (1828–1914), vintner, author, antiquarian, and bookseller; see 45:230–31.
Warren, Sarah (b. ca. 1812 in Norfolk), a widow with adult children (see 41:96TC to JAC, 17 Nov. 1864), cook and housekeeper at Cheyne Row Nov. 1864–Sept. 1875.
Watt, Thomas Fowler (1838–62), stepson of John A. Carlyle; went to Australia, 1861, and d. on his return (see 38:115TC to JWC, 2 July 1862).

Watt, Henry (1839–1913), stepson of John A. Carlyle; at sea from 1854 (see 29:121TC to JCA, 30 June 1854), then master mariner and shipowner in Liverpool; he m., 1863, Jane Wilson, b. Hunter (1837–1908), da. of John A. Carlyle’s friends John and Helen Hunter (see above); by 1875 they had seven children.

Watt, Arthur Chorley (1840–85), stepson of John A. Carlyle; joined the civil service 1862, and was currently an Assistant Judge in Poona, India; he m., 1869, Henrietta Vary, b. Hunter (b. 1846), younger da. of John and Helen Hunter; they had a da. (b. 1870), and two sons (b. 1873 and June 1875).
Watt, William (b. 1842), stepson of John A. Carlyle; an officer in the Dragoons, m., 1866, Mary, b. Smith, da. of E. H. Smith of Grouville, Jersey.

Wellmer, Meta (1826–89; see 43:21TC to MW, 4 Dec. 1865, and 45:207MA to MW, 3 Dec. 1868), German writer, teacher, feminist, vegetarian, and spiritualist. Her publications included Deutsche Erzieherinnen und deren Wirkungskreis [German Educators and their Sphere of Influence] (Leipzig, 1877).

Welsh, Alexander (Alick) (b. 1816), son of JWC’s maternal uncle John; m., ca. 1849, Sophy, b. Martin (b. ca. 1824). Their children were John (Jackie) (ca. 1853–64), Isabella Helen (b. 1856; see 31:201JWC to TC, [29 Aug. 1856]), Margaret (b. 1858), and Jean (b. 1860); they lived at Sandown Park, Wavertree, Liverpool.

Welsh, Ann (1799–1877), Elizabeth (1792–1877), and Grace (1801–67), JWC’s paternal aunts (see 14:67TC to JWC, 10 March 1842, and 16:219JWC to JW, [26 June 1843]), living at Craigen Villa, Morningside, Edinburgh.
Welsh, Grace, b. Welsh (1782–1842), JWC’s mother; m., 1800, John Welsh (1776–1819; see 1:202–3), JWC’s father, doctor in Haddington.

Welsh, John (1785–1853; see 28:286–87TC to JCA, 12 Oct. 1853), JWC’s maternal uncle, brass and copper founder, who had lived at 20 Maryland St., Liverpool; m., 1808,
Mary, b. Colliver (d. 1838; see 10:200TC to AC, 15 Oct. 1838); their children were Helen (ca. 1813–53); Walter; Alexander; Jeannie (see Chrystal); John (1820–60); Margaret; and Mary.

Welsh, Margaret (Maggie) (1821–29 April 1875), da. of JWC’s maternal uncle John; lived in Auchtertool with her brother Walter. She was JWC’s nurse, Dec. 1863–May 1864, and helped look after TC after JWC’s death, late April–mid- Aug. 1866, and June–Oct. 1867, and continued to visit regularly thereafter.

Welsh, Mary (1823–79), da. of JWC’s maternal uncle John; usually lived in Auchtertool with her brother Walter, but had been living in the Perth Asylum since 1869 being treated for her opium addiction.

Welsh, Rev. Walter (1815–1879; see 16:12JWC to JW, [8 Jan. 1843]), son of JWC’s maternal uncle John; minister at Auchtertool, Fife, since 1842. His sisters Margaret (Maggie) and Mary usually lived with him.

Wilson, Thomas (b. 1811; see 22:xiii22:introduction and 26:30426:introduction), scholar, old friend of TC’s, now teaching in Weimar; see 40:23540:biographical notes and 47:73–74TC to [Thomas Wilson], [early Oct. 1870]. He m., 1861, a German wife, unidentified further.

Woolner, Thomas (1825–92; ODNB; see 26:37TC to TW, [21 Feb. 1851], and 29:176–77TC to LA, 20 Oct. 1854), sculptor and poet; he lived at 29 Welbeck St., London. He m., 1864, Alice Gertrude, b. Waugh (b. 1845); they had six children, including Amy (b. 1865), Hugh (1866–1925), and Geoffrey (1867–82).
